title: Family accused of taking nearly $375,000 in copper from interstate construction projects
text:
EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE/Gray News) - Authorities say hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of copper has been stolen from construction projects along Interstate 69.
Indiana authorities said several thefts have been reported to Evansville police, the Warrick County Sheriff’s Office and the Vanderburgh County Sheriff’s Office.
According to the Indiana Department of Transportation, copper was reported stolen from work zone lighting projects at the I-69 and Interstate 64 interchange.
According to investigators, scrap yards across the Tri-State shared information that Jason Fulks and members of his family were selling large amounts of copper.
Construction crews estimated more than $367,000 in wire was stolen.
Records show Fulks was arrested earlier this month after a traffic stop with a warrant also out for his arrest tied to the copper-theft case.
Investigators noted that tools and copper were also found in Fulks’ truck.
Natalee Fairchild and Sherry Beasley are additionally facing charges of corrupt business influence stemming from the investigation, authorities said.
Indiana authorities added that surveillance video, license plate readers and cell phone data helped their several-month investigation.
Indiana’s Department of Transportation said its team is continuing to evaluate the impacts of the theft regarding the lighting projects.

title: Vote to protect right to reproductive healthcare
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Lisa Margulies is vice president of public affairs for Planned Parenthood Maine Action Fund PAC.
In a state known for its peace and quiet, Mainers are facing a relentless amount of noise: political ads everywhere, all the time. The stakes are high, and our votes matter in high-profile races that will determine the national political landscape just as much as they matter in races getting less attention.
Every seat in the state Legislature is up for grabs, and while many of those contests aren’t making headlines, they are critical to protecting our rights. The buck stops in Augusta in ensuring Maine remains a safe harbor for access to reproductive health care.
Our freedoms here in Maine are not secure from election to election. Though we have strong state laws protecting our reproductive rights, our laws can change if state leaders choose to change them. Unlike states like Vermont, we have no state constitutional amendment protecting reproductive autonomy. And we don’t need to look far to understand how elections impact care, with the New Hampshire Executive Council voting just a few years ago to defund Planned Parenthood of Northern New England.
Along with 186 voting seats in the Maine legislature, the governor’s office is also up for grabs and the pro-reproductive rights majority in Augusta is at stake. In 2024, the Maine House majority was determined by only 60 votes across three districts — yes, 60 individuals making the decision to cast their ballot. Some races were decided by just a handful of votes. One race in Sanford was decided by just one, singular vote.
The threats are real. Republican gubernatorial candidate Bobby Charles has said he’ll work with President Donald Trump to “defund abortion clinics” and that he opposes the state-level protections Maine lawmakers put in place after the U.S. Supreme Court overturned federal protections for abortion. Unenrolled candidate Rick Bennett claims to care, but his record — including calling to defund Planned Parenthood and opposing Mainers’ voting on a referendum to enshrine reproductive autonomy in the state constitution — shows us otherwise.
Every legislative session, lawmakers propose bills aimed at taking away our rights and access to essential care. Last session, proposals included creating barriers to essential medical care, requiring medical professionals to provide dangerous misinformation, and even repealing our state’s abortion laws full stop and potentially criminalizing patients and providers. These bills aren’t a fluke. In fact, the 2026 Maine Republican Party platform, like platforms from years before, opposes abortion.
But Mainers know better, and we don’t want politicians or political parties making personal private medical decisions for us. Each legislative session Planned Parenthood Maine Action Fund has fought alongside dedicated Mainers to defeat these harmful proposals, and we are grateful to our champions at the statehouse who have worked tirelessly to protect our rights and access to care.
The bottom line is: With your vote in this election, you can have real impact on critical races in our state. Your vote, one singular vote, can determine the result of a competitive state legislative race. Showing up matters.
Luckily, there are lots of ways to vote on or before Nov. 3. You can register to vote in-person at your local town clerk’s office and cast your absentee ballot there before election day. Maine also offers same-day in-person voter registration through election day. You can find your polling place, sample ballot, and more at Maine’s voter information lookup service.
Need help understanding which candidates share your values? Planned Parenthood Maine Action Fund PAC is proud to endorse Hannah Pingree for governor — the only candidate we can trust to protect our rights and access to care — and has also vetted and endorsed more than 100 candidates in Maine legislative races, all of whom you can find on our website.
We are committed to cutting through the noise and helping you find candidates that will fight for our rights. Your vote matters, and it could be your vote that determines the outcome of a critical race.

title: Only thing ‘crystal clear’ on Navatek allegations is Collins’ innocence
text:
An Oct. 1 report insinuated Sen. Susan Collins’ guilt in a campaign finance scheme (“The laws tied to the Susan Collins-Navatek allegations are ‘crystal clear.’ Enforcing them is another matter.”). There is no guilt; I know this because my agency investigated it.
As a commissioner on the Federal Election Commission, we investigated Navatek in 2021 in coordination with the Department of Justice. After three years, the FEC fined the company $325,000, and the Biden Justice Department convicted the CEO in 2022.
Our investigators found “no information in the factual record” that Sen. Collins or her campaign knowingly took illegal money. We dismissed every potential violation against the super PAC supporting her. And the DOJ made no attempt to charge the Collins campaign.
The idea that the FBI was still pursuing Collins in 2025 is not credible. The conduct happened in 2019, and prosecutors had five years to bring charges.
What remains is a convicted felon’s self-serving story. Recycling his claims before Election Day is not news. It’s a political hit.
Sean Cooksey
Former FEC Commissioner (2021-2025)
Washington, D.C.

title: Happy birthday, Sonny. Keep the memories coming.
text:
It’s amazing to think that one year ago I tore myself in two to push out a screaming potato and now, as I write this, there is a tiny chaos goblin in my office, pulling books off a desk and blowing raspberries.
As cliché as it is to say, the days have been long (and the nights even longer) but the year was short. It feels like it’s been forever and also like just yesterday I was flying down 295 to Maine Med at 4 a.m. Somehow we have all survived, with marriage and developmental milestones intact.
I was worried that I would lose my own identity in motherhood; I’ve read and spoken to a lot of women who felt that happened to them. I’ve been lucky so far; I still feel like exactly who I’ve always been, just with more add-on, after-market features.
I don’t know if it’s because I’ve only been a mom for a year, or because I only have one kid, or maybe I just have a particularly strong sense of self. It’s felt more like in a video game where suddenly you hit a new level or find a treasure chest and then your character can wield the Flaming Sword of Vengeance, except in this case it’s just the ability to prepare an entire baby lunch one-handed with the other arm holding a 20-pound child. I come equipped with new items too, like the Dumbbells of Lesser Back Pain, the Midnight Cookie Tupperware (can only be accessed in the dark) and the Diaper Bag of Endless Wonders.
I’ve also unlocked vast stores of patience that I had no idea were there, like an enormous underwater aquifer that just got discovered accidentally by a septic tank crew. There is no one else on Earth who can scream at me for two hours between 1 and 3 in the morning and I will respond with nothing but love and snuggles. I’m able to cope with sensory issues that would normally overstimulate me.
I mean, do you know how many slimy textured food items I’ve touched today alone? So many. And yet when it’s for my kiddo I don’t feel like tearing off my skin like I normally do. Last week there was a day where Sonny vomited on me. Twice. And I didn’t even have a meltdown.
Sonny is developing a real personality now. When we’re out and about he is fairly laid back — indeed, yesterday at the grocery store the cashier said he was “the chilliest baby she’s ever seen” — casually observing everything quietly, taking it all in and I assume processing it somehow. He doesn’t freak out too much at strangers. At home, though — well, there’s a reason my wife’s name for his alter ego is “Chaos Boy.”
Currently his favorite activities are pulling piles of things off shelves. I stack (and restack) board books for him on coffee tables for just this purpose and throwing food at the dogs, sometimes to indicate he’s done eating but sometimes just, apparently, for funsies. We play little games with each other.
He is constantly pulling himself up to standing using various objects to balance. He seems to have this insatiable, unstoppable inner drive to move forward. Once he learned to sit, he started lunging forward from a sitting position until he figured out crawling. Now he crawls and still wants to go further, farther and always upward (he’s also constantly trying to climb me and his other mom).
When we take him for walks in the stroller he is constantly twisting around and swiveling, trying to look at absolutely everything in the world. He has a particular fascination with staring at the stroller wheels turning, and in throwing his pacifiers out the side to see what happens.
I find myself staring at him with a stupid happy grin on my face all the time. (Well, maybe not at 2 a.m.) I feel so lucky that I get to hang out with this cool little dude all the time. We start our day on the floor of the nursery, him with his milk and me with my cup of coffee and I just feel so joyful. When he smiles at me it feels like the way taking the first sip of a glass of wine felt and I just want more and more.
I don’t take these moments of joy for granted. I’m sure I’ll go into it in a whole column at some point, but for the first few months after Sonny’s birth, I had postpartum depression pretty badly. I was worried I would never feel the joy in parenthood that other moms talked about or even just joy in general). I’m happy to report that the joy and fun has kicked in.
I can’t wait to see what Sonny does next. Which, at time of this writing, is crawling at top speed for the dog’s chew toy.

title: Maine Mariners lose to Worcester in season opener
text:
Worcester’s Matt DeMelis scored 15 seconds into the game, Sam Stange and Jordan Kaplan struck just over a minute apart early in the second period, and the Maine Mariners opened their ECHL season Saturday night with a 4-2 loss to the Railers in Worcester, Massachusetts.
The Railers led 1-0 after one period, then quickly extended their lead to 3-0 in the second. Stange scored at 1:02, and Kaplan converted a breakaway at 2:15 after a lead pass from Michael Suda.
The Mariners got their first goal of the season when Jack Bar scored 7:54 into the third. But Worcester answered just 29 seconds later, as Declan McDonald scored on the Railers’ only shot of the third period to make it 4-1.
Owen Gallatin scored a power-play goal for Maine with 3:49 remaining.
Parker Gahagen made 26 saves for the Railers. Maine’s Luke Cavallin finished with nine saves.
The teams meet again next weekend for two afternoon games in Portland, on Saturday and Sunday.

title: Disappointed in Jackson’s debate behavior
text:
After watching the recent debates, I will probably vote for Troy Jackson. However, his aggressive posture toward Sen. Collins and persistence in recounting debunked conspiracies make him a distasteful choice.
There was no evidence of even a hint of a gentleman in his performance. It’s fine to strongly point out differences but to spew repeated accusations makes me think he will be marginally effective in the Senate.
If he ultimately gets my vote, it will only be to change the balance of power in our federal government.
Michael Hudson
Brunswick

title: Reason, not ideology, will move Portland forward
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
I attended the Oct. 7 candidates night, sponsored by the Back Cove Neighborhood Association for District 4 and at-large candidates for the Portland City Council. It was well attended and all candidates attended.
The two candidates who stood out to me as worthy of election were Jake Viola and Kate Snyder. Both understood the need to creatively analyze existing problems facing Portland and figure out what works. Neither one is pushing a political agenda that supports ideological solutions that are ineffective. Having attended a Planning Board meeting two years ago, I was saddened that decisions were being made on wishful thinking and not reality in dealing with how to increase housing units. These two candidates will bring a refreshing approach that just might accomplish something worthwhile instead of pushing ideological, unworkable ideas.
Jacqueline Cohen
Portland

title: The Mills-Pingree machine crushed small business in Maine. Hannah Pingree will finish the job.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rick Savage, an entrepreneur, former owner and founder of the Sunday River Brewing Company in Bethel, is an advocate for small business rights.
Small business owners in Maine don’t ask for handouts.
We ask for a fair shot, a clear set of rules and a state government that stays off our backs so we can feed our families and employ our neighbors. But under the administration of Gov. Janet Mills (where Hannah Pingree served as a chief architect of policy, as director of the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future), Maine became a hostile environment for independent enterprise.
I know this firsthand. As the former co-owner of Sunday River Brewing Company, I lived through the heavy-handed, punitive overreach of an administration that treated hard-working entrepreneurs not as partners, but as subjects to be controlled.
In the spring of 2020, small businesses across Maine were strung along with moving goalposts and false reopening promises. When it became clear that state officials were operating behind closed doors without accountability, I spoke out. I went on national television and gave out Gov. Mills’ cellphone number so everyday Mainers, the people whose livelihoods were being systematically destroyed, could finally get an answer.
What followed was a targeted campaign of government retaliation.
Rather than working with small business owners trying to safely operate, state regulators moved in. Inspectors from the Department of Health and Human Services and state liquor licensing enforcement targeted my establishment, scrutinizing our operations and stripping our health and liquor licenses to force our doors shut. In my view, state agencies were weaponized to make an example out of anyone who dared to challenge Augusta’s dictates.
Our legal team estimates that the state spent nearly $500,000 in taxpayer resources, deploying state attorneys, inspectors and enforcement officials, just to crush one brewpub in Bethel. While the official court filings reflect a drawn-out legal war over licensing enforcement, the sheer waste of public funds to dismantle a local business tells you everything you need to know about the priorities of the Mills-Pingree administration.
Hannah Pingree cannot distance herself from this legacy. As one of Gov. Mills’ top policy advisers, Pingree sat at the right hand of an administration that oversaw a disastrous business climate. Her office helped shape the economic and regulatory framework that shut down small shops, pushed workers out of state and prioritized government mandates over economic survival.
The economic damage inflicted on Maine wasn’t an accident; it was the direct result of a top-down, central-planning mindset championed by bureaucrats like Pingree. When state government believes it can arbitrarily decide which businesses are “essential” and which are disposable, local economies suffer.
That is why I am standing firmly behind Bobby Charles for governor.
Bobby Charles understands what it takes to confront administrative overreach and dismantle the bureaucratic machine in Augusta.
Unlike the entrenched politicians who view government regulation as the solution to every problem, Bobby recognizes that free enterprise and small business are the lifeblood of Maine’s economy. He has the strength, vision and determination to restore accountability, rein in rogue state agencies and make sure no entrepreneur ever faces the kind of government persecution my family experienced.
Maine cannot afford four more years of the Mills-Pingree agenda. Small business owners are tired of high taxes, red tape and an administrative state that views free enterprise as a threat. We need leadership that respects working Mainers, honors the hard work of local entrepreneurs and stands up for our constitutional rights.
Bobby Charles is the leader Maine needs to close the book on this era of government overreach and rebuild a state where small businesses can actually thrive.

title: County Sweeps PVC Coaching Honors, Wins Three Team Championships
text:
County Cross Country Shines at PVC Championships With Three Team Titles, Two Individual Wins and Three Coaching Honors
Aroostook County had plenty to celebrate Saturday at the Penobscot Valley Conference Cross Country Championships in Old Town.
Three team championships, two individual victories and three PVC Coach of the Year honors highlighted an outstanding afternoon for County athletes and coaches.
Houlton/GHCA captured the Small School Boys championship, Presque Isle won the Large School Girls title, and Caribou finished first in the Large School Boys competition.
Caribou's Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves added individual championships, while two County coaches received recognition for their work throughout the season.
Caribou's Thomas Beckum was named PVC Girls Large School Coach of the Year, Presque Isle's Dylan Marrero earned PVC Boys Large School Coach of the Year honors, and Houlton's Chris Rines was named PVC Boys Small School Coach of the Year.
From the front of the varsity races to the junior varsity competition, County runners turned in strong performances across the board.
County Coaches Earn PVC Coach of the Year Honors
It wasn't just the runners bringing home recognition Saturday.
Caribou's Thomas Beckum was selected as the PVC Girls Coach of the Year, while Presque Isle's Dylan Marrero received the PVC Boys Coach of the Year award.
Both honors add to an impressive championship weekend for the County's cross country programs.
Beckum's Caribou girls finished third in the Large School team competition, led by individual champion Emma Graves. The Vikings also placed Jenna Strid and Isabella Albert among the top ten.
Marrero's Presque Isle boys finished third in one of the closest team races of the afternoon. Just six points separated the top three Large School Boys teams, with the Wildcats finishing behind Caribou and John Bapst.
The two coaching awards were another highlight of a day that saw County programs bring home championships in three of the four varsity divisions.
PVC Small School Boys: Houlton/GHCA Captures Team Championship
Houlton/GHCA put together one of the day's most impressive team performances, winning the Small School Boys championship with 36 points.
The Shires placed three runners among the top four and four among the top eight, finishing ahead of George Stevens Academy with 45 points and Orono with 47.
Malachi Witmer led Houlton/GHCA with a second-place finish in 17:16.06.
Brayden Drake finished third in 17:18.52, followed almost immediately by Wyatt Quint in fourth at 17:18.58. Only six-hundredths of a second separated the two teammates.
Logan Witmer added an eighth-place finish, while Stephen Cormier completed the Shires' scoring five.
Orono's Brady Cox won the individual championship in 17:11.53.

title: No Kings rallies across U.S. urge voters to cast ballots early ahead of midterms
text:
(AP) - Rallies organized by the No Kings network opposed to President Donald Trump were held Saturday in cities and communities across the U.S., with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections.
The hundreds of planned events were billed as nonpartisan, though they sought to build on nearly two years’ worth of No Kings marches and demonstrations by people upset with Trump’s presidency.
A band entertained what appeared to be a few hundred people in caps and coats at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington. Despite the chilly weather, many in the crowd danced to the tunes. “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!” were among the many signs held aloft.
At an Atlanta rally, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd to urge others to vote ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
“The Constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?” he said.
“You don’t see Superman giving up his power,” Bond continued. “You don’t see Black Panther giving up his power. You don’t see Wonder Woman giving up her magic lasso. So why would you give up your right, your power, your obligation to vote? Be a super hero, use your power. Go to the polls and vote.”
Trump has long been suspicious of mail voting and has claimed without evidence that voting fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election.
His administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for the midterm elections from people whom the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
On Friday the Justice Department warned that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution.
Earlier that day Democratic Sens. Alex Padilla of California, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Dick Durbin of Illinois wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified.

title: Joanne Shirley (Masellis) Gooley (1936-2026)
As an Oregon community mourns 4 killed in school shooting, 2 wounded survivors remain hospitalized
text:
BEND, Oregon (AP) — A special-needs teacher and student wounded in a deadly shooting at an Oregon elementary school remained hospitalized Saturday. But friends said their survival was a spot of hope in a community in mourning.
The youngest shooting survivor, 7-year-old Saylor Graham, is a feisty, vibrant fighter with a sweet nature whose story inspired other children, said Matt Sampson, executive director of Sparrow Clubs, where she was a member. She has a genetic disorder, usually uses a wheelchair and is non-verbal, but “she doesn’t even need words to connect with people,” he said.
“She’s just an amazing spirit who just immediately draws people to her and you just feel inspired by Saylor when you meet her,” Sampson said. “And she’s always wearing these iconic glasses, whether they’re pink or they’re red. She’s just such a cutie.”
Teacher Becky Drury, 54, is recovering in a Bend hospital with wounds to her arm and hand but hopes to go home soon, said Zack Hall, a family friend who is serving as her family’s spokesperson.
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and a teacher were killed at the Silver Rail Elementary school in Bend, Oregon, Thursday when a former student there, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, entered a special needs classroom and began firing with a shotgun.
One teacher was grappling with John for the weapon when the father of two students came in and shot him to death. They were credited with stopping the rampage and saving many people’s lives.
While police continued to investigate John’s motive, distraught parents, teachers and others gathered outside the school Saturday to leave flowers, pray and cry.
Savannah Patton, a mother who has a 1st and 4th grader at the school, sat on the grass Saturday across from a memorial of flowers, stuffed animals and balloons, and wiped tears from her eyes.
She told an Associated Press reporter that the teacher who died, Megan Lambert, 25, had been a substitute for her daughter’s class last year.
Patton said she has struggled to explain what happened to her daughter, who asked her, “Mommy, why would someone want to take a gun and kill us at school?” Patton said it was a question she didn’t know how to answer.
Physical challenges won’t keep her from “living with joy”
For several years, Saylor worked with students from Bend High School through the Sparrow Clubs, a volunteer group whose mission is to empower “kids to help kids in medical need” through kindness and community service, according to their website.
In a video on the Sparrow Clubs page, Saylor introduces herself, saying she loves watching Bluey and being around other kids, especially her brother. She said that while she is challenged by physical and cognitive issues, she can communicate with her eyes and a computer tablet.
“I prove every day that I’m a fighter who doesn’t give up,” she wrote in the video. “Living with CASK-related challenges is full of unknowns, which can be very hard and scary for my whole family,” she said, “But it doesn’t keep me from smiling, laughing and living with joy!”
Some of the high school students who worked with Saylor said helping her gave them hope that there is still humanity in this world.
After the shooting, she was taken to a hospital in Portland. A Go-Fund-Me for her family has raised almost $400,000.
“We will not let her name be forgotten”
Devon Johnson visited the memorial outside the school Saturday morning. Her husband teaches at Bend High School, and she is a volleyball coach at High Desert Middle School, so they are close with many of the staff at the elementary school.
“It’s just hard to take in,” she said. “I’m so glad to see that Bend is rallying and just wrapping their arms around this community, but it’s going to take a long time to get through this.”
Heidi Wood, the director of the Central Oregon Volleyball Club where Lambert coached, said in a social media post that she was “an amazing coach, ”an amazing teacher” and “an amazing person who would do anything” for her students.
“To the shooter, she would have given you the shirt off her back,” Wood said. “But you didn’t give her a chance.”
Wood said that Lambert wouldn’t take her volleyball coaching pay in her first year so the money could be used for scholarships for players who couldn’t afford to play instead.
“That was her, and that is her,” Wood said. “We will carry on her love, her passion and we will not let her name be forgotten.”
___
Bellisle reported from Seattle. Associated Press writer Haven Daley contributed to his report.

title: Crowd in Portland rallies around electing Maine Democrats on ‘No Kings Day’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — With just over two weeks until the midterm elections, about 400 people gathered in Deering Oaks on Saturday to rally around voting Democrats into office in Maine and ousting five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins from the U.S. Senate.
Organized by Indivisible Greater Portland, the event coincided with the fourth national “No Kings” day. Previous “No Kings” protests drew thousands of Mainers who condemned Trump administration actions they said reflect a monarchy rather than a democracy. This year, the same protesters are focused on encouraging people to vote early in the midterm elections, ensuring that democracy prevails, in their view.
“I feel there’s a very significant undercurrent of bitterness and feeling that our government is betraying us,” said Chris Beasley, 86, of Cape Elizabeth. He held a ribbon-adorned sign on a long wooden stick that said “Vote.” “This brings attention to our choice of representatives that reflect the values of democratic society.”
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree, U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson and U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., were three of several speakers at the event. The trio criticized President Donald Trump and discussed issues such as healthcare, the war in Iran, rising heating oil costs, immigration and abortion. They blamed Collins for affordability challenges in Maine and emphasized the importance of voting.
“Democracy is on the line here in Maine and across the country,” Pingree said. “Don’t leave it to chance.”
The race between Jackson and Collins is seen as particularly consequential — Democrats view it as one of their best shots at gaining a majority in the U.S. Senate. The competitors faced off in their fourth and final debate Thursday. Election Day is Nov. 3.
Sentiments against Collins and Trump at the rally were strong, with people holding signs that said “Retire Susan,” “Dump King Corruption” and “Susan Collins is complicit.” The senator has tried to distance herself from the president as his approval ratings wane, while Jackson’s campaign has pushed to present the two as a package.
Ben Bernard, 55, of Cliff Island, compared Collins to a teacher who helps a bullied child get some of their lunch money back, but won’t stand up to the bully. He was referring to Collins’ negotiations to remove some Maine items from Canada’s tariff list, a result of the trade war started by Trump.
“Collins is enabling Trump every day,” Bernard said.
Some came to the protest with specific policies in mind. Leah Campbell, 77, of Portland, held a sign that said “What happened to affordable healthcare for all?”
“I and people I know are impacted by healthcare cuts that have already been done,” Campbell said. “I have Medicare. I want to make sure that’s not cut. I have Social Security. I want to make sure that’s not cut. These are programs I have paid into all my life.”
Holly Parker, 52, of Cape Elizabeth, and Nancy Timberlake, 78, of Portland, said they already voted and came to the rally to surround themselves with positive energy after feeling drained by the most important issues in the elections.
“I had to buy heating oil this week, and it was excruciating,” Parker said. “I feel bad for a lot of people who are in a worse position than I am in terms of heating their homes and putting gas in their car.”
Prices of heating oil and gas have risen sharply since the start of the war in Iran.
Parker said she thinks the rally would be worth it if it persuades one more person to vote.
The event presented opportunities for Mainers to sign up to knock on doors and make calls to encourage their neighbors to vote. A band called “Singing Resistance” sang songs in between speakers who discussed voting and defeating Collins.
“A Senate seat does not belong to a person who’s held it for 30 years,” Jackson said. “It belongs to the people of Maine … I owe the people of Maine everything.”

title: Trump puts new Russia sanctions passed by Congress on hold, saying waiver is in US national interest
text:
Trump puts new Russia sanctions passed by Congress on hold, saying waiver is in US national interest
President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest.
Trump personally signed the legislation just last month. Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, it had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.
Trump's unexpected move comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.
An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president's handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump's approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress on Election Day on Nov. 3.
Sanctions were seen as part of Graham's legacy
Graham died in July but had advocated for stricter U.S. sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine. His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation — then changed his mind Friday.
The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest.
The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress.
Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, had remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large majorities in the House and Senate following Graham's sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy.
Trump's action follows announced diesel deal with Putin
The president's latest action also followed him announcing last week that he had reached an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump said Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.
Trump's decision to strike a deal with Putin on diesel on the world market has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine -- without making a different to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump's war on Iran.
The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centerpiece for Sen. Darline Graham, the late senator's sister who was appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term. She is now running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.
In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham — who has Trump's endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week — said she had been "so proud" to help get the measure passed but acknowledged it was the president's purview as to how he implemented it.
"It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions," Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. "So that's up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall."

title: New PFAS treatment system targets contamination near Kennebec River
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) -A new PFAS treatment system began operating this summer at the Greater Augusta Utility District, one of only a few facilities of its kind in Maine.
District found PFAS above state limit in 2024
In 2024, the Greater Augusta Utility District learned one of its largest water sources, located near the Kennebec River, contained PFAS levels above the state’s regulatory limit.
Though often called “forever chemicals,” PFAS are man-made compounds that can break down or fade over time.
“They’re in everyday products. They’re in a bunch of things. It can be waterproofing. It can be coating systems. It can be cosmetics. It’s in a lot of things,” said Andy Begin, assistant general manager and chief engineer for the Greater Augusta Utility District.
Officials cite improved detection technology
Though PFAS may have been in the environment for decades, officials say improved testing technology is now allowing scientists to detect the compounds at much lower levels.
“We’ve developed detection technologies that allow us to get more repeatably and reliably into these parts-per-trillion ranges. So, as we’ve been able to do that, of course, we can find more things in the environment,” said Brian Tarbuck, general manager of the Greater Augusta Utility District.
District installed six treatment vessels
After more than a year of testing, planning and construction, the district installed six large treatment vessels.
The vessels may sound like filters, but the system uses ion exchange.
“They’re these tiny little beads. It’s a media that chemically bonds the PFAS compound to it. So, it’s an adsorption process. The water flows down through that media,” Begin said.
The vessels are arranged in pairs, with backup units allowing the district to replace the resin beads without shutting down treatment. The resin beads are expected to last about a year and a half to two years.
Begin said that though PFAS levels have risen, the contamination remains manageable with the new technology.

title: Zacharia makes first statement since leaving job as White House press secretary
text:
Zacharia makes first statement since leaving job as White House press secretary
Katie Zacharia said working for President Donald Trump was an honor.
Zacharia makes first statement since leaving job as White House press secretary
Katie Zacharia said working for President Donald Trump was an honor.
Katie Zacharia is reportedly transitioning out of her role as White House press secretary after less than a week on the job.
Zacharia did not confirm her departure outright Friday but referred to her job in the past tense in a brief social media post.
"President Trump is a kind, wonderful, gracious, thoughtful, enthusiastic, and hardworking man. I wish more Americans appreciated him. No one will ever make America great the way he has and continues to. It was an honor to work for him," Zacharia said.
Zacharia's performance was widely criticized after an unusually short press briefing Tuesday. She took just three questions over roughly 14 minutes.
Zacharia's resume has also been under scrutiny. She has repeatedly represented herself as a lawyer but later revealed that she has not passed a bar exam. She said she worked as a lawyer in China and argued that these credentials were not relevant to her role as press secretary, as she was not hired to give legal advice.
President Donald Trump foreshadowed the staff change earlier Friday. He told reporters that he advised her to reconsider the role because she had been treated "unfairly" by the press.
"She's been treated, I would say, pretty nastily, and I said to Katie just two minutes ago, I said, 'Katie, you know, you don't have to do this if you don't want.' She said, 'This is a lot tougher.' I said, 'Welcome to the world of Trump,'" Trump said.
Trump has yet to name a replacement, but he told reporters that a lot of people want the job.
The White House did not immediately respond to emailed questions about the timeline for filling the position and who would conduct briefings in the meantime. Since Karoline Leavitt, the former press secretary, left the job, a rotating cast of Trump's cabinet members has been filling in at the podium.

title: Colby football coach Jack Cosgrove temporarily stepping away from team
text:
WATERVILLE — Colby College football coach Jack Cosgrove is temporarily stepping away from the program, the school announced.
In a statement obtained by the Morning Sentinel on Saturday, Colby said Cosgrove “has temporarily stepped away to prioritize providing care for a family member facing unforeseen health concerns.” WABI Bangor first reported the news Friday.
Offensive coordinator Mark Clements coached Colby in a home game against Amherst on Saturday. The Mules led 12-0 early in the second quarter but ultimately lost 21-15 to fall to 0-5 on the season.
Since being named Colby’s head coach in December 2017, Cosgrove has amassed a 26-41 record. He led the Mules to a 6-3 season last year, marking the program’s first winning record since 2005.
Cosgrove previously coached at the University of Maine from 1993-2015. He guided the Black Bears to three Coastal (formerly Colonial) Athletic Association titles and five Football Championship Subdivision playoff appearances.
Clements will be the head coach in Cosgrove’s absence. Defensive coordinator Liam Hobbins will serve as associate head coach in addition to his current role.
Colby’s next game is at Hamilton (1-4) at noon next Saturday.

title: Youngest Oregon school shooting victim was a fearless climber who loved stuffed animals
text:
Youngest Oregon school shooting victim was a fearless climber who loved stuffed animals
The youngest child killed in a shooting at an Oregon school was a fast runner and a fearless climber who also loved reading and his stuffed animals, his aunt said Friday.
Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of three children killed along with a teacher in the shooting Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 in central Oregon. The other two children killed were ages 8 and 11, and a fourth student and another teacher were wounded, police have said.
"He never met a stuffie that he didn't think needed to be rescued and cared for," said Swan Sheridan, whose sister is Summer's mother.
Sheridan said Summer liked for all of his sea creature stuffed animals to be in his favorite color: rainbow.
"He had a great fondness for sharks and dinosaurs and creatures that were in his words, 'misunderstood,'" she said.
Sheridan said her nephew would climb and jump off anything and was an "incredibly fast" runner, even from a young age. "He was a little ball of energy from the moment he was born," she said.
"He was a very, very happy child," she said.
Teacher Meghan Lambert, 25, was killed, said police Chief Mike Krantz at a Friday afternoon news conference. Police confirmed Summer was one of those killed but won't release names of the other children who died at the request of families.
Lambert had her "dream job," her family said in statement read at the news conference. Lambert grew up in Bend, graduated from Boise State in 2023, had a passion for sports, especially volleyball, and was a local coach, relatives said.
They described her as funny and opinionated and said she "lit up the room."
"Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart," her family said in the statement. "She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs."
Police said 16-year-old Griffin J. John II got into the school by shooting through locked doors. Authorities said John had been a special needs student at the school and attacked a classroom with special needs students.
Krantz said a parent saw John shooting outside the school, followed him inside and shot him several times.
The parent was Kaylub Giamanco, said his mother, Kenda Freeman, in a statement read Friday to reporters.
Police found John dead in the school minutes after the first calls for help, Krantz said.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, and drew community members Friday, including Brooke Olsen. She said she was feeling grateful that her daughter — a kindergartner — was safe while also trying to "grieve and process and recover."
"This is an extremely painful day of grief for everybody in Bend, especially Silver Rail families," Olsen said.
A wounded teacher was identified by family as Becky Drury. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on Facebook that she had injuries to her left arm and right hand and was recovering from surgery. Her husband, Will Drury, said in a statement that they're focusing on her recovery at an "unimaginably difficult time."
Blake Brinker said he came to a memorial at the school on Friday to pray.
"Life is such a delicate thing and I don't think anything brings that message across more than the loss of young life," he said.
___
Stengle contributed to this report from Dallas. Associated Press journalists Ed White in Detroit and Philip Marcelo in New York contributed to this report.

title: 3 men sentenced to more than 158 years for the killings of Australian, US surfers in Mexico
text:
ENSENADA, Mexico (AP) — A judge on Friday sentenced three Mexican men to more than 158 years in prison each for the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, a case that tarnished Mexico’s image by exposing the risks foreigners face when visiting the tourism-dependent country.
The sentencing, which came a week after the men were found guilty, marked the end of a lengthy legal process over the killings of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson, and American Carter Redd Rhoad. Their bodies were found in May 2024, and at least four people were arrested for their alleged involvement in the crime.
A judge in the coastal city of Ensenada, in Baja California state, ruled that Jesús Gerardo García, known as “el Kekas,” Irineo Francisco “N” and Ángel Jesús “N” would each serve 158 years and nine months in prison for murder, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
Antonio Otañez, president of the Baja California surfers’ association, welcomed the outcome, saying “justice has been served.” But he acknowledged that the killings had caused a “major drop” in tourist visits, particularly by surfers, to the region known for its beautiful beaches.
Here is a look at the key facts and events in the case:
Surfing trip ends in tragedy
The Robinson brothers — Callum and Jake — and their American friend decided to travel to Mexico in late April 2024 to pursue one of their passions, surfing, at a beach in Punta San José, about 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the city of Ensenada in Baja California state.
Unaware of the risks they faced, the three friends decided to camp on the beach on the night of April 27, 2024.
Their attackers confronted them there, shot them dead in the early morning hours and then dumped their bodies into a well more than 15 meters (50 feet) deep. The bodies were found on May 3 after several days of searching.
The Baja California prosecutor’s office announced on May 5, 2024, that it had arrested García, known as “el Kekas,” identifying him as the suspected gunman in the killings of the three foreigners.
State authorities said García had a criminal history in Ensenada involving alleged drug dealing, unlawful entry into a home, domestic violence and vehicle theft.
García’s former partner, Ary Gisell Silva Raya, and two of his alleged accomplices, Irineo Francisco “N” and Ángel Jesús “N,” were also arrested in the case.
Silva Raya, whom authorities found in possession of a cellphone belonging to one of the victims, agreed to an abbreviated trial and in November was sentenced to 20 years in prison for aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
The prosecution’s account and evidence
State prosecutor María Elena Andrade alleged that the attackers wanted to steal the tires from the foreigners’ pickup truck and that the victims resisted.
“The attackers pull out a gun they were carrying and kill the person who initially resisted the robbery, then turn on the other two,” she added.

title: UMaine football’s losing streak extended to six games
text:
A second-half comeback bid fell short Saturday as UMaine suffered its sixth consecutive football defeat, losing 17-14 to Bryant in Orono.
Maine’s only touchdown was an 11-yard pass from Caden Drezek to Rashawn Marshall early in the third quarter. Noah Carpenter rushed for the 2-point conversion to cut the Black Bears’ deficit to 14-11.

title: 71-year-old man killed by 12-foot alligator while fishing alongside lake
text:
(AP) - A 71-year-old man fishing on the shore of a Florida lake was killed Friday by a nearly 12-foot alligator, the second fatal attack reported this year.
Steven Hamilton of Winter Garden was standing on the shore of Lake Apopka at Dr. Bradford Memorial Park, 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Orlando, when he was attacked around 5 p.m., the Winter Garden Police Department said.
The presence of other active alligators in the water complicated any chance of rescuing Hamilton, whose body was recovered about two hours later, Winter Garden Fire Chief Jose Gainza told FOX35.
Police Capt. Michael Mason said authorities were not alerted in advance that an alligator was near the lake’s shore, possibly because it “has tons of alligators in it.” He said police launched a joint investigation with the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission, whose trappers captured and killed the alligator.
Mason reminded people to be aware of their surroundings and respect wildlife.
“Keep your distance,” he said. “It looks like it’s docile, it looks like your Florida emblem, but it can be dangerous.”
After a 31-year-old Oviedo woman, Brittany Clark, was killed by a 13-foot alligator near her home in June, Republican U.S. Rep. Greg Steube introduced a resolution calling for the Comptroller General and U.S. Department of the Interior to study the impacts of the American alligator’s listing as “threatened due to similarity of appearance” on Florida’s ability to remove nuisance alligators from residential and commercial waterways.
He said the species has been fully recovered since 1987 but remains protected to prevent trafficking and hunting of the similar-looking American crocodile.
Using Florida state data, the two 2026 deaths bring the total number of individuals killed by alligators since 1948 to 34. Among them were a 61-year-old woman tipped out of her canoe by an alligator in 2025 and an 85-year-old widow who was dragged out of her backyard by an alligator while walking her dog in 2023.

title: Fire crews battle Southern California blaze that burned 6 homes, led to the evacuation of 16,000
text:
SAN JUAN CAPISTRANO, Calif. (AP) — Fire crews in Southern California worked Saturday to contain a wind-driven blaze that charred hills and burned at least six large coastal homes, prompting the evacuation of thousands of people.
Hundreds of firefighters worked through the night on a blaze burning on the hills that straddle the coastal cities of San Juan Capistrano and San Clemente, in Orange County. On a scenic hill popular with hikers, only an American flag remained among the scorched terrain.
The fast-moving Norte Fire sparked Friday in San Clemente amid hot, strong Santa Ana winds that drove it into San Juan Capistrano, prompting the evacuation of about 16,000 residents.
It was one of several fires in the region hit by dry, warm gusts known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior and toward the coast. The strongest winds hit the area Friday afternoon. But conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday night, with a heat advisory in effect until 8 p.m. Saturday on the Orange County and San Diego County coast, the National Weather Service said.
The blaze was just under a square mile (2 square kilometers) and 5% contained Saturday, when firefighters were still dousing water on smoldering debris from a home that burned.
The fire has damaged or destroyed at least six homes — some of them hillside homes with sweeping ocean views, officials said.
Some evacuation orders were lifted Saturday, but authorities said the large majority remained in effect and urged people to stay away from the area.
“We do have an active fire line, we do have wind, and we have a heat advisory in effect so there is still a risk so, we please ask everybody to please cooperate and heed our advice and stay out of those areas,” said Greg Balta, a spokesperson with the Orange County Fire Authority.

title: Florida art dealer gets nearly 4 years in prison for scheme to sell fake Andy Warhol artworks
text:
Florida art dealer gets nearly 4 years in prison for scheme to sell fake Andy Warhol artworks
He must also pay back nearly $2.6 million that he earned from the scheme
Florida art dealer gets nearly 4 years in prison for scheme to sell fake Andy Warhol artworks
He must also pay back nearly $2.6 million that he earned from the scheme
A South Florida art dealer has been sentenced to nearly four years in federal prison for a scheme that involved selling fake Andy Warhol artworks.
Related video above: A painting bought for $30 at an estate sale may soon sell at auction for up to $250,000
Leslie Howard Roberts, 63, was sentenced in Miami federal court this month to three years and 10 months after pleading guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud. He must also pay back nearly $2.6 million that he earned from the scheme.
Roberts, the owner of Miami Fine Art Gallery in Coconut Grove, was arrested in April 2025. According to court records, he fraudulently represented art as original pieces created by renowned artist Andy Warhol. Prosecutors said Roberts falsely claimed that he acquired the artwork directly from the Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts and provided fake and fraudulent invoices.
"He exploited the trust that collectors place in art dealers and the authenticity of the works they purchase," U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Florida Jason Reding Quiñones said in a statement.
As part of the conspiracy, Carlos Rodriguez Melendez posed as an employee of a New York-based auction company and falsely authenticated artwork to conceal that it was forged, investigators said. Rodriguez Melendez pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit wire fraud last year and was sentenced to probation.
Another South Florida art dealer was sentenced in 2023 to two years and three months in federal prison for selling fake Warhols. Daniel Elie Bouaziz, who owned two galleries in Palm Beach County, had pleaded guilty to a single count of money laundering, while prosecutors agreed to drop 16 other counts related to fraud and embezzlement.
Warhol was an American visual artist and filmmaker most associated with the pop art movement of the 1960s.

title: Need help caring for an older Mainer? Start here
text:
Aging in Maine is presented by AARP Maine
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Caring for an aging Mainer can be overwhelming, but you don’t have to navigate it alone.
From respite care and transportation to counseling and legal help, a range of resources is available to support older Mainers and the family members and friends caring for them.
Here are some key agencies in each county and a look at what they offer.
As Maine’s population ages, taking care of its older residents is becoming an increasingly urgent issue. From the stress of rural isolation to a shortage of workers to complicated federal Medicare guidelines, this guide helps Mainers learn about the services, technology and resources available to caregivers and the parents, spouses, neighbors and friends they’re caring for.
ANDROSCOGGIN, FRANKLIN AND OXFORD COUNTIES
SeniorsPlus is based in Lewiston and has satellite offices in Norway and Wilton.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Care coordination (connecting people with home care services from respite to in-home community service (assistance with living independently)
- Fiscal intermediary services for clients with long-term care needs (handling employer and employee paperwork, payroll, tax filings and workers’ compensation coverage)
- Nutrition services (access to the Meals on Wheels meal delivery program, social dining opportunities and restaurant vouchers that offer reduced prices at participating locations)
- Specialized services (coordination of emergency response systems, respite in a facility, environmental modification and assistive technology).
Connect at seniorsplus.org and 207-795-4010.
AROOSTOOK COUNTY
Aroostook Agency on Aging, based in Presque Isle, serves older people in northern Maine.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Home care personal support (in-home help with daily activities)
- MaineCare in-home services, care partner education and support
- Volunteer programs and the Money Minders program (free bill-paying service where trained volunteers can help with setting up a budget, paying bills and managing a checkbook).
- MaineCare Toolkit which provides help with navigating community MaineCare or MaineCare in-home services applications and securing financial assistance for them.
Connect at aroostookaging.org and 207-764-3396.
For transportation needs, head to aroostooktransportation.org to access Aroostook Regional Transportation, which helps people throughout Aroostook County get to appointments, shop and stay active in their community.
CUMBERLAND AND YORK COUNTIES
Southern Maine Agency on Aging provides resources, services and information to empower adults, adults with disabilities and their caregivers.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Information for older Mainers about day programs, nutrition (including the Meals on Wheels meal delivery program) and fall prevention
- Medicare counseling
- Money Minders (help with money management/bill paying)
- Phone Pal program, which pairs volunteers who will call 1-3 times a week for friendly conversations
- Resources for assistance with caregiving, including information on benefit programs, adult day programming and community resources
- Classes are offered on topics such as caring for someone with dementia, finding community resources, stress management and problem solving
- Southern Maine Agency on Aging’s State Respite Care Program supports family caregivers of people with dementia, and in some cases the program reimburses some of the cost for someone else to provide care
- Regularly scheduled support groups take place at the Biddeford office, and in the community to help connect caregivers with one another
Connect at smaaa.org and 207-396-6500.
HANCOCK, PENOBSCOT, PISCATAQUIS AND WASHINGTON COUNTIES
Eastern Area Agency on Aging, based in Brewer, provides information, options and services for older adults, adults with disabilities and caregivers.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Family Caregiver Program (information and assistance, respite program and support groups)
- Commodity Supplemental Food Program (30-pound monthly food boxes with shelf stable grocery items and cheese available to low-income adults 60 years or older)
- Legal services for Maine elders, Medicare counseling, Meals on Wheels (meal delivery program)
- Money Minders (help with money management/bill paying).
Connect at eaaa.org and 207-941-2865.
KENNEBEC, KNOX, LINCOLN, SAGADAHOC, SOMERSET AND WALDO COUNTIES
Spectrum Generations is based in Augusta, and also has offices in Waterville, Damariscotta, Belfast, Hallowell and Brunswick.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- We Sustain Maine (locally grown food provided from Maine farms)
- Meals on Wheels (meal delivery program)
- MaineCare services (assistance with arranging home care programs)
- Money Minders (help with money management/bill paying)
- Caregiving services (support groups, adult day programs, state respite care program).
Spectrum Generations also covers Brunswick and Harpswell in Cumberland County.
Connect at spectrumgenerations.org and 800-639-1553.
OTHER RESOURCES
- Legal Services for Maine Elders is based in Augusta. Its mission is to protect the rights of older Mainers by providing free legal services to people ages 60 and older. They also advocate for people facing challenges when accessing Medicare benefits. Connect at maineelse.org and 207-623-1797.
- Office of Aging and Disability Services supports Maine’s older population by promoting the highest level of independence, health and safety throughout Maine. They oversee several programs for older adults, including long-term care programs. Connect at maine.gov/dhhs/oads and 207-287-9200.
- Maine Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program provides free, confidential advocacy for people receiving long-term care services and their families. The program investigates complaints and helps consumers understand their rights and options when problems arise with nursing homes, assisted living, home care, hospice and other services. Staff can also answer questions about finding and paying for care, and what to do if services are denied, reduced or terminated. Connect at maineombudsman.org and 207-621-1079.
- The Iris Network is a Portland-based nonprofit that helps Mainers who are blind or have low vision live independently. Services include low-vision evaluations and rehabilitation, mobility and orientation training, adaptive technology and help with everyday tasks. The organization serves people of all ages, including older adults experiencing age-related vision loss. Connect at theiris.org and 207-774-6273.

title: Happy birthday, Sonny. Keep the memories coming.
text:
It’s amazing to think that one year ago I tore myself in two to push out a screaming potato and now, as I write this, there is a tiny chaos goblin in my office, pulling books off a desk and blowing raspberries.
As cliché as it is to say, the days have been long (and the nights even longer) but the year was short. It feels like it’s been forever and also like just yesterday I was flying down 295 to Maine Med at 4 a.m. Somehow we have all survived, with marriage and developmental milestones intact.
I was worried that I would lose my own identity in motherhood; I’ve read and spoken to a lot of women who felt that happened to them. I’ve been lucky so far; I still feel like exactly who I’ve always been, just with more add-on, after-market features.
I don’t know if it’s because I’ve only been a mom for a year, or because I only have one kid, or maybe I just have a particularly strong sense of self. It’s felt more like in a video game where suddenly you hit a new level or find a treasure chest and then your character can wield the Flaming Sword of Vengeance, except in this case it’s just the ability to prepare an entire baby lunch one-handed with the other arm holding a 20-pound child. I come equipped with new items too, like the Dumbbells of Lesser Back Pain, the Midnight Cookie Tupperware (can only be accessed in the dark) and the Diaper Bag of Endless Wonders.
I’ve also unlocked vast stores of patience that I had no idea were there, like an enormous underwater aquifer that just got discovered accidentally by a septic tank crew. There is no one else on Earth who can scream at me for two hours between 1 and 3 in the morning and I will respond with nothing but love and snuggles. I’m able to cope with sensory issues that would normally overstimulate me.
I mean, do you know how many slimy textured food items I’ve touched today alone? So many. And yet when it’s for my kiddo I don’t feel like tearing off my skin like I normally do. Last week there was a day where Sonny vomited on me. Twice. And I didn’t even have a meltdown.
Sonny is developing a real personality now. When we’re out and about he is fairly laid back — indeed, yesterday at the grocery store the cashier said he was “the chilliest baby she’s ever seen” — casually observing everything quietly, taking it all in and I assume processing it somehow. He doesn’t freak out too much at strangers. At home, though — well, there’s a reason my wife’s name for his alter ego is “Chaos Boy.”
Currently his favorite activities are pulling piles of things off shelves. I stack (and restack) board books for him on coffee tables for just this purpose and throwing food at the dogs, sometimes to indicate he’s done eating but sometimes just, apparently, for funsies. We play little games with each other.
He is constantly pulling himself up to standing using various objects to balance. He seems to have this insatiable, unstoppable inner drive to move forward. Once he learned to sit, he started lunging forward from a sitting position until he figured out crawling. Now he crawls and still wants to go further, farther and always upward (he’s also constantly trying to climb me and his other mom).
When we take him for walks in the stroller he is constantly twisting around and swiveling, trying to look at absolutely everything in the world. He has a particular fascination with staring at the stroller wheels turning, and in throwing his pacifiers out the side to see what happens.
I find myself staring at him with a stupid happy grin on my face all the time. (Well, maybe not at 2 a.m.) I feel so lucky that I get to hang out with this cool little dude all the time. We start our day on the floor of the nursery, him with his milk and me with my cup of coffee and I just feel so joyful. When he smiles at me it feels like the way taking the first sip of a glass of wine felt and I just want more and more.
I don’t take these moments of joy for granted. I’m sure I’ll go into it in a whole column at some point, but for the first few months after Sonny’s birth, I had postpartum depression pretty badly. I was worried I would never feel the joy in parenthood that other moms talked about or even just joy in general). I’m happy to report that the joy and fun has kicked in.
I can’t wait to see what Sonny does next. Which, at time of this writing, is crawling at top speed for the dog’s chew toy.

title: 91-year-old man attacked by raccoon while walking to his mailbox
text:
Barrington, R.I. (WJAR) - A 91-year-old man in Barrington, Rhode Island, was attacked by a raccoon during a routine trip to the mailbox.
Hal Hamilton said it happened right at the front steps of his home.
“Four, five ... hit me here. Down I go,” he said.
Hamilton said that on the fifth step, a raccoon snuck up on him, throwing him off balance.
“Right here is where the raccoon regained its composure, having been kicked off the stairs, and looked like it was going to have an assault number two,” Hamilton said.
The mailbox isn’t far from Hamilton’s front door, and lucky for him, he had his cane handy.
“I was able to hit him with my cane and crack it over the head and then it went out this way down the wall into the congressional church,” Hamilton said.
Hamilton reached out to the Department of Fish and Wildlife for details on what to do next and eventually reported it to the Department of Health and local leaders.
But Hamilton didn’t realize just how much damage the raccoon had done until later, when he found puncture marks on his clothing.
“I looked at the other side of the tracksuit bottoms, there is no mark,” Hamilton said. “So, what I feel is that those little claws pulled that up and they got a clear shot at the flesh there and gave me a rip. And as you can see the two teeth, two fangs and the bell underneath ones there.”
Hamilton needed a rabies vaccine but said urgent care couldn’t treat him and sent him to Newport Hospital.
Instead, Hamilton had a plan of his own.
“I went to CVS and they did have the vaccine ready there,” he said.
But the vaccine cost him.
“The copay does not take on this particular vaccine. $440 it was. And I said, ‘I don’t care if you multiply that by five, get it in there,” Hamilton said.

title: Skowhegan considers public vote on separating town clerk, treasurer roles
It was a week of good, bad and ugly sports stories in Maine
text:
Rarely do we get a week in Maine chock full of sports stories that make you do a double take. This week, we got three.
These three stories will make you nod your head in gratitude, or just make you shake your head. They’ll tear at your faith in humanity, then build it back up.
The good: Joe Russo retires
The good isn’t that Russo retired after 36 season coaching the Portland High boys basketball team, it’s that we got three and a half decades of Russo and he was able to step away on his own terms.
Russo is one of 10 coaches in state history to win at least 500 games, and he won his sixth state championship this past season. Russo’s final season may have been his best coaching job. Take away the fact that some of his players missed early season practices while they prepared for the Class A football state championship game. Set aside injuries to key players throughout the regular season. Those are issues coaches have dealt with for years.
This season, with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement running around the state under the guise of the grotesquely named “Operation Catch of the Day,” Russo had at times 17% of his team out of school, kept home by parents fearful of their son being yanked off the street and taken to God knows where.
Through the most stressful time many of those teenagers have lived through, Russo kept them together. Winning 517 games and leaving a healthy collection of Gold Balls in the trophy case are fine benchmarks, but being there when your players are facing serious life-changing threats, that’s the mark of a truly great coach.
The bad: Police investigate fight at youth football game in Livermore Falls
Yeah, shouldn’t be surprised by this one. Adults have behaved like oafs at youth sports for decades. There hasn’t been a bar to sink below for years. That bar is buried cable. You need a backhoe and a dig-safe permit to reach it.
The latest incident occurred at a youth football game in Livermore Falls last Saturday. A video of the incident shows parent Donna Jewell approach coach Dylan Rider, as she’s holding a puppy. She appears to make contact with Rider as he turned toward her. Rider pushed Jewell to the ground, then made his way toward another fight between a pair of men, one of them his father.
You can be sure everyone involved is 100% confident they are in the right. In whatever heat of the moment can happen at a youth football game, nobody every stops to consider that they’re about to play the fool. In those moments, people forget youth sports should be about teaching the game and instilling fondness and respect for the game.
It’s especially disappointing that one of those involved, Rider, is an Androscoggin County Sheriff’s deputy. If anyone should be in position to de-escalate a situation like that, it’s a police officer.
It should be simple. If you’re at a youth sports game, cheer for the kids. If something happens that draws your concern, address it with calm tact, please.
Let’s review that the next time this happens, OK?
The ugly: Westbrook athletes caught in nasty online harassment
Let’s applaud the Westbrook community for standing up to bullies. When a Facebook post suggested two members of the Blue Blazes girls soccer team are transgender, Westbrook rallied around its student athletes.
Mayor David Morse released a statement calling out the abhorrent behavior. Superintendent Peter Lancia condemned the social media posts, as did State Rep. Sue Salisbury.
There’s honest discussion and debate to have on the issue of transgender athletes. It’s apparent there are bad actors who don’t want to have anything close to civil discourse. They’d rather point fingers and bully teenagers. That is abject cowardice. They don’t have a position, they have propaganda.
Thankfully, Westbrook High leadership and others stepped up and quickly came to the defense of its students. We saw how Westbrook comes together last year when the city rallied around its state-title winning football team. It’s nice to see that happen when the reason to come together isn’t a celebration.

title: Maine groups spay, neuter 44 community cats for National Feral Cat Day
text:
WINTHROP, Maine (WABI) -Local animal organizations teamed up for National Feral Cat Day to provide free spay and neuter services for cats across Maine.
PALS Low-Cost Feline Vet Service in Winthrop partnered with Cat Life Maine, Laurie and Dave Mountain to organize a mega spay-and-neuter event called “50 Cats, 50 Eartips, 50 Surgeries, One Day.”
Volunteers caught cats ahead of event
Throughout the week leading up to the event, local volunteers, under the guidance of animal organizations like Camp Emmett, caught 44 community cats to be spayed or neutered and given eartips to signal they were fixed.
Though organizers did not reach their goal of 50 because of factors including weather and the cats’ eating patterns, they said the effort still made a meaningful difference for cats from across the state.
“We frequently respond—or we call them—the invisible cats of Maine because nobody pays attention. You don’t know they’re there until you see them. And then once the blinders are off, they’re everywhere,” said Kate Downey, founder and executive director of Cat Life Maine.
Organizers hope to reduce stigma
Organizers also hope events like this can help remove the stigma around feral cats by showing that they are community animals that deserve care.
PALS was able to perform all 44 surgeries for free thanks to support from several partner organizations: Best Friends, Idexx, Boehringer Ingelheim, PetCo Love, AdopterLuv Microchip Registry, Maine Humane and Meow Cat Lounge.

title: Woman previously convicted of killing husband arrested again on new charge
text:
EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE/Gray News) — A 58-year-old Indiana woman with a reckless homicide conviction is facing a new charge after deputies said she was found intoxicated and parked in the middle of a street early Monday.
Wendy Payne was booked just after midnight Monday on a charge of driving while intoxicated. She was held on a $2,500 bond.
Deputies describe scene
Vanderburgh County deputies said they found Payne parked in the middle of Van Ness Avenue, near Kedzie Avenue, on the west side.
Deputies said Payne was so intoxicated she nearly fell several times. She allegedly told them she had been drinking at Leroy’s Tavern.
At the jail, deputies say a breath test showed Payne’s blood alcohol content was 0.228, nearly three times the legal limit.
Authorities said Payne was convicted of driving while intoxicated in Henderson in July.
Prior conviction in Evansville
Payne was also found guilty of reckless homicide in 2021 after stabbing her husband, Edward, to death in 2019 at their Glenview Drive home.
Payne was sentenced to five years in prison, but had credit for time served. Several people testified on her behalf at the sentencing hearing.

title: How a driver, a dad and a teacher tried to stop the Oregon school shooter
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — In the middle of an October day, a 16-year-old boy tossed a shotgun over a low chain-link fence. Then he climbed over it himself.
There was a playground and a broad grass field leading to an elementary school he once attended. Inside were hundreds of children, including a handful attending a special needs class — just like he had.
There was also a red truck. It was driven by the first of at least three people who would risk their own lives to try to stop him, according to accounts from police and school officials.
The driver yelled, and the boy started shooting. He hit the truck at least three times, but the driver wasn’t hurt — he drove down the road and called 911.
Nearby was another driver, Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter. He saw the boy shooting at the red truck and heading toward the school, Silver Rail Elementary. Giamanco’s children go there.
The boy walked along the school to a locked door. He blasted through its glass panes with the shotgun.
Giamanco drove into the parking lot. He had a gun too — a .40-caliber pistol legally stored in his vehicle.
In the classroom next to the broken door there were teachers and four children. Another teacher had taken a first-grader to the bathroom.
The boy entered a classroom next to the door. He pumped the shotgun and pulled the trigger. Over and over.
The teacher and the first-grader who had gone to the restroom heard the gunshots. They hid under a table in a nearby office.
Giamanco could hear the shooting too. He went toward it.
One of the teachers in the classroom threw a phone at the shooter. Then, police say, she tackled him.
Inside the school Giamanco saw a woman wrestling with the boy for control of the shotgun. He shot the boy several times, killing him.
The teacher who wrestled with the boy wasn’t hurt. But three of the children in the classroom were killed. They were 5, 8 and 11 years old. Another was critically wounded.
One teacher in the classroom was killed: 25-year-old Megan Lambert. Her family said teaching was her dream job. Another teacher was shot in the arm and in the hand.
Linda Sanchez is the mother of the first-grade boy who hid under the table with his teacher. She got a robocall about the lockdown and heard ambulances and police cars rushing toward the school.
“My heart was just like pounding because he was in there,” Sanchez said.
The entire series of events spanned just a few minutes. Police arrived quickly, just before Giamanco shot the boy, Griffin John II. In the aftermath investigators found as many as 15 spent shell casings. The boy had about 44 more unused rounds.
At a news conference Friday, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz and others expressed their appreciation for those who did not stand by.
“I don’t think we can underestimate or underappreciate that courage,” Krantz said. “When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognize that. The quick thinking to observe, to then park and follow someone into the school is incredible and undoubtedly saved people.
“If it came natural as a protective father, that’s terrific,” Krantz said.
“The teacher who’s willing to stand and fight for her children — incredible,” the chief added. “We all recognize that is true heroism. We don’t see that a lot in society.”
___
Johnson reported from Seattle.
