title: School bus carrying 6 nonverbal kids was missing for 4 hours, probe finds
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) — A school bus carrying six nonverbal students went missing for four hours, authorities in New York City said.
Investigation details timeline
Anastasia Coleman is the head of the Special Commissioner of Investigation for the New York City School District, an independent watchdog group. She said a former Consolidated Bus Transit driver and matron failed to drop off the 6- to 8-year-old students at P.S. 289 by 9 a.m. on Dec. 16 of last year.
According to Coleman, the driver was filling in that day and told investigators he drove to two incorrect Brooklyn-area schools before getting the correct address from dispatch around 10:40 that morning.
“They’re nonverbal, so they can’t tell you what happened,” Coleman said. “One of the children was lying down and had her diaper off and had urinated.”
Around 10 a.m., school staff tried calling Consolidated Bus Transit to locate the children and notified the Department of Education at 11:45 a.m. The school called Consolidated again and was told the bus would arrive by noon.
A parent tracking her children on the bus using AirTags called the school in a panic, and the New York City Police Department was alerted.
The bus arrived at PS 289 at 1:25 p.m.
“He said that he was near the school and he’d be there in 15 minutes, and it took hours after that,” one parent said.
Investigators said the bus matron, who was also on temporary assignment that day, did not alert anyone to the events that morning.
Company response
Consolidated Bus Transit released a statement saying both employees have been on administrative leave since the incident 10 months ago, pending investigation proceedings as required by the labor collective agreement. The company said the employees are not permitted on any of its buses and have no student interactions.
“Knowing all the buses, I’d definitely be in a panic,” one parent said.
Parents said they hope an incident like this does not happen again.

title: Joanne Shirley (Masellis) Gooley (1936-2026)
Outgoing, incoming general store owners followed similar paths to Owls Head
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Ownership of the Owls Head General Store is changing hands.
Both the outgoing owner and the incoming one followed similar paths to this coastal community.
Maya Newsam Sousa said the sale of the building and business is scheduled to be finalized Monday, Oct. 19. The new owner will be Catie Sheehan who was already working in the kitchen this week.
But the staff and the store’s well-known “Seven Napkin Burger” will continue with the ownership change.
The General Store, located next to the town’s post office, was built in 1880 and has operated as a general store since around the 1920s.
Newsam Sousa said she decided to sell because the time commitment to run a store was in conflict with the time needed to be with her 2-year-old child.
Newsam Sousa’s ties to Owls Head run deep. Her great-great grandfather was Pete Reed and she has spent every summer in Owls Head. She was managing a bar in Salem, Mass. when she and her husband got “temporarily” laid off during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. They came to Owls Head and purchased the General Store.
She said the community was supportive and helped make the operation a success. The store had been closed for three years before she purchased it in June 2020.
Sheehan had been a school teacher for many years and later ran a gift shop in New York but decided she wanted out after her business flooded twice. That was timed with the graduation of her daughter.
Sheehan said her father’s family was from Machias and South Portland. She spent holidays in Maine.
Sheehan said her mother saw online that the store was up for sale while she was in South Portland. Sheehan moved quickly and negotiated the purchase.
She said she was excited by the opportunity.
“It’s my baby,” Sheehan said.
The store received national attention in 2009 when the Food Network named its burger as the best burger in Maine.
Newsam Sousa purchased the store in June 2020 from 319 Enterprises, LLC and its manager Richard Craig. That company bought it in July 2012 from Luttrell Enterprises, LLC and its member Tom Luttrell. Luttrell purchased it in 2008 from McNeilly and Maher, LLC. That company purchased it from Dale and Constance Beal in 1997 who purchased it in 1991 from Charles and Marion Stevens who bought it in 1973 from Gladys Daucett who with Capser Daucett had owned it since 1950.
The store sells groceries, gifts, and prepared foods. The store is within walking distance from Owls Head Harbor.

title: County Sweeps PVC Coaching Honors, Wins Three Team Championships
text:
County Cross Country Shines at PVC Championships With Three Team Titles, Two Individual Wins and Three Coaching Honors
Aroostook County had plenty to celebrate Saturday at the Penobscot Valley Conference Cross Country Championships in Old Town.
Three team championships, two individual victories and three PVC Coach of the Year honors highlighted an outstanding afternoon for County athletes and coaches.
Houlton/GHCA captured the Small School Boys championship, Presque Isle won the Large School Girls title, and Caribou finished first in the Large School Boys competition.
Caribou's Pierce Gorneault and Emma Graves added individual championships, while two County coaches received recognition for their work throughout the season.
Caribou's Thomas Beckum was named PVC Girls Large School Coach of the Year, Presque Isle's Dylan Marrero earned PVC Boys Large School Coach of the Year honors, and Houlton's Chris Rines was named PVC Boys Small School Coach of the Year.
From the front of the varsity races to the junior varsity competition, County runners turned in strong performances across the board.
County Coaches Earn PVC Coach of the Year Honors
It wasn't just the runners bringing home recognition Saturday.
Caribou's Thomas Beckum was selected as the PVC Girls Coach of the Year, while Presque Isle's Dylan Marrero received the PVC Boys Coach of the Year award.
Both honors add to an impressive championship weekend for the County's cross country programs.
Beckum's Caribou girls finished third in the Large School team competition, led by individual champion Emma Graves. The Vikings also placed Jenna Strid and Isabella Albert among the top ten.
Marrero's Presque Isle boys finished third in one of the closest team races of the afternoon. Just six points separated the top three Large School Boys teams, with the Wildcats finishing behind Caribou and John Bapst.
The two coaching awards were another highlight of a day that saw County programs bring home championships in three of the four varsity divisions.
PVC Small School Boys: Houlton/GHCA Captures Team Championship
Houlton/GHCA put together one of the day's most impressive team performances, winning the Small School Boys championship with 36 points.
The Shires placed three runners among the top four and four among the top eight, finishing ahead of George Stevens Academy with 45 points and Orono with 47.
Malachi Witmer led Houlton/GHCA with a second-place finish in 17:16.06.
Brayden Drake finished third in 17:18.52, followed almost immediately by Wyatt Quint in fourth at 17:18.58. Only six-hundredths of a second separated the two teammates.
Logan Witmer added an eighth-place finish, while Stephen Cormier completed the Shires' scoring five.
Orono's Brady Cox won the individual championship in 17:11.53.

title: Explore the wild backcountry of the Nahmakanta Public Land
text:
Perched comfortably on a shelf of granite just above the shoreline of Sixth Debsconeag Pond, I am both entertained and awed by the brook trout leaping out of the water like little dolphins. Must be something mighty tasty they’re feasting on. My campfire crackles next to me as I chow down on a pouch of backpacker food. The sun behind my back has sunk into the trees, and try as I might to stay awake, I’m thinking it will be an early night in the bag.
Sixth Debsconeag Pond lies at the heart of the Debsconeag Backcountry in the northeast corner of Nahmakanta Public Land, a sprawling 43,000-acre expanse that ranges across four unorganized townships—T1 R12 WELS, T1 R11 WELS, Rainbow Township and T2 R12 WELS—in the northern reaches of Maine’s famed 100-Mile Wilderness. Low but rugged mountains, dense forests and pristine waters characterize this remote region.
The Debsconeag Backcountry Trail threads through this sector of the Nahmakanta for 12 miles, making a figure-eight loop past Fifth, Sixth, Seventh and Eighth Debsconeag ponds as well as one named Stink Pond (I’d love to know the origin of that name, for sure). Several miles along Nahmakanta Lake form the outer portion of the upper loop. Mossy ledge outcrops dot the terrain and offer wonderful views of the wild country all around.
A great horned owl makes its presence known from the woods up along the pond’s northern edge. And although I haven’t noticed loons on Sixth Debsconeag Pond, in the gathering darkness I hear two call from below on Nahmakanta Lake. I stand still for a few moments amid the fragrant spruce trees on the rocky point, nip of bourbon in hand, and just listen and look. Stars begin to populate the inky black sky above. Absolutely perfect.
Tomorrow, I’ll don my ultralight daypack and finish off the rest of the Debsconeag hike before returning to camp, breaking down, and packing out to the trailhead. For now, though, I am happy to simply revel in the quiet of the night, far from any errant noise, light or traffic. No wonder, though, given that I’m situated in the midst of a 9,200-acre roadless area that makes up the lion’s share of 11,800 acres of ecological reserve. This is the place to be.
Nahmakanta Public Land, established in 1990, is a key connector in a nearly continuous corridor of conservation lands stretching from Moosehead Lake to Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument. Owned by the state and managed for multiple uses by the Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands, the Nahmakanta features 35 miles of hiking trails (plus a segment of the Appalachian Trail) and a host of backcountry and roadside campsites.
Along the southern boundary of the Nahmakanta is the Turtle Ridge Trail, another figure-eight loop that meanders over several ridgetops and past a series of pristine ponds for 8 miles. On the southeastern edge is the Tumbledown Dick Trail, which leads past a couple more ponds and to tumbling Tumbledown Dick Falls. The Appalachian Trail winds through the Nahmakanta for 9 miles, along the namesake lake and over Nesuntabunt Mountain.
For a truly grand backpacking adventure, hikers can take to the Great Circle Trail, a 30-mile circuit that meanders through the best of the Nahmakanta terrain. This terrific new route, completed just five years ago after 15 years of trail work, connects several previously existing trails — Tumbledown Dick, the Debsconeag Backcountry Trail, a few miles of the AT, and Turtle Ridge — to several new trail segments, specifically the Pollywog Trail along Pollywog Pond to Wadleigh Pond, the Wadleigh Trail to the top of Wadleigh Mountain, and the Third Musquash Trail.
Tackle the entire Great Circle Trail loop, and you’ll gain more than 3,000 feet of elevation. There are several established campsites along the way, but you can also wild camp (except in the AT corridor), provided you practice the principles of “Leave No Trace.”
Nahmakanta Lake is, of course, the land’s magnificent centerpiece, so some time well spent there admiring its beauty is warranted. Next summer, I think I’ll bring my canoe, camping gear and cooler, and explore the 1,100-acre water body with paddle power. I’ve seen those beautiful beach campsites from high above, after all, and can just picture my camp chair there on the sand, me with cold beer in hand. Good living, that.
Carey Kish of Mount Desert Island is a Triple Crown hiker, freelance writer, and author of three hiking guides. Connect with Carey on Facebook and Instagram and at [email protected].

title: Crowd in Portland rallies around electing Maine Democrats on ‘No Kings Day’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — With just over two weeks until the midterm elections, about 400 people gathered in Deering Oaks on Saturday to rally around voting Democrats into office in Maine and ousting five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins from the U.S. Senate.
Organized by Indivisible Greater Portland, the event coincided with the fourth national “No Kings” day. Previous “No Kings” protests drew thousands of Mainers who condemned Trump administration actions they said reflect a monarchy rather than a democracy. This year, the same protesters are focused on encouraging people to vote early in the midterm elections, ensuring that democracy prevails, in their view.
“I feel there’s a very significant undercurrent of bitterness and feeling that our government is betraying us,” said Chris Beasley, 86, of Cape Elizabeth. He held a ribbon-adorned sign on a long wooden stick that said “Vote.” “This brings attention to our choice of representatives that reflect the values of democratic society.”
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree, U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson and U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., were three of several speakers at the event. The trio criticized President Donald Trump and discussed issues such as healthcare, the war in Iran, rising heating oil costs, immigration and abortion. They blamed Collins for affordability challenges in Maine and emphasized the importance of voting.
“Democracy is on the line here in Maine and across the country,” Pingree said. “Don’t leave it to chance.”
The race between Jackson and Collins is seen as particularly consequential — Democrats view it as one of their best shots at gaining a majority in the U.S. Senate. The competitors faced off in their fourth and final debate Thursday. Election Day is Nov. 3.
Sentiments against Collins and Trump at the rally were strong, with people holding signs that said “Retire Susan,” “Dump King Corruption” and “Susan Collins is complicit.” The senator has tried to distance herself from the president as his approval ratings wane, while Jackson’s campaign has pushed to present the two as a package.
Ben Bernard, 55, of Cliff Island, compared Collins to a teacher who helps a bullied child get some of their lunch money back, but won’t stand up to the bully. He was referring to Collins’ negotiations to remove some Maine items from Canada’s tariff list, a result of the trade war started by Trump.
“Collins is enabling Trump every day,” Bernard said.
Some came to the protest with specific policies in mind. Leah Campbell, 77, of Portland, held a sign that said “What happened to affordable healthcare for all?”
“I and people I know are impacted by healthcare cuts that have already been done,” Campbell said. “I have Medicare. I want to make sure that’s not cut. I have Social Security. I want to make sure that’s not cut. These are programs I have paid into all my life.”
Holly Parker, 52, of Cape Elizabeth, and Nancy Timberlake, 78, of Portland, said they already voted and came to the rally to surround themselves with positive energy after feeling drained by the most important issues in the elections.
“I had to buy heating oil this week, and it was excruciating,” Parker said. “I feel bad for a lot of people who are in a worse position than I am in terms of heating their homes and putting gas in their car.”
Prices of heating oil and gas have risen sharply since the start of the war in Iran.
Parker said she thinks the rally would be worth it if it persuades one more person to vote.
The event presented opportunities for Mainers to sign up to knock on doors and make calls to encourage their neighbors to vote. A band called “Singing Resistance” sang songs in between speakers who discussed voting and defeating Collins.
“A Senate seat does not belong to a person who’s held it for 30 years,” Jackson said. “It belongs to the people of Maine … I owe the people of Maine everything.”

title: No Kings rallies across U.S. urge voters to cast ballots early ahead of midterms
text:
(AP) - Rallies organized by the No Kings network opposed to President Donald Trump were held Saturday in cities and communities across the U.S., with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections.
The hundreds of planned events were billed as nonpartisan, though they sought to build on nearly two years’ worth of No Kings marches and demonstrations by people upset with Trump’s presidency.
A band entertained what appeared to be a few hundred people in caps and coats at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington. Despite the chilly weather, many in the crowd danced to the tunes. “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!” were among the many signs held aloft.
At an Atlanta rally, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd to urge others to vote ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
“The Constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?” he said.
“You don’t see Superman giving up his power,” Bond continued. “You don’t see Black Panther giving up his power. You don’t see Wonder Woman giving up her magic lasso. So why would you give up your right, your power, your obligation to vote? Be a super hero, use your power. Go to the polls and vote.”
Trump has long been suspicious of mail voting and has claimed without evidence that voting fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election.
His administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for the midterm elections from people whom the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
On Friday the Justice Department warned that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution.
Earlier that day Democratic Sens. Alex Padilla of California, Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island and Dick Durbin of Illinois wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified.

title: Rep. Ilhan Omar's attorneys demand return of property seized in federal search of her home
text:
Rep. Ilhan Omar's attorneys demand return of property seized in federal search of her home
Attorneys for Rep. Ilhan Omar asked the Justice Department on Friday to immediately return property that federal agents seized from her home this week, arguing that the search stemming from an immigration fraud investigation was "neither justified nor lawful."
In a letter obtained by The Associated Press, lawyers for the Democrat from Minnesota described the investigation as a baseless effort to go after a longtime political target of Republican President Donald Trump, noting that the search was conducted just weeks before the midterm elections, in which Omar is on the ballot.
Omar's attorneys wrote that there is "no legitimate basis for any suggestion that she has violated any law concerning her citizenship status."
"This vindictive, retributive, and politically motivated criminal investigation into one of the President's chief congressional critics violates Representative Omar's constitutional rights and threatens the separation of powers," Omar's legal team wrote in the letter first reported by The Wall Street Journal.
A Justice Department spokesperson didn't immediately respond to a message seeking comment Friday evening.
Monday's search of Omar's Washington, D.C., home this week drew swift condemnation from Democrats, as the Justice Department has historically sought to avoid public investigative actions involving a candidate within 60 days of a primary or general election.
Federal authorities seized Omar's phone in the search and have issued more than a dozen grand jury subpoenas, including to some of her relatives, a person briefed on the probe told the AP this week.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, though Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has suggested that authorities were examining potential crimes related to her family's immigration paperwork. Separately, Washington's U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro has said "there are several investigations going on" related to Omar and her office is probing issues concerning the lawmaker's financial disclosures.
In the letter, Omar's attorneys accused the Justice Department of violating longstanding agency policy designed to avoid potentially influencing an election. They also raised concerns about whether the department appropriately followed all of the specific instructions by the magistrate judge who approved the search.
In addition to the return of her property, Omar's attorneys are demanding that the Justice Department preserve any audio and video that was taken during the search, according to the letter.
Omar has repeatedly refuted allegations about her marriage and immigration status raised by conservative critics, even before she joined Congress.
According to her House biography, Omar has said she and her family fled Somalia's civil war when she was 8: "The family spent four years in a refugee camp in Kenya before coming to the United States in 1990s. In 1997, she moved to Minneapolis with her family." She became a lawfully naturalized U.S. citizen in 2000, according to her lawyers.
Conservative online sites have alleged that Omar married a brother to commit immigration fraud. Omar has broadly denied the allegations as "disgusting lies" and called the insinuation "absurd and offensive."
The search of her home came just days after Trump referred pejoratively to Omar at a rally in Tennessee as coming from a country of "crime and squalor" and suggested that Vice President JD Vance "and our people" were investigating her. Hours after the search, Trump told reporters he had "nothing to do" with it and it's "really up to the DOJ."

title: Susan Collins not to blame for birthing center closures
text:
Recent political commercials regarding the closing of birthing centers in this state — linking them to Medicare cuts and blaming Sen. Susan Collins — are blatantly false.
As a member of the Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services Committee in the Maine Legislature, I have heard loud and clear from these hospitals that these closures are due to staff recruiting and hiring difficulties, low birth rates in the rural areas of the state and limited advancement and training opportunities for new doctors practicing here in Maine — not Medicare cuts.
Sen. Collins was the author of the Rural Health Transformation Program that brought $190 million to the state of Maine to support our rural hospitals, not to close them. I realize this is the silly campaign season but one should know the truth when subjected to false claims such as the ones depicted in these ads.
Rep. Robert Foley
Wells

title: 81-year-old man killed during home invasion; suspect shoots himself in bathroom, authorites say
text:
NEW ALBANY, Miss. (WTVA/Gray News) - An 81-year-old Mississippi man was shot and killed during a home invasion, authorities said.
Union County Sheriff Jimmy Edwards said the shooting happened around 4 a.m. Thursday at a home.
An 81-year-old man identified as Bobby McGill and a woman were in bed when the suspect, Eric Basco, allegedly entered the home.
The woman escaped and called 911, while McGill tried to fight off Basco.
Authorities said the suspect allegedly got ahold of McGill’s gun and killed the 81-year-old man.
Edwards said Basco appeared to have entered the home to burglarize it. He then went into a bathroom and shot himself, the sheriff said.
Basco is recovering at a hospital.

title: Carrot Top announces return to Las Vegas show, thanks supporters for their well-wishes
text:
LAS VEGAS (Gray News) — Comedian and Las Vegas headliner Carrot Top will return to the stage next week.
Carrot Top, whose real name is Scott Thompson, was hospitalized last month following a reported mental health crisis, leading to the cancellation of several performances at his long-running comedy show at the Luxor hotel-casino.
On Saturday, according to a press release, Carrot Top was ready to return to the stage on Oct. 19.
“The laughs are coming back. Legendary comedian and Las Vegas headliner Carrot Top will return ... resuming his award-winning comedy residency at Luxor,” the release said.
The entertainer also took to social media to thank everyone for the support he has received.
“I’m truly overwhelmed by the outpouring of love, support, prayers, and well wishes I’ve received over the past couple of weeks. Every message, text, and kind thought has meant more to me than you know,” Carrot Top shared.
Carrot Top, 61, is known for prop comedy, multicolor outfits and his large and unruly mane of red hair. He has had a residency at the Luxor in Las Vegas since 2005.
“While I haven’t been able to respond to everyone individually, please know that I’ve felt your love and appreciate each and every one of you from the bottom of my heart,” his post continued. “Thank you for being there for me during this time. It truly means the world to me!”

title: Technology is helping older adults age in place. Can Maine take advantage of it?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
When Peter Carrier fell down his front steps a couple of years ago, he didn’t want to bother anyone.
Carrier, 72, lives alone in his mobile home in Poland. He was headed out to the garage when he slipped and landed on his back. Unhurt and “more embarrassed than anything,” he said it wasn’t worth calling his son.
If something more serious happens, he hopes he can rely on smart technology to make that call for him.
Carrier is one of hundreds of people to receive free smart home devices in the last year amid a push to make Maine a better place to age. Lifelong Maine, one program leading the charge, has installed 606 smart speakers in homes from York to Caribou, focusing on people over the age of 65.
As workforce shortages and burnout afflict caregivers across the country, assistive technology is assuming a bigger role in the independence and comfort of older adults. The state has projected there will be nearly 75,000 more Mainers age 65 and older between now and 2032, and 88% of older adults say they want to live and age at home, according to a 2024 AARP survey.
Maine’s age-friendly advocates say adding technology to those plans supports safety, well-being and connections to others.
Within two months of Lifelong Maine’s distribution, 72% of recipients said they felt comfortable using the palm-sized smart speakers, which are called Echo Dots and powered by Amazon’s voice service, Alexa.
Some ask their speaker to play music. Others call family members whose phone numbers they’ve forgotten. When hooked up with smart lightbulbs, the devices can save people a trip to the light switch and reduce their risk of falls.
“If they’re comfortable using the device now, they’re going to be more comfortable using it when they might need it more,” said Patricia Oh, founder of Lifelong Maine’s Echo Dot distribution program.
THE COST OF CONNECTIVITY
While technology is an important solution for aging Mainers, it isn’t infallible. By late 2024, about 9,000 homes and businesses in Maine had no access to internet service or technology of any kind, and hundreds of towns and cities are still underserved, according to the Maine Connectivity Authority, the state’s broadband office.
Those who are connected tread a minefield of scams and the rising use of artificial intelligence.
And cost remains a barrier for Maine’s older adults, more than half of whom are unable to afford basic expenses where they live, according to U.S. Census Bureau data and the ALICE threshold, which is calculated for each county using household income and the cost of food, housing and other needs.
Lani Carlson, director of Maine Community Inclusion through Technology, the state’s federally funded assistive technology program, said it’s important to remember that hiking sticks and cardholders also fall under the umbrella of assistive technology.
“We use it every day,” Carlson said. “Normalizing assistive technology in everyday use is so important because these tools can help us remain independent and live a better quality of life.”
At Maine CITE’s assistive technology lending library in Augusta, Carlson’s team matches patrons with devices that can help with hearing, vision, learning, recreation or daily activities. Some check out a pocket talker, a personal listening device that fits over the ears like headphones and amplifies nearby sound.
Sock pullers are helpful for back and hip issues. There’s even a robotic cat designed to provide companionship and stimulate brain activity in older adults with dementia. It communicates through meows that grow more insistent when it isn’t being pet, then responds to touch by purring and rolling over for belly rubs.
Carlson remembers holding a device demonstration with an older woman who said she was missing out on conversations but “didn’t want to really bother her hearing aid person.”
“She put on a pocket talker, and her eyes lit up,” Carlson said.
The woman returned the pocket talker and had her hearing aids adjusted by the end of the month.
Between 2023 and 2025, annual device loans nearly doubled to 994, which Carlson attributes in part to increased awareness of accessibility after the pandemic. People can browse and order from the library’s online catalog, while in-person device demonstrations are also available at partner sites in Sanford, Bath, Lewiston, Auburn and Farmington. Two new sites are set to open at North Star Pediatric Therapy and the Center for Advancement of Rural Living in Caribou.
It hasn’t all been growth, though. Maine CITE’s partner site in Portland, Spurwink ALLTECH, shuttered last month. Bart Beattie, chief operating officer of the statewide behavioral healthcare provider, said the closure was because of “program sustainability considerations and staffing changes.”
Carlson said it’s a loss for southern Mainers, who may face longer drives to try out devices.
“We’re trying hard to adapt to this change and create new networks and pathways,” Carlson said.
Oh also saw the Echo Dots as an opportunity to fill gaps. She asked volunteers in every corner of the state to identify older community members who needed extra support at home. Hundreds received Echo Dots, smart lightbulbs and smart plugs, which connect household appliances to voice control.
Many have incorporated the devices into routines around the home, from medication reminders to music. Betsey Pace, 78, and Donna Beveridge, 83, ask it about local business hours before they leave their Saco apartment.
But the Echo Dots didn’t work for everybody. Andy Chandler, a South Portland resident with lifelong hearing loss who advocates for assistive technology, said he was unable to hear Alexa’s responses. This year, with his feedback, Oh and her team are matching people who are deaf or hard of hearing with screened Echo Shows, which can provide captions for Alexa.
The smart devices were paid for with a $35,000 grant from the University of New England. Maine CITE’s $510,000 annual budget comes entirely from the federal government, and municipalities with age-friendly programs, like Saco and Lewiston, are increasingly funding their own technology distributions.
BARRIERS TO TECHNOLOGY
Carrier learned that he could receive a free Echo Dot and device training through his Sailing Life Solo group, which meets monthly in Lewiston. He said the group helps get him out of his house: A single-story, rambling space with a wooden rocking chair and walls filled with family photos.
His windows face several neighboring homes, but Carrier hasn’t introduced himself to anyone.
“It gets lonely sometimes,” he said. “I wish the cat would talk, but I have a conversation with her whether she’s listening or not.”
So he drives to Lewiston to meet other people who are aging alone. He texts his best friend. And he goes on Facebook, “where most problems arise.”
Carrier’s savings were depleted last year after he was scammed out of $27,000 by someone he met online. He is now living paycheck to paycheck on Social Security and pension payments. With the exception of a smart watch that he bought for less than $70, the smart devices he uses at home were all gifts or the result of a distribution program like Lewiston’s.
More than 40% of Americans age 50 and older have had money stolen because of fraud, according to a report from AARP. The nonprofit offers cybersecurity workshops and resources to avoid more than 70 types of scams. Chandler, the assistive technology advocate, also delivers in-person presentations on artificial intelligence and fraud at community spaces across Maine.
While urging caution when using the internet, Chandler also can’t help but share his excitement. He spent decades relying on intermediaries to transcribe conversations and relay responses. Today, advances in automatic speech recognition allow him to see live captioning for every phone call, Zoom meeting or TV show he watches.
He can’t wait for the day that smart glasses with live captioning hit the mainstream market.
“Absolutely,” Chandler said, “assistive technology has been my best friend.”
Many are also betting on technology as a solution to loneliness. The Maine Connectivity Authority has provided millions in grants to improve technology access at community centers in Lewiston, Caribou and other underserved areas. The real goal, said Digital Opportunity Senior Manager Jessica Perez, is “social connectivity.”
Then there’s ElliQ, a robotic care companion that just arrived in Maine CITE’s library.
The lamp-shaped robot peppers the user with questions, jokes and requests for conversation, adapting to their personality and needs over time. When Carlson requested a reminder to take her medicine, ElliQ wondered if she’d like a nudge to eat food first.
To hug, the little lamp-shaped robot leaned into Carlson’s hand on its “metallic shoulder.”
The push to embrace technology will only grow with Maine’s older population. Carrier said he wouldn’t mind a robotic companion, but first he wants to learn how to use the devices already in front of him.
He still needs to figure out how to add an emergency contact to his smart watch, so it automatically calls his son if he falls. He’d like to see his best friend’s face when they catch up, for once. And he doesn’t want the dangers of the internet to keep him from connecting with others.
“I’m trying to just keep up,” he said. “I don’t want to get left behind, because I know you’ll miss out on a lot.”

title: ‘Tragedy’: 1 child, 1 adult killed after vehicle drives into soccer game at sports complex, police say
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - Two people were killed, and several other people were hurt when a truck drove through a soccer game at the Stryker Sports Complex in east Wichita, Kansas.
Wichita police said a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man, both from McPherson, died Saturday afternoon.
The two were not related, police said.
Eleven other people were taken to the hospital with traumatic injuries. They include a 5-year-old girl, a 5-year-old boy, two 8-year-old boys, a 9-year-old girl, a 28-year-old woman, a 32-year-old man, a 59-year-old woman, a 65-year-old woman and a 68-year-old man. A 61-year-old woman was taken to the hospital for medical, non-traumatic treatment.
Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses said the driver of the truck is a 34-year-old woman from Garden City. She is currently police custody.
Two girls who were in the car with her at the time of the deadly accident. He would not say what happened to the children or where they are now.
Moses said the woman had a child playing soccer at Stryker but not on the field where the deadly crash occurred. He also said she had a valid driver’s license. Now, police are working to determine how and why the crash occurred.
Anyone with information is asked to call WPD Investigations at 316-268-4407, Crime Stoppers at 316-267-2111 or 911.
This is a developing story.

title: Maranacook girls, Winthrop boys win MVC cross country titles
text:
AUGUSTA — William Morris of Dirigo and Reagan Mattson of Maranacook dominated their competition Saturday while winning individual titles in the Mountain Valley Conference cross country championships at University of Maine at Augusta’s Elvin Fields.
Winthrop cruised to the boys team championship with 30 points, far ahead of Maranacook (72) and Boothbay/Wiscasset (93). Mattson helped Maranacook (51 points) edged Boothbay/Wiscasset (59) for the girls team title.
Morris, a senior, finished the 5-kilometer course with a time of 16:20.26, more than 35 seconds quicker than Winthrop’s Alfie Cognata (16:55.68) and Sawyer Wess (16:56.00).
“It’s not a very fast course, I wasn’t going for any (personal records),” Morris said. “Maybe it’s a lack of confidence or something, but I’m always scared I’m going to get passed. My coach has always drilled into me to never look back, but I just never seem to lose that fear, and push (as if) someone is going to pass me.”
Morris, who swept the MVC, Class C South and Class C state titles last season, has had another successful fall. He was runner-up to Scarborough’s Atticus Merriam by 0.15 seconds at the Festival of Champions in Belfast on Oct. 3.
“I’m feeling pretty good about states and regionals,” Morris said. “I feel like MVC is the strongest Class C conference. If you can place well here, you can place well at states.”
Mattson, a freshman, finished in 19:35.31, more than 1:15 faster than runner-up McKenzie Boyle (20:50.52) of Dirigo. Mattson’s teammate, Kira Pelletier, placed third (21:07.85).
“It felt good (to win), I was kind of cold to start,” Mattson said. “It was kind of rough, but I got warmed up and it was fun to run with the girls in the woods. It’s definitely a goal of mine to get out and separate myself (from the group), then you just try to take your mind off the race and try to expand the gap.”
Mattson has already made a name for herself in her freshman year. She won her first high school race, the Scot Laliberte Invitational at Cony High in Augusta, set a Winthrop course record with a time of 19.56.84 on Sept. 17, and was the top freshman girls runner (18:55) at the Festival of Champions.
“She’s been so strong all season long, she’s just a real talent,” said Maranacook coach Casey Spencer. “She consistently works hard at everything she does and it continues to pay off.”
The Winthrop boys had five runners in the top 10 in the boys race. Aside from Cognata and Wess, Sam St. Germain (17:56.67) placed seventh, Michael Van Tassel (18:04.73) was eighth and Gianni Haefele (18:53.30) finished 10th.
The Winthrop boys won MVC and Class C South titles last year but finished runner-up at the state meet to Houlton/Greater Houlton Christian Academy.
“We had a plan and we executed it,” said Winthrop coach Ed Van Tassel. “I’m happy. I think next week at regionals, we’ll have a similar type of performance. And we’ve had states circled (on our calendars) since last year.”
Maranacook’s Harper Olmstead (22:46.11) finished eighth in the girls race, giving the Black Bears three top-10 finishers.
“The team’s worked really hard,” Spencer said. “We’re feeling pretty good. We really have our eyes on the next two weekends (at regionals and states), to tell the truth. We worked really hard this past week and did our best (today), and it worked out really well for the girls.”
Temperatures were in the low 50s with a strong breeze, chilly for spectators but good conditions for runners as they danced in and out of the woods.
Morris and Mattson were named the MVC Runners of the Year. Van Tassel and Spencer are the Coaches of the Year.

title: Immigration’s economic impact highlighted ahead of midterms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Inflation has been a major topic of conversation as voters head to the polls for next month’s midterm elections. Economists point to several factors, but some Democratic lawmakers say President Donald Trump’s immigration policies are part of the problem.
Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.) said the impact of immigration enforcement is being felt across multiple industries.
“ICE is an affordability issue. Everyone in this country is paying the ‘ICE tax,’” Espaillat said.
Some politicians argue the Trump administration’s immigration policy is hitting Americans’ pocketbooks, calling the economic fallout from mass deportations the “ICE tax.”
“When a construction site screeched to a halt because no one is left to build homes, that’s the ‘ICE tax’. When our elders cannot receive the care that they need because their caretakers and nurses are gone, that’s the ‘ICE tax,’” Espaillat said.
While Democrats such as Espaillat are focusing on the consequences, others see the immigration crackdown as a positive.
Joe Chatham with the Federation for American Immigration Reform supports Trump’s immigration agenda, claiming it’s boosting the U.S. economy. He said fewer foreign workers means a better deal for Americans.
“What you see is employers across the board, they start to raise those wages and there’s upward pressure because there’s less workers available. And then in addition, the working conditions start to improve. So American workers will come back into those jobs, and they’ll be able to sustain a middle-class lifestyle,” Chatham said.
Chatham said it’s a give and take, pointing to the housing market. In his view, while fewer foreign workers could make labor more expensive, housing access is a “zero-sum game.” He said more deportations means less demand for housing, lowering the cost.
“You’re also putting more money in the pocket of American workers who can then go out and buy houses, then go out and buy new products,” Chatham said.
The Brookings Institute studied cities with the most ICE activity in 2025. It found nearly 670,000 jobs were lost, with at least one in six being jobs held by American-born workers.

title: Winds calm overnight, a chilly morning, then a placid week
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - Tonight will be quite chilly with the first 20s showing up for those who haven’t seen them yet. Sunday will be warmer than Saturday. The wind will back off substantially and it will be a sunny day. The beginning of next week will be much calmer and quieter weather wise.
Tonight: Hard freeze likely, clouds clear out
Clouds will clear out almost completely into the evening. And as the winds die off temps will drop quickly into the 20s. Many areas that have not seen the 20s yet will probably see them Saturday night. Winds will decrease quickly and almost go calm in several locations.
Sunday: A much calmer and warmer day
Things will calm down considerably Sunday as the low fully departs. Winds will only be 5-10 mph and highs will reach back into the 50s for most of us with a few still stuck in the 40s. The sun will also return for pretty much everyone. The northern reaches of the county may see some clouds throughout the day, likely the only place that will.
Sunday night: Calm and cold again
Winds will go calm Sunday night and many areas will fall into the low 30s again with colder spots in the 20s. So it will be a cold start to your Sunday pretty much everywhere but a comfortable day for the most part.
Monday and beyond: A very calm weather week
After a week of rain and very diverse weather next week will mainly be the opposite. High pressure will dominate and highs in the 50s and low 60s with lows mostly in the 30s will be the consistent theme of the week. It will certainly be a very pleasant fall like week across much of the state.
Today: Cold and blustery. Highs in the 30s and 40s. Winds NW at 20-30 mph and gusts to 40 mph. Wind chills in the 20s for most.
Tonight: Winds calm down and temps drop. Lows mainly in the 20s. Winds W at 5-10 mph.
Sunday: Calmer and clear. Mainly sunny with highs in the 50s. Winds W at 5-10 mph.
Sunday night: Clear and cold. Lows in the 20s and 30s. Winds light.
Monday: Mainly sunny. Highs in the 50s. Winds W at 5-10 mph.
Monday night: Some clouds with lows in the 30s and 40s. Winds N at 5-10 mph

title: Disappointed in Jackson’s debate behavior
text:
After watching the recent debates, I will probably vote for Troy Jackson. However, his aggressive posture toward Sen. Collins and persistence in recounting debunked conspiracies make him a distasteful choice.

title: FlyDubai passenger who survived hijacking attempt speaks out
text:
'Miracle': FlyDubai passenger who survived hijacking attempt speaks out
A FlyDubai passenger whose flight plunged thousands of feet during an attack in the cockpit spoke about his experience on Thursday.
Almog Italie shared his story and said it was a “miracle” he and his family survived.
Video above: Co-pilot of an Israel-bound Flydubai flight tried to hijack the plane after stabbing the captain
Italie, his wife and two teenage children were returning home from a family trip when the plane dropped about 17,000 feet in seconds, he said.
“We were looking down, and suddenly we felt like [we were] free falling for 30 seconds, like a roller coaster, but way, way, way, way faster,” Italie said.
The plane jolted upward before stabilizing.
Italie initially thought the crew was dealing with a technical problem. He said he only realized there was an attack after passengers were told that one pilot had stabbed the other.
Several passengers intervened and subdued the attacker before the plane landed safely in Saudi Arabia, Italie said.
“If we continued dropping for 10 or 15 seconds, I wouldn’t be here,” he said. “So I feel very, very lucky. It’s a miracle.”
Italie said his wife told him she had held God’s hand and prayed to remain alive after the plane landed. He said he wanted his story to be about survival and faith.
“You don’t believe it will happen, but when it does happen, you don’t think about losing life,” Italie said. “You think about how to save life.”
Video below: Brother of FlyDubai passenger speaks about flight where captain was stabbed
In the weeks since the alleged hijacking, Italie has been traveling across the world to speak about what he saw on Flight FZ1073.
Italie said recounting those moments has proven to be a healing experience as he learns to cope with what he and others on the plane endured.

title: Hockey transfer Lee Parks having immediate effect at UMaine with 3-game goals streak
text:
After losing the team’s top four scorers and players who produced 52.6% of its goals a year ago, University of Maine sixth-year head hockey coach Ben Barr and his staff brought in a number of players designed to help fill that void.
One of those players was UMass Lowell transfer right wing Lee Parks. Just four games into the season, he has already scored goals in his last three games. He has three goals and an assist over that span, including the game-winner in the second period of last Saturday’s 5-3 win over nationally ranked Quinnipiac.
That goal was set up by a perfectly placed cross-ice pass from linemate Will Gerrior, who has also been one of his best friends since eighth grade when they went to school together in the Ottawa suburbs and were teammates for one year.
Gerrior had made a similar pass to him the previous night resulting in UMaine’s only goal in a 2-1 loss to Quinnipiac.
Parks scored his first goal as a Black Bear in a 3-2 overtime loss to Holy Cross, netting the tying goal that forced the overtime with just 2:38 left in regulation. Sophomore defenseman Lukas Peterson had the only assist.
“I owe a lot to my teammates and what they’ve been doing for me around the puck and around the net. Gerrior has set me up pretty well a couple of times now,” said Parks, a native of Stittsville, Ontario. “It’s definitely more of a team effort than just me.”
Parks is a power forward, using his 6-foot-2, 209-pound frame to full advantage by winning puck battles and getting to the net.
“He is a great power forward,” UMaine defenseman Dru Krebs said. “He moves his feet well, he has good hands and he really drives the net. He is tenacious around the puck.”
Parks is physical and great in the corners, Barr said.
“He just has to believe he can do it. He is starting to show he can and believe in himself,” Barr added.
When Parks entered the NCAA transfer portal and got the opportunity to come to UMaine, he didn’t hesitate.
“It was something I knew I had to do,” Parks said. “With the team we have here and what we’re building and the tradition. Obviously the fans as well as an opportunity to play with one of my best friends. This was what was best for me, hockey-wise.”
Parks played in 69 games in his two seasons at UMass Lowell and garnered 14 goals and 14 assists.
He said he loved playing for UMass Lowell head coach Norm Bazin and his coaching staff and appreciated everything they did for him.
“I’m happy for the opportunity here and looking forward to it,” Parks said.
He has always been a productive scorer, notching 30 goals and 28 assists in 62 regular season games for the Fargo Force in the United States Hockey League during the 2023-24 season. He amassed 23 goals and 25 assists in 50 games for the Vernon Vipers of the British Columbia Junior Hockey League the previous year.
He has been happy with his start but noted that it’s early on in the season. And even though he has been a consistently prolific scorer, he pointed out that nothing comes easy.
“I spend a lot of time working on little things after practice,” he said.
He said everything has been amazing so far in his transition to UMaine.
“It’s everything I could have asked for. Everybody comes to the rink every day with the right attitude. We push each other to get better. We’re all working towards the goal of winning a championship,” Parks said.
Knowing he is one of the players being relied upon to put pucks in the net hasn’t put any additional pressure on him.
“I just have to be me. There are plenty of guys on this team who are capable of scoring goals. It’s a matter of executing when the time comes,” Parks said. “I’m sure as the season goes along, we will see a lot of players step up in different moments.”
Gerrior and Parks have been linemates for all four games. Gerrior has been the left wing and they have been centered by Jaden Lipinski for the first three games and Max Scott for the fourth.
Even though they played only one season together prior to coming to UMaine, Gerrior said they have trained together every summer since they were 15 and also hang out together.
Gerrior is now 22 and Parks turned 22 on Friday.
Gerrior thoroughly enjoys being on a line with him.
“It has been great. He makes it easy for me,” Gerrior said. “He is a big guy who can protect the puck well and move it. He’s a great player.”
The Black Bears are 2-2 and will have the weekend off before hosting ECAC team Colgate for a two-game series on Friday and Saturday nights, Oct. 23 and 24, at 7 p.m.
Parks said the win over Quinnipiac will be good for the team’s confidence but he also said there are still plenty of things to work on.
“You can’t be too happy about just one win because it’s a long season and we have to keep getting better,” Parks said.

title: 91-year-old man attacked by raccoon while walking to his mailbox
text:
Barrington, R.I. (WJAR) - A 91-year-old man in Barrington, Rhode Island, was attacked by a raccoon during a routine trip to the mailbox.
Hal Hamilton said it happened right at the front steps of his home.
“Four, five ... hit me here. Down I go,” he said.
Hamilton said that on the fifth step, a raccoon snuck up on him, throwing him off balance.
“Right here is where the raccoon regained its composure, having been kicked off the stairs, and looked like it was going to have an assault number two,” Hamilton said.
The mailbox isn’t far from Hamilton’s front door, and lucky for him, he had his cane handy.
“I was able to hit him with my cane and crack it over the head and then it went out this way down the wall into the congressional church,” Hamilton said.
Hamilton reached out to the Department of Fish and Wildlife for details on what to do next and eventually reported it to the Department of Health and local leaders.
But Hamilton didn’t realize just how much damage the raccoon had done until later, when he found puncture marks on his clothing.
“I looked at the other side of the tracksuit bottoms, there is no mark,” Hamilton said. “So, what I feel is that those little claws pulled that up and they got a clear shot at the flesh there and gave me a rip. And as you can see the two teeth, two fangs and the bell underneath ones there.”
Hamilton needed a rabies vaccine but said urgent care couldn’t treat him and sent him to Newport Hospital.
Instead, Hamilton had a plan of his own.
“I went to CVS and they did have the vaccine ready there,” he said.
But the vaccine cost him.
“The copay does not take on this particular vaccine. $440 it was. And I said, ‘I don’t care if you multiply that by five, get it in there,” Hamilton said.

title: ‘Very happy child’: Loved ones remembering 5-year-old killed in Oregon school shooting
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — The youngest child killed in a shooting at an Oregon school was a fast runner and a fearless climber who also loved reading and his stuffed animals, his aunt said Friday.
Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of three children killed along with a teacher in the shooting Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 in central Oregon. The other two children killed were ages 8 and 11, and a fourth student and another teacher were wounded, police have said.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” said Swan Sheridan, whose sister is Summer’s mother.
Sheridan said Summer liked for all of his sea creature stuffed animals to be in his favorite color: rainbow.
“He had a great fondness for sharks and dinosaurs and creatures that were in his words, ‘misunderstood,’” she said.
Sheridan said her nephew would climb and jump off anything and was an “incredibly fast” runner, even from a young age. “He was a little ball of energy from the moment he was born,” she said.
“He was a very, very happy child,” she said.
Teacher Megan Lambert, 25, was killed, said police Chief Mike Krantz at a Friday afternoon news conference. Police confirmed Summer was one of those killed but won’t release names of the other children who died at the request of their families.
Lambert had her “dream job,” her family said in statement read at the news conference. Lambert grew up in Bend, graduated from Boise State in 2023, had a passion for sports, especially volleyball, and was a local coach, relatives said.
They described her as funny and opinionated and said she “lit up the room.”
“Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart,” her family said in the statement. ”She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs.”
Police said 16-year-old Griffin J. John II got into the school by shooting through locked doors. Authorities said John had been a special needs student at the school and attacked a classroom with special needs students.
Krantz said a parent saw John shooting outside the school, followed him inside and shot him several times.
The parent was Kaylub Giamanco, said his mother, Kenda Freeman, in a statement read Friday to reporters.
Police found John dead in the school minutes after the first calls for help, Krantz said.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, and drew community members Friday, including Brooke Olsen. She said she was feeling grateful that her daughter — a kindergartner — was safe while also trying to “grieve and process and recover.”
“This is an extremely painful day of grief for everybody in Bend, especially Silver Rail families,” Olsen said.
Police identified the wounded teacher as Becky Drury, 54. Police said her injuries were serious but not life threatening, and she was hospitalized. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on Facebook that she had injuries to her left arm and right hand and was recovering from surgery. Her husband, Will Drury, said in a statement that they’re focusing on her recovery at an “unimaginably difficult time.”
Blake Brinker said he came to a memorial at the school on Friday to pray.
“Life is such a delicate thing and I don’t think anything brings that message across more than the loss of young life,” he said
___
This story has been updated to correct the name of the teacher killed Thursday. She is Megan Lambert, not Meghan Lambert as police originally reported.
___
Stengle contributed to this report from Dallas. Associated Press journalists Ed White in Detroit and Philip Marcelo in New York also contributed to this report.

title: Maine Mariners lose to Worcester in season opener
text:
Worcester’s Matt DeMelis scored 15 seconds into the game, Sam Stange and Jordan Kaplan struck just over a minute apart early in the second period, and the Maine Mariners opened their ECHL season Saturday night with a 4-2 loss to the Railers in Worcester, Massachusetts.
The Railers led 1-0 after one period, then quickly extended their lead to 3-0 in the second. Stange scored at 1:02, and Kaplan converted a breakaway at 2:15 after a lead pass from Michael Suda.
The Mariners got their first goal of the season when Jack Bar scored 7:54 into the third. But Worcester answered just 29 seconds later, as Declan McDonald scored on the Railers’ only shot of the third period to make it 4-1.
Owen Gallatin scored a power-play goal for Maine with 3:49 remaining.
Parker Gahagen made 26 saves for the Railers. Maine’s Luke Cavallin finished with nine saves.
The teams meet again next weekend for two afternoon games in Portland, on Saturday and Sunday.

title: Lawsuit alleges DHS effort to collect detailed state voter data violates federal law
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A lawsuit filed Thursday challenges the Trump administration’s sprawling effort to collect and analyze Americans’ voter data, alleging the government has obtained voter files from at least 47 states and handled the data in a way that violates federal law.
The 42-page complaint filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., claims the Department of Homeland Security’s secretive probe of the voter data, including a policy to combine it with commercial datasets, disregards federal safeguards and flouts the privacy rights of millions of Americans.
The case, brought by the League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center and the League of United Latin American Citizens, is the latest in a torrent of legal challenges that have emerged in response to President Donald Trump’s crusade against noncitizen voting, a concern he views as a serious problem but which research shows is exceedingly rare.
The Trump administration has consistently sought to exert more power over elections, even as the Constitution grants that authority to states and, in some cases, Congress. Judges have consistently upheld states’ rights to decline to hand over their lists to the federal government.
DHS didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Thursday’s lawsuit alleges the Trump administration has obtained voter lists from 47 states, even as 30 states refused to turn them over to the administration. It calls for the court to declare the administration’s collection of voter data illegal, block the policy and order DHS to delete and stop using the voter information it already has collected.
The lawsuit comes less than three weeks before Election Day, as the administration has continued to escalate threats to states alleging they are not doing enough to remove noncitizens from their voter rolls.
On Thursday, the administration sued California election officials, alleging they didn’t act quickly enough to review names the federal government identified as “likely” noncitizens, and asking a judge to bar the state from counting those people’s mail ballots for next month’s midterm elections. The secretary of state’s office said it was given just 48 hours to review 20,000 names without the Justice Department providing any evidence to substantiate its claims.

title: Husson, UNE pick up football victories
text:
Husson University of Bangor and Biddeford’s University of New England picked up small college football wins on Saturday.
Husson beat New England College 42-0 for its second straight win and UNE dealt Castine’s Maine Maritime Academy its 38th straight loss, 62-14.
The state’s other three NCAA Division III teams, New England Small College Athletic Conference schools Colby, Bates and Bowdoin remained winless after absorbing their fifth losses of the season.
Amherst edged Colby 21-15, Wesleyan topped Bates 34-8 and Hamilton bested Bowdoin 26-7.
At Henniker, N.H., Daniel Ruiz Cantu ran for 157 yards and three touchdowns and Anthony Santacroce rushed for 87 yards and two touchdowns as Husson improved to 2-4 overall and 2-1 in the Conference of New England.
New England College, in just its third season after reviving its program since dropping it in 1972, fell to 1-5 and 0-3, respectively.
Ruiz Cantu scored on runs of 30, 26 and 25 yards and Santacroce scored on a pair of four-yard runs. Brody Gibson threw an eight-yard TD pass to Jacob Lenz.
Gibson completed 11 of 15 passes for 106 yards and a TD.
Caden Crocker and Lenz each caught four passes for 37 and 29 yards, respectively.
Calvin Casavant had five tackles including two and a half sacks and he also forced a fumble.
Jayden Horton, J.T. Wright and Cooper McNamara were each involved in four tackles and McNamara had a sack and an interception.
Brody Sobotka completed 11 of 23 passes for 51 yards for NEC, Isaiah Turner caught two passes for 30 yards and Ethan Cenesca had a game-high 17 tackles with DaShawn Fairfax being involved in nine.
In Biddeford, Damien Jones, Nathan Delgado and Gavin Martin rushed for 95, 84 and 81 yards respectively and combined to score five touchdowns with Jones and Delgado notching two apiece.
Javin Willis, Noah Federico and Steven Rosario also had touchdown runs and C.J. Cooper returned an interception 47 yards for a TD.
UNE is now 1-5 and 1-2 in the CNE while MMA is 0-6 and 0-3.
Auston Harris led MMA with 115 rushing yards on 12 carries including a 55-yard TD run. Harris Stone completed 21 of 41 passes for 176 yards including a six-yard TD pass to Evan Flowers.
Ty Regis and Flowers had seven receptions apiece for 104 and 45 yards, respectively.
Kyle Danson had nine tackles for UNE and Jack Grant had seven while MMA’s Theo Blanke, Lucas Houghton and Anthony Mazza Jr. had 15, 14 and 11 tackles, respectively.

title: Androscoggin County requests tax abatements for properties in Auburn
text:
The Androscoggin County administrator filed for a tax abatement in August with the city of Auburn for nine county properties bought in 2022 to build a sheriff’s office.
The properties initially included four homes, land and the former Subaru dealership at 774 Center St. in Auburn, though one of the homes was sold this week.
County commissioners in 2025 could not agree on a price for renovations to the former dealership and surrounding properties. This year, they decided to sell those properties. They purchased the former Maine Public building at 1450 Lisbon St. in Lewiston for $1.4 million in August to become a public safety center.
The city of Auburn taxed the properties purchased for the public safety building at nearly $68,000. The city assessor agreed to abate about $32,000 for the former dealership for one year with the intent to tax it after that, county Administrator Jeff Chute said.
The 774 Center St. building qualifies for an abatement because the property was determined to have served a public purpose, Auburn assessor Karen Scammon said in September. The other properties were not deemed to qualify for a tax exemption.
The taxes on the remaining properties are nearly $36,000. The city assessor has asked to inspect the interiors of the properties as part of the abatement process to verify the information on the property record cards, Chute said. The inspection would consist of a quick walkthrough of the interior. The exterior has already been completed as part of the revaluation process.
His reason for requesting the 100% abatements listed on the forms “is the property is owned by Androscoggin County, which is a political subdivision of the state of Maine and exempt from taxation” by state law.
Auburn conducts annual reviews of all tax exemptions across the city, where nearly 25% of assessed property is exempt.
“The legal basis for our decision (on the county taxes) was straightforward,” Joe St. Peter, Auburn deputy assessor, wrote in September, noting that under Maine tax law, taxation is the rule and exemption is the exception. Because the county is holding the land without actively using it for county operations, the “land-banked” property remains taxable, he said.
There was a brief discussion Sept. 30 at the county’s Budget Advisory Committee meeting about why the county was taxed, and how that impacts all towns and cities in the county, which fund county operations.
Lisa Cesare of Minot, chairperson of the budget committee and the Minot Select Board, called it an unfair taxation to all county towns. She mentioned that Auburn will pay about 25% of those taxes.
Chute said he tried to permit the buildings as a warehouse, public safety, training and other uses but was told by city representatives it could not be done. The building had been used in the past for training, storage and other activities.

title: Colby football coach Jack Cosgrove temporarily stepping away from team
text:
WATERVILLE — Colby College football coach Jack Cosgrove is temporarily stepping away from the program, the school announced.
In a statement obtained by the Morning Sentinel on Saturday, Colby said Cosgrove “has temporarily stepped away to prioritize providing care for a family member facing unforeseen health concerns.” WABI Bangor first reported the news Friday.
Offensive coordinator Mark Clements coached Colby in a home game against Amherst on Saturday. The Mules led 12-0 early in the second quarter but ultimately lost 21-15 to fall to 0-5 on the season.
Since being named Colby’s head coach in December 2017, Cosgrove has amassed a 26-41 record. He led the Mules to a 6-3 season last year, marking the program’s first winning record since 2005.
Cosgrove previously coached at the University of Maine from 1993-2015. He guided the Black Bears to three Coastal (formerly Colonial) Athletic Association titles and five Football Championship Subdivision playoff appearances.
Clements will be the head coach in Cosgrove’s absence. Defensive coordinator Liam Hobbins will serve as associate head coach in addition to his current role.
Colby’s next game is at Hamilton (1-4) at noon next Saturday.

title: Many Maine fire departments are understaffed, new study finds
text:
MAINE (WABI) - A new study from the Maine Fire Marshal’s Office and the University of Maine finds many fire departments are understaffed.
219 of Maine’s nearly 400 fire departments took part. 47% say they don’t have enough people, even as call volumes have risen nearly 80% in the last decade.
Researchers say financial pressures, work schedules and family obligations keep Mainers from volunteering.

title: Carrot Top announces return to Las Vegas show, thanks supporters for their well-wishes
text:
LAS VEGAS (Gray News) — Comedian and Las Vegas headliner Carrot Top will return to the stage next week.
Carrot Top, whose real name is Scott Thompson, was hospitalized last month following a reported mental health crisis, leading to the cancellation of several performances at his long-running comedy show at the Luxor hotel-casino.
On Saturday, according to a press release, Carrot Top was ready to return to the stage on Oct. 19.
“The laughs are coming back. Legendary comedian and Las Vegas headliner Carrot Top will return ... resuming his award-winning comedy residency at Luxor,” the release said.
The entertainer also took to social media to thank everyone for the support he has received.
“I’m truly overwhelmed by the outpouring of love, support, prayers, and well wishes I’ve received over the past couple of weeks. Every message, text, and kind thought has meant more to me than you know,” Carrot Top shared.
Carrot Top, 61, is known for prop comedy, multicolor outfits and his large and unruly mane of red hair. He has had a residency at the Luxor in Las Vegas since 2005.
“While I haven’t been able to respond to everyone individually, please know that I’ve felt your love and appreciate each and every one of you from the bottom of my heart,” his post continued. “Thank you for being there for me during this time. It truly means the world to me!”
