title: Animal Welfare Society hosts free rabies vaccination and microchip clinic for hundreds in Kennebunk
text:
Animal Welfare Society hosts free rabies vaccination and microchip clinic for hundreds in Kennebunk
Over one hundred cats and dogs were given a rabies vaccination for free on Saturday at an event hosted by the Animal Welfare Society.
According to A.W.S., they hold two to three of these clinics a year due to a great demand in the community.
"These clinics are really important to our community," said marketing communications director for A.W.S. Suz Madore. "But care can be very expensive as well as inaccessible for a lot of folks in our communities."
According to Madore, once animals have reached 12 weeks old, it's time to get the rabies vaccine. Following the original shot, the pet should receive the shot every three years.
"Having a rabies vaccination is incredibly important," added Madore. "Maine CDC recently said that we are in an endemic wildlife population right now with rabies. So it's incredibly important, even if you don't think your pets are outside that much. It is something that's crucial. Rabies is something that can spread animal to animal or even animal to human."
Madore said that the clinics are typically held in the spring and the fall.
Each January in the state of Maine, every dog must be registered with its municipality. With that, proof of a rabies vaccination is required.

title: Technology is helping older adults age in place. Can Maine take advantage of it?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Aging in Maine is presented by AARP Maine
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
When Peter Carrier fell down his front steps a couple of years ago, he didn’t want to bother anyone.
Carrier, 72, lives alone in his mobile home in Poland. He was headed out to the garage when he slipped and landed on his back. Unhurt and “more embarrassed than anything,” he said it wasn’t worth calling his son.
If something more serious happens, he hopes he can rely on smart technology to make that call for him.
Carrier is one of hundreds of people to receive free smart home devices in the last year amid a push to make Maine a better place to age. Lifelong Maine, one program leading the charge, has installed 606 smart speakers in homes from York to Caribou, focusing on people over the age of 65.
As Maine’s population ages, taking care of its older residents is becoming an increasingly urgent issue. From the stress of rural isolation to a shortage of workers to complicated federal Medicare guidelines, this guide helps Mainers learn about the services, technology and resources available to caregivers and the parents, spouses, neighbors and friends they’re caring for.
As workforce shortages and burnout afflict caregivers across the country, assistive technology is assuming a bigger role in the independence and comfort of older adults. The state has projected there will be nearly 75,000 more Mainers age 65 and older between now and 2032, and 88% of older adults say they want to live and age at home, according to a 2024 AARP survey.
Maine’s age-friendly advocates say adding technology to those plans supports safety, well-being and connections to others.
Within two months of Lifelong Maine’s distribution, 72% of recipients said they felt comfortable using the palm-sized smart speakers, which are called Echo Dots and powered by Amazon’s voice service, Alexa.
Some ask their speaker to play music. Others call family members whose phone numbers they’ve forgotten. When hooked up with smart lightbulbs, the devices can save people a trip to the light switch and reduce their risk of falls.
“If they’re comfortable using the device now, they’re going to be more comfortable using it when they might need it more,” said Patricia Oh, founder of Lifelong Maine’s Echo Dot distribution program.
THE COST OF CONNECTIVITY
While technology is an important solution for aging Mainers, it isn’t infallible. By late 2024, about 9,000 homes and businesses in Maine had no access to internet service or technology of any kind, and hundreds of towns and cities are still underserved, according to the Maine Connectivity Authority, the state’s broadband office.
Those who are connected tread a minefield of scams and the rising use of artificial intelligence.
And cost remains a barrier for Maine’s older adults, more than half of whom are unable to afford basic expenses where they live, according to U.S. Census Bureau data and the ALICE threshold, which is calculated for each county using household income and the cost of food, housing and other needs.
Lani Carlson, director of Maine Community Inclusion through Technology, the state’s federally funded assistive technology program, said it’s important to remember that hiking sticks and cardholders also fall under the umbrella of assistive technology.
“We use it every day,” Carlson said. “Normalizing assistive technology in everyday use is so important because these tools can help us remain independent and live a better quality of life.”
At Maine CITE’s assistive technology lending library in Augusta, Carlson’s team matches patrons with devices that can help with hearing, vision, learning, recreation or daily activities. Some check out a pocket talker, a personal listening device that fits over the ears like headphones and amplifies nearby sound.
Sock pullers are helpful for back and hip issues. There’s even a robotic cat designed to provide companionship and stimulate brain activity in older adults with dementia. It communicates through meows that grow more insistent when it isn’t being pet, then responds to touch by purring and rolling over for belly rubs.
Carlson remembers holding a device demonstration with an older woman who said she was missing out on conversations but “didn’t want to really bother her hearing aid person.”
“She put on a pocket talker, and her eyes lit up,” Carlson said.
The woman returned the pocket talker and had her hearing aids adjusted by the end of the month.
Between 2023 and 2025, annual device loans nearly doubled to 994, which Carlson attributes in part to increased awareness of accessibility after the pandemic. People can browse and order from the library’s online catalog, while in-person device demonstrations are also available at partner sites in Sanford, Bath, Lewiston, Auburn and Farmington. Two new sites are set to open at North Star Pediatric Therapy and the Center for Advancement of Rural Living in Caribou.
It hasn’t all been growth, though. Maine CITE’s partner site in Portland, Spurwink ALLTECH, shuttered last month. Bart Beattie, chief operating officer of the statewide behavioral healthcare provider, said the closure was because of “program sustainability considerations and staffing changes.”
Carlson said it’s a loss for southern Mainers, who may face longer drives to try out devices.
“We’re trying hard to adapt to this change and create new networks and pathways,” Carlson said.
Oh also saw the Echo Dots as an opportunity to fill gaps. She asked volunteers in every corner of the state to identify older community members who needed extra support at home. Hundreds received Echo Dots, smart lightbulbs and smart plugs, which connect household appliances to voice control.
Many have incorporated the devices into routines around the home, from medication reminders to music. Betsey Pace, 78, and Donna Beveridge, 83, ask it about local business hours before they leave their Saco apartment.
But the Echo Dots didn’t work for everybody. Andy Chandler, a South Portland resident with lifelong hearing loss who advocates for assistive technology, said he was unable to hear Alexa’s responses. This year, with his feedback, Oh and her team are matching people who are deaf or hard of hearing with screened Echo Shows, which can provide captions for Alexa.
The smart devices were paid for with a $35,000 grant from the University of New England. Maine CITE’s $510,000 annual budget comes entirely from the federal government, and municipalities with age-friendly programs, like Saco and Lewiston, are increasingly funding their own technology distributions.
BARRIERS TO TECHNOLOGY
Carrier learned that he could receive a free Echo Dot and device training through his Sailing Life Solo group, which meets monthly in Lewiston. He said the group helps get him out of his house: A single-story, rambling space with a wooden rocking chair and walls filled with family photos.
His windows face several neighboring homes, but Carrier hasn’t introduced himself to anyone.
“It gets lonely sometimes,” he said. “I wish the cat would talk, but I have a conversation with her whether she’s listening or not.”
So he drives to Lewiston to meet other people who are aging alone. He texts his best friend. And he goes on Facebook, “where most problems arise.”
Carrier’s savings were depleted last year after he was scammed out of $27,000 by someone he met online. He is now living paycheck to paycheck on Social Security and pension payments. With the exception of a smart watch that he bought for less than $70, the smart devices he uses at home were all gifts or the result of a distribution program like Lewiston’s.
More than 40% of Americans age 50 and older have had money stolen because of fraud, according to a report from AARP. The nonprofit offers cybersecurity workshops and resources to avoid more than 70 types of scams. Chandler, the assistive technology advocate, also delivers in-person presentations on artificial intelligence and fraud at community spaces across Maine.
While urging caution when using the internet, Chandler also can’t help but share his excitement. He spent decades relying on intermediaries to transcribe conversations and relay responses. Today, advances in automatic speech recognition allow him to see live captioning for every phone call, Zoom meeting or TV show he watches.
He can’t wait for the day that smart glasses with live captioning hit the mainstream market.
“Absolutely,” Chandler said, “assistive technology has been my best friend.”
Many are also betting on technology as a solution to loneliness. The Maine Connectivity Authority has provided millions in grants to improve technology access at community centers in Lewiston, Caribou and other underserved areas. The real goal, said Digital Opportunity Senior Manager Jessica Perez, is “social connectivity.”
Then there’s ElliQ, a robotic care companion that just arrived in Maine CITE’s library.
The lamp-shaped robot peppers the user with questions, jokes and requests for conversation, adapting to their personality and needs over time. When Carlson requested a reminder to take her medicine, ElliQ wondered if she’d like a nudge to eat food first.
To hug, the little lamp-shaped robot leaned into Carlson’s hand on its “metallic shoulder.”
The push to embrace technology will only grow with Maine’s older population. Carrier said he wouldn’t mind a robotic companion, but first he wants to learn how to use the devices already in front of him.
He still needs to figure out how to add an emergency contact to his smart watch, so it automatically calls his son if he falls. He’d like to see his best friend’s face when they catch up, for once. And he doesn’t want the dangers of the internet to keep him from connecting with others.
“I’m trying to just keep up,” he said. “I don’t want to get left behind, because I know you’ll miss out on a lot.”

title: Explore the wild backcountry of the Nahmakanta Public Land
text:
Perched comfortably on a shelf of granite just above the shoreline of Sixth Debsconeag Pond, I am both entertained and awed by the brook trout leaping out of the water like little dolphins. Must be something mighty tasty they’re feasting on. My campfire crackles next to me as I chow down on a pouch of backpacker food. The sun behind my back has sunk into the trees, and try as I might to stay awake, I’m thinking it will be an early night in the bag.
Sixth Debsconeag Pond lies at the heart of the Debsconeag Backcountry in the northeast corner of Nahmakanta Public Land, a sprawling 43,000-acre expanse that ranges across four unorganized townships—T1 R12 WELS, T1 R11 WELS, Rainbow Township and T2 R12 WELS—in the northern reaches of Maine’s famed 100-Mile Wilderness. Low but rugged mountains, dense forests and pristine waters characterize this remote region.
The Debsconeag Backcountry Trail threads through this sector of the Nahmakanta for 12 miles, making a figure-eight loop past Fifth, Sixth, Seventh and Eighth Debsconeag ponds as well as one named Stink Pond (I’d love to know the origin of that name, for sure). Several miles along Nahmakanta Lake form the outer portion of the upper loop. Mossy ledge outcrops dot the terrain and offer wonderful views of the wild country all around.
A great horned owl makes its presence known from the woods up along the pond’s northern edge. And although I haven’t noticed loons on Sixth Debsconeag Pond, in the gathering darkness I hear two call from below on Nahmakanta Lake. I stand still for a few moments amid the fragrant spruce trees on the rocky point, nip of bourbon in hand, and just listen and look. Stars begin to populate the inky black sky above. Absolutely perfect.
Tomorrow, I’ll don my ultralight daypack and finish off the rest of the Debsconeag hike before returning to camp, breaking down, and packing out to the trailhead. For now, though, I am happy to simply revel in the quiet of the night, far from any errant noise, light or traffic. No wonder, though, given that I’m situated in the midst of a 9,200-acre roadless area that makes up the lion’s share of 11,800 acres of ecological reserve. This is the place to be.
Nahmakanta Public Land, established in 1990, is a key connector in a nearly continuous corridor of conservation lands stretching from Moosehead Lake to Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument. Owned by the state and managed for multiple uses by the Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands, the Nahmakanta features 35 miles of hiking trails (plus a segment of the Appalachian Trail) and a host of backcountry and roadside campsites.
Along the southern boundary of the Nahmakanta is the Turtle Ridge Trail, another figure-eight loop that meanders over several ridgetops and past a series of pristine ponds for 8 miles. On the southeastern edge is the Tumbledown Dick Trail, which leads past a couple more ponds and to tumbling Tumbledown Dick Falls. The Appalachian Trail winds through the Nahmakanta for 9 miles, along the namesake lake and over Nesuntabunt Mountain.
For a truly grand backpacking adventure, hikers can take to the Great Circle Trail, a 30-mile circuit that meanders through the best of the Nahmakanta terrain. This terrific new route, completed just five years ago after 15 years of trail work, connects several previously existing trails — Tumbledown Dick, the Debsconeag Backcountry Trail, a few miles of the AT, and Turtle Ridge — to several new trail segments, specifically the Pollywog Trail along Pollywog Pond to Wadleigh Pond, the Wadleigh Trail to the top of Wadleigh Mountain, and the Third Musquash Trail.
Tackle the entire Great Circle Trail loop, and you’ll gain more than 3,000 feet of elevation. There are several established campsites along the way, but you can also wild camp (except in the AT corridor), provided you practice the principles of “Leave No Trace.”
Nahmakanta Lake is, of course, the land’s magnificent centerpiece, so some time well spent there admiring its beauty is warranted. Next summer, I think I’ll bring my canoe, camping gear and cooler, and explore the 1,100-acre water body with paddle power. I’ve seen those beautiful beach campsites from high above, after all, and can just picture my camp chair there on the sand, me with cold beer in hand. Good living, that.
Carey Kish of Mount Desert Island is a Triple Crown hiker, freelance writer, and author of three hiking guides. Connect with Carey on Facebook and Instagram and at [email protected].

title: The Mills-Pingree machine crushed small business in Maine. Hannah Pingree will finish the job.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rick Savage, an entrepreneur, former owner and founder of the Sunday River Brewing Company in Bethel, is an advocate for small business rights.
Small business owners in Maine don’t ask for handouts.
We ask for a fair shot, a clear set of rules and a state government that stays off our backs so we can feed our families and employ our neighbors. But under the administration of Gov. Janet Mills (where Hannah Pingree served as a chief architect of policy, as director of the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future), Maine became a hostile environment for independent enterprise.
I know this firsthand. As the former co-owner of Sunday River Brewing Company, I lived through the heavy-handed, punitive overreach of an administration that treated hard-working entrepreneurs not as partners, but as subjects to be controlled.
In the spring of 2020, small businesses across Maine were strung along with moving goalposts and false reopening promises. When it became clear that state officials were operating behind closed doors without accountability, I spoke out. I went on national television and gave out Gov. Mills’ cellphone number so everyday Mainers, the people whose livelihoods were being systematically destroyed, could finally get an answer.
What followed was a targeted campaign of government retaliation.
Rather than working with small business owners trying to safely operate, state regulators moved in. Inspectors from the Department of Health and Human Services and state liquor licensing enforcement targeted my establishment, scrutinizing our operations and stripping our health and liquor licenses to force our doors shut. In my view, state agencies were weaponized to make an example out of anyone who dared to challenge Augusta’s dictates.
Our legal team estimates that the state spent nearly $500,000 in taxpayer resources, deploying state attorneys, inspectors and enforcement officials, just to crush one brewpub in Bethel. While the official court filings reflect a drawn-out legal war over licensing enforcement, the sheer waste of public funds to dismantle a local business tells you everything you need to know about the priorities of the Mills-Pingree administration.
Hannah Pingree cannot distance herself from this legacy. As one of Gov. Mills’ top policy advisers, Pingree sat at the right hand of an administration that oversaw a disastrous business climate. Her office helped shape the economic and regulatory framework that shut down small shops, pushed workers out of state and prioritized government mandates over economic survival.
The economic damage inflicted on Maine wasn’t an accident; it was the direct result of a top-down, central-planning mindset championed by bureaucrats like Pingree. When state government believes it can arbitrarily decide which businesses are “essential” and which are disposable, local economies suffer.
That is why I am standing firmly behind Bobby Charles for governor.
Bobby Charles understands what it takes to confront administrative overreach and dismantle the bureaucratic machine in Augusta.
Unlike the entrenched politicians who view government regulation as the solution to every problem, Bobby recognizes that free enterprise and small business are the lifeblood of Maine’s economy. He has the strength, vision and determination to restore accountability, rein in rogue state agencies and make sure no entrepreneur ever faces the kind of government persecution my family experienced.
Maine cannot afford four more years of the Mills-Pingree agenda. Small business owners are tired of high taxes, red tape and an administrative state that views free enterprise as a threat. We need leadership that respects working Mainers, honors the hard work of local entrepreneurs and stands up for our constitutional rights.
Bobby Charles is the leader Maine needs to close the book on this era of government overreach and rebuild a state where small businesses can actually thrive.

Hiker rescued after falling cactus hits her in the head
text:
SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) — A woman was taken to a trauma center after she was hit on the head by a cactus while hiking in Arizona.
Shortly after 7 a.m., first responders were called to the Bell Pass Trail in the McDowell Mountains after reports of an injured woman. According to the Scottsdale Fire Department, she had been on a trail when a falling cactus hit her on the head.
The fire department said Scottsdale technical rescue found the woman about two miles from the trailhead. Crews used a big wheel and a utility terrain vehicle to get her back safely.
She was then taken to a local trauma center for further evaluation.

title: Zelenskyy urges support for new US sanctions on Russia after Trump puts them on hold
text:
Zelenskyy urges support for new US sanctions on Russia after Trump puts them on hold
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged supporters Saturday to speak out in defense of new U.S. sanctions against Russia, hours after President Donald Trump signed an executive order pausing a sweeping package of restrictions targeting the Russian economy.
Related video above: Trump waives new sanctions on Russia under law named for late Sen. Graham
The White House decision has further raised fears that Ukraine could be left exposed to Moscow’s escalating assaults with winter approaching.
Russian attacks overnight killed at least four people, including an ambulance driver, and wounded dozens, officials said. Ukrainian drones killed a woman in a Russian border region and disrupted flights at Moscow's airports, according to Russian authorities.
In a statement on social media, Zelenskyy described Trump's move to put sanctions on hold as unfortunate but did not directly criticize the U.S. leader despite deepening tensions between Ukraine and Washington in recent days.
“A decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end,” Zelenskyy wrote.
He separately thanked Democrats and Republicans who backed the legislation. He said blocking it would encourage Russia to continue killing, and limiting Ukraine’s ability to retaliate against Russian attacks would not bring peace.
“Nevertheless, we very much hope — and I personally hope — that the president of the United States of America will do everything possible to make (Russian President Vladimir) Putin stop the killing, stop the attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war,” he said.
Asked about contacts with Washington, Zelenskyy said that Ukraine’s lead negotiator, Rustem Umerov, met with U.S. presidential envoy Jared Kushner, who is also Trump's son-in-law, on Friday. He said that the U.S. was working to arrange a trilateral meeting with both him and Putin. He said it could take place in the Middle East, Europe or the U.S.
Critics say Trump's decision helps Putin
Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war against Ukraine. The bill had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.
Trump personally signed the legislation just last month, and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. The president told Congress that the pause was in the national interest but gave no further details.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, who co-drafted the bill, said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on “the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies.”
“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said.
Trump’s unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.
Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”
The decision has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike, who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine — without making a difference to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war on Iran.
Kyiv says Moscow carried out a ‘massive’ energy strike
Zelenskyy also said Saturday that Moscow had carried out a massive strike on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 sites across the country.
“The sheer scale and unrelenting pace of Russia’s strikes, specifically against our energy sector, are unfortunately having severe consequences,” he said.
Ukraine’s air force said that Russian forces launched four cruise missiles and 332 attack drones overnight. All of the missiles and 289 of the drones had been suppressed or destroyed, it said.
Russia’s heavy bombardment of the power grid ahead of winter has been an annual feature of the war, aimed at wearing down Ukraine’s appetite for the fight by denying civilians heat and running water. Ukrainian officials have warned that Russia is stockpiling ballistic missiles for more attacks in the coming months.
Russian attacks killed three people in the Ukrainian city of Sloviansk, Vadym Liakh, head of the city military administration, said Saturday. Writing on social media, Liakh said that two apartment blocks were partially destroyed and other homes damaged.
A Russian strike also killed an ambulance driver in Ukraine’s Kherson region, head of the local military administration Yaroslav Shanko said. The strike, which used guided bombs, injured at least 33 others, he said.
Ukrainian drones kill 1, ground hundreds of flights at Moscow airports
Elsewhere, a Russian woman was killed in a Ukrainian drone attack in the Russian border region of Belgorod, local officials said.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Saturday that its forces had shot down 610 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 Russian regions, as well as the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black Sea.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that more than 100 drones were shot down en route to the Russian capital. More than 350 flights were canceled or delayed at Moscow's airports, local media reported, as planes were grounded in response to incoming drones.
The Kremlin announced Saturday that Russian President Vladimir Putin had approved a government program to help restore trade and logistics facilities damaged in drone attacks.

title: Top runners prevail at KVAC cross country championships
text:
AUGUSTA — There was little drama at the finish line of the Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference cross country championships Saturday. Instead, the conference’s top runners made it look easy.
Bangor’s Sam Bergmark (large school boys), Medomak Valley’s Colby Daigle (small school boys), Hampden Academy’s Addison Elliott (large school girls) and Lincoln Academy’s Karen Higgins (small school girls) won titles at Cony High School. All did so easily, with the average margin of victory between the four coming in at 1 minute, 12.8 seconds.
“It’s very hilly (here), but I enjoy it; I really like the hilly course,” said Higgins, who repeated as KVAC Small School champion. “(The conditions were good); there was only like one spot where it was a little bit slippery, but I’d say since it’s been dry, it’s absorbed it all into the trails, so it was good.”
Hampden (53 points) beat Mt. Blue (84 points) for the KVAC Large boys title, while the Lincoln boys (68) claimed the Small crown over Morse (101). Hampden and Lincoln were the girls teams champions. Hampden (21) had a wide margin over Camden Hills (65), and Lincoln (42) edged Waterville (48).
Donning the No. 1 bib, Bergmark was widely expected to lead the pack and did so, beating Lucas Demarco (17:15.6) of Mt. Blue by 36.6 seconds. Mt. Blue’s Wyatt Oliver (17:33.7), Hampden’s Jack Scott (17:38.6) and Noah Seigh (17:45.8) of Camden Hills rounded out the top five.
“I just wanted to go kind of hard because I didn’t want it to be a race — I just wanted to win,” said Bergmark, who placed third in the KVAC race year and won the Class A North title. “I just wanted to see how things were going to go, and once we got on the gravel, I went at my own speed.
Daigle’s margin of victory was even larger. The senior’s time of 17:36.9 was more than a minute faster than Cony’s Brady Cloutier (18:37.4). Lincoln’s Holden Nehrboss (18:45.4), Erskine Academy’s Brayden Dow (18:48.1) and Gardiner’s Abrahm Hasty (19:01.7) also earned top-five finishes.
Elliott and Higgins were way out in front of the girls field. Elliott’s winning time of 18:39.0 beat teammate Isabelle Clark by 1:50.2. Also finishing in the top five in the Large division were Charlotte Crowe of Mt. Ararat (20:35.9), Elsie Mann of Camden Hills (20:38.3) and Emeline Cournane of Hampden (20:43.8).
Hampden claimed its third consecutive team title. In addition to Elliott, Clark and Cournane, Silvia Ruge (21:18.6) finished sixth, Mackenzie Elliott (21:24.5) took seventh, Erin Curtis (22:18.0) placed 11th and Aubrey Shaw (22:21.3) was 12th.
“I’m just so proud of our girls,” Elliott said. “We keep getting better, and I think we ran really, really well today. I think that shared energy between (us) really fed into how we did today. … I thought (the course) was going to be really muddy and uneven, but except for the start, it was great.”
Higgins’ time of 18:56.9 was nearly a minute and a half ahead of the runner-up in the Small divison, Frida Wright of Morse (21:21.8). Hallie Coots of Nokomis (21:32.5) placed third, Carson Dunn of Waterville (21:42.6) claimed fourth, and August Miller of Lincoln (22:06.5) finished fifth.
Although the Large and Small divisions were scored separately, runners competed in the same race, creating an interesting dynamic. Elliott and Higgins were neck-and-neck for a while. It wasn’t until midway through the race that Elliott began to separate herself from Higgins, who said that going head-to-head with one of the state’s best runners was a good springboard to regionals and states.
“It was nice to have her with me, because that definitely pushed me to go under 19,” Higgins said. “Running with her, at least for the first bit, that was fun. … I think Twin Brook (next Saturday for the Class B South regional) is going to feel a bit easier compared to this.”

title: Only thing ‘crystal clear’ on Navatek allegations is Collins’ innocence
text:
An Oct. 1 report insinuated Sen. Susan Collins’ guilt in a campaign finance scheme (“The laws tied to the Susan Collins-Navatek allegations are ‘crystal clear.’ Enforcing them is another matter.”). There is no guilt; I know this because my agency investigated it.
As a commissioner on the Federal Election Commission, we investigated Navatek in 2021 in coordination with the Department of Justice. After three years, the FEC fined the company $325,000, and the Biden Justice Department convicted the CEO in 2022.
Our investigators found “no information in the factual record” that Sen. Collins or her campaign knowingly took illegal money. We dismissed every potential violation against the super PAC supporting her. And the DOJ made no attempt to charge the Collins campaign.
The idea that the FBI was still pursuing Collins in 2025 is not credible. The conduct happened in 2019, and prosecutors had five years to bring charges.
What remains is a convicted felon’s self-serving story. Recycling his claims before Election Day is not news. It’s a political hit.
Sean Cooksey
Former FEC Commissioner (2021-2025)
Washington, D.C.

title: UNE football easily beats MMA for 1st win of season
text:
The University of New England rushed for 399 yards and rolled to a 62-14 win over Maine Maritime Academy in a college football game Saturday in Biddeford.
Damien Jones rushed six times for 95 yards and two touchdowns, while Nathan Delgado had 84 yards and two TDs for UNE (1-5, 1-2 Conference of New England). Gavin Martin added 81 yards and a score.
Jack Lambert completed 4 of 5 passes for 63 yards and a touchdown.
Harris Stone threw for 176 yards, a touchdown and an interception for MMA (0-6, 0-3). Auston Harris had 119 yards and a touchdown on 12 carries.
HUSSON 42, NEW ENGLAND COLLEGE 0: Daniel Ruiz Cantu rushed for 157 yards and three touchdowns, and the Eagles (2-4, 2-1 CNE) earned their second straight victory, beating the Pilgrims (1-5, 0-3) in Henniker, New Hampshire.
Anthony Santacroce added 87 yards rushing and two touchdowns, while Brody Gibson completed 11 of 15 passes for 106 yards and a score.
The Eagles held NEC to five first downs and 71 yards.
AMHERST 21, COLBY 15: Marek Hill thew a 4-yard touchdown pass to Michael Dunmore with 24 seconds left, and the Mammonths (5-0) beat the Mules (0-4) in a NESCAC game in Waterville.
Hill also scored on a 1-yard run in the fourth quarter to pull Amherst within 15-13.
Colby went up 5-0 in the first quarter on a 42-yard field goal by Avi Gotshalk and a safety. The Mules pushed it to 12-0 on a 12-yard pass from Jack Matera to Jack Nye in the second quarter. Hill scored on a 3-yard run later in the quarter, but Gotshalk kicked a 22-yard field goal with five seconds left.
HAMILTON 26, BOWDOIN 7: The Continentals (1-4) jumped out to a 17-point lead and beat the Bobcats (0-5) in Brunswick.
Connor Laverty scored a pair of touchdowns in the first quarter and Carmelo Velardo kicked a 38-yard field goal in the first half. Velardo added field goals of 32, 27 and 37 yards in the second half.
Michael Wolfendale caught a 23-yard touchdown pass from Soren Hummel in the third quarter for Bowdoin.
WESLEYAN 34, BATES 8: The Cardinals (5-0) held the Bobcats (0-5) to 142 yards in a win in Middletown, Connecticut.
Matt Fitzsimons completed 19 of 33 passes for 243 yards and a touchdown for Wesleyan. Matt Diaz rushed 20 times for 105 yards and two scores.
Ryan Foley scored on a 6-yard run in the fourth quarter for Bates.

title: Woman previously convicted of killing husband arrested again on new charge
text:
EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE/Gray News) — A 58-year-old Indiana woman with a reckless homicide conviction is facing a new charge after deputies said she was found intoxicated and parked in the middle of a street early Monday.
Wendy Payne was booked just after midnight Monday on a charge of driving while intoxicated. She was held on a $2,500 bond.
Deputies describe scene
Vanderburgh County deputies said they found Payne parked in the middle of Van Ness Avenue, near Kedzie Avenue, on the west side.
Deputies said Payne was so intoxicated she nearly fell several times. She allegedly told them she had been drinking at Leroy’s Tavern.
At the jail, deputies say a breath test showed Payne’s blood alcohol content was 0.228, nearly three times the legal limit.
Authorities said Payne was convicted of driving while intoxicated in Henderson in July.
Prior conviction in Evansville
Payne was also found guilty of reckless homicide in 2021 after stabbing her husband, Edward, to death in 2019 at their Glenview Drive home.
Payne was sentenced to five years in prison, but had credit for time served. Several people testified on her behalf at the sentencing hearing.

title: 71-year-old man killed by 12-foot alligator while fishing alongside lake
text:
(AP) - A 71-year-old man fishing on the shore of a Florida lake was killed Friday by a nearly 12-foot alligator, the second fatal attack reported this year.
Steven Hamilton of Winter Garden was standing on the shore of Lake Apopka at Dr. Bradford Memorial Park, 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Orlando, when he was attacked around 5 p.m., the Winter Garden Police Department said.
The presence of other active alligators in the water complicated any chance of rescuing Hamilton, whose body was recovered about two hours later, Winter Garden Fire Chief Jose Gainza told FOX35.
Police Capt. Michael Mason said authorities were not alerted in advance that an alligator was near the lake’s shore, possibly because it “has tons of alligators in it.” He said police launched a joint investigation with the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission, whose trappers captured and killed the alligator.
Mason reminded people to be aware of their surroundings and respect wildlife.
“Keep your distance,” he said. “It looks like it’s docile, it looks like your Florida emblem, but it can be dangerous.”
After a 31-year-old Oviedo woman, Brittany Clark, was killed by a 13-foot alligator near her home in June, Republican U.S. Rep. Greg Steube introduced a resolution calling for the Comptroller General and U.S. Department of the Interior to study the impacts of the American alligator’s listing as “threatened due to similarity of appearance” on Florida’s ability to remove nuisance alligators from residential and commercial waterways.
He said the species has been fully recovered since 1987 but remains protected to prevent trafficking and hunting of the similar-looking American crocodile.
Using Florida state data, the two 2026 deaths bring the total number of individuals killed by alligators since 1948 to 34. Among them were a 61-year-old woman tipped out of her canoe by an alligator in 2025 and an 85-year-old widow who was dragged out of her backyard by an alligator while walking her dog in 2023.

title: Need help caring for an older Mainer? Start here
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Caring for an aging Mainer can be overwhelming, but you don’t have to navigate it alone.
From respite care and transportation to counseling and legal help, a range of resources is available to support older Mainers and the family members and friends caring for them.
Here are some key agencies in each county and a look at what they offer.
ANDROSCOGGIN, FRANKLIN AND OXFORD COUNTIES
SeniorsPlus is based in Lewiston and has satellite offices in Norway and Wilton.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Care coordination (connecting people with home care services from respite to in-home community service (assistance with living independently)
- Fiscal intermediary services for clients with long-term care needs (handling employer and employee paperwork, payroll, tax filings and workers’ compensation coverage)
- Nutrition services (access to the Meals on Wheels meal delivery program, social dining opportunities and restaurant vouchers that offer reduced prices at participating locations)
- Specialized services (coordination of emergency response systems, respite in a facility, environmental modification and assistive technology).
Connect at seniorsplus.org and 207-795-4010.
AROOSTOOK COUNTY
Aroostook Agency on Aging, based in Presque Isle, serves older people in northern Maine.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Home care personal support (in-home help with daily activities)
- MaineCare in-home services, care partner education and support
- Volunteer programs and the Money Minders program (free bill-paying service where trained volunteers can help with setting up a budget, paying bills and managing a checkbook).
- MaineCare Toolkit which provides help with navigating community MaineCare or MaineCare in-home services applications and securing financial assistance for them.
Connect at aroostookaging.org and 207-764-3396.
For transportation needs, head to aroostooktransportation.org to access Aroostook Regional Transportation, which helps people throughout Aroostook County get to appointments, shop and stay active in their community.
CUMBERLAND AND YORK COUNTIES
Southern Maine Agency on Aging provides resources, services and information to empower adults, adults with disabilities and their caregivers.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Information for older Mainers about day programs, nutrition (including the Meals on Wheels meal delivery program) and fall prevention
- Medicare counseling
- Money Minders (help with money management/bill paying)
- Phone Pal program, which pairs volunteers who will call 1-3 times a week for friendly conversations
- Resources for assistance with caregiving, including information on benefit programs, adult day programming and community resources
- Classes are offered on topics such as caring for someone with dementia, finding community resources, stress management and problem solving
- Southern Maine Agency on Aging’s State Respite Care Program supports family caregivers of people with dementia, and in some cases the program reimburses some of the cost for someone else to provide care
- Regularly scheduled support groups take place at the Biddeford office, and in the community to help connect caregivers with one another
Connect at smaaa.org and 207-396-6500.
HANCOCK, PENOBSCOT, PISCATAQUIS AND WASHINGTON COUNTIES
Eastern Area Agency on Aging, based in Brewer, provides information, options and services for older adults, adults with disabilities and caregivers.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Family Caregiver Program (information and assistance, respite program and support groups)
- Commodity Supplemental Food Program (30-pound monthly food boxes with shelf stable grocery items and cheese available to low-income adults 60 years or older)
- Legal services for Maine elders, Medicare counseling, Meals on Wheels (meal delivery program)
- Money Minders (help with money management/bill paying).
Connect at eaaa.org and 207-941-2865.
KENNEBEC, KNOX, LINCOLN, SAGADAHOC, SOMERSET AND WALDO COUNTIES
Spectrum Generations is based in Augusta, and also has offices in Waterville, Damariscotta, Belfast, Hallowell and Brunswick.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- We Sustain Maine (locally grown food provided from Maine farms)
- Meals on Wheels (meal delivery program)
- MaineCare services (assistance with arranging home care programs)
- Money Minders (help with money management/bill paying)
- Caregiving services (support groups, adult day programs, state respite care program).
Spectrum Generations also covers Brunswick and Harpswell in Cumberland County.
Connect at spectrumgenerations.org and 800-639-1553.
OTHER RESOURCES
- Legal Services for Maine Elders is based in Augusta. Its mission is to protect the rights of older Mainers by providing free legal services to people ages 60 and older. They also advocate for people facing challenges when accessing Medicare benefits. Connect at maineelse.org and 207-623-1797.
- Office of Aging and Disability Services supports Maine’s older population by promoting the highest level of independence, health and safety throughout Maine. They oversee several programs for older adults, including long-term care programs. Connect at maine.gov/dhhs/oads and 207-287-9200.
- Maine Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program provides free, confidential advocacy for people receiving long-term care services and their families. The program investigates complaints and helps consumers understand their rights and options when problems arise with nursing homes, assisted living, home care, hospice and other services. Staff can also answer questions about finding and paying for care, and what to do if services are denied, reduced or terminated. Connect at maineombudsman.org and 207-621-1079.
- The Iris Network is a Portland-based nonprofit that helps Mainers who are blind or have low vision live independently. Services include low-vision evaluations and rehabilitation, mobility and orientation training, adaptive technology and help with everyday tasks. The organization serves people of all ages, including older adults experiencing age-related vision loss. Connect at theiris.org and 207-774-6273.

title: Troy Jackson rallies with Dropkick Murphys as Senate campaign enters final stretch

text:
Troy Jackson rallies with Dropkick Murphys as Senate campaign enters final stretch
Concerts and speeches were a part of Maine AFL-CIO's 'Rally for the Working Class'
Troy Jackson rallies with Dropkick Murphys as Senate campaign enters final stretch
Concerts and speeches were a part of Maine AFL-CIO's 'Rally for the Working Class'
With the debates behind them, Maine’s candidates for U.S. Senate have a little more than 2 weeks to make their final case to voters before Election Day on Nov. 3.
Democrat Troy Jackson spent Friday night with some Boston musical royalty, joining the Dropkick Murphys at the "Rally for the Working Class" in Biddeford hosted by the Maine AFL-CIO.
The band played an acoustic set for the crowd at The Foundry. Before the performance,  attendees heard from union workers, including a nurse from Central Maine Medical Center.  Nurses at the hospital recently joined the Maine Nurses Union. Every speaker called for more union voices in the U.S. Senate.
"We need to stand up to corporate greed. We need to place people like you and me in a position where they can speak for us," said nurse Katie Grinell. "The biggest changes have been accomplished when people stand together. We need to stand together and fight for a better tomorrow. We're building a movement. It's time we stand up, fight back and let corporate greed know that we are not for sale."
Jackson’s push continues this weekend with town halls and get-out-the-vote events alongside Massachusetts Democratic Sen. Elizabeth Warren.

title: Mom hunts ‘once-in-a-lifetime’ moose 4 days after C-section birth
text:
BEULAH, N.D. (KFYR/Gray News) — A North Dakota family has a hunting story and a photo to go with it after Shayla Beckler shot a moose four days after giving birth to her daughter, Stella.
Stella was born weighing 6 pounds, 12 ounces.
“She is the best baby, just happy as can be all the time,” Shayla Beckler said.
A once-in-a-lifetime tag
Shayla Beckler, of Beulah, shot the moose on opening day of rifle season.
She had a C-section earlier this month on Monday, went home from the hospital on Wednesday and was hunting by Friday.
“It’s a once-in-a-lifetime tag,” Shayla Beckler said. “There was no way I was giving it up.”
Shayla Beckler, her husband Jacob and her brothers spent weeks tracking the moose. She had hoped to get the moose during archery season, but missed her shot.
“I hadn’t bow hunted in 10 years,” Shayla Beckler said. “We got pretty close, and when I got set up for the shot, I missed.”
“It was awesome,” Shayla Beckler said of the rifle season hunt.
Dad on baby duty
Jacob Beckler stayed in the truck with Stella during the hunt, keeping her warm while keeping an eye on his wife.
“I know she’s a strong woman who would make anything work,” Jacob Beckler said.
Shayla Beckler said getting a photo of Stella was part of her motivation to fill the tag.
“The No. 1 thing I want is a picture of Stella with her stuffed moose on the moose, and she fit perfectly right on the antlers,” Shayla Beckler said.
The family will process the moose meat themselves, Shayla Beckler said, and Stella will be there for that too.
Jacob Beckler said he is a little jealous of his wife’s harvest. He has applied for moose tags for years and has never been drawn.
Stella’s older brother, Bryson, missed the hunt because of a football game.

title: Trump puts new Russia sanctions that he recently signed into law on hold, citing national interest
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest.
Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. It drew shift condemnation from congressional Democrats.
Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.
Trump’s unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.
An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president’s handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump’s approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress after midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Sanctions were seen as part of Graham’s legacy
Graham, a close ally and friend of the president, had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. He had advocated for stricter U.S. sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine.
His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation — then changed his mind Friday.
The package had been meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbor more than four years ago. The bill, also drafted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.
It also directed Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Blumenthal said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on “the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies.”
“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said.
Democratic Virginia Rep. Don Beyer noted on social media shortly after the announcement of the sanctions being suspended that he and others had “warned” Trump might make such a move. The veteran congressman, who spoke out against the bill as it was debated, called on Congress to “fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine.”
The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest. The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress.
Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, had remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large majorities in the House and Senate following Graham’s sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy.
Trump’s action follows announced diesel deal with Putin
Under last week’s agreement, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”
Trump’s striking a diesel deal with Putin has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine -- without making a different to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war on Iran.
The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centerpiece for Sen. Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term. She is now running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.
Darline Graham said in a statement after Trump signed the bill, “I wish Lindsey were here to celebrate this historic day.” In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham — who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week — said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed.
She acknowledged, however, that it was the president’s purview as to how he implemented it.
“It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.”

title: ‘Tragedy’: 1 child, 1 adult killed after vehicle drives into soccer game at sports complex, police say
text:
WICHITA, Kan. (KWCH/Gray News) - Two people were killed, and several other people were hurt when a truck drove through a soccer game at the Stryker Sports Complex in east Wichita, Kansas.
Wichita police said a 6-year-old boy and a 35-year-old man, both from McPherson, died Saturday afternoon.
The two were not related, police said.
Eleven other people were taken to the hospital with traumatic injuries. They include a 5-year-old girl, a 5-year-old boy, two 8-year-old boys, a 9-year-old girl, a 28-year-old woman, a 32-year-old man, a 59-year-old woman, a 65-year-old woman and a 68-year-old man. A 61-year-old woman was taken to the hospital for medical, non-traumatic treatment.
Wichita Police Capt. Aaron Moses said the driver of the truck is a 34-year-old woman from Garden City. She is currently police custody.
Two girls who were in the car with her at the time of the deadly accident. He would not say what happened to the children or where they are now.
Moses said the woman had a child playing soccer at Stryker but not on the field where the deadly crash occurred. He also said she had a valid driver’s license. Now, police are working to determine how and why the crash occurred.
Anyone with information is asked to call WPD Investigations at 316-268-4407, Crime Stoppers at 316-267-2111 or 911.
This is a developing story.

title: Women of Maine, your vote is not a Valentine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maria Padian is a novelist and freelance writer who lives in Brunswick. She has previously worked as a news reporter and a congressional press secretary.
Something surprised me this month as I’ve been knocking on doors and doing some political canvassing: There are a lot of older women who plan to vote for both Hannah Pingree and Sen. Susan Collins.
As a Medicare-eligible female myself, I’ll confess: this struck me as some profound cognitive dissonance; these two candidates are very different. But despite my impulse to exclaim, “Seriously?” at my fellow women of a certain age, I remembered that good canvassing includes listening. So I asked them to … explain.
Their reasons were remarkably personal.
Regarding Pingree, a Democrat running for governor in Maine, many said, “Oh, I love Hannah.” Like she’s the smart daughter we’re super proud of.
Regarding Collins, the five-term incumbent Republican running for U.S. Senate, they spoke as if she were a trusted friend or sister. “She saved my job,” one said. “She understands us,” said another. “She’s a real Mainer.”
Here’s the thing: those gals have been voting for Collins for decades. They hold fast to the Susan they knew 20-plus years ago, who molded herself as a moderate. It didn’t matter if I pointed out that the current Susan has abandoned those moderate impulses. That today’s Susan votes with President Trump 96% of the time and marches lock-step with the MAGA-aligned values of a GOP that past Maine Republican women like Margaret Chase Smith would not recognize today.
I realized I wasn’t going to change their minds at the front stoop. But I did say this: Your vote is not a Valentine. It’s a calculated chess move.
Because in the game we’re playing right now, “our senator” (that’s the logo on the Collins’ campaign bus) is no friend. She’s no sister. She’s no powerful chess queen, wielding her influence as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Instead, she’s played the past two years like an ineffective pawn. And her repeated caving to Trump has hurt Maine.
Someone who understands Mainers would know that bombing Iran would disrupt world oil prices and leave us out in the cold. So this winter, thank Susan Collins when we pay 75% more for heating oil. She voted repeatedly to support this now-forever war, back when Trump called it a military “action” that would last six weeks. Decades worth of past presidents from both parties knew better. Collins knew better.
Someone who cares about Maine jobs and Mainers’ health wouldn’t support Trump’s “big,
beautiful bill,” which Collins voted to advance. 
That bill’s devastating Medicaid cuts will not only shutter hundreds of hospitals nationwide, it’s projected to eliminate Medicaid for 31,000 Mainers and, according to the Maine Center for Economic Policy, might close four hospitals in Maine, resulting in the loss of tens of million in wages.
Speaking of health: measles is back. It was declared “eliminated” in U.S. in 2000, but so far this year we’re at more than 4,000 cases. All thanks to the anti-vaccination misinformation spread by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whom “our senator” voted to confirm.
With all due respect to my fellow senior women: chess, like democracy, is a long game. And sometimes, winning requires being strategic — and retiring a piece.

title: High schools Saturday: Gorham football slips past Scarborough
text:
Isaac Vail returned a kickoff 71 yards with just over a minute remaining, setting up his 11-yard touchdown reception that gave Gorham a 28-21 win over Scarborough in a Class A South football game Saturday in Gorham.

York’s Ava Hickey made 16 saves.

Vivienne Provencher, Emmaline Ellison and Emelia Michaud were the other goal scorers.

title: High school football team’s season canceled as police investigate multiple serious reports
text:
ST. LOUIS. (KMOV/Gray News) - A St. Louis football team’s season was canceled as police investigate “inappropriate behavior.”
In a statement Friday, Saint Louis Public Schools announced it canceled the Clyde C. Miller/Sumner co-op football team’s remaining season.
The district said it canceled the season after reports of “seriously inappropriate behavioral and physical conduct involving students” associated with the team."
Officials said the police department received complaints from multiple people on Thursday, the day before the announcement.
St. Louis Metropolitan Police confirmed that it is in the early stages of the investigation, which primarily involves the student-athletes.
The district says its leadership is working to connect students who may have been impacted and their families with resources and to address safety concerns.
Authorities did not answer questions about the complaints or investigation.

title: Oxford Hills football shuts out Portland for big Class A North win
text:
SOUTH PARIS — The Oxford Hills football team needed to bounce back after a blowout loss to Bonny Eagle last week.
The Vikings did in a big way, dominating defending Class A North champion Portland 29-0 on Saturday afternoon.
“We knew it was just a bad night for us at Bonny Eagle and we just had to get past it and keep moving forward, ” Oxford Hills quarter Toby Oufiero said of the Vikings’ 45-6 loss to the Scots on Oct. 9. “Work hard this week, which we did. Came out here and put up a good fight and won.”
Oufiero had a touchdown pass and ran for a touchdown to lift the Vikings past the Bulldogs, who are ranked fifth in the Varsity Maine poll. The win moves the Vikings (5-1) into first place in Class A North, a position they will try to solidify in the final two games against Noble and Bangor.
Portland drops to second at 5-2.
“We just got to keep battling,” Oufiero said. “It’s not over yet, and hard work every day.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
Oxford Hills took the lead on a 4-yard rushing touchdown by Keegan Ridley in the second quarter and stretched it to 15-0 when Tucker Hilden took a shovel pass from Oufiero into the end zone from 3 yards out with 49 seconds left in the first half.
Portland struggled to sustain anything offensively. Oxford Hills pulled away in the second half with a 1-yard rushing touchdown by Oufiero and a 45-yard run by Carter Davis.
UNSUNG HERO
Mason Ridley was a playmaker throughout. He caught a 2-point conversion pass in the second quarter, was a factor defensively, and racked up yards as a punt returner.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “Having only 27 guys on the team, it’s tough to, when you face teams like Bonny Eagle, when you face teams like Portland with (Alex Martin), to simulate the speed and the strength of their lines and stuff like that, so we really worked hard on just mentally being prepared.” — Oxford Hills coach Nate Danforth
• “Play a great team, you get better from that. That’s always a positive, right? Iron sharpens iron, especially in the regular season. So we’re grateful to have this experience. There’s a lot of positives we’re going to pull from it and a lot of teachable moments we’re going to pull from it.” — Portland coach Dylan Rottkov
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Oxford Hills: Toby Oufiero (8 of 13 passing, 62 yards, touchdown; 13 rushes, 55 yards, touchdown), Keegan Ridley (eight rushes, 38 yards, touchdown; two interceptions)
• Portland: Alex Martin (23 carries, 75 yards)

Maine Tech Week returns to Portland next week, bringing together entrepreneurs, researchers and industry leaders to explore how technology is shaping the state's future.

title: University official dies in freak accident while on walking tour at historic landmark
text:
SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A senior leader of a Brazilian university died Friday afternoon in what is being called a freak accident while on a walking tour of Frank Lloyd Wright’s historic Taliesin West home in Scottsdale.
According to the Scottsdale Fire Department, Rogério Renato Mateucci, rector of the Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná, was struck by roofing material dislodged by strong winds.
Mateucci was said to be with a group on a walking tour at the late architect’s home when he was hit.
Fire officials said Mateucci, only identified as a Brazilian tourist by crews, died instantly and was pronounced dead at the scene.
No foul play was suspected. Police said they are investigating the death as a weather-related accident.
The National Weather Service reported east winds of 22 mph in Scottsdale around 2 p.m. Friday, with gusts up to 32 mph.
Taliesin West was closed to the public until further notice following Mateucci’s death.
“The Foundation extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of the individual,” the foundation’s CEO Joe Spector said in a statement.
The historic home, built in 1937, served as Wright’s winter home and desert laboratory in the foothills of the McDowell Mountains. It is now a National Historic Landmark and home to the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation.
In an Instagram post, the university said classes will be canceled Saturday and Monday, and administrative offices will be closed Monday, to mourn its highest-ranking official.

title: ‘Itchiest bite’: Tick-borne syndrome leaves woman allergic to red meat
text:
ROSS TOWNSHIP, Pa. (KDKA) — A Pennsylvania woman is sharing her experience with a rare and potentially deadly tick-borne disease.
Angela Lundy was bitten by a tick over the summer and is now allergic to red meat.
“It was the itchiest bite I had ever had,” Lundy said.
Her sickness developed after she ate a bratwurst, a German sausage link.
After speaking with a doctor, Lundy was diagnosed with alpha-gal syndrome.
“I woke up with severe stomach pain right along where my bra line is, and it lasted about three hours,” Lundy said.
Lundy is now carrying an EpiPen as an extra precaution.
According to the CDC, alpha-gal can cause an allergy to meats like beef, pork and venison. About 300 people test positive for the tick-borne disease each year.
The best prevention is to spray DEET or wash clothes with specialized bug-repellent detergent.

title: Suspected midcoast drug deal leads to discovery of starving dogs
text:
A man was charged Thursday night, Oct. 15 with possession of a firearm by a prohibited person.
When officers went to the home where the gun was located, officers found two caged dogs who were malnourished to the point that the outlines of their bones were visible.
Seth Young, 28, of Camden was only initially charged with the gun offense. But an affidavit filed by the Knox County Sheriff’s Office said it is gathering evidence on the situation with the dogs.
A deputy first spotted Young as a passenger in a car at Andes Variety in Warren. The officer suspected a drug deal was occurring and spoke to the driver and Young. When the officer informed Young he was going to conduct a check of his residence, which is allowed under terms of probation, Young said the officer would find a gun in his bedroom.
When officers went to the home, there were two dogs, each in its own cage. The cages were filled with feces and feces was throughout the house. One of the dogs had a sore.
Young is being held on a probation hold. Judge John Martin set bail on the weapon charge at $2,500 cash during a brief initial appearance held via Zoom in the state court in Knox County.

title: Maine Trust for Local News wins more than 100 awards at annual press contest
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Trust for Local News, the state’s largest news organization, won more than 100 combined awards at an annual ceremony hosted Saturday by the Maine Press Association.
The Maine Trust, the parent company of the Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram, the Sun Journal in Lewiston, Kennebec Journal in Augusta and Morning Sentinel in Waterville, won top awards in a number of general categories. For general excellence among daily/weekend newspapers, the Sun Journal won first place, followed by the Kennebec Journal in second and the Bangor Daily News in third.
The Portland Press Herald won first place for general excellence in advertising, followed by the Sun Journal in second and Central Maine Sunday in third.
For general excellence in digital, the Portland Press Herald’s website, pressherald.com, won first place. Placing second in digital was the Maine Monitor’s website, themainemonitor.org, and third was Centralmaine.com, the website of the Kennebec Journal and Morning Sentinel.
Allison McCann, vice president of advertising and business development for the Maine Trust for Local News, was selected as “Businessperson of the Year.” The award recognizes an employee on the business side of a news organization whose work has been distinguished over a period of time.
“I’ve worked alongside Alli for more than a decade, and I can say without hesitation that I wouldn’t want to do this work without her,” said Stefanie Manning, president and publisher of the Maine Trust for Local News. “She understands our business, believes deeply in what we do and brings an incredible amount of energy, creativity and determination to making us successful. When Alli is in the room, I know our interests are well represented. She’s a trusted partner, a strong leader and someone who genuinely cares about the people she works with. This recognition is so well deserved, and I couldn’t be happier for her.”
In addition, Melissa Pritchard, who retired recently as the longtime creative services director at the Maine Trust, was selected as the “Mentor of the Year.” The award honors an employee who has offered support, encouragement or advice that has helped others in their organization grow or achieve in the news industry.
“It was an exceptional year of journalism across Maine,” Executive Editor Carolyn Fox said. “Congratulations to our company recipients on the well-deserved recognition as well as the rest of the MPA winners.”
The press association’s conference and awards ceremony was held at the DoubleTree by Hilton Hotel in Portland, and also featured a Hall of Fame induction ceremony for three former Maine Trust journalists.
JOURNALISM HONORS
The Press Herald won 56 individual awards, including 26 first-place wins.
Among some of the journalists recognized with top awards was Kelley Bouchard, for news coverage exploring how a Maine couple gave their $1.3 million retirement savings to bitcoin scammers; Drew Bonifant, for a sports news story examining why concussions are high in girls soccer; and Megan Gray, for an outdoors story describing the 250-mile Can-Am Crown International Sled Dog Races in Aroostook County.
Gregory Rec, chief photographer for the Press Herald, won the “Best in Show” photography award for his Dec. 30, 2025, photo of Dillon Gray of Mt. Blue taking down Brady Ouellette of Noble during the Noble Wrestling Invitational at Noble High School in Berwick.
For the second year in a row, Press Herald columnists Travis Lazarczyk and Leslie Bridgers also won top honors for their columns about sports and culture, respectively.
The Sun Journal had 17 individual awards, including five first-place wins. Some of the top awards went to Matthew Jaroncyk, for a spot news story about Lewiston residents cleaning up after a destructive water main break; and Rose Lincoln, for a lifestyle feature story about a Newry man who keeps game from going to waste for hunters who can’t cool their own meat before its processed.
The Kennebec Journal and Morning Sentinel had 21 individual awards, including five first-place awards. Top winners included Joe Phelan, for an online news video that goes behind the scenes at Brownville’s food pantry for deer; and Anna Chadwick, who had best spot news photo for the scene after a home explosion and best people photo from a dress rehearsal for “The Nutcracker.”
HALL OF FAME
The Maine Press Association also inducted three veteran journalists — Andy Molloy, Mike Lowe and Tux Turkel — into its Hall of Fame during a luncheon. The association said the three honorees made lasting contributions to Maine journalism through photojournalism, sports reporting and enterprise coverage, reflecting a shared commitment to accuracy and informing their communities.
Molloy spent 30 years as a photojournalist at the Kennebec Journal in Augusta, earning recognition for his news instincts, compelling images and deep connections throughout central Maine. Molloy, who died this spring at 57 after a decade-long battle with a rare form of cancer, was also an accomplished journalist who frequently broke news and developed sources across the region. Beyond his journalism, Molloy was remembered for mentoring colleagues and providing practical and personal support to fellow journalists and community members facing difficult circumstances.
Lowe spent four decades covering sports for the Portland Press Herald and Maine Sunday Telegram, where his work ranged from major national and international events to high school championships across Maine. During his career, which began in 1982 and ended with his retirement in 2022, Lowe covered seven Super Bowls, the Portland Pirates’ Calder Cup championship run, the Little League World Series and the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing. He also produced enterprise and investigative reporting on issues including concussions, the cost of youth sports, depression among athletes and race in Maine sports. His work earned numerous honors, including four Maine Sports Writer of the Year awards from the National Sports Media Association.
Tux Turkel retired from the Portland Press Herald in 2023 after more than 40 years covering energy, environmental and utility issues, building a reputation for explaining complex subjects and holding powerful institutions accountable. His reporting examined some of Maine’s most consequential energy debates, including the closure of the Maine Yankee Nuclear Power Plant, radioactive waste storage, offshore wind development, the Central Maine Power and Hydro-Québec transmission corridor and the state’s persistently high electricity costs. Turkel became known for digging through public records and regulatory filings, scrutinizing official explanations and seeking independent experts to put technical information into context. He continues to report as a freelance journalist, including for The Maine Monitor.

title: Police respond to 'mass casualty incident' at Kansas sports complex
text:
2 killed, multiple injured after vehicle drives onto field during soccer game at Wichita sports complex
A child and an adult were killed and multiple others were injured when a vehicle drove onto a field during a youth soccer game in Wichita, Kansas, on Saturday, authorities said.
The driver of the vehicle is in custody and “there is no additional ongoing threat to the public from that driver,” said Aaron Moses of the Wichita Police Department.
Two “juveniles” were inside the vehicle when it drove through Stryker Sports Complex around 3:25 p.m. local time, Moses said. The vehicle remained at the scene, he added.
“This is a tragedy,” Moses told reporters outside the complex.
An attendee told the station he was with his family when a black pickup truck jumped the curb and drove onto the field. Two witnesses also described hearing a loud noise at the time.
Vanessa Trammell was at her 13-year-old son’s soccer game nearby when she saw the truck drive across the neighboring field, striking several people, she told CNN.
Video below: Officials speak after two were killed when a vehicle drove through a youth soccer game
“We thought it was going to stop, but then it like kept going,” she said.
Her son’s soccer game had just ended, and the team was in a huddle on the sidelines of the field when she said the truck drove near the sidelines.
The incident drew a large law enforcement response to the soccer field, which is fenced off and has a concrete runway leading to a parking lot, KWCH reported. It’s not yet clear how the vehicle breached the gate or how fast it was driving, Moses said.
Children were gathered in their red sports uniforms by emergency vehicles and yellow police tape at the scene, video shows.
The incident shocked families and children at the field as dozens of first responders swarmed the scene.
“It was pure panic,” Trammell said. “I didn’t know what was going on – just that people were being hit. I’m pretty sure I probably screamed, but absolutely, just pure panic was going through me.”
Younger children play at the soccer fields in the complex, including the one where the truck came barreling through, Trammell said.
“I don’t know if people tried to stop it or what happened. I was a little more focused on the chaos and trying to find my son first,” Trammell said, adding that her son’s coach then ran towards the area to help victims before the paramedics arrived on site.
Those killed have not been identified. Officials are working to notify family members of the victims and are not yet releasing their ages, Moses said. It’s unclear what soccer clubs were on the field, he said.
All events at Stryker Sports Complex have been canceled until further notice, the facility said. “We ask that you keep all individuals and families affected in your thoughts and prayers during this difficult time,” the statement said.
The complex hosts recreational and competitive youth soccer leagues for players ranging from under-5 age groups through high school, as well as adult leagues, according to its website. It has 11 outdoor turf fields and an indoor facility.
Flag football state championship games scheduled at an adjacent field have also been suspended as police probe the scene, the Kansas State High School Activities Association said in a statement.
Wichita Mayor Lily Wu said she’s “heartbroken” and advised people to avoid the area, adding, “My thoughts and prayers are with everyone affected, especially the children and families involved.”
Police asked for the public’s help as they search for video from the sports complex. Officials are expected to hold another news conference to provide more information Saturday evening, Moses said.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

title: Record-setting 60-year-old flamingo hatches 2 chicks at Louisville Zoo
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — The Louisville Zoo announced the arrival of brand-new Chilean flamingo chicks on Thursday.
One of the zoo’s Chilean flamingos just became a parent at 60 years old, a record-setting age for a female Chilean flamingo to produce chicks. She produced two.
The flock has welcomed six chicks in total this season, and all of them are being hand-reared by the zoo’s bird keeper staff.
Flamingo chicks hatch covered in snowy white down that transitions to gray before they turn into the famous flamingo pink as they grow.

title: Bruins rally in 3rd period to beat Ducks
text:
ANAHEIM, Calif. — Elias Lindholm assisted on the tying goal and scored the go-ahead goal in the third period, leading the Boston Bruins past the Anaheim Ducks 4-2 on Friday night for their fourth straight victory.
David Pastrnak scored a tying power-play goal and Frederic Brunet got his first NHL goal for the Bruins, who roared back from an early two-goal deficit and improved to 6-2-0.
Less than five minutes after Pastrnak converted a give-and-go with Lindholm, the Ducks failed to mark Lindholm during a power play and allowed him to tap in a pass from Pavel Zacha with 11:39 to play. Matthew Poitras added another goal with 3:40 left on James Hagens’ second assist of the night.
Michael DiPietro made 25 saves in his second start of the season for the Bruins.
Beckett Sennecke got his fifth goal and Tim Washe also scored for the Ducks, who have lost three straight home games while giving up 13 goals. Lukas Dostal stopped 18 shots.
Ducks captain Mikael Granlund sat out with an upper-body injury, and goal-scoring winger Cutter Gauthier filled in by moving to center for the first time in his NHL career.
Anaheim had the best chances in the first period, and it took a lead with two goals 20 seconds apart in the final minute. After Washe’s long shot went in through the legs of screening teammate Jeff Malott, Sennecke finished a strong passing sequence with Gauthier and Nikita Nesterenko.
Brunet trimmed Anaheim’s lead with his first goal early in the second, connecting on a power play in the 23-year-old defenseman’s sixth NHL game.
After the Ducks failed to score on a four-minute power play, Pastrnak’s 423rd career goal broke a tie with Brad Marchand for the fourth-most in Bruins history.
The Ducks have sold out Honda Center for the first four games of a new season for the first time since 2007, when the team was coming off its lone Stanley Cup title.
Up next
Bruins: At Los Angeles on Saturday.
Ducks: At New York Rangers on Monday.
