title: Obituary: Janet McGraves
text:
BRUNSWICK – Janet McGraves, passed away peacefully on Oct. 11, 2026 in a loving send-off from her close family.
Born in Topsham, Maine in 1947, she was a proud lifelong resident of Brunswick. Janet grew up in a loving home with her parents, Donald and Velma, her older brother Doug, and her identical twin sister, Jane, along with a menagerie of well-loved family pets. She could recite Brunswick High School cheers and we can still hear her singing “Get back, get back, get back to the woods…”
Janet dedicated 30 years to owning and operating the Lisbon Falls Dairy Maid, carrying on the family business her parents established 30 years earlier in 1952. Janet mentored countless young women and men working their first summer jobs at the ice cream and pizza stand, teaching them the value of hard work and the importance of treating customers right, always sprinkled with a little humor and compassion. A lifetime hard worker, she spent six days a week in the summer running the Dairy Maid, switching to L.L.Bean in the winter, then right back to summers at the Dairy Maid.
Prior to its closing, a member of Senator Angus King’s staff presented to Janet, Jane and the McGraves family a Senatorial Congratulations recognizing the Lisbon Falls Dairy Maid for 64 years as a cultural landmark.
Janet was known for her unmatched sense of humor. Janet delighted those around her with her impressions, silly faces, and quick wit. The younger Janet and crew could be seen tooling around Brunswick and Harpswell in her white Mustang with bright red interior. Even toward the end of her life, she found ways to bring laughter to her nurses and caregivers, sharing her gift for humor right up until the end.
Janet found joy in life’s simple pleasures, including Reese’s Peanut Butter Cups, a fresh lobster roll, and a suspenseful episode of Murder, She Wrote. She was also a fun-loving aunt to J.D. and Katie, known for sneaking enormous bags of candy into movie theaters and furnishing copious amounts of ice cream (from the Dairy Maid).
Janet’s loyalty and deep affection for those she loved were at the heart of who she was. Once, speaking to a tall young man she had known since birth, Janet teased him, “You used to look up to me.” He replied, “I still do.” That simple exchange captures the lasting place Janet held in the lives of those she cared about. She stood by the people she loved through life’s difficult moments and celebrated their happiest ones, always bringing laughter and joy along the way. Janet had a special gift for making others feel cared for, supported, and cherished—a true friend whose love and presence left a lasting mark.
Janet is survived by her identical twin sister, Jane, brother-in-law, Ken; nephew, J.D. (Vanessa), niece, Katie (Cole); five delightful great-nieces and great-nephews, Maeve, Grant, Ian, Colin, and Esmé; as well as many connections and friends along the way including lifelong friend, Chrissy Davis.
The family would like to express heartfelt gratitude to the caring staff at Friends In-Home Care (Dawn), BaySquare (Melissa, Sandra, Bri), and MaineHealth (Dr. Inger, Leslie, Nicole, Emma). For those working in memory care, please know that on your hardest days and in the hardest moments, you make a difference and leave a lasting impact on those in your care, even if they are never able to express it. We sincerely appreciate you and thank you.
A service honoring Janet’s full life will be held at 11 a.m. on Saturday, Oct. 24, at the Brunswick United Methodist Church, 320 Church Rd., Brunswick, ME 04011. Memories and condolences can be shared at http://www.brackettfh.com.

title: UNE football easily beats MMA for 1st win of season
text:
The University of New England rushed for 399 yards and rolled to a 62-14 win over Maine Maritime Academy in a college football game Saturday in Biddeford.
Damien Jones rushed six times for 95 yards and two touchdowns, while Nathan Delgado had 84 yards and two TDs for UNE (1-5, 1-2 Conference of New England). Gavin Martin added 81 yards and a score.
Jack Lambert completed 4 of 5 passes for 63 yards and a touchdown.
Harris Stone threw for 176 yards, a touchdown and an interception for MMA (0-6, 0-3). Auston Harris had 119 yards and a touchdown on 12 carries.
HUSSON 42, NEW ENGLAND COLLEGE 0: Daniel Ruiz Cantu rushed for 157 yards and three touchdowns, and the Eagles (2-4, 2-1 CNE) earned their second straight victory, beating the Pilgrims (1-5, 0-3) in Henniker, New Hampshire.
Anthony Santacroce added 87 yards rushing and two touchdowns, while Brody Gibson completed 11 of 15 passes for 106 yards and a score.
The Eagles held NEC to five first downs and 71 yards.

title: Trump says he jokingly called Google to float the idea of naming an ocean after himself
text:
(CNN) - President Donald Trump claimed he jokingly called Google to float the idea of naming an ocean after himself.
“I called up Google. And I said, let me ask just one question … First, they do the Gulf of America … They take a little small lake away from Canada. It’s not a small lake, but we have a lake. I said we’re going to do this strait … but then I said to him, we need an ocean,” Trump said.
The president made the remark during a rally in Dalton, Georgia, Friday.
“How do you feel about the Trump Ocean for the Atlantic or the Pacific? You know what they said, ‘We’ve had it. That’s enough. We’re not doing it anymore.’ I said I agree. No, I was only kidding. No, I sent them a little picture of where it says: The Trump Ocean. And they called back. They said, ‘Sir, look, OK. This one we can’t do. Oceans are different. Oceans cover many, many countries. We can’t do it.
I said I was only kidding. That time I was. Although it’s not the worst idea I’ve ever heard, it’s not one of the greatest ideas.”
Trump signed an executive order in August to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America,” following his effort last year to rename the Gulf of Mexico as “Gulf of America.”

title: Peaks woman tells late sister’s story to caution against faith healing
text:
PEAKS ISLAND — On the last weekend of September, as she has since 2004, Janis Price placed a memorial in the Maine Sunday Telegram for her younger sister, Nancy. Nancy, who didn’t live past the age of 7, would have been 70 this year.
Price believes no obituary ever ran where they grew up in Texas and, despite her efforts, hasn’t been able to locate an autopsy report. From what Price has gathered from records, Nancy died overnight on a Saturday and was cremated that Monday. Her death certificate lists the cause as “probably malignant lymphoma.” As far as Price knows, Nancy never saw a doctor. No one in her family did.
“That Sunday morning, they woke me up and said, ‘Nancy’s gone,’ and that was it,” recalled Price, whose parents wouldn’t explain what happened.
Price was 8 years old at the time — Irish twins, her mother called them. The oldest of five siblings, the sisters did everything together: rode bikes and horses, played kickball and pick-up sticks. At a green wrought-iron table that’s now in Price’s living room on Peaks Island, they’d sit and eat mangoes with their toes curled around the bars at the base.
Eventually, though, Nancy couldn’t play anymore or go to school, either. She vomited all the time, and lumps had formed on her neck — these were the effects of not being faithful enough, she was told.
Letters from a prominent Christian Science practitioner, which Price found among her late mother’s belongings, tell Nancy that, if she truly believed God could make her neck heal, the lumps would go away.
Price thinks her mother, who grew up exposed to Christian Science, became avid about faith healing after her own sister was treated with medication for appendicitis and was never the same. In a way, she can understand her mother’s thinking. In more ways, she can’t.
Both of her parents were educated; her mother graduated from Southern Methodist University, and her father was a lawyer, which makes it harder for Price to fathom how he could go along with it.
The church says it doesn’t prohibit its members from seeing doctors but that they often choose prayer-based healing because they have found it effective.
Price feels lucky not to have had a life-threatening illness as a child, though she remembers a badly stubbed toe that she was left to tend to herself when it started oozing and being put to bed after falling off a swing set and hitting her head.
The emotional pain of being raised this way, however, has taken its own toll.
Price since has become an advocate for eliminating religious exemptions to child-neglect laws and vaccine mandates, lending her support to organizations still trying to make those changes in places like Idaho, where children in faith-healing families continue to die from treatable illnesses.
In Maine, she’s told her story to legislators and written letters to the editor, as she felt compelled to do in February after the state started reporting new cases of measles.
She keeps all the public records and research she’s gathered — with her thoughts written on pink and yellow sticky notes — in a filing cabinet in the corner of her bedroom.
Underneath her bed is a box with more personal items related to her sister: sympathy notes to their mother and letters Nancy wrote herself, along with her red pencil case from school and favorite book, “The Lonely Doll Learns a Lesson.”
Hanging above her pillow are portraits of her and Nancy, painted by their grandmother, and beside the bed are two rocking chairs, one a little bigger than the other, where the sisters used to sit. They remind Price of how close they were.
“She was once here. She was a real person,” Price said.
PATH TO HEALING
Being on Peaks Island, where she can watch the crashing ocean waves, has been healing for Price. It took her a long time to get to this point.
Looking back on her childhood after 50 years of therapy, she can see how the effects of her sister’s death started to take hold.
Within a few months, she was wetting the bed. Streaming tears would come out of nowhere, like when her sixth-grade choir started singing “Puff, the Magic Dragon.” In eighth grade, when she heard another girl vomiting in the bathroom, she ran out with her hands covering her ears.
When she left home, it took a more self-destructive form — risky behavior, failed marriages, severed friendships and suicide attempts.
“It just seemed like a blinding series of one trauma or crisis after another,” Price said.
While she was living in Lexington, Kentucky, a chance encounter at a restaurant with a man from Vinalhaven led Price to visit Maine. She made return trips for years, until she ended up moving to Peaks in 1999, raising two of her daughters here and starting to find peace.
“I wanted something completely different, like nothing I’d ever seen before, and, boy, did I get it,” said Price, who gets around the island in a green golf cart.
In 2003, she held the memorial service that her sister never had, with photos and candles set up at a friend’s house overlooking the ocean. She had a band play “Puff, the Magic Dragon” and served tacos, one of Nancy’s favorite foods.
Price has given testimony in front of the Maine State Legislature, including in 2005, for a bill that removed religious exemptions to reporting child abuse; in 2019, for one that eliminated non-medical exemptions for vaccines; and again last year, when there was an attempt to restore them.
“Nancy’s story is just, I guess, really compelling,” she said, proudly adding that the state’s vaccination rate has since risen to at least 95%.
She wants as many people as possible to know what her sister went through and what other children still do, which is why she runs the remembrance in the newspaper every year.
Price credits Nancy with saving her life, by providing an example of bravery on her darkest days.
“I don’t want her to be forgotten,” she said.
Price still plugs her ears at the sound of choking. She takes antidepressants to relieve her overwhelming sadness and help her sleep. She doesn’t talk to her other siblings, because they don’t see eye to eye on much. But she has close friends now and a longtime partner who lives in Saco and takes her on sailing trips. She’s in the island’s ukulele band, a drumming circle and the Spanish club.
Several years ago, she moved to Windham, to be closer to her first grandchild, but started struggling and felt the need to get back to Peaks. She applied for senior housing on the island but was told it would be a long time before she’d hear anything.
One night, when she was feeling like she couldn’t go on living any longer, she thought of all that Nancy endured to help her get through it. The next day, she got a call saying an apartment had become available on the island.
She believes her sister is still thinking of her, too.

title: Maine Mariners lose to Worcester in season opener
text:
Worcester’s Matt DeMelis scored 15 seconds into the game, Sam Stange and Jordan Kaplan struck just over a minute apart early in the second period, and the Maine Mariners opened their ECHL season Saturday night with a 4-2 loss to the Railers in Worcester, Massachusetts.

title: Bruins rally in 3rd period to beat Ducks
text:
ANAHEIM, Calif. — Elias Lindholm assisted on the tying goal and scored the go-ahead goal in the third period, leading the Boston Bruins past the Anaheim Ducks 4-2 on Friday night for their fourth straight victory.
David Pastrnak scored a tying power-play goal and Frederic Brunet got his first NHL goal for the Bruins, who roared back from an early two-goal deficit and improved to 6-2-0.
Less than five minutes after Pastrnak converted a give-and-go with Lindholm, the Ducks failed to mark Lindholm during a power play and allowed him to tap in a pass from Pavel Zacha with 11:39 to play. Matthew Poitras added another goal with 3:40 left on James Hagens’ second assist of the night.
Michael DiPietro made 25 saves in his second start of the season for the Bruins.
Beckett Sennecke got his fifth goal and Tim Washe also scored for the Ducks, who have lost three straight home games while giving up 13 goals. Lukas Dostal stopped 18 shots.
Ducks captain Mikael Granlund sat out with an upper-body injury, and goal-scoring winger Cutter Gauthier filled in by moving to center for the first time in his NHL career.
Anaheim had the best chances in the first period, and it took a lead with two goals 20 seconds apart in the final minute. After Washe’s long shot went in through the legs of screening teammate Jeff Malott, Sennecke finished a strong passing sequence with Gauthier and Nikita Nesterenko.
Brunet trimmed Anaheim’s lead with his first goal early in the second, connecting on a power play in the 23-year-old defenseman’s sixth NHL game.
After the Ducks failed to score on a four-minute power play, Pastrnak’s 423rd career goal broke a tie with Brad Marchand for the fourth-most in Bruins history.
The Ducks have sold out Honda Center for the first four games of a new season for the first time since 2007, when the team was coming off its lone Stanley Cup title.
Up next
Bruins: At Los Angeles on Saturday.
Ducks: At New York Rangers on Monday.

title: Obituary: Sidney H. Geller
text:
WATERVILLE – Sidney Herbert Geller, 89, of Waterville, Maine, passed away peacefully in his sleep on Oct. 15, 2026.
“Sid” was born in Portland on April 5, 1937, to Mary (nee Blumenthal) and Harry Geller. A proud Mainer, he was born and raised in Portland and spent his adult life living in Waterville. Upon retirement, he enjoyed winters in Boca Raton, Fla., and summers at “the camp” on East Pond in Oakland.
He graduated from Deering High School, attended Northeastern University, and earned his bachelor’s degree from Drake University. He later attended Boston University School of Law before earning his law degree from the University of Maine School of Law. True to his sense of humor, he always joked that he was never at the top of his class.
After passing the Maine Bar Exam, Sid moved to Waterville to pursue his career in law. He practiced law in Waterville for 63 years. Throughout his life, he remained deeply committed to giving back to his community. He was very philanthropic and particularly devoted to supporting his synagogue, Beth Israel in Waterville, and The Cedars in Portland.
Sidney was predeceased by his parents; his brother, Arnold; and many beloved aunts and uncles.
He is survived by his wife of 61 years, Elizabeth “Liz” Geller; his three sons, David, his wife Jenny of Waterville, Michael, his partner Clinton O’Dell of Rumford, R.I., and Stephen Geller of Cape Cod, Mass.; and his three grandchildren, Chloe Geller and her partner David Barre of York, and Ian and Ava Geller both of Waterville. He also leaves behind his beloved sisters-in-law Susan Goldberg and Barbara McPherson; along with many nieces, nephews, and cousins.
Sid leaves behind a legacy of family, community, loyalty, and laughter. He will be dearly missed and fondly remembered by all who had the privilege of knowing him.
A funeral will be held at the Levey Chapel in Portland, on Sunday, Oct. 18, at 12 p.m.

Waterville, ME 04903-1882, or
The Cedars,
630 Ocean Ave.,
Portland, ME 04103

title: A bitter Michigan Senate race rattles Jewish and Muslim voters already on edge over the war in Gaza
text:
WEST BLOOMFIELD, Mich. (AP) — For many voters in Michigan, the U.S. Senate race has become about far more than which party controls Washington.
In the Detroit suburbs, some Jewish Democrats are confronting deeply personal questions about faith and identity as they weigh whether they can support their party’s nominee. Just miles away in Dearborn, Arab American leaders who backed President Donald Trump two years ago are growing increasingly alarmed by Republican rhetoric.
The concerns are rippling through communities already shaken by Israel’s war in Gaza. Now they are central players in the bitter open-seat race between Republican Mike Rogers, a onetime congressman, and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official who would be the country’s first Muslim senator if elected on Nov. 3.
Rogers has increasingly portrayed El-Sayed as an extremist and a threat to Jewish voters as the Republican tries to win over a traditionally Democratic constituency. Rogers laughed when a visiting Republican senator said El-Sayed slept in an Osama bin Laden jersey, and he agreed with a social media post calling El-Sayed a terrorist.
Emotions were already raw before the latest escalation.
In West Bloomfield, a synagogue recovering from an attack this year is only a half-hour drive from the “Wall of Tears” in downtown Dearborn memorializing children killed in Gaza.
The race has even divided close friends like Lori Goldman and Mimi Price-Miletic.
Goldman, a Jewish Democratic activist, described Rogers’ message as “a fear campaign.”
“It’s spreading and it’s not spreading slowly,” she said. “It’s spreading insidiously and widely and effectively.”
Price-Miletic, a member of the Michigan Democratic Jewish Caucus, sees things differently. She is not supporting El-Sayed and has not ruled out voting for Rogers.
“Lori Goldman is my best friend,” said Price-Miletic. “This summer I said we cannot discuss Abdul. I don’t want to hear his name. We’ve agreed to disagree and we don’t talk about it.”
“She adores him,” she added. “And I feel the exact opposite of her.”
Republicans look to win over Jewish voters
Central to Rogers’ strategy has been winning over Jewish voters after the fierce Democratic primary between El-Sayed and U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in which Israel became a focal point.
Stevens, one of Israel’s staunchest supporters in Congress, benefited from roughly $30 million in spending by groups affiliated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC.
Stevens represents much of Oakland County, just north of Detroit and home to a significant portion of Michigan’s Jewish population. Rogers has focused heavily on the area and is holding an event later in October with U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, that’s billed as “Who Will Keep Us Safe? Rogers vs. El-Sayed in the Wake of October 7th and the Temple Israel Attack.”
Vance Patrick, chair of the Oakland County Republican Party, said Rogers was “definitely making some headway” among Jewish voters and that the community is “listening to the Republican Party this time.”
Patrick added that Rogers has visited synagogues across the county, including Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, where a man rammed a truck loaded with fireworks and gasoline into the building and exchanged gunfire with a security guard in March.
The attacker, a naturalized citizen originally from Lebanon who lived in Dearborn Heights, had recently lost family members in an Israeli airstrike in his native country.
El-Sayed condemned the Temple Israel attack but drew criticism for saying “hurt people hurt people.” He later apologized by saying “to anyone who feels like my comments might have been hurtful, I’m really sorry.”
Rogers and his allies have repeatedly invoked those comments, with Rogers claiming El-Sayed “can’t condemn terrorism in our own country because he’s so close to the people who are supporting the Muslim Brotherhood.”
Trump went further Wednesday, claiming El-Sayed was a member of the Muslim Brotherhood.
There is no evidence that El-Sayed has any affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood. His half-sister, Eman Abdelhadi, wrote on social media in 2012 that “my family has long been MB” and described a conversation with her mother about involvement in the Muslim Brotherhood in the early 1970s.
El-Sayed, who was born in Michigan to Egyptian immigrant parents and was raised by his father, told NBC this week the social media posts are “hearsay.”
The Trump administration designated the Egyptian, Jordanian and Lebanese branches of the Muslim Brotherhood as terrorist organizations earlier this year.
Democrats face divisions over El-Sayed’s candidacy
Democrats are still struggling to unite behind El-Sayed after the primary exposed deep disagreements over Israel.
Oakland County is one of Michigan’s largest and most politically consequential counties, with roughly 1.3 million residents. Once a Republican stronghold, it has shifted steadily toward Democrats over the past two decades.
But many of the country’s top Democrats have kept an arm’s length from El-Sayed.
State Sen. Jeremy Moss, who is Jewish and is running for a U.S. House seat encompassing much of Oakland County, has not endorsed El-Sayed. Stevens has endorsed El-Sayed, but has not campaigned with him.
Price-Miletic, who supported Stevens in the primary, said part of the reason she will not vote for El-Sayed is his past appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker, who has made comments described as antisemitic.
Goldman, the founder of grassroots organization Fems for Dems, said she believes much of the rhetoric spread about El-Sayed is not true and that Republicans “are preying upon the fears that are engendered in every Jewish person because past is prologue.”
Surrogates for El-Sayed, including local leaders and high-profile Democratic officials, have been holding house party events throughout the state to talk with undecided Jewish voters. Former U.S. Rep. Andy Levin of Michigan, who is Jewish and is supporting El-Sayed, has taken part in many of them.
“We don’t take a hard sell approach at all,” Levin said. “It’s more like a bunch of Jews coming together and saying, ‘OK, let’s all talk about our fears, our hopes, our anxieties.’”
There’s a backlash in the nation’s largest Arab American community
Dearborn, just south of Oakland County, has been a focal point for political divisions over Gaza. Many Arab American voters turned against Democrats in 2024 over President Joe Biden’s support for Israel. Trump won the city of nearly 100,000 residents by 6 percentage points.
But the community has grown increasingly critical of Trump since he took office in January 2025. The rhetoric from Rogers and other Republicans about El-Sayed has added to those frustrations.
Dearborn Mayor Abdullah Hammoud, a Democrat who did not endorse in the 2024 election, said Republicans’ words about El-Sayed and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, another prominent Muslim politician, have been “very problematic.”
“You’ve seen Sen. Cruz and other U.S. senators bringing poster boards onto the Senate floor, basically trying to tie them to terrorist organizations or call them terrorists themselves, just because of their faith,” Hammoud said.
The criticism has also come from some of the Arab American leaders who were instrumental when Trump won the state two years ago.
“Any attack based on a person’s religion is not acceptable,” said Bishara Bahbah, who helped lead Trump’s outreach in Michigan in 2024. “Abdul El-Sayed was born and raised in the United States. He’s as American as they come.”
Bahbah, who renamed his group Arab Americans for Trump to Arab Americans for Peace early in Trump’s term, said the president’s rhetoric toward El-Sayed crossed a “red line.”
“President Trump several times thanked the Arab American population for their support of his candidacy. I think the people around him should remember that,” Bahbah said. “Because elections are coming up.”

title: Man shot, killed on subway platform in midtown Manhattan
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — An argument on a subway platform in midtown Manhattan turned deadly Saturday, leaving one man fatally shot and train service disrupted.
The shooting happened around 12:20 p.m. at the station at 7th Avenue and 53rd Street, a short walk from several Broadway theaters and Carnegie Hall.
Police found an adult man with a gunshot wound to his chest. A police spokesperson said the shooting took place on the E train platform. The dispute involved two or three men.
Emergency crews responded and transported the victim to Bellevue Hospital, where he was pronounced dead.
No arrests were immediately reported. Trains that normally stop at that station were bypassing the area as a police investigation took place.
Violent crime has been dropping steadily in New York City since a spike during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic, and deadly violence inside the subway system remains rare, despite the trains being used by millions of people each day.
Through mid-October, the city was on pace to have its lowest number of killings in decades, with reported homicides down 20% from the same point last year.

Families could check out a variety of hands-on activities designed to foster creativity in young minds, while exposing them to potential career paths for the future.
Kids could build their own cars, blast off to space with virtual reality, practice coding with a robot, and even get a chance to try out being a reporter.

title: You might be overlooking something unusual in a flock of Canada geese
text:
Outdoors
The BDN outdoors section brings readers into the woods, waters and wild places of Maine. It features stories on hunting, fishing, wildlife, conservation and recreation, told by people who live these experiences. This section emphasizes hands-on knowledge, field reports, issues, trends and the traditions that define life outside in Maine. Read more Outdoors stories here. 
I enjoy goose-hunting this time of year, but not the kind of goose-hunting you might be thinking of. Canada geese are roaming the state. They are one of the few Canadian products currently entering the United States without a tariff.
Canada geese are found throughout North America, sometimes in nuisance numbers. It’s hard to imagine that a hundred years ago, they were on the brink of extinction in many areas due to overhunting. They have bounced back remarkably, a testament to their adaptability.
Besides aquatic vegetation, Canada geese forage on grains, grasses and berries. They are not only comfortable around people, but they take advantage of increased development. Parks, golf courses and lawns provide food and a wide view of approaching predators. Geese quickly learn where they are safe from hunting. Thousands of autumn geese gather in fire ponds and mill ponds, especially in Aroostook County.
Even Canada goose chicks are adaptable. Goslings can swim within one day of hatching. They stick together in tight groups, making it easier for parents to guard them, which the parents do ferociously.
Too many geese can be worse than not enough. They damage cornfields, endanger aircraft, and soil neighborhoods. Just 50 geese will deposit 2.5 tons of poop in a year. I don’t know exactly how that figure was determined, but somewhere there is a grad student who got the worst research assignment ever.
Hunting pressure may be the only thing keeping the Canada goose population in check. During Maine’s September hunting season, the bag limit is 8 to 10 per day, and up to 30 in possession. A freezer big enough to hold that many geese would not fit in my garage.
It’s common to see flocks of Canada geese flying in V formation. Every goose except the leader benefits from an aerodynamic upwash created by the goose ahead. When the leader tires, it rotates to the back, and another goose takes over.
You’ve likely noticed that geese in V formation fly in all directions, not just south. They typically spend the night in a wetland where they are safe from land-based predators. When daylight arrives, they roam around looking for good places to forage.
Canada geese migrate during the day. They can travel great distances quickly. With a tailwind, they can fly from Bangor to Orlando in one day. However, they prefer a more relaxed pace, stopping to forage at well-known rest stops along the way. Many of America’s National Wildlife Refuges are located along migratory coastal flyways in the mid-Atlantic states.
Some geese don’t migrate at all. The subspecies used to restore Canada goose populations a century ago was largely non-migratory. Meanwhile, migratory subspecies have adapted to a changing landscape and warming climate, migrating less. They take advantage of corn stubble that was once snow-covered and open water that was formerly frozen. They crowd into developed areas, safe from hunting. Why migrate if it’s not necessary for survival?
A species that is successful and widespread often evolves subspecies within distinct geographic regions. Seven subspecies of Canada goose are currently recognized. The one we primarily see — the Atlantic Canada goose — is the most widespread in the east. The Pacific Northwest hosts at least three different subspecies of Canada goose, each with a very limited range.
Although all Canada geese resemble each other, one subspecies is so small that it was reclassified as a separate species 22 years ago. The cackling goose breeds in the far north, and winters west of the Mississippi. A few vagrants show up in Maine each fall. Finding this duck-sized pipsqueak is one of the things that makes goose-hunting fun this time of year.
Snow geese migrate in huge numbers, primarily on a route west of Maine. Ross’s goose is a smaller, rarer species resembling the snow goose that is mostly restricted to midcontinent. When one shows up in Maine, it’s apt to draw a crowd of birders.
Greater white-fronted geese are abundant midcontinent birds that stray into Maine. Pink-footed geese and barnacle geese are European birds that nest no closer than Greenland, but visit Maine on rare occasions. A big flock of Canada geese may have any of these interlopers hiding among them.
Finally, let me get this off my chest. It’s called a Canada goose, not a Canadian goose. Don’t call it a Canadian goose unless you’re in Canada. I made this same admonition in a column 12 years ago, and what name did the editors use to caption the photo with the article? “Canadian Goose.”

title: Family heirloom found to be unspent WWI artillery shell prompts emergency response
text:
Family heirloom found to be an unspent WWI artillery shell prompts emergency response
An unspent World War I artillery shell was found at a Paxton, Massachusetts, residence on Wednesday, prompting an emergency response.
The Paxton Fire Department said the ordnance was found at a home and the shell had been passed down as a family heirloom from the homeowner's grandfather.
Realizing the hazard the ordnance posed, the homeowner immediately contacted the Massachusetts State Police.
State police coordinated a response with local, state and military personnel to safely remove the item.
"While these historic military relics are fascinating pieces of history, many remain unstable even more than 100 years after they were manufactured," the Paxton Fire Department wrote in a news release. "In this case, the shell, which was approximately 110 years old, presented a serious risk within the home and required specialized handling by trained explosive ordnance personnel."
No injuries were reported, and at no point was there any danger to neighboring homes.
The artillery shell was transported to Devens, Massachusetts, where it will be destroyed under controlled conditions.
Officials remind the public not to touch any old military munitions, explosives or other suspicious items they encounter and to call 911.

title: Bryant deals UMaine football a sixth straight loss
text:
It was more of the same for the University of Maine’s football team on Saturday at Morse Field in Alfond Stadium in Orono as Sean Green made his debut as interim offensive coordinator after Mikahael Waters was let go nearly two weeks ago.
Mistakes, dropped passes and an inability to score touchdowns yielded yet another loss as Bryant University carved out its first ever win in six games in Orono, 17-14.
Bryant improved to 5-2 overall and 3-0 in the Coastal Athletic Association while UMaine suffered its sixth straight loss and fell to 1-6 overall, 1-3 in the conference.
UMaine is now 0-3 at home this season.
The losing streak is the longest since UMaine dropped nine in a row spanning the 2022 and 2023 seasons.
Trailing 17-14 with 3:23 left in the game, UMaine took over the ball at its own 25-yard line and used a diving catch by Major Leak off a Caden Drezek pass to set itself up at the Bryant 42.
Redshirt junior Drezek was making his first career full-time start. He shared the role with Eddie Buehler two weeks ago.
But an illegal procedure penalty on tackle Andrew Kocan and a one-yard run by Drezek left the Black Bears in a second-and-14 yards to go predicament and three poor Drezek throws resulted in incompletions which turned the ball over to Bryant and the Bulldogs ran out the clock.
“We just weren’t able to build off that play,” said UMaine head coach Jordan Stevens, referring to Leak’s reception.
UMaine had won the last four meetings between the two in both venues.
It was another inept performance from the UMaine offense in the first half and only a goal line stand by the Black Bear defense late in the half kept them within striking distance at 14-3.
UMaine’s offense managed just 73 yards, running back/slot back Nick Laughlin coughed up two fumbles and Black Bear receivers dropped three passes.
They dropped two more in the second half for a total of five in the game.
UMaine came into the game with the worst offense in the CAA and one of the worst among 124 teams in the Football Championship Subdivision. It was last in the CAA in points (14.5) and total yards (270.2) per game. It was 121st and 115th in the country in those categories, respectively.
The first drop occurred on UMaine’s first drive of the game and proved costly as a potential touchdown pass from Drezek to Corey Rideout went through the hands of the open receiver in the end zone.
So UMaine had to settle for Sam Tremblay’s 40-yard field goal.
Bryant took the lead on the ensuing possession, covering 75 yards on six plays with quarterback Brennan Myer capping the drive with a 30-yard pass to Jose Leon in the left corner of the end zone.
The drive was extended by a 34-yard pass from Myer to a diving Leon on third-and-nine and a holding penalty on UMaine’s Jamaree Gibson on third-and-10.
UMaine put together a promising drive early in the second period after getting great field position at the 50 courtesy of a personal foul penalty on Bryant.
A 17-yard scamper by Drezek moved the chains but, on a third-and-four from the Bryant 32-yard line, Laughlin fumbled and Bryant linebacker Drake Lusk recovered it.
On Bryant’s first play, UMaine safety Jeremiah McGill dropped a potential interception and the Bulldogs made them pay, putting together an eight-play, 63-yard drive finished off by O.J. Ross’ three-yard run.
Myer completed passes of 19 yards to Maximlus Nosler and 16 yards to Shamar Fowles during the drive.
Laughlin then lost another fumble and Bryant moved down to the five-yard line.
But, on fourth-and-one, the Black Bear defense stuffed running back Deshon Jenkins shy of first down yardage. Noah Carpenter and Farradi Titkipina were credited with the tackles.
UMaine strung together its only touchdown drive of the game to start the third quarter, going 75 yards on just six plays.
Laughlin made a terrific one-handed catch along the right sideline for a 28-yard completion and Drezek hooked up with Evan Wallace on a 31-yard pass as Wallace took a short throw in the backfield on a screen and weaved his way through traffic down to the B-10 yard line.
On third-and-goal from the 11, Marshall took a short pass from Drezek in the right flats and fought his way to the goal line, extending the ball with his right hand into the end zone.
The Black Bears then used a trick play for a two-point conversion as linebacker Carpenter took a direct snap and ran up the middle with help from a push from behind by a beefy teammate.
The Black Bears forced a three-and-out by Bryant and regained the ball at its own 16-yard line.
But Drezek was sacked and fumbled the ball and Bryant’s Lucian DePino recovered at the UMaine 9 yard line.
Again, the UMaine defense bailed out the offense by holding Bryant to a 26-yard field goal by Nicholas Stoyanovich.
UMaine put together a 20-play, 78-yard drive spanning the third and fourth quarters and reached the Bryant 7-yard line.
But on third-and-four, they tried a pitch out to the right side to Rashawn Marshall and he was nailed for a sizable loss by Toby Brown Jr. so, again, UMaine had to settle for a Tremblay field goal, this time from 32 yards.
“Congrats to Bryant. I thought they played hard and played in the manner they’ve played all year,” said Jordan Stevens. “They didn’t turn the ball over, they created takeaways. We turned the ball over.
“This is on me to start in terms of not playing with more discipline in terms of ball security. Penalties on special teams. Those hurt us the most within the game,” said Stevens. “We were in position to win the game at the end but just came up short.”
UMaine outgained Bryant 352-287 in total yards but the three turnovers resulted in 10 Bryant points, and the Bulldogs didn’t turn the ball over.
UMaine was penalized eight times for 62 yards while Bryant had five penalties for 45 yards.
Myer completed 12 of 21 passes for 157 yards and one touchdown. O.J Ross carried the ball 11 times for 61 yards and Fowles caught five passes for 43 yards.
Linebacker Lusk had a team-high 12 tackles, a sack, two fumble recoveries and he forced a fumble. Linebacker Anthony Ottinot had eight tackles, two and a half for lost yardage, and he forced a fumble.
Drezek completed 18 of 34 passes for 234 yards and a TD. He added nine rushes for 35 yards. Marshall had a game-high 62 rushing yards on 19 carries. Laughlin had a game-high seven catches for 86 yards and Wallace had three for 59 yards.
Linebacker Sam Oppenheimer had a game-high 15 tackles including half a sack. Carpenter had 11. Defensive end Kye Pressley had eight tackles.
UMaine will host Campbell (NC) for Homecoming on Saturday at 1 pm while Bryant will host Stony Brook at 2 pm.

title: Vatican says Pope Leo to be released from the hospital Saturday, 4 days after lung cancer surgery
Peaks woman tells late sister’s story to caution against faith healing
text:
PEAKS ISLAND — On the last weekend of September, as she has since 2004, Janis Price placed a memorial in the Maine Sunday Telegram for her younger sister, Nancy. Nancy, who didn’t live past the age of 7, would have been 70 this year.
Price believes no obituary ever ran where they grew up in Texas and, despite her efforts, hasn’t been able to locate an autopsy report. From what Price has gathered from records, Nancy died overnight on a Saturday and was cremated that Monday. Her death certificate lists the cause as “probably malignant lymphoma.” As far as Price knows, Nancy never saw a doctor. No one in her family did.
“That Sunday morning, they woke me up and said, ‘Nancy’s gone,’ and that was it,” recalled Price, whose parents wouldn’t explain what happened.
Price was 8 years old at the time — Irish twins, her mother called them. The oldest of five siblings, the sisters did everything together: rode bikes and horses, played kickball and pick-up sticks. At a green wrought-iron table that’s now in Price’s living room on Peaks Island, they’d sit and eat mangoes with their toes curled around the bars at the base.
Eventually, though, Nancy couldn’t play anymore or go to school, either. She vomited all the time, and lumps had formed on her neck — these were the effects of not being faithful enough, she was told.
Letters from a prominent Christian Science practitioner, which Price found among her late mother’s belongings, tell Nancy that, if she truly believed God could make her neck heal, the lumps would go away.
Price thinks her mother, who grew up exposed to Christian Science, became avid about faith healing after her own sister was treated with medication for appendicitis and was never the same. In a way, she can understand her mother’s thinking. In more ways, she can’t.
Both of her parents were educated; her mother graduated from Southern Methodist University, and her father was a lawyer, which makes it harder for Price to fathom how he could go along with it.
The church says it doesn’t prohibit its members from seeing doctors but that they often choose prayer-based healing because they have found it effective.
Price feels lucky not to have had a life-threatening illness as a child, though she remembers a badly stubbed toe that she was left to tend to herself when it started oozing and being put to bed after falling off a swing set and hitting her head.
The emotional pain of being raised this way, however, has taken its own toll.
Price since has become an advocate for eliminating religious exemptions to child-neglect laws and vaccine mandates, lending her support to organizations still trying to make those changes in places like Idaho, where children in faith-healing families continue to die from treatable illnesses.
In Maine, she’s told her story to legislators and written letters to the editor, as she felt compelled to do in February after the state started reporting new cases of measles.
She keeps all the public records and research she’s gathered — with her thoughts written on pink and yellow sticky notes — in a filing cabinet in the corner of her bedroom.
Underneath her bed is a box with more personal items related to her sister: sympathy notes to their mother and letters Nancy wrote herself, along with her red pencil case from school and favorite book, “The Lonely Doll Learns a Lesson.”
Hanging above her pillow are portraits of her and Nancy, painted by their grandmother, and beside the bed are two rocking chairs, one a little bigger than the other, where the sisters used to sit. They remind Price of how close they were.
“She was once here. She was a real person,” Price said.
PATH TO HEALING
Being on Peaks Island, where she can watch the crashing ocean waves, has been healing for Price. It took her a long time to get to this point.
Looking back on her childhood after 50 years of therapy, she can see how the effects of her sister’s death started to take hold.
Within a few months, she was wetting the bed. Streaming tears would come out of nowhere, like when her sixth-grade choir started singing “Puff, the Magic Dragon.” In eighth grade, when she heard another girl vomiting in the bathroom, she ran out with her hands covering her ears.
When she left home, it took a more self-destructive form — risky behavior, failed marriages, severed friendships and suicide attempts.
“It just seemed like a blinding series of one trauma or crisis after another,” Price said.
While she was living in Lexington, Kentucky, a chance encounter at a restaurant with a man from Vinalhaven led Price to visit Maine. She made return trips for years, until she ended up moving to Peaks in 1999, raising two of her daughters here and starting to find peace.
“I wanted something completely different, like nothing I’d ever seen before, and, boy, did I get it,” said Price, who gets around the island in a green golf cart.
In 2003, she held the memorial service that her sister never had, with photos and candles set up at a friend’s house overlooking the ocean. She had a band play “Puff, the Magic Dragon” and served tacos, one of Nancy’s favorite foods.
Price has given testimony in front of the Maine State Legislature, including in 2005, for a bill that removed religious exemptions to reporting child abuse; in 2019, for one that eliminated non-medical exemptions for vaccines; and again last year, when there was an attempt to restore them.
“Nancy’s story is just, I guess, really compelling,” she said, proudly adding that the state’s vaccination rate has since risen to at least 95%.
She wants as many people as possible to know what her sister went through and what other children still do, which is why she runs the remembrance in the newspaper every year.
Price credits Nancy with saving her life, by providing an example of bravery on her darkest days.
“I don’t want her to be forgotten,” she said.
Price still plugs her ears at the sound of choking. She takes antidepressants to relieve her overwhelming sadness and help her sleep. She doesn’t talk to her other siblings, because they don’t see eye to eye on much. But she has close friends now and a longtime partner who lives in Saco and takes her on sailing trips. She’s in the island’s ukulele band, a drumming circle and the Spanish club.
Several years ago, she moved to Windham, to be closer to her first grandchild, but started struggling and felt the need to get back to Peaks. She applied for senior housing on the island but was told it would be a long time before she’d hear anything.
One night, when she was feeling like she couldn’t go on living any longer, she thought of all that Nancy endured to help her get through it. The next day, she got a call saying an apartment had become available on the island.
She believes her sister is still thinking of her, too.

title: Immigration’s economic impact highlighted ahead of midterms
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Inflation has been a major topic of conversation as voters head to the polls for next month’s midterm elections. Economists point to several factors, but some Democratic lawmakers say President Donald Trump’s immigration policies are part of the problem.
Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-N.Y.) said the impact of immigration enforcement is being felt across multiple industries.
“ICE is an affordability issue. Everyone in this country is paying the ‘ICE tax,’” Espaillat said.
Some politicians argue the Trump administration’s immigration policy is hitting Americans’ pocketbooks, calling the economic fallout from mass deportations the “ICE tax.”
“When a construction site screeched to a halt because no one is left to build homes, that’s the ‘ICE tax’. When our elders cannot receive the care that they need because their caretakers and nurses are gone, that’s the ‘ICE tax,’” Espaillat said.
While Democrats such as Espaillat are focusing on the consequences, others see the immigration crackdown as a positive.
Joe Chatham with the Federation for American Immigration Reform supports Trump’s immigration agenda, claiming it’s boosting the U.S. economy. He said fewer foreign workers means a better deal for Americans.
“What you see is employers across the board, they start to raise those wages and there’s upward pressure because there’s less workers available. And then in addition, the working conditions start to improve. So American workers will come back into those jobs, and they’ll be able to sustain a middle-class lifestyle,” Chatham said.
Chatham said it’s a give and take, pointing to the housing market. In his view, while fewer foreign workers could make labor more expensive, housing access is a “zero-sum game.” He said more deportations means less demand for housing, lowering the cost.
“You’re also putting more money in the pocket of American workers who can then go out and buy houses, then go out and buy new products,” Chatham said.
The Brookings Institute studied cities with the most ICE activity in 2025. It found nearly 670,000 jobs were lost, with at least one in six being jobs held by American-born workers.

title: UMaine holds 14th annual march against domestic violence
text:
ORONO, Maine (WABI) - The 14th annual UMaine March Against Domestic Violence kicked off Friday evening from the steps of the Fogler Library and continued around the Mall back to the Memorial Union.
Organizers said the public show of support for survivors helps break the stigma around domestic abuse.
The event also serves as a way to connect college students with resources, with a number of local organizations tabling after the walk.
Speeches memorialize lives lost
There were also speeches, including one memorializing Makayla Rose DeSantis, the 23-year-old Connecticut woman who was shot to death in Carrabasset Valley earlier this year.
Her boyfriend is charged with her murder.
“A question that I would like everyone to keep in mind and consider and sit with is: What do we owe victims of domestic violence when we witness or become aware of their abuse? How can we shift from passive bystanders to active allies?” said Sophie Lauritano, president, Triota.
“Consider taking action that goes beyond awareness, that makes lasting change in our communities and that change must start with you,” said Amanda Cost, executive director, Partners for Peace.
The event concluded with a ceremony for lives lost to domestic violence.
If you or someone you know is experiencing domestic violence, Partners for Peace has a 24-hour helpline available at 1-800-863-9909. For additional resources, visit https://www.partnersforpeaceme.org/.

title: Hiker rescued after falling cactus hits her in the head
text:
SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. (AZFamily/Gray News) — A woman was taken to a trauma center after she was hit on the head by a cactus while hiking in Arizona.
Shortly after 7 a.m., first responders were called to the Bell Pass Trail in the McDowell Mountains after reports of an injured woman. According to the Scottsdale Fire Department, she had been on a trail when a falling cactus hit her on the head.
The fire department said Scottsdale technical rescue found the woman about two miles from the trailhead. Crews used a big wheel and a utility terrain vehicle to get her back safely.

title: Happy birthday, Sonny. Keep the memories coming.
text:
It’s amazing to think that one year ago I tore myself in two to push out a screaming potato and now, as I write this, there is a tiny chaos goblin in my office, pulling books off a desk and blowing raspberries.
As cliché as it is to say, the days have been long (and the nights even longer) but the year was short. It feels like it’s been forever and also like just yesterday I was flying down 295 to Maine Med at 4 a.m. Somehow we have all survived, with marriage and developmental milestones intact.
I was worried that I would lose my own identity in motherhood; I’ve read and spoken to a lot of women who felt that happened to them. I’ve been lucky so far; I still feel like exactly who I’ve always been, just with more add-on, after-market features.
I don’t know if it’s because I’ve only been a mom for a year, or because I only have one kid, or maybe I just have a particularly strong sense of self. It’s felt more like in a video game where suddenly you hit a new level or find a treasure chest and then your character can wield the Flaming Sword of Vengeance, except in this case it’s just the ability to prepare an entire baby lunch one-handed with the other arm holding a 20-pound child. I come equipped with new items too, like the Dumbbells of Lesser Back Pain, the Midnight Cookie Tupperware (can only be accessed in the dark) and the Diaper Bag of Endless Wonders.
I’ve also unlocked vast stores of patience that I had no idea were there, like an enormous underwater aquifer that just got discovered accidentally by a septic tank crew. There is no one else on Earth who can scream at me for two hours between 1 and 3 in the morning and I will respond with nothing but love and snuggles. I’m able to cope with sensory issues that would normally overstimulate me.
I mean, do you know how many slimy textured food items I’ve touched today alone? So many. And yet when it’s for my kiddo I don’t feel like tearing off my skin like I normally do. Last week there was a day where Sonny vomited on me. Twice. And I didn’t even have a meltdown.
Sonny is developing a real personality now. When we’re out and about he is fairly laid back — indeed, yesterday at the grocery store the cashier said he was “the chilliest baby she’s ever seen” — casually observing everything quietly, taking it all in and I assume processing it somehow. He doesn’t freak out too much at strangers. At home, though — well, there’s a reason my wife’s name for his alter ego is “Chaos Boy.”
Currently his favorite activities are pulling piles of things off shelves. I stack (and restack) board books for him on coffee tables for just this purpose and throwing food at the dogs, sometimes to indicate he’s done eating but sometimes just, apparently, for funsies. We play little games with each other.
He is constantly pulling himself up to standing using various objects to balance. He seems to have this insatiable, unstoppable inner drive to move forward. Once he learned to sit, he started lunging forward from a sitting position until he figured out crawling. Now he crawls and still wants to go further, farther and always upward (he’s also constantly trying to climb me and his other mom).
When we take him for walks in the stroller he is constantly twisting around and swiveling, trying to look at absolutely everything in the world. He has a particular fascination with staring at the stroller wheels turning, and in throwing his pacifiers out the side to see what happens.
I find myself staring at him with a stupid happy grin on my face all the time. (Well, maybe not at 2 a.m.) I feel so lucky that I get to hang out with this cool little dude all the time. We start our day on the floor of the nursery, him with his milk and me with my cup of coffee and I just feel so joyful. When he smiles at me it feels like the way taking the first sip of a glass of wine felt and I just want more and more.
I don’t take these moments of joy for granted. I’m sure I’ll go into it in a whole column at some point, but for the first few months after Sonny’s birth, I had postpartum depression pretty badly. I was worried I would never feel the joy in parenthood that other moms talked about or even just joy in general). I’m happy to report that the joy and fun has kicked in.
I can’t wait to see what Sonny does next. Which, at time of this writing, is crawling at top speed for the dog’s chew toy.

title: 81-year-old man killed during home invasion; suspect shoots himself in bathroom, authorites say
text:
NEW ALBANY, Miss. (WTVA/Gray News) - An 81-year-old Mississippi man was shot and killed during a home invasion, authorities said.
Union County Sheriff Jimmy Edwards said the shooting happened around 4 a.m. Thursday at a home.
An 81-year-old man identified as Bobby McGill and a woman were in bed when the suspect, Eric Basco, allegedly entered the home.
The woman escaped and called 911, while McGill tried to fight off Basco.
Authorities said the suspect allegedly got ahold of McGill’s gun and killed the 81-year-old man.
Edwards said Basco appeared to have entered the home to burglarize it. He then went into a bathroom and shot himself, the sheriff said.

title: Family accused of taking nearly $375,000 in copper from interstate construction projects
text:
EVANSVILLE, Ind. (WFIE/Gray News) - Authorities say hundreds of thousands of dollars’ worth of copper has been stolen from construction projects along Interstate 69.
Indiana authorities said several thefts have been reported to Evansville police, the Warrick County Sheriff’s Office and the Vanderburgh County Sheriff’s Office.
According to the Indiana Department of Transportation, copper was reported stolen from work zone lighting projects at the I-69 and Interstate 64 interchange.
According to investigators, scrap yards across the Tri-State shared information that Jason Fulks and members of his family were selling large amounts of copper.
Construction crews estimated more than $367,000 in wire was stolen.
Records show Fulks was arrested earlier this month after a traffic stop with a warrant also out for his arrest tied to the copper-theft case.
Investigators noted that tools and copper were also found in Fulks’ truck.
Natalee Fairchild and Sherry Beasley are additionally facing charges of corrupt business influence stemming from the investigation, authorities said.
Indiana authorities added that surveillance video, license plate readers and cell phone data helped their several-month investigation.
Indiana’s Department of Transportation said its team is continuing to evaluate the impacts of the theft regarding the lighting projects.

title: ‘Itchiest bite’: Tick-borne syndrome leaves woman allergic to red meat
text:
ROSS TOWNSHIP, Pa. (KDKA) — A Pennsylvania woman is sharing her experience with a rare and potentially deadly tick-borne disease.
Angela Lundy was bitten by a tick over the summer and is now allergic to red meat.
“It was the itchiest bite I had ever had,” Lundy said.
Her sickness developed after she ate a bratwurst, a German sausage link.
After speaking with a doctor, Lundy was diagnosed with alpha-gal syndrome.
“I woke up with severe stomach pain right along where my bra line is, and it lasted about three hours,” Lundy said.
Lundy is now carrying an EpiPen as an extra precaution.
According to the CDC, alpha-gal can cause an allergy to meats like beef, pork and venison. About 300 people test positive for the tick-borne disease each year.
The best prevention is to spray DEET or wash clothes with specialized bug-repellent detergent.

title: Top runners prevail at KVAC cross country championships
text:
AUGUSTA — There was little drama at the finish line of the Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference cross country championships Saturday. Instead, the conference’s top runners made it look easy.
Bangor’s Sam Bergmark (large school boys), Medomak Valley’s Colby Daigle (small school boys), Hampden Academy’s Addison Elliott (large school girls) and Lincoln Academy’s Karen Higgins (small school girls) won titles at Cony High School. All did so easily, with the average margin of victory between the four coming in at 1 minute, 12.8 seconds.
“It’s very hilly (here), but I enjoy it; I really like the hilly course,” said Higgins, who repeated as KVAC Small School champion. “(The conditions were good); there was only like one spot where it was a little bit slippery, but I’d say since it’s been dry, it’s absorbed it all into the trails, so it was good.”
Hampden (53 points) beat Mt. Blue (84 points) for the KVAC Large boys title, while the Lincoln boys (68) claimed the Small crown over Morse (101). Hampden and Lincoln were the girls teams champions. Hampden (21) had a wide margin over Camden Hills (65), and Lincoln (42) edged Waterville (48).
Donning the No. 1 bib, Bergmark was widely expected to lead the pack and did so, beating Lucas Demarco (17:15.6) of Mt. Blue by 36.6 seconds. Mt. Blue’s Wyatt Oliver (17:33.7), Hampden’s Jack Scott (17:38.6) and Noah Seigh (17:45.8) of Camden Hills rounded out the top five.
“I just wanted to go kind of hard because I didn’t want it to be a race — I just wanted to win,” said Bergmark, who placed third in the KVAC race year and won the Class A North title. “I just wanted to see how things were going to go, and once we got on the gravel, I went at my own speed.
Daigle’s margin of victory was even larger. The senior’s time of 17:36.9 was more than a minute faster than Cony’s Brady Cloutier (18:37.4). Lincoln’s Holden Nehrboss (18:45.4), Erskine Academy’s Brayden Dow (18:48.1) and Gardiner’s Abrahm Hasty (19:01.7) also earned top-five finishes.
Elliott and Higgins were way out in front of the girls field. Elliott’s winning time of 18:39.0 beat teammate Isabelle Clark by 1:50.2. Also finishing in the top five in the Large division were Charlotte Crowe of Mt. Ararat (20:35.9), Elsie Mann of Camden Hills (20:38.3) and Emeline Cournane of Hampden (20:43.8).
Hampden claimed its third consecutive team title. In addition to Elliott, Clark and Cournane, Silvia Ruge (21:18.6) finished sixth, Mackenzie Elliott (21:24.5) took seventh, Erin Curtis (22:18.0) placed 11th and Aubrey Shaw (22:21.3) was 12th.
“I’m just so proud of our girls,” Elliott said. “We keep getting better, and I think we ran really, really well today. I think that shared energy between (us) really fed into how we did today. … I thought (the course) was going to be really muddy and uneven, but except for the start, it was great.”
Higgins’ time of 18:56.9 was nearly a minute and a half ahead of the runner-up in the Small divison, Frida Wright of Morse (21:21.8). Hallie Coots of Nokomis (21:32.5) placed third, Carson Dunn of Waterville (21:42.6) claimed fourth, and August Miller of Lincoln (22:06.5) finished fifth.
Although the Large and Small divisions were scored separately, runners competed in the same race, creating an interesting dynamic. Elliott and Higgins were neck-and-neck for a while. It wasn’t until midway through the race that Elliott began to separate herself from Higgins, who said that going head-to-head with one of the state’s best runners was a good springboard to regionals and states.
“It was nice to have her with me, because that definitely pushed me to go under 19,” Higgins said. “Running with her, at least for the first bit, that was fun. … I think Twin Brook (next Saturday for the Class B South regional) is going to feel a bit easier compared to this.”

title: Only thing ‘crystal clear’ on Navatek allegations is Collins’ innocence
text:
An Oct. 1 report insinuated Sen. Susan Collins’ guilt in a campaign finance scheme (“The laws tied to the Susan Collins-Navatek allegations are ‘crystal clear.’ Enforcing them is another matter.”). There is no guilt; I know this because my agency investigated it.
As a commissioner on the Federal Election Commission, we investigated Navatek in 2021 in coordination with the Department of Justice. After three years, the FEC fined the company $325,000, and the Biden Justice Department convicted the CEO in 2022.
Our investigators found “no information in the factual record” that Sen. Collins or her campaign knowingly took illegal money. We dismissed every potential violation against the super PAC supporting her. And the DOJ made no attempt to charge the Collins campaign.
The idea that the FBI was still pursuing Collins in 2025 is not credible. The conduct happened in 2019, and prosecutors had five years to bring charges.
What remains is a convicted felon’s self-serving story. Recycling his claims before Election Day is not news. It’s a political hit.
Sean Cooksey
Former FEC Commissioner (2021-2025)
Washington, D.C.

Mainers offer 6 tips for family caregivers
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Karen Groves has been taking care of her 93-year-old mother, Jean Groves, for five years.
Her mom lives at Berwick Estates, an assisted living facility near Groves’ home in South Berwick, but Groves sees her mother almost daily, taking her to twice-weekly dialysis treatments, plus other medical and hair appointments.
The retired Portsmouth Naval Shipyard engineer is never far away in case she gets a call from Berwick Estates — her mom has a variety of health, mobility and cognitive issues and has already been hospitalized four times this year.
“I feel very tied down,” said Groves, 69. “Usually once a year, one of my kids will cover for me for a few days. Then I can go away without waiting for the phone to ring. Last year I went to Vermont for four days and the mental break was amazing.”
Making time for yourself is one piece of advice Groves and other family caregivers offered to those who may be new to or still struggling with challenges that come with caring for an aging relative.
Nancy Jo Polito, 78, of Portland, wrote a book, “Taking Care of Business: Tales of a Caregiver,” about caring for her mother, Isabel Profenno Polito, who died in 2010 at age 93.
Her mother suffered from multiple health problems throughout her life, so Polito began helping out around the house when she was 5 years old and never stopped. When her mother fell and broke her wrist at age 89, she moved to a skilled nursing facility.
Polito’s concerns about the quality of care her mother received there led her to become a super advocate, regularly monitoring her mother’s meals, medications, bathing schedule, foot care and even doctor’s orders for medical tests and treatments.
“You just can’t admit someone and walk away and feel good about it,” Polito said. “You have to be an advocate to make sure they’re getting the right care.”
Here are some tips from the front lines of caregiving:
1. Get comfortable with being an advocate
It can be challenging, but it’s probably the most valuable role in caregiving — being an advocate and a witness to ensure a loved one receives proper care. That includes medical appointments, for in-home services and in long-term care facilities.
Visit and call regularly, ask questions and stop by randomly to see how living conditions measure up.
“You have to keep open communication and you have to stay on top of it,” Polito said. “I was told I was too pushy, but they like it when you don’t come in all the time.”
2. Learn what services are available
Search the internet for family caregiver programs that are available in your area. Elder care and social service agencies can help. AgeMaine, formerly Southern Maine Agency on Aging, is a good place to start.
“Be resourceful,” said Marvella Heard, 56, of Biddeford, who cares for her 79-year-old father, Samuel. “I wasn’t ready for all this. It’s complicated, like they don’t want it to be easy. It’s trial and error, but you figure things out.”
3. Meet with an elder law attorney
Whether you are a caregiver charged with overseeing a loved one’s finances and personal affairs, or you want to make long-range plans for yourself, an elder law attorney can help.
In addition to estate planning, which includes wills, trusts, powers of attorney, healthcare proxies and advanced directives, elder law attorneys handle asset protection, long-term care plans, government benefits, guardianships and elder abuse prevention.
Clare Herrmann, of Portland, cares for her husband, Jim Vollmar. The couple, both 78, found some peace of mind meeting with an elder law attorney.
“It takes all the questions out of it,” Herrmann said. “Who will take care of your finances? Who will make sure you have proper care as you age? All of that needs to be in writing and it’s hard to come up with all the ‘what ifs’ on your own.”
To find an elder law attorney, check the Maine State Bar Association’s Lawyer Referral Service or the National Academy of Elder Law Attorneys.
4. Put family controversy aside
Caring for an aging family member is often challenging on its own. Don’t let old grudges with siblings or other relatives make it more difficult.
“Put personal feeling aside and focus on caring for the person,” Heard said. “It’s very important to stick together at times like this. Be there for each other and one person won’t be overwhelmed.”
5. Take care of yourself
Reach out for assistance through elder care agencies, peer support groups and community organizations. Engage in activities that connect you with others outside the sphere of caregiving. Make time to do what makes you happy, even if it’s only for a few hours.
For Groves, that means treating any free day like an adventure, so she goes hiking or to a museum. She also enjoys volunteering and still makes time for it, teaching balance exercise classes for older adults.
“I find it gratifying and inspiring,” Groves said. “Volunteering was always going to be a big part of my retirement and I don’t want to give that up.”
6. Cut yourself some slack
It’s easy to feel guilty if you think you’re not doing enough as a caregiver, especially when a loved one gets sick or injured in a fall.
“You get waves of that,” Polito said. “You blame yourself when things happen. You feel you should have done more. You just have to let it go. It’s insurmountable at times. You can’t do it all.”

title: What’s on the ballot in Wells this November?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Wells voters will weigh in on five referendums in this fall’s election, including the town’s widely discussed mobile home lot rent stabilization ordinance.
Residents will also vote in state Legislature races and for York County sheriff.
Early voting is now open at the Wells town clerk’s office during normal business hours. There’s also special Saturday hours on Oct. 24 from 8 a.m. to noon.
Election Day is Nov. 3, with voting held at the Wells Junior High School gym from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.
Here’s what Wells voters can expect to see on their ballots this fall.
EMS QUESTION
The first referendum on the ballot asks whether the town should authorize 14 full-time positions to replace Wells Emergency Medical Services. Earlier this year, the organization notified the town that it would cease operations following a settlement involving alleged Medicare fraud.
If approved, the authorization would allow the town to provide emergency medical and ambulance services previously provided by WEMS.
The total cost is estimated at about $1,388,072, or $99,148 per position. That includes benefit costs.
Both the Board of Selectmen and Budget Committee unanimously recommend passage of this article.
OTHER REFERENDUMS
One referendum question will have voters decide whether to approve the relocation of a drainage easement. According to the town engineer’s proposal, a newly built home’s foundation encroaches on the current easement, but if voters approve, then the drainage can be redirected into an adjacent parcel of land.
The next article asks voters whether to let the select board issue up to $5,500,000 in general obligation bonds for the existing fire station on Log Cabin Lane. That funding would go towards renovating, expanding and equipping the station and its personnel.
Residents will also decide whether to approve an ordinance that would establish a retroactive moratorium on data centers. The 180-day moratorium, retroactive to June 16, would pause any data center developments 100,000 square feet or larger.
Finally, voters will consider a rent stabilization ordinance for mobile home lots. Residents of Wells mobile home parks have said they’ve been struggling with rent increases in recent years.
Diane Whiteside, 79, said lot rents at Blueberry Ridge Mobile Home Park were around $395 a month in 2015. Now, her rent is $625, with some newcomers even paying upward of $900.
“I’m still working because I have to keep my home,” Whiteside said. “I have an 82 year-old neighbor who has to borrow money to afford her lot.”
The Board of Selectmen previously approved a 60-day moratorium on lot rent increases to temporarily protect residents from further hikes prior to the vote.
STATE CANDIDATES
Residents in House District 145, which covers a majority of Wells, will decide between two newcomers, Democrat Kristin Davis and Republican Caleb Chase, as a state representative.
House District 146 covers a portion of the coast of Wells, as well as York and Ogunquit, where voters will decide between Democratic incumbent Gerry Runte Jr., serving his second term, and former District 149 Rep. Bradley Moulton, a Republican.
All Wells voters will also decide between current Kennebunk state Rep. Dan Sayre, a Democrat, or Jonathan Fallon, a Republican, to succeed current Democrat Joe Rafferty as their state senator.
All York County residents will also decide on a referendum abolishing a county treasurer position, as well as electing a sheriff. Incumbent Democrat William King is seeking a fifth term against Republican David Corbett. (Independent Brian Pellerin withdrew from the race and was recently hired as the new police chief in Wells, though he will still appear on the ballot.)

title: Smoked salmon recalled over listeria risk
text:
(FDA/CNN) - The Food and Drug Administration says there is a voluntary recall of frozen smoked salmon sold in six states.
Officials say “Starfish Seafood Premium Cold Smoked Norwegian Salmon” carries a potential risk of listeria.
The product was sold in New York, Florida, Georgia, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Ohio.
The distributor, Krasnyi Oktyabr, issued a voluntary recall after the New York State Department of Agriculture and Markets found potential listeria contamination.
No illnesses have been reported.
Consumers who have purchased the smoked salmon can return it to the retailer they purchased it from for a full refund.

title: Popular roller coaster shut down at Six Flags’ Cedar Point after bracket comes loose from ride
text:
SANDUSKY, Ohio (WOIO/Gray News) - The Millennium Force roller coaster at Cedar Point was shut down Friday after a small bracket became dislodged from a car on the ride.
According to Sara Gordon of Six Flags Entertainment, the bracket landed in a guest area and didn’t hit any park visitors or Cedar Point employees.
No injuries were reported.
According to Six Flags, the ride was immediately shut down in accordance with protocols and would remain closed pending an internal review and additional state inspection to ensure safety before reopening.
This comes on the heels of a tragic accident at Six Flags Over Georgia, where a man fell from the Goliath coaster and died on Monday.
Six Flags temporarily shut down nine rides across six parks that were similar to the Goliath.

title: 3 men sentenced to more than 158 years for the killings of Australian, US surfers in Mexico
text:
ENSENADA, Mexico (AP) — A judge on Friday sentenced three Mexican men to more than 158 years in prison each for the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, a case that tarnished Mexico’s image by exposing the risks foreigners face when visiting the tourism-dependent country.
The sentencing, which came a week after the men were found guilty, marked the end of a lengthy legal process over the killings of Australians Callum and Jake Robinson, and American Carter Redd Rhoad. Their bodies were found in May 2024, and at least four people were arrested for their alleged involvement in the crime.
A judge in the coastal city of Ensenada, in Baja California state, ruled that Jesús Gerardo García, known as “el Kekas,” Irineo Francisco “N” and Ángel Jesús “N” would each serve 158 years and nine months in prison for murder, robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
Antonio Otañez, president of the Baja California surfers’ association, welcomed the outcome, saying “justice has been served.” But he acknowledged that the killings had caused a “major drop” in tourist visits, particularly by surfers, to the region known for its beautiful beaches.
Here is a look at the key facts and events in the case:
Surfing trip ends in tragedy
The Robinson brothers — Callum and Jake — and their American friend decided to travel to Mexico in late April 2024 to pursue one of their passions, surfing, at a beach in Punta San José, about 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the city of Ensenada in Baja California state.
Unaware of the risks they faced, the three friends decided to camp on the beach on the night of April 27, 2024.
Their attackers confronted them there, shot them dead in the early morning hours and then dumped their bodies into a well more than 15 meters (50 feet) deep. The bodies were found on May 3 after several days of searching.
The Baja California prosecutor’s office announced on May 5, 2024, that it had arrested García, known as “el Kekas,” identifying him as the suspected gunman in the killings of the three foreigners.
State authorities said García had a criminal history in Ensenada involving alleged drug dealing, unlawful entry into a home, domestic violence and vehicle theft.
García’s former partner, Ary Gisell Silva Raya, and two of his alleged accomplices, Irineo Francisco “N” and Ángel Jesús “N,” were also arrested in the case.
Silva Raya, whom authorities found in possession of a cellphone belonging to one of the victims, agreed to an abbreviated trial and in November was sentenced to 20 years in prison for aggravated robbery with violence and vehicle theft with violence.
The prosecution’s account and evidence
State prosecutor María Elena Andrade alleged that the attackers wanted to steal the tires from the foreigners’ pickup truck and that the victims resisted.
“The attackers pull out a gun they were carrying and kill the person who initially resisted the robbery, then turn on the other two,” she added.
Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved.
