Need help caring for an older Mainer? Start here
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Caring for an aging Mainer can be overwhelming, but you don’t have to navigate it alone.
From respite care and transportation to counseling and legal help, a range of resources is available to support older Mainers and the family members and friends caring for them.
Here are some key agencies in each county and a look at what they offer.
ANDROSCOGGIN, FRANKLIN AND OXFORD COUNTIES
SeniorsPlus is based in Lewiston and has satellite offices in Norway and Wilton.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Care coordination (connecting people with home care services from respite to in-home community service (assistance with living independently)
- Fiscal intermediary services for clients with long-term care needs (handling employer and employee paperwork, payroll, tax filings and workers’ compensation coverage)
- Nutrition services (access to the Meals on Wheels meal delivery program, social dining opportunities and restaurant vouchers that offer reduced prices at participating locations)
- Specialized services (coordination of emergency response systems, respite in a facility, environmental modification and assistive technology).
Connect at seniorsplus.org and 207-795-4010.
AROOSTOOK COUNTY
Aroostook Agency on Aging, based in Presque Isle, serves older people in northern Maine.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Home care personal support (in-home help with daily activities)
- MaineCare in-home services, care partner education and support
- Volunteer programs and the Money Minders program (free bill-paying service where trained volunteers can help with setting up a budget, paying bills and managing a checkbook).
- MaineCare Toolkit which provides help with navigating community MaineCare or MaineCare in-home services applications and securing financial assistance for them.
Connect at aroostookaging.org and 207-764-3396.
For transportation needs, head to aroostooktransportation.org to access Aroostook Regional Transportation, which helps people throughout Aroostook County get to appointments, shop and stay active in their community.
CUMBERLAND AND YORK COUNTIES
Southern Maine Agency on Aging provides resources, services and information to empower adults, adults with disabilities and their caregivers.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Information for older Mainers about day programs, nutrition (including the Meals on Wheels meal delivery program) and fall prevention
- Medicare counseling
- Money Minders (help with money management/bill paying)
- Phone Pal program, which pairs volunteers who will call 1-3 times a week for friendly conversations
- Resources for assistance with caregiving, including information on benefit programs, adult day programming and community resources
- Classes are offered on topics such as caring for someone with dementia, finding community resources, stress management and problem solving
- Southern Maine Agency on Aging’s State Respite Care Program supports family caregivers of people with dementia, and in some cases the program reimburses some of the cost for someone else to provide care
- Regularly scheduled support groups take place at the Biddeford office, and in the community to help connect caregivers with one another
Connect at smaaa.org and 207-396-6500.
HANCOCK, PENOBSCOT, PISCATAQUIS AND WASHINGTON COUNTIES
Eastern Area Agency on Aging, based in Brewer, provides information, options and services for older adults, adults with disabilities and caregivers.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- Family Caregiver Program (information and assistance, respite program and support groups)
- Commodity Supplemental Food Program (30-pound monthly food boxes with shelf stable grocery items and cheese available to low-income adults 60 years or older)
- Legal services for Maine elders, Medicare counseling, Meals on Wheels (meal delivery program)
- Money Minders (help with money management/bill paying).
Connect at eaaa.org and 207-941-2865.
KENNEBEC, KNOX, LINCOLN, SAGADAHOC, SOMERSET AND WALDO COUNTIES
Spectrum Generations is based in Augusta, and also has offices in Waterville, Damariscotta, Belfast, Hallowell and Brunswick.
Here are some of the services they offer:
- We Sustain Maine (locally grown food provided from Maine farms)
- Meals on Wheels (meal delivery program)
- MaineCare services (assistance with arranging home care programs)
- Money Minders (help with money management/bill paying)
- Caregiving services (support groups, adult day programs, state respite care program).
Spectrum Generations also covers Brunswick and Harpswell in Cumberland County.
Connect at spectrumgenerations.org and 800-639-1553.
OTHER RESOURCES
- Legal Services for Maine Elders is based in Augusta. Its mission is to protect the rights of older Mainers by providing free legal services to people ages 60 and older. They also advocate for people facing challenges when accessing Medicare benefits. Connect at maineelse.org and 207-623-1797.
- Office of Aging and Disability Services supports Maine’s older population by promoting the highest level of independence, health and safety throughout Maine. They oversee several programs for older adults, including long-term care programs. Connect at maine.gov/dhhs/oads and 207-287-9200.
- Maine Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program provides free, confidential advocacy for people receiving long-term care services and their families. The program investigates complaints and helps consumers understand their rights and options when problems arise with nursing homes, assisted living, home care, hospice and other services. Staff can also answer questions about finding and paying for care, and what to do if services are denied, reduced or terminated. Connect at maineombudsman.org and 207-621-1079.
- The Iris Network is a Portland-based nonprofit that helps Mainers who are blind or have low vision live independently. Services include low-vision evaluations and rehabilitation, mobility and orientation training, adaptive technology and help with everyday tasks. The organization serves people of all ages, including older adults experiencing age-related vision loss. Connect at theiris.org and 207-774-6273.

title: BDN reporter wins Maine Press Association's Journalist of the Year
text:
A Bangor Daily News investigative reporter and editor was named Maine Press Association’s Journalist of the Year at the association’s annual conference Saturday in South Portland.
Callie Ferguson, deputy investigations editor for the BDN’s Maine Focus team, won the award in recognition of her reporting on the impact of controversial federal policies on the state
BDN Politics and Investigations Editor Michael Shepherd called Ferguson the paper’s “lead voice on two of last year’s biggest stories in Maine: immigration enforcement and the Trump administration’s fight with the state over federal money.”
Ferguson had been “the most decorated newspaper journalist in Maine who has not yet won” the Maine Journalist of the Year nod, Shepherd wrote in a letter nominating her for the honor.
“Her career has been built on holding police and other powerful people accountable,” Shepherd wrote. “What I think makes Callie special is her ability to work with sources on really difficult topics while also getting what she needs, but doing it all in a way that still keeps her in good standing. She works in such a way that she maintains a great deal of credibility among sources who are often the target of her reporting.”
Earlier this month, Ferguson was named the AP Sevellon Brown NE Journalist of the Year, a prize named in honor of the late journalist Sevellon Brown.
The AP award recognized Ferguson’s coverage of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s raids and arrests in Maine, highlighting the lives of working immigrants who found themselves caught up in President Donald Trump’s push to ramp up deportations.
Also on Saturday, Ferguson and Josh Keefe of The Maine Monitor were honored by The Center for Integrity in News Reporting for a series they co-wrote titled ‘Stop Punching Him,’ about a Limerick man who was repeatedly punched in his face by a Maine State Trooper who pinned him to the ground after he had been handcuffed.
Ferguson and BDN Investigative Reporter Sawyer Loftus on Saturday also received the MPA’s Judy Meyer Freedom of Information Award in the contest’s daily weekend division, for their reporting on ICE detentions in Maine. Kathleen Phalen Tomaselli, a reporter for the BDN-owned The County newspaper in Aroostook County, won the Judy Meyer Award in the weekly division for her reporting on public surveillance cameras in Houlton.
Other honors Ferguson has received include being named a 2022 Livingston Award finalist, a 2023 New York Times local investigations fellow, and winning the New England First Amendment Coalition’s Michael Donoghue Freedom of Information Award and a Sidney Award for her contribution to the BDN’s “Lawmen Off Limits” series investigating the lack of accountability among Maine’s sheriffs.
BDN Staff members were awarded several individual honors at the conference.
First-place awards in writing and editorial categories:
Courts Story – Callie Ferguson, Police turned off the cameras
Editorial – BDN Editorial Board, Threats and dysfunction
Continuing story – Sawyer Loftus, Billy Kobin and Michael Shepherd: Graham Platner fallout
Business/Economics Story – Daniel O’Connor, Train grinds life to a halt
Sports Headline – Larry Mahoney, How much do these high school players love hockey? They travel 100 miles just to practice
Editorial Cartoonist – George Danby
In advertising, first-place wins went to Marcie Coombs, Campaign or Series; Callie Picard, Best Supplement Cover; and Amy Allen, Supplement/Special Section.
The paper also earned several second- and third-place awards.
Second-place advertising and marketing winners were Coombs, Allen and the BDN Philanthropy Team, with Allen, Coombs and Picard also earning third-place honors.
Linda Coan O’Kresik was awarded second-place photography honors in both the People and Spot News categories, and she picked up a third-place win for a scenic photo.
Second-place design honors went to Becky Bowden, Front Page Design; and the BDN Editorial Board, Editorial Page.
Second-place writing awards went to Mahoney, Ferguson, Loftus, Elizabeth Walztoni, Judy Harrison, Marie Weidmayer and Rob Glover. Third-place honors went to Walztoni, O’Connor, the BDN Editorial Board, Kathleen O’Brien, Kasey Turman, Weidmayer, Mahoney, Bill Trotter and columnist Bob Duchesne.
Leela Stockley earned a third-place nod in the Illustration/Graphic category, while Linda Kamp-Davis took home a third-place award for the BDN Sports Section.
The Bangor Daily News won third-place honors in the contest’s Print Excellence category.
An earlier version of this story contained inaccurate information about which city where the conference was held.

title: Peaks woman tells late sister’s story to caution against faith healing
text:
PEAKS ISLAND — On the last weekend of September, as she has since 2004, Janis Price placed a memorial in the Maine Sunday Telegram for her younger sister, Nancy. Nancy, who didn’t live past the age of 7, would have been 70 this year.
Price believes no obituary ever ran where they grew up in Texas and, despite her efforts, hasn’t been able to locate an autopsy report. From what Price has gathered from records, Nancy died overnight on a Saturday and was cremated that Monday. Her death certificate lists the cause as “probably malignant lymphoma.” As far as Price knows, Nancy never saw a doctor. No one in her family did.
“That Sunday morning, they woke me up and said, ‘Nancy’s gone,’ and that was it,” recalled Price, whose parents wouldn’t explain what happened.
Price was 8 years old at the time — Irish twins, her mother called them. The oldest of five siblings, the sisters did everything together: rode bikes and horses, played kickball and pick-up sticks. At a green wrought-iron table that’s now in Price’s living room on Peaks Island, they’d sit and eat mangoes with their toes curled around the bars at the base.
Eventually, though, Nancy couldn’t play anymore or go to school, either. She vomited all the time, and lumps had formed on her neck — these were the effects of not being faithful enough, she was told.
Letters from a prominent Christian Science practitioner, which Price found among her late mother’s belongings, tell Nancy that, if she truly believed God could make her neck heal, the lumps would go away.
Price thinks her mother, who grew up exposed to Christian Science, became avid about faith healing after her own sister was treated with medication for appendicitis and was never the same. In a way, she can understand her mother’s thinking. In more ways, she can’t.
Both of her parents were educated; her mother graduated from Southern Methodist University, and her father was a lawyer, which makes it harder for Price to fathom how he could go along with it.
The church says it doesn’t prohibit its members from seeing doctors but that they often choose prayer-based healing because they have found it effective.
Price feels lucky not to have had a life-threatening illness as a child, though she remembers a badly stubbed toe that she was left to tend to herself when it started oozing and being put to bed after falling off a swing set and hitting her head.
The emotional pain of being raised this way, however, has taken its own toll.
Price since has become an advocate for eliminating religious exemptions to child-neglect laws and vaccine mandates, lending her support to organizations still trying to make those changes in places like Idaho, where children in faith-healing families continue to die from treatable illnesses.
In Maine, she’s told her story to legislators and written letters to the editor, as she felt compelled to do in February after the state started reporting new cases of measles.
She keeps all the public records and research she’s gathered — with her thoughts written on pink and yellow sticky notes — in a filing cabinet in the corner of her bedroom.
Underneath her bed is a box with more personal items related to her sister: sympathy notes to their mother and letters Nancy wrote herself, along with her red pencil case from school and favorite book, “The Lonely Doll Learns a Lesson.”
Hanging above her pillow are portraits of her and Nancy, painted by their grandmother, and beside the bed are two rocking chairs, one a little bigger than the other, where the sisters used to sit. They remind Price of how close they were.
“She was once here. She was a real person,” Price said.
PATH TO HEALING
Being on Peaks Island, where she can watch the crashing ocean waves, has been healing for Price. It took her a long time to get to this point.
Looking back on her childhood after 50 years of therapy, she can see how the effects of her sister’s death started to take hold.
Within a few months, she was wetting the bed. Streaming tears would come out of nowhere, like when her sixth-grade choir started singing “Puff, the Magic Dragon.” In eighth grade, when she heard another girl vomiting in the bathroom, she ran out with her hands covering her ears.
When she left home, it took a more self-destructive form — risky behavior, failed marriages, severed friendships and suicide attempts.
“It just seemed like a blinding series of one trauma or crisis after another,” Price said.
While she was living in Lexington, Kentucky, a chance encounter at a restaurant with a man from Vinalhaven led Price to visit Maine. She made return trips for years, until she ended up moving to Peaks in 1999, raising two of her daughters here and starting to find peace.
“I wanted something completely different, like nothing I’d ever seen before, and, boy, did I get it,” said Price, who gets around the island in a green golf cart.
In 2003, she held the memorial service that her sister never had, with photos and candles set up at a friend’s house overlooking the ocean. She had a band play “Puff, the Magic Dragon” and served tacos, one of Nancy’s favorite foods.
Price has given testimony in front of the Maine State Legislature, including in 2005, for a bill that removed religious exemptions to reporting child abuse; in 2019, for one that eliminated non-medical exemptions for vaccines; and again last year, when there was an attempt to restore them.
“Nancy’s story is just, I guess, really compelling,” she said, proudly adding that the state’s vaccination rate has since risen to at least 95%.
She wants as many people as possible to know what her sister went through and what other children still do, which is why she runs the remembrance in the newspaper every year.
Price credits Nancy with saving her life, by providing an example of bravery on her darkest days.
“I don’t want her to be forgotten,” she said.
Price still plugs her ears at the sound of choking. She takes antidepressants to relieve her overwhelming sadness and help her sleep. She doesn’t talk to her other siblings, because they don’t see eye to eye on much. But she has close friends now and a longtime partner who lives in Saco and takes her on sailing trips. She’s in the island’s ukulele band, a drumming circle and the Spanish club.
Several years ago, she moved to Windham, to be closer to her first grandchild, but started struggling and felt the need to get back to Peaks. She applied for senior housing on the island but was told it would be a long time before she’d hear anything.
One night, when she was feeling like she couldn’t go on living any longer, she thought of all that Nancy endured to help her get through it. The next day, she got a call saying an apartment had become available on the island.
She believes her sister is still thinking of her, too.

title: UMaine football looking to snap 5-game losing streak
text:
The University of Maine’s football team, mired in its first five-game losing streak since the 2022 season, will look to snap its skid when it entertains Bryant University on Saturday at 1 p.m.
UMaine has won the last four meetings between the two teams, and seven of the last eight.
UMaine is 1-5 overall and 1-2 in the Coastal Athletic Association while Bryant, which was picked ninth in the coaches’ preseason poll, is a surprising 4-2 and 2-0, respectively.
Sean Green, the former state championship head coach at Portland and Cape Elizabeth High Schools, will make his debut as interim offensive coordinator/quarterbacks coach in the game after replacing Mikahael Waters. Waters was fired after UMaine’s 24-16 loss to Sacred Heart on Oct. 3.
The Black Bears didn’t play last weekend.
Bryant lost to in-state rival Brown University last Saturday, 28-13, even though Bryant junior quarterback Brennan Myer completed 29 of 37 passes for 308 yards and sophomore wide receiver Shamar Fowles caught 12 of those passes for 135 yards. They hooked up on one touchdown pass.
UMaine’s offense is dead last among 13 teams in the conference in points (14.5) and yards per game (270.2) and the Black Bears will be facing a Bryant defense that is third best in the conference in points allowed (23.3).
UMaine head football coach Jordan Stevens called Bryant a very good football team.
“They’re a really disciplined team. They take care of the ball really well,” Stevens said. “They play complementary football in all three phases (offense, defense, special teams). You’ve seen that throughout the season.”
Bryant has great receivers, Stevens added.
“That’s going to be a challenge for us. They have size as well and they’re going to go get the ball. And they have a run game to go along with that,” Stevens said.
Defensively, Stevens said Bryant has a tough, physical, swarming defense.
Bulldogs head coach Chris Merritt said he has a “tremendous amount of respect for Maine” and said his team is in for a dogfight.
“Even though they may be a different team than they’ve been the past two years, they’ve taken us behind the shed in the first half of each game and gotten after us, outscoring us 69-0,” Merritt said.
For the first time this season, UMaine alternated quarterbacks in the Sacred Heart game with regular starter Eddie Buehler completing just one of his five passes for 13 yards before Caden Drezek came on to complete 12 of 28 passes for 141 yards and a touchdown and he finished the game.
On the season, Buehler has completed 54.6 percent of his passes for 828 yards and four touchdowns with six interceptions. Drezek has completed 42.5 percent of his passes for 201 yards and a TD without being intercepted.
A resurgent Rashawn Marshall has rushed for 172 yards on 27 carries in his last two games for an average of 6.4 yards per carry. He has rushed for 348 yards on 77 carries on the season.
Nick Laughlin and Evan Wallace have been the top receivers. Laughlin has 23 catches for 211 yards and Wallace has 18 for 154.
Linebackers Sam Oppenheimer (58 tackles) and Noah Carpenter (42 tackles) and strong safety Jeremiah McGill (44 tackles) have led the UMaine defense and defensive end Chris Bacon has a team-high three sacks.
Oppenheimer is third in the conference in tackles and second in solo tackles (36). He is seventh in the country among players at 124 Football Championship Subdivision teams in solo tackles.
He also has two interceptions and a forced fumble.
For Bryant, Myer has completed 63.2 percent of his passes for 1,075 yards and four TDs with two interceptions. Sean Wilson Jr. has snared 24 passes for 304 yards, Fowles has caught 22 for 322 yards and Jose Leon has 17 for 164 yards including 14 catches in his last two games.
O.J. Ross (66 carries-277 yards) and Jordan Bennett (53-for-224) are the Bulldogs’ leading rushers.
Linebacker Drake Lusk (48 tackles), cornerback Olatunde Mkparu (33 tackles) and free safety Ezra Carter (30) are their top tacklers.
The six Maine Division III football teams will also be in action on Saturday.
Bangor’s Husson University, 1-4 overall and 1-1 in the Conference of New England, will travel to Henniker, New Hampshire, for a conference game against New England College (1-4, 0-2) at noon. New England College is in just its third season of football since reinstating the program following a 51-year absence.
The state’s two other Conference of New England programs, Biddeford’s University of New England and Castine’s Maine Maritime Academy, will square off in Biddeford at noon with each gunning for its first victory of the season. Both are 0-5 and 0-2.
Maine Maritime Academy has lost 37 consecutive games.
The three New England Small College Athletic Conference teams are all 0-4 for the first time since the 2019 season. And they are all taking on 4-0 teams.
Bates will visit Wesleyan and Colby will entertain Amherst in 1 p.m. contests, and Bowdoin will trek to Trinity for a 1:30 p.m. game.

title: America's politically divided Jewish community braces for Israel's elections
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — Jewish Americans feel they have a lot at stake in this month’s contentious elections in Israel as three years of Mideast conflicts rile up emotions across the United States, from street protests to the midterm races.
But they are sharply divided along political, religious and often generational lines on the preferred outcome in a vote that’s perceived as a referendum on Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and held against the backdrop of the enduring trauma of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, which triggered the war in Gaza.
Netanyahu’s supporters, especially among Orthodox Jews, believe he’s protecting a country they love as central to their identity. Many liberal and younger Jewish Americans believe his policies have harmed Israel’s global standing, engendering widespread anger that threatens them in the U.S., too.
The moment is particularly fraught as antisemitism and antisemitic violence grow. Even harsh critics of Netanyahu’s actions, whether over Gaza or Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank, argue that blame for attacks against Jews can’t solely be laid at his feet.
“A lot of American Jews are really torn. They want to shout from the rooftops, ‘Stop the pogroms in the West Bank,’ but also yell at everybody, ‘Stop with allegations of genocide and double standards against Israel,’” said Rabbi Dan Levin of Temple Beth El in Boca Raton, Florida.
Israel is important to Jewish Americans’ identity
Levin’s large Reform synagogue is one of many across the U.S. hosting educational programs this fall because congregants feel “deeply emotionally invested” in the Israeli elections, even if, as non-citizens, they can’t vote.
Under Israel’s complex, multiparty political system, the Oct. 27 election outcome is impossible to forecast. Polls suggest a tight race between a Netanyahu-led bloc and an alliance of rivals for control of the government.
Many Jewish Americans have Israeli friends and family. More broadly, support for Israel is a key component of the religious identity of many U.S. Jewish adults ages 45 and older, particularly those who identify as religiously Jewish, according to a recent AP-NORC poll.
The largest Jewish denomination in the United States is Reform, which emphasizes progressive values. Many Reform Jews see no contradiction between their liberalism and their Zionism — understood as the Jewish people’s aspiration “to live as a free people in our land,” said Rabbi Josh Weinberg of the Union for Reform Judaism, an umbrella group for more than 800 Reform synagogues in North America.
But they worry about the growing power of the ultra-Orthodox in Israel’s political and religious life, as well as settlement policies and the treatment of Palestinians in the West Bank, that they perceive as contrary to their values, Weinberg added.
“If Netanyahu wins, I worry very much about the young generation of American Jews who may continue to be, I’ll put it nicely, disenchanted, and who might just say ‘OK, that’s it. I’m giving up on Israel,’” he said.
Only about 4 in 10 religious Jewish adults under 45 in the United States say that supporting Israel is “extremely” or “very” important for their Jewish identity, prioritizing instead other forms of connection, like celebrating Jewish holidays, according to the AP-NORC poll.
Antisemitism is a key concern
In the same poll, a majority of Jewish adults said prejudice against Jewish people is an “extremely” or “very” serious problem in the United States today.
As the Israeli elections approach, many communities are worrying about their effects on antisemitism.
“Some American Jews believe a different style of prime minister, one more similar to earlier ones who constantly talked about the desire for peace, will change the way American Jews themselves are viewed,” said Jonathan Sarna, professor emeritus of American Jewish History at Brandeis University.
Even Netanyahu critics, however, don’t believe antisemitic acts would stop if Israel changes its government, especially when outrage at his administration’s actions toward Palestinians is used to incite violence against all Jews regardless of nationality or political leanings.
“‘There is only one solution, intifada revolution’ — we hear that as a call to rise up and use violence against Jews,” Weinberg said of a popular protest chant referring to the violent Palestinian uprising. “So when someone says that in Ramallah, that’s one thing. When someone says that in Minneapolis, what exactly are they calling for? That seems pretty clearly to us antisemitic.”
But some think different Israeli policies would help stem the tide.
“Somebody who decides that they’re going to drive a car into a synagogue or attack Jews on the street, that is their responsibility. You can’t blame that on Israel’s actions,” said Rabbi Jill Jacobs, CEO of T’ruah, a rabbinic human rights organization. “But … I think that it’s going to be a very scary time for Jews around the world if there’s another Netanyahu government and if it continues on its policy of expanding occupation, ethnic cleansing, and forever war.”
Stanley Weinstein, an Orthodox Jew from Florida, rejects much of the criticism of the Israeli military and policymaking, especially given the threats the state faces from militant groups like Hamas in Gaza as well as in other conflicts that keep simmering despite tenuous ceasefires, including in Lebanon and with Iran.
Weinstein sees Israel’s security as crucial, especially given the rise in anti-Israel and antisemitic rhetoric among left- and right-wing American political figures that he has observed even from his home in the diverse and vibrant Jewish community of Miami Beach.
“I am appalled as an American. I am appalled as a Jew. And I say, thank God there is an Israel,” he said.
Netanyahu, Trump and close elections with unity at stake
For Jewish Americans, Israel also looms large in the U.S. midterms — when voters decide who controls Congress for the next two years. The Nov. 3 elections come a week after Israelis go to their polls.
From New York City to Michigan and beyond, support for Palestinians, and withdrawal of U.S. aid to Israel, are rising issues among Democratic voters.
Both the Israeli and U.S. elections could affect the two countries’ longstanding alliance. It has been particularly close — though not without recent strains, especially over the joint Iran war — under the Trump and Netanyahu administrations.
Even as some Israeli policies have become controversial in the United States, among American Jews there is still substantial support for the state of Israel, said Jason Isaacson, chief policy officer for the American Jewish Committee, a prominent advocacy group that strives to broadly represent Jews in the U.S. and abroad.
“There is strong support for the continuation of the U.S.-Israel relationship and for the necessity of Israel’s survival,” he said.
Regardless of their faith and politics, some Jewish Americans are most concerned about the prospect of further divisions driven by Israel’s elections.
“This may be the most consequential election in modern Israeli history, because the nature of the current administration is so fraught with division that it’s ripping the people apart,” said Levin, the Reform rabbi in Boca Raton.
Weinstein, the Orthodox congregant in Miami Beach, believes Netanyahu has been doing “a terrific job.” But he shares the same worry for the future.
“The biggest issue in Israel today, which doesn’t exist, is unity. To me, that is what is at stake,” he said. “Is there a way to unify the country, unify the people?”
___

title: It’s not just you. There are more Maine political ads than ever this year.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The gym. The doctor’s office. The living room. The car.
The store. The salon. The restaurant and bar.
Whether out and about or trying to relax at home, Mainers have heard or seen more than their fair share of political ads ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election headlined by races for the U.S. Senate, House of Representatives and governor. And don’t forget the glossy pamphlets — sometimes multiple in one day — that have arrived in mailboxes.
Mainers’ collective feelings — frustration, annoyance, ignorance or acceptance — cross ideological and demographic lines, putting political advertising in a rare category of grievances that largely foster bipartisan agreement.
That extends to politics in general. The Pew Research Center found in a 2024 survey that 65% of Americans reported feeling “exhausted” most or all of the time when thinking about politics.
“I am so sick, as most Mainers are, of the negative take and dark tone of the visuals of these ads,” said Kat Taylor, 70, an unenrolled voter who lives in Argyle Township in Penobscot County.
The retiree who previously worked at the University of Maine said she is hit with ads throughout her day, from when she tunes into NEWS CENTER Maine in the early morning to when she walks outside to check the mailbox.
Inside a Portland bar on a recent evening, a college football game was on one of the TVs. Nearly every commercial break featured at least one campaign ad.
The refrains are familiar by now, such as the “I’m Troy Jackson” opening line in one of the pro-Jackson ads, or the “Taxin’ Jackson” criticism in an ad from a pro-Republican group. (That negative ad recently and erroneously went on air in Portland, Oregon, instead of Portland, Maine.)
For those wondering if there are actually more ads in front of them this election year in Maine, the answer is yes.
The numbers prove it.
THOUSANDS UPON THOUSANDS OF ADS
The total number of ads that have aired in Maine’s official media markets of Portland-Auburn, Bangor and Presque Isle is dizzying.
According to the advertising tracking insight firm AdImpact, the Portland-Auburn market has seen more than 24,100 political ads air on TV since the week of Aug. 30. The Bangor market has seen more than 18,100 ads air since that week, while the Presque Isle region in northern Maine has seen roughly 2,750 since then.
In the first week of October alone, 5,787 ads aired on TV across the Portland-Auburn market, or about 827 ads each day, according to AdImpact.
This deluge is possible because of record spending on Maine’s highest profile races. Candidates, their affiliated political action committees, the campaign arms of national parties and dark money groups have so far spent and reserved $315 million on ads across various platforms this election cycle in Maine, per AdImpact.
That figure surpasses the state record of around $200 million in 2020 that mostly covered the U.S. Senate race between Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Sara Gideon.
Maine is the 42nd most populous state but is the 11th most expensive state for political ad spending this cycle, according to AdImpact, which said Tuesday that the total spending will likely get to around $400 million. Republican groups are outspending Democratic groups in Maine and nationally.
But there is some consolation for those tired of all the interruptions. AdImpact initially thought that number would get as high as $490 million in Maine.
DO THE ADS ACTUALLY CONVINCE PEOPLE?
Adding to the frustration of many Mainers: Political advertising is unlikely to move the needle much in any of Maine’s key races.
The gubernatorial race to succeed outgoing Gov. Janet Mills and the 2nd Congressional District contest to succeed U.S. Rep. Jared Golden have certainly drawn attention and outside interest, but ads tied to those elections are relatively few. In the 2nd District, they’re only targeted toward Mainers living in certain regions of the state.
The tight U.S. Senate race between Collins, the Republican seeking a sixth term, and former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic challenger, is a different story.
Ads upon ads have sought to sway the undecided voters who may decide the Senate contest.
An Axios analysis of dollars spent on cable, broadcast and social media along with estimates for streaming platforms found Maine has the priciest per capita Senate race in the nation, with Republican-aligned groups spending $96.99 for each Maine adult and Democratic-aligned groups spending $69.52.
But polls show the number of voters who haven’t made up their mind in that race is minuscule. And despite all of the time, money and effort that goes into producing these ads, past studies have found the effects of political spots to be small in terms of persuading voters.
The Washington Post and George Mason University’s Schar School of Policy and Government conducted a poll of Maine’s Senate race between Sept. 30 and Oct. 5, finding just 3% of respondents did not pick between Jackson and Collins.
In the 2020 election, about 819,000 voters cast a ballot in the race that saw Collins defy the polls to beat Gideon by a comfortable margin. If roughly 3% of the electorate this year is undecided, and the voting pool stays the same size, campaigns are fighting to reach about 24,500 voters.
DEALING WITH ‘THE NASTINESS’
Steve Hamblen, a 75-year-old unenrolled voter from Sanford, said he is getting inundated with ads and political canvassers at his doorstep — a reality that he said has reaffirmed his belief that the country’s campaign finance system needs reform. The U.S. Supreme Court, however, has removed limits on how much parties and corporations can spend on elections.
“The nastiness really annoys me, but people sit there and swallow it,” Hamblen said in late August. “Make up your own mind. Don’t listen to these political ads and just fall for the one-liners.”
The ads indeed make claims that are false, misleading or only partially backed up by citations in small print that are tough for the average viewer to digest in real time.
“The ads do nothing to sway my opinion. I have never been enrolled in any party and am a critical thinker,” Taylor, the Argyle Township resident, said on a recent weekday, adding that the printed ads in her mailbox “aren’t even good for starting my wood stove or composting.”
Whether the ads end up making a difference in the outcome of the Nov. 3 election is likely unmeasurable. Whether Mainers are ready for them to go away until the next cycle is an easier thing to observe.
Peggy Belkenny, an 83-year-old Democrat from Auburn, said last month she wants candidates and their ads to focus on what they would do to help people if they’re elected to office. And if they don’t?
“We’re gonna put them on a plane and send them all to Siberia,” she said. “One way.”
Staff Writer Randy Billings contributed to this report.

title: Coastal homes burn as hot winds fuel California fires
text:
Coastal homes burn as hot winds fuel California fires
A fast-moving fire fueled by high winds burned at least six homes in Southern California on Friday, engulfing expensive coastal properties and prompting thousands to evacuate.
Black smoke — visible from miles away — billowed over tennis courts and swimming pools while firefighters doused blazing homes in San Juan Capistrano in Orange County. Some homeowners sprayed water on their properties before heeding evacuation orders.
One firefighter suffered heat exhaustion in the blaze that was less than a square mile as of Friday evening, said Chief Mark Backoff with the Orange County Fire Authority. Officials have not said how it started.
Howard Hart, a councilmember for San Juan Capistrano, said he and his wife doused their roof with water and moved propane tanks away from their home before they evacuated Friday with a to-go bag.
Laura Hart hasn't had to evacuate due to fire in the more than five decades she's lived in the community, she said.
"This doesn't usually happen to us, we usually see it on the news," she said. "We always pray to God it's not us, but yeah, it was today."
The Norte Fire started in the coastal city of San Clemente and wind drove it into San Juan Capistrano. An evacuation shelter has opened in each city.
It was one of several fires in the region hit by dry, warm gusts known as Santa Anas, which blow from the interior and toward the coast. The strongest winds were expected through Friday afternoon but conditions that increase the fire risk were expected to last through Saturday night, with a heat advisory in effect until 8 p.m. Saturday on the Orange County and San Diego County coast, the National Weather Service said.
Tens of thousands of people in the state are without power after their electricity was turned off. A separate fire by the Marine Corps base Camp Pendleton shut down for hours a section of Interstate 5 that is a major artery connecting Orange County to San Diego. That added hours to commutes throughout Southern California.
The coastal cities are surrounded by hillsides. San Juan Capistrano, a city of 35,000, is known for horse trails and the historic Mission San Juan Capistrano. San Clemente, which is home to 62,000 people, is known as a "Spanish village by the sea" and popular with beachgoers and surfers.
"The fire is right up on the city," said Victor Cabral, a San Clemente council member. "It's on the perimeter of our homes on the north end."
Nine schools were also closed Friday in San Juan Capistrano, the Capistrano Unified School District said.
Nearby residents were also on edge as smoke darkened the sky.
Wyoming resident Shannon Needham was visiting her mother at her assisted living facility in Dana Point just north of San Clemente when she learned about the fire.
The facility director told her that two buses would be on standby in case they needed to evacuate, Needham said.
"You could hear the fire trucks, you could hear the helicopters and everything above. And it was so smoky, it was just dark smoke," Needham said.
Some of California's worst wildfires have been sparked by power equipment, and utilities in recent years have begun proactively shutting off power in dry winds. More than 200,000 customers in California were without electricity as of Friday, according to poweroutage.com.
The weather service also issued a red flag warning for parts of central and Northern California through Friday morning, saying any fires would spread rapidly.
___
Rodriguez reported from San Francisco. Associated Press writer Jaimie Ding contributed from Los Angeles.

title: School bus carrying 6 nonverbal kids was missing for 4 hours, probe finds
text:
NEW YORK (WABC) — A school bus carrying six nonverbal students went missing for four hours, authorities in New York City said.
Investigation details timeline
Anastasia Coleman is the head of the Special Commissioner of Investigation for the New York City School District, an independent watchdog group. She said a former Consolidated Bus Transit driver and matron failed to drop off the 6- to 8-year-old students at P.S. 289 by 9 a.m. on Dec. 16 of last year.
According to Coleman, the driver was filling in that day and told investigators he drove to two incorrect Brooklyn-area schools before getting the correct address from dispatch around 10:40 that morning.
“They’re nonverbal, so they can’t tell you what happened,” Coleman said. “One of the children was lying down and had her diaper off and had urinated.”
Around 10 a.m., school staff tried calling Consolidated Bus Transit to locate the children and notified the Department of Education at 11:45 a.m. The school called Consolidated again and was told the bus would arrive by noon.
A parent tracking her children on the bus using AirTags called the school in a panic, and the New York City Police Department was alerted.
The bus arrived at PS 289 at 1:25 p.m.
“He said that he was near the school and he’d be there in 15 minutes, and it took hours after that,” one parent said.
Investigators said the bus matron, who was also on temporary assignment that day, did not alert anyone to the events that morning.
Company response
Consolidated Bus Transit released a statement saying both employees have been on administrative leave since the incident 10 months ago, pending investigation proceedings as required by the labor collective agreement. The company said the employees are not permitted on any of its buses and have no student interactions.
“Knowing all the buses, I’d definitely be in a panic,” one parent said.
Parents said they hope an incident like this does not happen again.

title: Maine Trust for Local News wins more than 100 awards at annual press contest
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The Maine Trust for Local News, the state’s largest news organization, won more than 100 combined awards at an annual ceremony hosted Saturday by the Maine Press Association.
The Maine Trust, the parent company of the Portland Press Herald/Maine Sunday Telegram, the Sun Journal in Lewiston, Kennebec Journal in Augusta and Morning Sentinel in Waterville, won top awards in a number of general categories. For general excellence among daily/weekend newspapers, the Sun Journal won first place, followed by the Kennebec Journal in second and the Bangor Daily News in third.
The Portland Press Herald won first place for general excellence in advertising, followed by the Sun Journal in second and Central Maine Sunday in third.
For general excellence in digital, the Portland Press Herald’s website, pressherald.com, won first place. Placing second in digital was the Maine Monitor’s website, themainemonitor.org, and third was Centralmaine.com, the website of the Kennebec Journal and Morning Sentinel.
Allison McCann, vice president of advertising and business development for the Maine Trust for Local News, was selected as “Businessperson of the Year.” The award recognizes an employee on the business side of a news organization whose work has been distinguished over a period of time.
“I’ve worked alongside Alli for more than a decade, and I can say without hesitation that I wouldn’t want to do this work without her,” said Stefanie Manning, president and publisher of the Maine Trust for Local News. “She understands our business, believes deeply in what we do and brings an incredible amount of energy, creativity and determination to making us successful. When Alli is in the room, I know our interests are well represented. She’s a trusted partner, a strong leader and someone who genuinely cares about the people she works with. This recognition is so well deserved, and I couldn’t be happier for her.”
In addition, Melissa Pritchard, who retired recently as the longtime creative services director at the Maine Trust, was selected as the “Mentor of the Year.” The award honors an employee who has offered support, encouragement or advice that has helped others in their organization grow or achieve in the news industry.
“It was an exceptional year of journalism across Maine,” Executive Editor Carolyn Fox said. “Congratulations to our company recipients on the well-deserved recognition as well as the rest of the MPA winners.”
The press association’s conference and awards ceremony was held at the DoubleTree by Hilton Hotel in Portland, and also featured a Hall of Fame induction ceremony for three former Maine Trust journalists.
JOURNALISM HONORS
The Press Herald won 56 individual awards, including 26 first-place wins.
Among some of the journalists recognized with top awards was Kelley Bouchard, for news coverage exploring how a Maine couple gave their $1.3 million retirement savings to bitcoin scammers; Drew Bonifant, for a sports news story examining why concussions are high in girls soccer; and Megan Gray, for an outdoors story describing the 250-mile Can-Am Crown International Sled Dog Races in Aroostook County.
Gregory Rec, chief photographer for the Press Herald, won the “Best in Show” photography award for his Dec. 30, 2025, photo of Dillon Gray of Mt. Blue taking down Brady Ouellette of Noble during the Noble Wrestling Invitational at Noble High School in Berwick.
For the second year in a row, Press Herald columnists Travis Lazarczyk and Leslie Bridgers also won top honors for their columns about sports and culture, respectively.
The Sun Journal had 17 individual awards, including five first-place wins. Some of the top awards went to Matthew Jaroncyk, for a spot news story about Lewiston residents cleaning up after a destructive water main break; and Rose Lincoln, for a lifestyle feature story about a Newry man who keeps game from going to waste for hunters who can’t cool their own meat before its processed.
The Kennebec Journal and Morning Sentinel had 21 individual awards, including five first-place awards. Top winners included Joe Phelan, for an online news video that goes behind the scenes at Brownville’s food pantry for deer; and Anna Chadwick, who had best spot news photo for the scene after a home explosion and best people photo from a dress rehearsal for “The Nutcracker.”
HALL OF FAME
The Maine Press Association also inducted three veteran journalists — Andy Molloy, Mike Lowe and Tux Turkel — into its Hall of Fame during a luncheon. The association said the three honorees made lasting contributions to Maine journalism through photojournalism, sports reporting and enterprise coverage, reflecting a shared commitment to accuracy and informing their communities.
Molloy spent 30 years as a photojournalist at the Kennebec Journal in Augusta, earning recognition for his news instincts, compelling images and deep connections throughout central Maine. Molloy, who died this spring at 57 after a decade-long battle with a rare form of cancer, was also an accomplished journalist who frequently broke news and developed sources across the region. Beyond his journalism, Molloy was remembered for mentoring colleagues and providing practical and personal support to fellow journalists and community members facing difficult circumstances.
Lowe spent four decades covering sports for the Portland Press Herald and Maine Sunday Telegram, where his work ranged from major national and international events to high school championships across Maine. During his career, which began in 1982 and ended with his retirement in 2022, Lowe covered seven Super Bowls, the Portland Pirates’ Calder Cup championship run, the Little League World Series and the 2008 Summer Olympics in Beijing. He also produced enterprise and investigative reporting on issues including concussions, the cost of youth sports, depression among athletes and race in Maine sports. His work earned numerous honors, including four Maine Sports Writer of the Year awards from the National Sports Media Association.
Tux Turkel retired from the Portland Press Herald in 2023 after more than 40 years covering energy, environmental and utility issues, building a reputation for explaining complex subjects and holding powerful institutions accountable. His reporting examined some of Maine’s most consequential energy debates, including the closure of the Maine Yankee Nuclear Power Plant, radioactive waste storage, offshore wind development, the Central Maine Power and Hydro-Québec transmission corridor and the state’s persistently high electricity costs. Turkel became known for digging through public records and regulatory filings, scrutinizing official explanations and seeking independent experts to put technical information into context. He continues to report as a freelance journalist, including for The Maine Monitor.

title: It was a week of good, bad and ugly sports stories in Maine
text:
Rarely do we get a week in Maine chock full of sports stories that make you do a double take. This week, we got three.
These three stories will make you nod your head in gratitude, or just make you shake your head. They’ll tear at your faith in humanity, then build it back up.
The good: Joe Russo retires
The good isn’t that Russo retired after 36 season coaching the Portland High boys basketball team, it’s that we got three and a half decades of Russo and he was able to step away on his own terms.
Russo is one of 10 coaches in state history to win at least 500 games, and he won his sixth state championship this past season. Russo’s final season may have been his best coaching job. Take away the fact that some of his players missed early season practices while they prepared for the Class A football state championship game. Set aside injuries to key players throughout the regular season. Those are issues coaches have dealt with for years.
This season, with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement running around the state under the guise of the grotesquely named “Operation Catch of the Day,” Russo had at times 17% of his team out of school, kept home by parents fearful of their son being yanked off the street and taken to God knows where.
Through the most stressful time many of those teenagers have lived through, Russo kept them together. Winning 517 games and leaving a healthy collection of Gold Balls in the trophy case are fine benchmarks, but being there when your players are facing serious life-changing threats, that’s the mark of a truly great coach.
The bad: Police investigate fight at youth football game in Livermore Falls
Yeah, shouldn’t be surprised by this one. Adults have behaved like oafs at youth sports for decades. There hasn’t been a bar to sink below for years. That bar is buried cable. You need a backhoe and a dig-safe permit to reach it.
The latest incident occurred at a youth football game in Livermore Falls last Saturday. A video of the incident shows parent Donna Jewell approach coach Dylan Rider, as she’s holding a puppy. She appears to make contact with Rider as he turned toward her. Rider pushed Jewell to the ground, then made his way toward another fight between a pair of men, one of them his father.
You can be sure everyone involved is 100% confident they are in the right. In whatever heat of the moment can happen at a youth football game, nobody every stops to consider that they’re about to play the fool. In those moments, people forget youth sports should be about teaching the game and instilling fondness and respect for the game.
It’s especially disappointing that one of those involved, Rider, is an Androscoggin County Sheriff’s deputy. If anyone should be in position to de-escalate a situation like that, it’s a police officer.
It should be simple. If you’re at a youth sports game, cheer for the kids. If something happens that draws your concern, address it with calm tact, please.
Let’s review that the next time this happens, OK?
The ugly: Westbrook athletes caught in nasty online harassment
Let’s applaud the Westbrook community for standing up to bullies. When a Facebook post suggested two members of the Blue Blazes girls soccer team are transgender, Westbrook rallied around its student athletes.
Mayor David Morse released a statement calling out the abhorrent behavior. Superintendent Peter Lancia condemned the social media posts, as did State Rep. Sue Salisbury.
There’s honest discussion and debate to have on the issue of transgender athletes. It’s apparent there are bad actors who don’t want to have anything close to civil discourse. They’d rather point fingers and bully teenagers. That is abject cowardice. They don’t have a position, they have propaganda.
Thankfully, Westbrook High leadership and others stepped up and quickly came to the defense of its students. We saw how Westbrook comes together last year when the city rallied around its state-title winning football team. It’s nice to see that happen when the reason to come together isn’t a celebration.

title: Oxford Hills football shuts out Portland for big Class A North win
text:
SOUTH PARIS — The Oxford Hills football team needed to bounce back after a blowout loss to Bonny Eagle last week.
The Vikings did in a big way, dominating defending Class A North champion Portland 29-0 on Saturday afternoon.
“We knew it was just a bad night for us at Bonny Eagle and we just had to get past it and keep moving forward, ” Oxford Hills quarter Toby Oufiero said of the Vikings’ 45-6 loss to the Scots on Oct. 9. “Work hard this week, which we did. Came out here and put up a good fight and won.”
Oufiero had a touchdown pass and ran for a touchdown to lift the Vikings past the Bulldogs, who are ranked fifth in the Varsity Maine poll. The win moves the Vikings (5-1) into first place in Class A North, a position they will try to solidify in the final two games against Noble and Bangor.
Portland drops to second at 5-2.
“We just got to keep battling,” Oufiero said. “It’s not over yet, and hard work every day.”
HOW IT HAPPENED
Oxford Hills took the lead on a 4-yard rushing touchdown by Keegan Ridley in the second quarter and stretched it to 15-0 when Tucker Hilden took a shovel pass from Oufiero into the end zone from 3 yards out with 49 seconds left in the first half.
Portland struggled to sustain anything offensively. Oxford Hills pulled away in the second half with a 1-yard rushing touchdown by Oufiero and a 45-yard run by Carter Davis.
UNSUNG HERO
Mason Ridley was a playmaker throughout. He caught a 2-point conversion pass in the second quarter, was a factor defensively, and racked up yards as a punt returner.
HEARD IT HERE FIRST
• “Having only 27 guys on the team, it’s tough to, when you face teams like Bonny Eagle, when you face teams like Portland with (Alex Martin), to simulate the speed and the strength of their lines and stuff like that, so we really worked hard on just mentally being prepared.” — Oxford Hills coach Nate Danforth
• “Play a great team, you get better from that. That’s always a positive, right? Iron sharpens iron, especially in the regular season. So we’re grateful to have this experience. There’s a lot of positives we’re going to pull from it and a lot of teachable moments we’re going to pull from it.” — Portland coach Dylan Rottkov
STATISTICAL LEADERS
• Oxford Hills: Toby Oufiero (8 of 13 passing, 62 yards, touchdown; 13 rushes, 55 yards, touchdown), Keegan Ridley (eight rushes, 38 yards, touchdown; two interceptions)
• Portland: Alex Martin (23 carries, 75 yards)

title: Pumpkins spill onto roadway, causing major Halloween headache
text:
MOUNT PLEASANT, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — A load of pumpkins caused traffic delays in South Carolina Thursday afternoon.
An 18-wheeler struck a low-hanging tree limb coming off the Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge in Mount Pleasant, causing the accident.
The collision blocked the two right lanes of Coleman Boulevard as crews worked to clear the road. The road has since reopened.

title: Vatican says Pope Leo to be released from hospital Saturday, 4 days after lung cancer surgery
text:
Pope returns to Vatican days after surgery; surgeon says he should be fit for Latin America tour
Pope Leo XIV returned to the Vatican on Saturday days after lung cancer surgery, as his surgeon said there are "no clinical reasons" to prevent his planned trip to Latin America next month.
Related video above: Pope Leo's cancer diagnosis sparks push for more screenings
"The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery," Dr. Stefano Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery "in another 10 days or so."
Leo, 71, is scheduled to make an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Peru and Argentina, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes.
"As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place," Margaritora said.
Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. He left the hospital on Saturday, well ahead of the week-long hospital stay the Vatican had initially anticipated.
Pope says he feels 'much better'
"I am much better, thank you," the pope said when asked how he was as he was driven away in a black SUV.
Leo greeted patients inside the hospital accompanied by his surgeon, before waving to well-wishers outside who cried out "Holiness" as he walked to a waiting vehicle.
He paused when a 13-year-old Ukrainian girl presented him with a homemade papal doll that she said had helped her through successful cancer treatment. She had briefly met Leo at an audience in St. Peter's Square last December — an encounter she told reporters "gave her the strength to overcome the illness."
Since the surgery, Leo has shown signs of recovering well. He had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, held meetings with senior aides and celebrated Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.
He will take on his first official duty on Sunday, delivering the traditional Angelus blessing to the faithful in St. Peter's Square. It comes exactly one week after the pontiff revealed to throngs in the square that the nodule had been found and would be surgically removed — an unusually candid revelation for the Vatican.
Further tests being carried out
Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome's Gemelli hospital, also confirmed that the nodule was discovered by chance during routine abdominal examinations. It appeared as "a small spot" at the base of the lung, which extends down to the diaphragm, he said.
He added that if the spot had been higher up, "it certainly would not have been seen."
The cancer was in its early stages, and the pope had "no respiratory symptoms, and felt perfectly well," Margaritora said.
He described Tuesday's procedure to remove the lobe as "routine" and "without complications," but acknowledged that it "stirred deep feelings ... to operate on a pope, who for the first time – at least in modern history – is undergoing surgery for a malignant tumor."
The Vatican did not disclose that the tumor was malignant until after Tuesday's successful surgery. It later confirmed that the pope had undergone a biopsy before being admitted to Gemelli. Experts say the state-of-the-art Ion robotic bronchoscopy would have indicated whether the tumor was malignant and possibly whether cancer had spread to the lymph nodes.
Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor's molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor's genetic characteristics.
Margaritora said the pope's recovery so far had required "very little assistance from us."
"His determination to recover quickly has been effective in every respect. It was truly commendable," the surgeon said.

title: Top runners prevail at KVAC cross country championships
text:
AUGUSTA — There was little drama at the finish line of the Kennebec Valley Athletic Conference cross country championships Saturday. Instead, the conference’s top runners made it look easy.
Bangor’s Sam Bergmark (large school boys), Medomak Valley’s Colby Daigle (small school boys), Hampden Academy’s Addison Elliott (large school girls) and Lincoln Academy’s Karen Higgins (small school girls) won titles at Cony High School. All did so easily, with the average margin of victory between the four coming in at 1 minute, 12.8 seconds.
“It’s very hilly (here), but I enjoy it; I really like the hilly course,” said Higgins, who repeated as KVAC Small School champion. “(The conditions were good); there was only like one spot where it was a little bit slippery, but I’d say since it’s been dry, it’s absorbed it all into the trails, so it was good.”
Hampden (53 points) beat Mt. Blue (84 points) for the KVAC Large boys title, while the Lincoln boys (68) claimed the Small crown over Morse (101). Hampden and Lincoln were the girls teams champions. Hampden (21) had a wide margin over Camden Hills (65), and Lincoln (42) edged Waterville (48).
Donning the No. 1 bib, Bergmark was widely expected to lead the pack and did so, beating Lucas Demarco (17:15.6) of Mt. Blue by 36.6 seconds. Mt. Blue’s Wyatt Oliver (17:33.7), Hampden’s Jack Scott (17:38.6) and Noah Seigh (17:45.8) of Camden Hills rounded out the top five.
“I just wanted to go kind of hard because I didn’t want it to be a race — I just wanted to win,” said Bergmark, who placed third in the KVAC race year and won the Class A North title. “I just wanted to see how things were going to go, and once we got on the gravel, I went at my own speed.
Daigle’s margin of victory was even larger. The senior’s time of 17:36.9 was more than a minute faster than Cony’s Brady Cloutier (18:37.4). Lincoln’s Holden Nehrboss (18:45.4), Erskine Academy’s Brayden Dow (18:48.1) and Gardiner’s Abrahm Hasty (19:01.7) also earned top-five finishes.
Elliott and Higgins were way out in front of the girls field. Elliott’s winning time of 18:39.0 beat teammate Isabelle Clark by 1:50.2. Also finishing in the top five in the Large division were Charlotte Crowe of Mt. Ararat (20:35.9), Elsie Mann of Camden Hills (20:38.3) and Emeline Cournane of Hampden (20:43.8).
Hampden claimed its third consecutive team title. In addition to Elliott, Clark and Cournane, Silvia Ruge (21:18.6) finished sixth, Mackenzie Elliott (21:24.5) took seventh, Erin Curtis (22:18.0) placed 11th and Aubrey Shaw (22:21.3) was 12th.
“I’m just so proud of our girls,” Elliott said. “We keep getting better, and I think we ran really, really well today. I think that shared energy between (us) really fed into how we did today. … I thought (the course) was going to be really muddy and uneven, but except for the start, it was great.”
Higgins’ time of 18:56.9 was nearly a minute and a half ahead of the runner-up in the Small divison, Frida Wright of Morse (21:21.8). Hallie Coots of Nokomis (21:32.5) placed third, Carson Dunn of Waterville (21:42.6) claimed fourth, and August Miller of Lincoln (22:06.5) finished fifth.
Although the Large and Small divisions were scored separately, runners competed in the same race, creating an interesting dynamic. Elliott and Higgins were neck-and-neck for a while. It wasn’t until midway through the race that Elliott began to separate herself from Higgins, who said that going head-to-head with one of the state’s best runners was a good springboard to regionals and states.
“It was nice to have her with me, because that definitely pushed me to go under 19,” Higgins said. “Running with her, at least for the first bit, that was fun. … I think Twin Brook (next Saturday for the Class B South regional) is going to feel a bit easier compared to this.”

title: UMaine football’s losing streak extended to six games
text:
A second-half comeback bid fell short Saturday as UMaine suffered its sixth consecutive football defeat, losing 17-14 to Bryant in Orono.
Maine’s only touchdown was an 11-yard pass from Caden Drezek to Rashawn Marshall early in the third quarter. Noah Carpenter rushed for the 2-point conversion to cut the Black Bears’ deficit to 14-11.
Bryant (5-2, 3-0 CAA) answered with a 26-yard field goal from Nicholas Stoyanovich. Maine’s Samuel Tremblay kicked his second field goal of the game, from 32 yards, early in the fourth quarter, but the Black Bears (1-6, 1-3) got the ball only one more time and were stopped on downs just beyond midfield.
Drezek, making his first start for Maine, was 18 of 34 for 234 yards. Nick Laughlin caught seven passes for 86 yards, and Marshall gained 62 yards on 19 carries.

title: Kittens recovering after being buried alive in Florida backyard
text:
Surviving kittens recovering after being buried alive
Two of the five kittens a Florida sheriff's office says were buried in a backyard are recovering and being cared for by a foster family before they can be adopted.
Surviving kittens recovering after being buried alive
Two of the five kittens a Florida sheriff's office says were buried in a backyard are recovering and being cared for by a foster family before they can be adopted.
Investigators say Alba Chavez admitted to burying the kittens, some while they were still alive. Two kittens were found dead, two survived, and one has not been found.
The two surviving kittens, just 3 weeks old when they were discovered, are now showing signs of improvement while staying with foster caregiver Jennifer Jagdeo and her family.
Jagdeo said she received a call from the Humane Society on Friday and has been caring for the kittens ever since.
At first, the kittens were struggling to get around and eat on their own.
"They were a little bit sluggish, a little slower. Hadn't quite completely figured out the whole walking thing and the eating thing. But now it's a complete turnaround," Jagdeo said.
Despite their difficult start, she is optimistic about their future.
"I know. It's not even a hope. I know that they are going to do amazing things over the next couple of weeks with us," Jagdeo told Hearst sister station WPBF.
The Humane Society of the Treasure Coast has custody of the kittens and says they will need about two more months of care before they are ready for adoption.
Jagdeo said she expects them to continue growing and eventually find loving homes.
"They're going to continue to grow. They're going to be big fluffy little kittens and they're going to find their forever home, and it's going to be somebody that loves them even more than we do," she said.
For now, Jagdeo said the kittens have already shown how resilient they are.
"These two are fighters, for sure. And they are meant to be here. They have a purpose, whether it's, you know, to heal some child's heart or some family's heart or bring joy to them. They definitely have a purpose," she said.
The surviving kittens will remain in foster care until they are ready to be adopted. Those interested in adopting them are asked to visit the website for the Humane Society of the Treasure Coast.
Martin County jail records show Chavez remains in custody on animal cruelty charges and is being held on a $100,000 bond.

title: Mainers offer 6 tips for family caregivers
text:
Aging in Maine is presented by AARP Maine
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Karen Groves has been taking care of her 93-year-old mother, Jean Groves, for five years.
Her mom lives at Berwick Estates, an assisted living facility near Groves’ home in South Berwick, but Groves sees her mother almost daily, taking her to twice-weekly dialysis treatments, plus other medical and hair appointments.
The retired Portsmouth Naval Shipyard engineer is never far away in case she gets a call from Berwick Estates — her mom has a variety of health, mobility and cognitive issues and has already been hospitalized four times this year.
“I feel very tied down,” said Groves, 69. “Usually once a year, one of my kids will cover for me for a few days. Then I can go away without waiting for the phone to ring. Last year I went to Vermont for four days and the mental break was amazing.”
As Maine’s population ages, taking care of its older residents is becoming an increasingly urgent issue. From the stress of rural isolation to a shortage of workers to complicated federal Medicare guidelines, this guide helps Mainers learn about the services, technology and resources available to caregivers and the parents, spouses, neighbors and friends they’re caring for.
Making time for yourself is one piece of advice Groves and other family caregivers offered to those who may be new to or still struggling with challenges that come with caring for an aging relative.
Nancy Jo Polito, 78, of Portland, wrote a book, “Taking Care of Business: Tales of a Caregiver,” about caring for her mother, Isabel Profenno Polito, who died in 2010 at age 93.
Her mother suffered from multiple health problems throughout her life, so Polito began helping out around the house when she was 5 years old and never stopped. When her mother fell and broke her wrist at age 89, she moved to a skilled nursing facility.
Polito’s concerns about the quality of care her mother received there led her to become a super advocate, regularly monitoring her mother’s meals, medications, bathing schedule, foot care and even doctor’s orders for medical tests and treatments.
“You just can’t admit someone and walk away and feel good about it,” Polito said. “You have to be an advocate to make sure they’re getting the right care.”
Here are some tips from the front lines of caregiving:
1. Get comfortable with being an advocate
It can be challenging, but it’s probably the most valuable role in caregiving — being an advocate and a witness to ensure a loved one receives proper care. That includes medical appointments, for in-home services and in long-term care facilities.
Visit and call regularly, ask questions and stop by randomly to see how living conditions measure up.
“You have to keep open communication and you have to stay on top of it,” Polito said. “I was told I was too pushy, but they like it when you don’t come in all the time.”
2. Learn what services are available
Search the internet for family caregiver programs that are available in your area. Elder care and social service agencies can help. AgeMaine, formerly Southern Maine Agency on Aging, is a good place to start.
“Be resourceful,” said Marvella Heard, 56, of Biddeford, who cares for her 79-year-old father, Samuel. “I wasn’t ready for all this. It’s complicated, like they don’t want it to be easy. It’s trial and error, but you figure things out.”
3. Meet with an elder law attorney
Whether you are a caregiver charged with overseeing a loved one’s finances and personal affairs, or you want to make long-range plans for yourself, an elder law attorney can help.
In addition to estate planning, which includes wills, trusts, powers of attorney, healthcare proxies and advanced directives, elder law attorneys handle asset protection, long-term care plans, government benefits, guardianships and elder abuse prevention.
Clare Herrmann, of Portland, cares for her husband, Jim Vollmar. The couple, both 78, found some peace of mind meeting with an elder law attorney.
“It takes all the questions out of it,” Herrmann said. “Who will take care of your finances? Who will make sure you have proper care as you age? All of that needs to be in writing and it’s hard to come up with all the ‘what ifs’ on your own.”
To find an elder law attorney, check the Maine State Bar Association’s Lawyer Referral Service or the National Academy of Elder Law Attorneys.
4. Put family controversy aside
Caring for an aging family member is often challenging on its own. Don’t let old grudges with siblings or other relatives make it more difficult.
“Put personal feeling aside and focus on caring for the person,” Heard said. “It’s very important to stick together at times like this. Be there for each other and one person won’t be overwhelmed.”
5. Take care of yourself
Reach out for assistance through elder care agencies, peer support groups and community organizations. Engage in activities that connect you with others outside the sphere of caregiving. Make time to do what makes you happy, even if it’s only for a few hours.
For Groves, that means treating any free day like an adventure, so she goes hiking or to a museum. She also enjoys volunteering and still makes time for it, teaching balance exercise classes for older adults.
“I find it gratifying and inspiring,” Groves said. “Volunteering was always going to be a big part of my retirement and I don’t want to give that up.”
6. Cut yourself some slack
It’s easy to feel guilty if you think you’re not doing enough as a caregiver, especially when a loved one gets sick or injured in a fall.
“You get waves of that,” Polito said. “You blame yourself when things happen. You feel you should have done more. You just have to let it go. It’s insurmountable at times. You can’t do it all.”

title: Championship Season Is Here, and Saturday Is Loaded Across the County
text:
The County Scoreboard: Championship Season Arrives as County Athletes Prepare for a Busy Saturday
Friday's weather may have put Aroostook County high school sports on hold, but Saturday is shaping up to be one of the biggest days of the fall season.
From the PVC Cross Country Championships to New England golf qualifying and a full slate of soccer games, County athletes have plenty to compete for today.
With the final countable day for soccer now set for Wednesday, October 21, every remaining game carries a little more weight. Teams are looking to improve their playoff positions, while others are hoping to build momentum before tournament play begins.
County Runners Chase PVC Championships
The Penobscot Valley Conference Cross Country Championships take center stage today in Old Town, where some of the County's top runners will be looking to bring home conference titles.
Houlton/GHCA's boys are coming off an impressive performance at the Red Riot Challenge, where Malachi Witmer took first place and teammates Wyatt Quint, Logan Witmer and Brayden Drake joined him in the top five. The Shires finished first as a team.
Caribou's boys also have plenty of momentum after dominating last weekend's Pendale's meet in Hermon. Pierce Gorneault, Tewolde Stewart and Peyton Gorneault swept the top three spots to lead the Vikings to the team championship.
On the girls side, Caribou's Emma Graves is coming off another individual victory, while Presque Isle's girls are fresh off a team championship at Pendale's.
Aleah Rideout, Lillian Johnson and Taylor York helped lead the Wildcats to that victory, with Rideout finishing second and Johnson third.
Presque Isle's boys also finished second last weekend, led by Jeremy Charette's fourth-place performance.
With the postseason getting underway, Saturday should provide an excellent look at where the County's runners stand heading into the championship stretch.
County Golfers Looking for New England Berths
The high school golf season isn't finished for several County athletes.
Maine's New England Individual Golf Qualifier takes place today, with the boys competing at Prouts Neck and the girls at Natanis Golf Course.
The golfers who advance will earn an opportunity to compete at the New England Championships later this month in Connecticut.
Aroostook County is coming off a strong showing at the state championships.
Houlton's Beckett Peabody tied for third in Class C boys, while teammate Presley Goodwin finished third in the Class C girls competition.
Presque Isle's Alice Korzekwa tied for sixth in Class B girls, while Ashland's Averie Smith also finished sixth in Class C.
Those performances capped an impressive state championship weekend for County golf, and today offers another chance for local athletes to extend their seasons.
Soccer Playoff Race Enters Its Final Days
If Thursday's games were any indication, the final days of the soccer regular season could be something special.
We saw two overtime finishes, several one-goal games and some outstanding individual performances before Friday's weather forced postponements across the schedule.
Now, with October 21 marking the final countable day, teams have just a handful of opportunities left to improve their positions in the standings.
Presque Isle has a particularly interesting afternoon ahead with another meeting against John Bapst.
The Lady Wildcats pushed the Crusaders into double overtime earlier this week before falling 5-4. The boys also played a competitive game against Bapst, falling 4-2.
Both teams will be looking for a different outcome when they meet again today at Hampden Academy.
Caribou also has a rematch with Hermon.
Last weekend, the Hermon girls defeated Caribou 10-2, while the Viking boys earned a 2-0 shutout victory. Both matchups should provide another good test as the regular season winds down.
Elsewhere, Easton and Van Buren will finally get their postponed girls matchup played, while Fort Kent, Wisdom, Central Aroostook and Southern Aroostook are among the other County programs with games on the schedule.
There is plenty left to be decided before the postseason begins.
