title: NWS Skywarn weather spotter training coming in late fall
text:
NWS Skywarn weather spotter training coming in late fall
Become a SKYWARN Weather Spotter This Fall!
NWS Skywarn weather spotter training coming in late fall
Become a SKYWARN Weather Spotter This Fall!
Are you fascinated by the power of a winter storm, the development of severe weather, or the forces behind coastal flooding? Turn your passion for weather into an opportunity to make a difference!
SKYWARN Weather Spotter training is open to weather enthusiasts of all experience levels who want to learn more about recognizing and reporting important weather conditions. Whether you’re an avid storm watcher, a weather hobbyist, or simply curious about the science behind the forecast, these training sessions can help you take your interest to the next level. Join a session this fall and discover how you can help support weather awareness and keep your community informed when hazardous weather threatens.
The 2026 fall training schedule includes in-person and virtual sessions covering winter weather and coastal flooding. These sessions offer an opportunity to learn about weather spotting and help support weather awareness in local communities.

title: Women of Maine, your vote is not a Valentine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maria Padian is a novelist and freelance writer who lives in Brunswick. She has previously worked as a news reporter and a congressional press secretary.
Something surprised me this month as I’ve been knocking on doors and doing some political canvassing: There are a lot of older women who plan to vote for both Hannah Pingree and Sen. Susan Collins.
As a Medicare-eligible female myself, I’ll confess: this struck me as some profound cognitive dissonance; these two candidates are very different. But despite my impulse to exclaim, “Seriously?” at my fellow women of a certain age, I remembered that good canvassing includes listening. So I asked them to … explain.
Their reasons were remarkably personal.
Regarding Pingree, a Democrat running for governor in Maine, many said, “Oh, I love Hannah.” Like she’s the smart daughter we’re super proud of.
Regarding Collins, the five-term incumbent Republican running for U.S. Senate, they spoke as if she were a trusted friend or sister. “She saved my job,” one said. “She understands us,” said another. “She’s a real Mainer.”
Here’s the thing: those gals have been voting for Collins for decades. They hold fast to the Susan they knew 20-plus years ago, who molded herself as a moderate. It didn’t matter if I pointed out that the current Susan has abandoned those moderate impulses. That today’s Susan votes with President Trump 96% of the time and marches lock-step with the MAGA-aligned values of a GOP that past Maine Republican women like Margaret Chase Smith would not recognize today.
I realized I wasn’t going to change their minds at the front stoop. But I did say this: Your vote is not a Valentine. It’s a calculated chess move.
Because in the game we’re playing right now, “our senator” (that’s the logo on the Collins’ campaign bus) is no friend. She’s no sister. She’s no powerful chess queen, wielding her influence as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Instead, she’s played the past two years like an ineffective pawn. And her repeated caving to Trump has hurt Maine.
Someone who understands Mainers would know that bombing Iran would disrupt world oil prices and leave us out in the cold. So this winter, thank Susan Collins when we pay 75% more for heating oil. She voted repeatedly to support this now-forever war, back when Trump called it a military “action” that would last six weeks. Decades worth of past presidents from both parties knew better. Collins knew better.
Someone who cares about Maine jobs and Mainers’ health wouldn’t support Trump’s “big,
beautiful bill,” which Collins voted to advance. 
That bill’s devastating Medicaid cuts will not only shutter hundreds of hospitals nationwide, it’s projected to eliminate Medicaid for 31,000 Mainers and, according to the Maine Center for Economic Policy, might close four hospitals in Maine, resulting in the loss of tens of million in wages.
Speaking of health: measles is back. It was declared “eliminated” in U.S. in 2000, but so far this year we’re at more than 4,000 cases. All thanks to the anti-vaccination misinformation spread by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whom “our senator” voted to confirm.
With all due respect to my fellow senior women: chess, like democracy, is a long game. And sometimes, winning requires being strategic — and retiring a piece.

title: No Kings rallies across U.S. urge voters to cast ballots early ahead of midterms
text:
Rallies organized by the No Kings network opposed to President Donald Trump were being held Saturday in cities and communities across the U.S., with an aim of getting people out to vote early in the midterm elections.
The hundreds of planned events were being billed as nonpartisan, though they sought to build on nearly two years’ worth of No Kings marches and demonstrations by people upset with Trump’s presidency.
A band entertained what appeared to be a few hundred people in caps and coats Saturday at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C. Despite the chilly weather, many in the crowd danced to the tunes. “VOTE EARLY” and “HANDS OFF MY VOTE!” were among the many signs held aloft.
At an Atlanta rally, City Councilman Michael Julian Bond told the crowd to urge others to vote ahead of the Nov. 3 general election.
“The constitution gives you one power, right? That is the power to vote. Are you gonna use that power?” he asked.
“You don’t see Superman giving up his power,” Bond continued. “You don’t see Black Panther giving up his power. You don’t see Wonder Woman giving up her magic lasso. So why would you give up your right, your power, your obligation to vote? Be a super hero, use your power. Go to the polls and vote.”
Trump has long been suspicious of mail voting, and has claimed without evidence that voting fraud cost him the 2020 presidential election.
His administration sued California election officials Thursday, asking a judge to bar the state from counting mail-in ballots for the midterm elections from people whom the federal government has identified as “likely” noncitizens until their immigration status can be confirmed.
On Friday, the Justice Department warned that local officials who process and tabulate ballots submitted by suspected noncitizen voters are putting themselves at risk of criminal investigation and potential prosecution.
Earlier Friday, Sens. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., Sheldon Whitehouse, D-R.I., and Dick Durbin, D-Ill., wrote to Attorney General Todd Blanche demanding that the Justice Department commit to not seizing ballots or other election materials before the midterm elections are certified.

title: Championship Season Is Here, and Saturday Is Loaded Across the County
text:
The County Scoreboard: Championship Season Arrives as County Athletes Prepare for a Busy Saturday
Friday's weather may have put Aroostook County high school sports on hold, but Saturday is shaping up to be one of the biggest days of the fall season.
From the PVC Cross Country Championships to New England golf qualifying and a full slate of soccer games, County athletes have plenty to compete for today.
With the final countable day for soccer now set for Wednesday, October 21, every remaining game carries a little more weight. Teams are looking to improve their playoff positions, while others are hoping to build momentum before tournament play begins.
County Runners Chase PVC Championships
The Penobscot Valley Conference Cross Country Championships take center stage today in Old Town, where some of the County's top runners will be looking to bring home conference titles.
Houlton/GHCA's boys are coming off an impressive performance at the Red Riot Challenge, where Malachi Witmer took first place and teammates Wyatt Quint, Logan Witmer and Brayden Drake joined him in the top five. The Shires finished first as a team.
Caribou's boys also have plenty of momentum after dominating last weekend's Pendale's meet in Hermon. Pierce Gorneault, Tewolde Stewart and Peyton Gorneault swept the top three spots to lead the Vikings to the team championship.
On the girls side, Caribou's Emma Graves is coming off another individual victory, while Presque Isle's girls are fresh off a team championship at Pendale's.
Aleah Rideout, Lillian Johnson and Taylor York helped lead the Wildcats to that victory, with Rideout finishing second and Johnson third.
Presque Isle's boys also finished second last weekend, led by Jeremy Charette's fourth-place performance.
With the postseason getting underway, Saturday should provide an excellent look at where the County's runners stand heading into the championship stretch.
County Golfers Looking for New England Berths
The high school golf season isn't finished for several County athletes.
Maine's New England Individual Golf Qualifier takes place today, with the boys competing at Prouts Neck and the girls at Natanis Golf Course.
The golfers who advance will earn an opportunity to compete at the New England Championships later this month in Connecticut.
Aroostook County is coming off a strong showing at the state championships.
Houlton's Beckett Peabody tied for third in Class C boys, while teammate Presley Goodwin finished third in the Class C girls competition.
Presque Isle's Alice Korzekwa tied for sixth in Class B girls, while Ashland's Averie Smith also finished sixth in Class C.
Those performances capped an impressive state championship weekend for County golf, and today offers another chance for local athletes to extend their seasons.
Soccer Playoff Race Enters Its Final Days
If Thursday's games were any indication, the final days of the soccer regular season could be something special.
We saw two overtime finishes, several one-goal games and some outstanding individual performances before Friday's weather forced postponements across the schedule.
Now, with October 21 marking the final countable day, teams have just a handful of opportunities left to improve their positions in the standings.
Presque Isle has a particularly interesting afternoon ahead with another meeting against John Bapst.
The Lady Wildcats pushed the Crusaders into double overtime earlier this week before falling 5-4. The boys also played a competitive game against Bapst, falling 4-2.
Both teams will be looking for a different outcome when they meet again today at Hampden Academy.
Caribou also has a rematch with Hermon.
Last weekend, the Hermon girls defeated Caribou 10-2, while the Viking boys earned a 2-0 shutout victory. Both matchups should provide another good test as the regular season winds down.
Elsewhere, Easton and Van Buren will finally get their postponed girls matchup played, while Fort Kent, Wisdom, Central Aroostook and Southern Aroostook are among the other County programs with games on the schedule.
There is plenty left to be decided before the postseason begins.

title: The Mills-Pingree machine crushed small business in Maine. Hannah Pingree will finish the job.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Rick Savage, an entrepreneur, former owner and founder of the Sunday River Brewing Company in Bethel, is an advocate for small business rights.
Small business owners in Maine don’t ask for handouts.
We ask for a fair shot, a clear set of rules and a state government that stays off our backs so we can feed our families and employ our neighbors. But under the administration of Gov. Janet Mills (where Hannah Pingree served as a chief architect of policy, as director of the Office of Policy Innovation and the Future), Maine became a hostile environment for independent enterprise.
I know this firsthand. As the former co-owner of Sunday River Brewing Company, I lived through the heavy-handed, punitive overreach of an administration that treated hard-working entrepreneurs not as partners, but as subjects to be controlled.
In the spring of 2020, small businesses across Maine were strung along with moving goalposts and false reopening promises. When it became clear that state officials were operating behind closed doors without accountability, I spoke out. I went on national television and gave out Gov. Mills’ cellphone number so everyday Mainers, the people whose livelihoods were being systematically destroyed, could finally get an answer.
What followed was a targeted campaign of government retaliation.
Rather than working with small business owners trying to safely operate, state regulators moved in. Inspectors from the Department of Health and Human Services and state liquor licensing enforcement targeted my establishment, scrutinizing our operations and stripping our health and liquor licenses to force our doors shut. In my view, state agencies were weaponized to make an example out of anyone who dared to challenge Augusta’s dictates.
Our legal team estimates that the state spent nearly $500,000 in taxpayer resources, deploying state attorneys, inspectors and enforcement officials, just to crush one brewpub in Bethel. While the official court filings reflect a drawn-out legal war over licensing enforcement, the sheer waste of public funds to dismantle a local business tells you everything you need to know about the priorities of the Mills-Pingree administration.
Hannah Pingree cannot distance herself from this legacy. As one of Gov. Mills’ top policy advisers, Pingree sat at the right hand of an administration that oversaw a disastrous business climate. Her office helped shape the economic and regulatory framework that shut down small shops, pushed workers out of state and prioritized government mandates over economic survival.
The economic damage inflicted on Maine wasn’t an accident; it was the direct result of a top-down, central-planning mindset championed by bureaucrats like Pingree. When state government believes it can arbitrarily decide which businesses are “essential” and which are disposable, local economies suffer.
That is why I am standing firmly behind Bobby Charles for governor.
Bobby Charles understands what it takes to confront administrative overreach and dismantle the bureaucratic machine in Augusta.
Unlike the entrenched politicians who view government regulation as the solution to every problem, Bobby recognizes that free enterprise and small business are the lifeblood of Maine’s economy. He has the strength, vision and determination to restore accountability, rein in rogue state agencies and make sure no entrepreneur ever faces the kind of government persecution my family experienced.
Maine cannot afford four more years of the Mills-Pingree agenda. Small business owners are tired of high taxes, red tape and an administrative state that views free enterprise as a threat. We need leadership that respects working Mainers, honors the hard work of local entrepreneurs and stands up for our constitutional rights.
Bobby Charles is the leader Maine needs to close the book on this era of government overreach and rebuild a state where small businesses can actually thrive.

title: Record-setting 60-year-old flamingo hatches 2 chicks at Louisville Zoo
text:
LOUISVILLE, Ky. (WDRB+WAVE/Gray News) — The Louisville Zoo announced the arrival of brand-new Chilean flamingo chicks on Thursday.
One of the zoo’s Chilean flamingos just became a parent at 60 years old, a record-setting age for a female Chilean flamingo to produce chicks. She produced two.
The flock has welcomed six chicks in total this season, and all of them are being hand-reared by the zoo’s bird keeper staff.
Flamingo chicks hatch covered in snowy white down that transitions to gray before they turn into the famous flamingo pink as they grow.

title: US winter is likely to be wetter and warmer, forecasters say. If you want more snow, look south
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Winter in the United States looks like it will generally be wetter and warmer, but not necessarily snowier, according to the federal government’s seasonal outlook and other meteorologists’ forecasts. You can thank or blame El Niño.
El Niño is likely to shift weather patterns to bring more moisture, but with it higher temperatures. That should help erase persistent Western drought, but it won’t likely make Northern snow-lovers happy, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration said Thursday.
“This is going to be a winter that’s really difficult for them to find what they’re looking for,” said James Belanger, vice president of meteorology for the Weather Company.
El Niño, the natural but temporary warming in parts of the Pacific, generally warms the globe. Although it disrupts weather conditions around the world in dramatically different ways, its effects tend to follow predictable regional patterns, especially when El Niño is strong like it is right now. That gives forecasters greater confidence in what lies ahead.
All this is on top of a U.S. winter that has warmed about 4 degrees (2.2 degrees Celsius) in the past 50 years, predominantly from human-caused climate change, according to NOAA.
The best chance of snow could actually shift south
While the weather service doesn’t make seasonal snowfall predictions, their meteorologists said much of the northern parts of the country — including the Northeast, Great Lakes, Upper Midwest and Northern Rockies — should expect below-normal snow. The Southern Rockies, parts of the Southeast and Southwest may get more than they usually do.
“Listen, even in the winter months, it doesn’t mean you’re not going to have snow. It doesn’t mean you might not have a snowstorm,” National Weather Service Director Ken Graham said in a media briefing presenting the three-month winter outlook. “So it doesn’t erase the risk.”
The Northern snow shrinkage is also predicted by private meteorology firms. Salt Lake City is the only big metro area where AccuWeather expects above-normal winter snow amounts. Chicago, Boston, New York and Philadelphia are forecast to get about half or less of their normal winter snow, the firm said.
And a White Christmas? Consider a plane ride to the Southern Rockies, Belanger said. Otherwise, “Santa’s gonna find a barren landscape when he returns in late December.”
A warmer winter can still pack a punch
Part or all of 41 of the Lower 48 states are forecast to be warmer than normal. No states — or even parts of states — are forecast to be cooler than average. Florida, Louisiana, southern Georgia, Alabama and Mississippi are forecast to be near normal. There’s equal chance of warm, cold or normal in Texas, New Mexico, Arizona, Utah, Southern California, Nevada, Wyoming, western Oklahoma, Kansas and Nebraska.
And the dreaded polar vortex with its icy blast of Arctic air escaping into the United States? That shouldn’t happen as much as most winters, but that doesn’t mean it won’t happen at all, said National Weather Service meteorologist and branch chief Jon Gottschalck.
“It only takes one storm to flip the script, especially for the East Coast cities,” said AccuWeather lead long-range forecaster Paul Pastelok, who said to especially watch for Eastern snowstorms in late January and February.
AccuWeather is more bullish than NOAA for snow in the Rockies regions, calling for Denver to have 10 to 18 days with at least 2 inches (5 centimeters) of snow, which is more than the historical average of 9 inches (23 centimeters). The company’s overall snow forecast for Denver is still around average, but considerably more than last winter.
Drought relief comes with a downside
NOAA is forecasting that parts of 39 states will see a wetter-than-usual winter, with much of Montana and parts of Oregon, Idaho, Wisconsin and Michigan being drier.
“We anticipate drought conditions to improve or end for western portions of Oregon and western Washington state, the Southwest, the central and southern Rockies, the southern Great Plains, the lower Mississippi Valley, and areas in the East,” Gottschalck said.
Mike Bettes, a meteorologist at The Weather Channel, said it will likely be too much rain for California: “We’d anticipate numerous, high-impact atmospheric rivers that could bring extensive flooding and landslides this winter.”
Atmospheric rivers are long and relatively narrow bands of water vapor. They take water from oceans and flow through the sky, dumping rain in prodigious amounts.
Florida and parts of the Southeast should also be on guard for more tornadoes this winter and early spring because of El Niño, Gottschalck said.
A record El Niño puts forecasters in uncharted territory
Forecasters across the globe expect the current El Niño to reach record levels this fall or winter. Graham, the weather service chief, noted that a strong El Niño doesn’t mean its impacts are stronger, but it does make the weather easier to predict.
Winter weather expert Judah Cohen, an MIT research scientist, is waiting a couple more weeks before making his forecast. He says an unprecedented El Niño is “a reason not be more confident, but less confident.”
“We have no real historical analog or precedent,” Cohen said. “When every meteorologist on the planet is on the same side, I get nervous. We’re not that good.”

title: Obituary: Nancy G. Riter
text:
PORTLAND – “Nonnie”, just shy of her 86th birthday, peacefully passed away on Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026, at Maine Medical Center in Portland. Born Oct. 14, 1940, the daughter of Sal and Tac Riter, Nonnie left this world with the same spirit of determination, stubbornness, and grit that guided her well-lived life.
Born in Montclair, N.J., Nonnie spread her wings to homes from Florida, through the Jersey Shore to Falmouth, Maine, where she lived for over 20 years with her “boys”, two Maine Coon cats, Diesel and Benji.
She is survived by her devoted son, Scott and his wife, Maggie; her four grandchildren, Kelly, Patrick and his wife Shannon, Ian and his fiancée Victoria, Austin; and her two great-grandchildren, Roran and Rian. She is also survived by her beloved sister and best friend, Susie and her husband Dickie, brother Jen and his wife Janie, brother Mike and his wife Kim; a clutch of precious nieces and nephews; and a cadre of devoted friends too many to count. She will be deeply missed by all who knew and loved her.
Nonnie was a creative force, a devout and nurturing friend, a multi-talented professional, and a Jane-of-all-trades. From phlebotomist and medical office manager to horse show wrangler and real estate mogul, there was nothing she couldn’t tackle. Her most precious gift was always lending an ear, a shoulder, or a set of hands whenever someone needed them.
Her friends and loved ones remember snowy toboggan rides down Mountainside Park, Christmas Eve snuggles waiting to hear Santa on the roof, catching the record-setting grouper, river boating through Europe, dog-sledding and helicopter rides over Alaskan glaciers, snow birding between her happy places in Maine and Florida, ice cream, peanut butter, sipping coffee, breakfast for dinner, and deciding who loved turtles more.
A kind and sympathetic friend, Nonnie always put others before herself, spreading her warmth, humor, wisdom and kindness to all those she touched.
Nonnie’s eternal message to us all is to BELIEVE and to take comfort in knowing that her renewed spirit is soaring high above the clouds with the angels. She will be missed by all who knew her.
A celebration of life will follow at a later date.
Arrangements are under the direction of the Conroy-Tully Walker Cremation, Funeral and Gathering Center, 300 Allen Ave., Portland.

title: Grateful for the Democratic candidates in Maine
text:
I feel fortunate to have excellent candidates to vote for on Nov. 3. I can count on Democrat Troy Jackson to support my right to make my own decisions about when to have children. Temple

title: Video shows police officer punching, using Taser on man in chair
text:
DONORA, Pa. (KDKA) — A Pennsylvania resident is calling attention to an incident between a man and a police officer after sharing video of their encounter.
The situation began with a call to Donora police about a domestic disturbance report.
The video shows Shawn Bowman sitting in a chair as an officer tries to handcuff him after officers were called to his home for the alleged domestic disturbance.
In the video, Bowman moves his hand toward the officer’s hands. The officer then punches him in the face twice and uses a Taser. Bowman falls to the ground.
Dennis Hawkins Jr., a longtime Donora resident, said he reacted after seeing the video.
“I just started shaking. I can’t believe someone in our town is going through this from a person who is supposed to protect and serve the people of this community,” Hawkins said.
Criminal complaint details
In the criminal complaint, the officer wrote that after he used the Taser, he repeatedly ordered Bowman to get on the ground and put his hands behind his back before he complied.
“If they’re not resisting or causing any threat to you, that force shouldn’t be taken. It looks like a rogue officer exercising his right to do whatever he wants to do because he has a badge on,” Hawkins said.
Community reaction
Hawkins often uses his Facebook page to bring attention to community concerns. After he shared the video, questions about the officer’s use of force came in. He said the reaction goes beyond anger.
“People are scared. It seems like no one is safe cause that guy was probably 60 years old,” Hawkins said.
Donora police were asked whether they were aware of the video. The chief was not in, and there has been no response.
“It definitely should be investigated, but its like who’s going to investigate it,” Hawkins said.

title: Lawsuit alleges DHS effort to collect detailed state voter data violates federal law
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — A lawsuit filed Thursday challenges the Trump administration’s sprawling effort to collect and analyze Americans’ voter data, alleging the government has obtained voter files from at least 47 states and handled the data in a way that violates federal law.
The 42-page complaint filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., claims the Department of Homeland Security’s secretive probe of the voter data, including a policy to combine it with commercial datasets, disregards federal safeguards and flouts the privacy rights of millions of Americans.
The case, brought by the League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center and the League of United Latin American Citizens, is the latest in a torrent of legal challenges that have emerged in response to President Donald Trump’s crusade against noncitizen voting, a concern he views as a serious problem but which research shows is exceedingly rare.
The Trump administration has consistently sought to exert more power over elections, even as the Constitution grants that authority to states and, in some cases, Congress. Judges have consistently upheld states’ rights to decline to hand over their lists to the federal government.
DHS didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.
Thursday’s lawsuit alleges the Trump administration has obtained voter lists from 47 states, even as 30 states refused to turn them over to the administration. It calls for the court to declare the administration’s collection of voter data illegal, block the policy and order DHS to delete and stop using the voter information it already has collected.
The lawsuit comes less than three weeks before Election Day, as the administration has continued to escalate threats to states alleging they are not doing enough to remove noncitizens from their voter rolls.
On Thursday, the administration sued California election officials, alleging they didn’t act quickly enough to review names the federal government identified as “likely” noncitizens, and asking a judge to bar the state from counting those people’s mail ballots for next month’s midterm elections. The secretary of state’s office said it was given just 48 hours to review 20,000 names without the Justice Department providing any evidence to substantiate its claims.

title: Midcoast drifting sailboat saga nearing end after 18 months
text:
A year and a half ago, a sailboat washed up on the shores of Edgecomb, disappeared again, and then reappeared in Woolwich, setting off a saga of questions, deliberations, and pointed fingers.
Now, the back and forth is coming to a close.
At a Sept. 29 Edgecomb Select Board meeting, Chair Forrest Carver said Woolwich has agreed to scuttle the boat and split the cost of removal. Harbor Master Terry Stockwell said King’s Tide Marine, of Bath, is set to do the work and the cost is not set yet until it is determined whether the boat is floating. If the boat floats, it will cost the town $3,500. If it doesn’t, it will cost $6,500.
According to Edgecomb Tax Collector Jessica Mague, the money will come out of the remaining harbor master’s budget for 2027.
At the Sept. 29 meeting, the board approved the allocation of up to $2,700, the remainder to be paid next year.
“I’ll let them know that we fully intend to split the cost with them and that we appreciate their working with us,” Carver said.
In a Friday, Oct. 9 interview, Stockwell said the sailboat first appeared on Edgecomb’s shores near Fort Edgecomb in May 2025. The boat remained there for around a month and when someone told Stockwell they thought it belonged to someone who kept it in Wiscasset. He said he then towed it over and put it on one of the Wiscasset Yacht Club’s moorings.
“The yacht club and the Wiscasset harbor master called me up and said, “Get rid of it,” Stockwell said.
He then went on to tow the sailboat over to Edgecomb waters, where it stayed while the town tried to figure out who the original owner was. Stockwell said the boat had been last registered 52 years ago to a Westport Island man who is now deceased, and his wife was not interested in retaining ownership of the vessel.
As the town went through the process of declaring the sailboat as abandoned and preparing it to be auctioned, it disappeared again.
“I live on the Sheepscot River and I didn’t see it go by me,” Stockwell said.
After being missing for months, the sailboat landed in the waters off of Woolwich and the town requested Edgecomb get rid of the boat.
According to Stockwell, it has not yet been determined when the boat will be removed, which will also be determined whether it sinks or swims.
The Edgecomb Select Board will meet next at 6 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 27 at the town hall, at 16 Town Hall Road. For more information, call 882-7018 or go to edgecomb.org.

title: From Broadway to basilica: Lewiston’s revered Virgin Mary medallion finds a ‘proper’ home
text:
LEWISTON — For nearly a hundred years, a large medallion of the Blessed Virgin Mary gazed down upon worshipers at St. Mary’s Church in the section of the city known as Little Canada.
The medallion was adored. Venerated. Revered.
“It was always there,” said Roger Caron, who was an altar server at the church in the mid-1960s. “It was beautiful. It was part of the church and it was part of us.”
And then for more than a decade, after the closing of St. Mary’s at 46 Cedar St. in 2000, the Blessed Virgin gazed down upon comedians cracking off-color jokes, Halloween parties, Broadway shows, rock bands and a host of other events that were decidedly non-Catholic in nature.
The events were being offered by the Franco American Heritage Center, which had taken over the church, and it was generally agreed that the Mother Mary, known officially as Our Lady of Perpetual Help, was out of place.
“Groups would come in from out of town,” said Paul Dube, whose late wife, Rita, took an interest in the medallion. “They were non-Catholic groups and they didn’t want that statue up there. Rita had a nice curtain that could be lowered over it when there was one of those groups coming in.”
The thought of the Blessed Mother being concealed in such a manner was appalling to some, including Rita, who was a founding member of the Franco Center board.
Almost everybody agreed that the grand medallion, carved of wood and roughly 5 feet tall and 3 feet wide, should be taken down from the spot it had occupied since St. Mary’s was built in the early 1900s.
But what to do with such a magnificent statue of such a sacred religious figure?
One member of the Franco board thought it should be taken down and shipped to a mission in Haiti.
“Rita was totally against that,” Paul said. The medallion “was part of the church; part of the history. She fought that for a year and won.”
Eventually Elaine Roop, then board president of what had become the Franco Center, reached out to the Very Rev. Daniel Greenleaf, pastor of the Prince of Peace Parish, to see if he was interested in taking possession of the medallion.
He was. Very interested, as it turns out.
“It was such a significant piece for the people who went to Mass down in Little Canada,” said Greenleaf, whose Prince of Peace Parish includes the Basilica of Saints Peter and Paul on Ash Street in Lewiston. “It was a central piece of the church. And so we had some discussions and I said, ‘We’ll take it.'”
The rest of the congregation felt the same. The medallion needed to be preserved no matter what it took.
“We said, ‘We will not let this thing go to waste,'” said Caron, a longtime parishioner at St. Mary’s and now the basilica. “‘We will not have it destroyed or cut into pieces. Somehow, we’re going to preserve it and find a place for it.”
And the will of those people was strong enough to see the matter through. In 2022, the medallion was moved out of the former St. Mary’s Church and brought to the basilica.
Not that it was as simple as it sounds.
‘AWE-INSPIRING’
The medallion is estimated to weigh at least 500 pounds. Moving it was delicate work and required special equipment.
Since then, the medallion has been propped on saw horses while awaiting its new home in the basilica’s chapel. That’s another five years of strange history for The Blessed Virgin, but that part is almost over.
On Wednesday, the medallion will be on full display in the chapel, placed lovingly within an altar hand carved by 22-year-old Dave Madore, of Gray, the same carpenter who carved an altar for a Nativity scene brought from The Holy Land in 2023 by Greenleaf and a group of his parishioners. Madore, who is a member of the parish, produced the ornate table in front of the medallion as well as the reredos — the ornamental wooden wall that displays the medallion.
And on that same Wednesday, the Most Rev. James Ruggieri, bishop of the Diocese of Portland, will be at the basilica to consecrate the medallion — a Catholic service in which the statue will be deemed holy.
After that, at 6 p.m., the altar and its medallion will be presiding over Mass in the basilica’s lower chapel, with the Blessed Virgin Mary once again gazing down upon those who adore her.
“I got a sneak peak of it last week,” said Caron. “And I was just taken aback by how beautiful it looked, and how awe-inspiring. It’s a perfect fit for the chapel. It’s going to be a great addition to the basilica, and the history of St. Mary’s is going to be maintained and preserved.”
The chapel wall needed to be reinforced to accept the weight of the medallion, but everybody involved in the process considers it a labor of the very deepest kind of love.
“Placing the Blessed Virgin medallion from the former St. Mary’s Church in the refurbished lower chapel of the basilica,” said parishioner Maura Murphy, “shows us where the past, present and future of Lewiston’s Catholic and cultural heritage come together in a most meaningful, lovely way.”
ORIGINS UNKNOWN
The medallion features the carved figure of Mother Mary cradling a baby Jesus. The precise history of the piece is elusive — most of those familiar with it only know that it was part of St. Mary’s Church from the very beginning.
Construction of the church began 1907 and wasn’t completed until 20 years later, with worshipers gathering in a basement for services in the years between.
St. Mary’s had been established after the Saints Peter and Paul Parish was divided in 1907 to accommodate the quickly growing French-speaking mill-worker population. Located at the corner of Cedar and Oxford streets, the church would eventually become a cornerstone of the city’s Franco-American “Little Canada” neighborhood.
And the Blessed Virgin was the centerpiece of the church.
In 1930, a Boston newspaper published a photo of St. Mary’s and deemed it the most beautiful Church in New England. Until the day it closed in 2000, St. Mary’s continued to hold Masses in English and French.
The Norman-Gotchic-style church was designed by a pair of architects from Boston, according to historical sources. It is generally presumed that they also commissioned the creation of the grand medallion that became such an integral part of worship at St. Mary’s.
But who created the iconic medallion of Our Lady of Perpetual Help? Was it some studio, individual or an active member of the architectural firm O’Connell & Shaw?
Those details seem lost to history. But those who have adored the medallion for years are plenty happy that the Virgin Mother has a new home that is properly suited for her.
In fact, for some, the storied medallion features prominently in the best of their earliest memories.
“It had a lot of effect on me as a Franco-American boy growing up in Lewiston,” said Caron.
Elaine Roop, who spent 15 years trying to get the medallion into a proper home, said in a 2022 interview that it had always bothered her that the Virgin Mother had to be covered with a curtain for certain events at the Franco Center.
“It was such an important thing for me to see that she received the respect so rightfully deserved,” Roop said. “I wanted to find a proper place for her, not just some afterthought.
“I have been waiting for this moment,” she said, “since I made a promise to Mary that I would find her a proper place.”

title: Crowd in Portland rallies around electing Maine Democrats on ‘No Kings Day’
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
PORTLAND — With just over two weeks until the midterm elections, about 400 people gathered in Deering Oaks on Saturday to rally around voting Democrats into office in Maine and ousting five-term Republican incumbent Susan Collins from the U.S. Senate.
Organized by Indivisible Greater Portland, the event coincided with the fourth national “No Kings” day. Previous “No Kings” protests drew thousands of Mainers who condemned Trump administration actions they said reflect a monarchy rather than a democracy. This year, the same protesters are focused on encouraging people to vote early in the midterm elections, ensuring that democracy prevails, in their view.
“I feel there’s a very significant undercurrent of bitterness and feeling that our government is betraying us,” said Chris Beasley, 86, of Cape Elizabeth. He held a ribbon-adorned sign on a long wooden stick that said “Vote.” “This brings attention to our choice of representatives that reflect the values of democratic society.”
Democratic gubernatorial candidate Hannah Pingree, U.S. Senate candidate Troy Jackson and U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., were three of several speakers at the event. The trio criticized President Donald Trump and discussed issues such as healthcare, the war in Iran, rising heating oil costs, immigration and abortion. They blamed Collins for affordability challenges in Maine and emphasized the importance of voting.
“Democracy is on the line here in Maine and across the country,” Pingree said. “Don’t leave it to chance.”
The race between Jackson and Collins is seen as particularly consequential — Democrats view it as one of their best shots at gaining a majority in the U.S. Senate. The competitors faced off in their fourth and final debate Thursday. Election Day is Nov. 3.
Sentiments against Collins and Trump at the rally were strong, with people holding signs that said “Retire Susan,” “Dump King Corruption” and “Susan Collins is complicit.” The senator has tried to distance herself from the president as his approval ratings wane, while Jackson’s campaign has pushed to present the two as a package.
Ben Bernard, 55, of Cliff Island, compared Collins to a teacher who helps a bullied child get some of their lunch money back, but won’t stand up to the bully. He was referring to Collins’ negotiations to remove some Maine items from Canada’s tariff list, a result of the trade war started by Trump.
“Collins is enabling Trump every day,” Bernard said.
Some came to the protest with specific policies in mind. Leah Campbell, 77, of Portland, held a sign that said “What happened to affordable healthcare for all?”
“I and people I know are impacted by healthcare cuts that have already been done,” Campbell said. “I have Medicare. I want to make sure that’s not cut. I have Social Security. I want to make sure that’s not cut. These are programs I have paid into all my life.”
Holly Parker, 52, of Cape Elizabeth, and Nancy Timberlake, 78, of Portland, said they already voted and came to the rally to surround themselves with positive energy after feeling drained by the most important issues in the elections.
“I had to buy heating oil this week, and it was excruciating,” Parker said. “I feel bad for a lot of people who are in a worse position than I am in terms of heating their homes and putting gas in their car.”
Prices of heating oil and gas have risen sharply since the start of the war in Iran.
Parker said she thinks the rally would be worth it if it persuades one more person to vote.
The event presented opportunities for Mainers to sign up to knock on doors and make calls to encourage their neighbors to vote. A band called “Singing Resistance” sang songs in between speakers who discussed voting and defeating Collins.
“A Senate seat does not belong to a person who’s held it for 30 years,” Jackson said. “It belongs to the people of Maine … I owe the people of Maine everything.”

title: Letter: We’re all paying for Republicans’ failure to stand up to Trump
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
I just got my first home heating oil bill of the season at $6.38 per gallon, more than twice the $3.18 of a year ago, adding to our inflated prices of diesel, gas, groceries and more. I’m not happy about this and I’m sure no one else in Maine is either.
We citizens of Maine are hurting and I think nothing but a big overhaul in Congress will be able to change this in the next two years. I believe this overhaul needs to start here by electing a new senator for the State of Maine — Troy Jackson — and a new representative for the 2nd Congressional District — Matt Dunlap.
The problems we face are largely caused by the feckless policies and actions of our president and his meek majority of followers in both chambers of Congress who mostly bow to his every whim. The ill-conceived and endless war in Iran, outrageous tariffs and lost medical coverage and care are placing extreme burdens on all Mainers.
Our current senator Susan Collins votes nearly all the time in support of Trump. Paul LePage has spent most of his time in recent years in Florida and is the self-proclaimed Trump before Trump. I think they are part of the problem, not part of the solution.
I believe Troy Jackson and Matt Dunlap are dedicated to improving the lives of Maine citizens, have proven themselves with decades of fine public service and have earned our votes.
Hugh Townsend
Belfast

title: Vote ‘No’ on Lewiston’s proposed needle exchange restrictions
text:
No one wants syringe waste in public places. Question 1 on the Lewiston ballot seems to address the problem by allowing drug users to receive only as many clean needles as they return. It mandates that syringe services exist in a single location, and bans mobile units.
Banning mobile units is a particularly terrible idea. Lewiston has a single syringe provider: Spurwink, located nearly at the turnpike exit on Lisbon Street. Most of the neediest and most vulnerable drug users live downtown, and can neither walk nor pay for the bus to get there.
If mobile units cannot come to them, people will reuse and share needles. Used needles spread disease and burden taxpayers with the costs of treating them. Mobile syringe units meet people where they are, connect users with services, and are demonstrably effective in helping people toward sobriety. If passed, Question 1 will do none of those things.
Mary Hunter
Lewiston

title: Colby football coach Jack Cosgrove temporarily stepping away from team
text:
WATERVILLE — Colby College football coach Jack Cosgrove is temporarily stepping away from the program, the school announced.
In a statement obtained by the Morning Sentinel on Saturday, Colby said Cosgrove “has temporarily stepped away to prioritize providing care for a family member facing unforeseen health concerns.” WABI Bangor first reported the news Friday.
Offensive coordinator Mark Clements coached Colby in a home game against Amherst on Saturday. The Mules led 12-0 early in the second quarter but ultimately lost 21-15 to fall to 0-5 on the season.
Since being named Colby’s head coach in December 2017, Cosgrove has amassed a 26-41 record. He led the Mules to a 6-3 season last year, marking the program’s first winning record since 2005.
Cosgrove previously coached at the University of Maine from 1993-2015. He guided the Black Bears to three Coastal (formerly Colonial) Athletic Association titles and five Football Championship Subdivision playoff appearances.
Clements will be the head coach in Cosgrove’s absence. Defensive coordinator Liam Hobbins will serve as associate head coach in addition to his current role.
Colby’s next game is at Hamilton (1-4) at noon next Saturday.

title: Letter: BDN editorial overplayed election disruption fears
text:
Letters submitted by BDN readers are verified by BDN Opinion Page staff. Send your letters to letters@bangordailynews.com
The Oct. 10 Bangor Daily News editorial, “Worried about election interference? Vote now,” offers sensible advice: If you have made your choices, early voting is a convenient option. My concern is how the editorial presents the reasons for that advice.
Statements about deploying troops or immigration agents at polling places deserve scrutiny, as do attempts to impose new restrictions on mail ballots. But readers need a clear distinction between troubling statements, confirmed plans, and the likelihood of disruptions in their own communities.
The editorial does not establish how likely those disruptions are in Maine. It also omits the Department of Homeland Security’s stated position that ICE does not plan to patrol polling places. That assurance does not settle every concern, but it belongs in the discussion.
The editorial quotes Secretary of State Shenna Bellows saying the election should be business as usual. That reassurance deserves as much weight as the possibilities raised in the opening paragraphs.
I am not asking the newspaper to dismiss threats. I am asking it to apply the same care to warnings that it applies to reassurances.
Encourage early voting. Explain the risks. But help readers distinguish what could happen from what there is evidence to expect.
Danny Coombs
Bucksport

title: Pumpkins spill onto roadway, causing major Halloween headache
text:
MOUNT PLEASANT, S.C. (WCSC/Gray News) — A load of pumpkins caused traffic delays in South Carolina Thursday afternoon.
An 18-wheeler struck a low-hanging tree limb coming off the Arthur Ravenel Jr. Bridge in Mount Pleasant, causing the accident.
The collision blocked the two right lanes of Coleman Boulevard as crews worked to clear the road. The road has since reopened.
The pumpkins, which were from New Mexico, were to be sold by Hibben United Methodist Church; the proceeds were to be given to local and state nonprofit organizations.

title: Mom hunts ‘once-in-a-lifetime’ moose 4 days after C-section birth
text:
BEULAH, N.D. (KFYR/Gray News) — A North Dakota family has a hunting story and a photo to go with it after Shayla Beckler shot a moose four days after giving birth to her daughter, Stella.
Stella was born weighing 6 pounds, 12 ounces.
“She is the best baby, just happy as can be all the time,” Shayla Beckler said.
A once-in-a-lifetime tag
Shayla Beckler, of Beulah, shot the moose on opening day of rifle season.
She had a C-section earlier this month on Monday, went home from the hospital on Wednesday and was hunting by Friday.
“It’s a once-in-a-lifetime tag,” Shayla Beckler said. “There was no way I was giving it up.”
Shayla Beckler, her husband Jacob and her brothers spent weeks tracking the moose. She had hoped to get the moose during archery season, but missed her shot.
“I hadn’t bow hunted in 10 years,” Shayla Beckler said. “We got pretty close, and when I got set up for the shot, I missed.”
“It was awesome,” Shayla Beckler said of the rifle season hunt.
Dad on baby duty
Jacob Beckler stayed in the truck with Stella during the hunt, keeping her warm while keeping an eye on his wife.
“I know she’s a strong woman who would make anything work,” Jacob Beckler said.
Shayla Beckler said getting a photo of Stella was part of her motivation to fill the tag.
“The No. 1 thing I want is a picture of Stella with her stuffed moose on the moose, and she fit perfectly right on the antlers,” Shayla Beckler said.
The family will process the moose meat themselves, Shayla Beckler said, and Stella will be there for that too.
Jacob Beckler said he is a little jealous of his wife’s harvest. He has applied for moose tags for years and has never been drawn.
Stella’s older brother, Bryson, missed the hunt because of a football game.
Copyright 2026 KFYR via Gray Local Media, Inc. All rights reserved.

title: High school football team’s season canceled as police investigate multiple serious reports
text:
ST. LOUIS. (KMOV/Gray News) - A St. Louis football team’s season was canceled as police investigate “inappropriate behavior.”
In a statement Friday, Saint Louis Public Schools announced it canceled the Clyde C. Miller/Sumner co-op football team’s remaining season.
The district said it canceled the season after reports of “seriously inappropriate behavioral and physical conduct involving students” associated with the team."
Officials said the police department received complaints from multiple people on Thursday, the day before the announcement.
St. Louis Metropolitan Police confirmed that it is in the early stages of the investigation, which primarily involves the student-athletes.
The district says its leadership is working to connect students who may have been impacted and their families with resources and to address safety concerns.
Authorities did not answer questions about the complaints or investigation.

title: DoorDash driver dies, teen brother critical after being ambushed while delivering food, father says
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - A man and his younger brother delivering food were allegedly ambushed by gunfire Thursday night at an apartment complex in the Nashville area.
Metro Nashville police said the shooting occurred at the Birchstone Village Apartments.
The reported victims, identified by their father as 22-year-old Jhon Diaz Santos and 14-year-old Alan, were said to be working for DoorDash that evening and drove into the apartment complex parking lot in a black Infiniti sedan.
According to authorities, a man approached Santos’ car and began shooting, police said. Two more men walked up, and one of them also started firing.
Police said Santos attempted to get away, backing his car into a fence. All three men ran off afterward.
Santos’ father, Juan Díaz, said his son had been a DoorDash delivery driver for more than a year.
Diaz said they were eating dinner as a family when Santos told him that night he was going to bring Alan out with him to make deliveries.
The father said his sons had gone out together before for food deliveries and reported nothing suspicious.
“They’d go out for two, three hours. They would come back safe. They never mentioned to us at any time at any time any suspicion,” Diaz said.
According to the father, he found out about what happened when a police officer knocked on their door, telling him his sons had an accident.
“I say, ‘Was it a car accident? Where was it?’ I say, ‘Can we go? Can you take me? I’ll follow you,” he said.
The father said it “shattered his soul” to learn that one of his sons had died.
“We don’t believe what is happening to us. One is not prepared for such a loss or news of this size,” Diaz said.
Fourteen-year-old Alan was also taken to the hospital in critical condition after being shot in the head, the father said.
Nashville authorities noted they were working on several leads while the shooting remains under investigation.
Copyright 2026 WSMV via Gray Local Media, Inc. All rights reserved.

title: Chilly, breezy, and a cold night ahead
text:
Chilly, breezy, and a cold night ahead
Chilly, breezy, and a cold night ahead
Saturday will be seasonably cold and breezy, with wind gusts reaching 25 to 35 mph. The northwest direction of the wind will help make conditions feel extra chilly. High temperatures today will be in the 40s, and some feels-like conditions will be in the 30s.
Tonight will be the coldest night of the season so far, and a widespread hard freeze is expected. Calmer winds and clear skies will help temperatures dip significantly. Temperatures will mainly be in the 20s, with some areas along the coast getting closer to 30 degrees.
Wintry precipitation is possible through Saturday morning in high terrain. Hikers must keep in mind the dangerous conditions this weekend. Conditions will be slick from the snow and freezing rain, and wind chill values will be in the single digits and even below zero above the tree line.
Temperatures will increase during the first half of the week, and we have a nice, dry forecast for the next few days.

title: It’s not just you. There are more Maine political ads than ever this year.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The gym. The doctor’s office. The living room. The car.
The store. The salon. The restaurant and bar.
Whether out and about or trying to relax at home, Mainers have heard or seen more than their fair share of political ads ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election headlined by races for the U.S. Senate, House of Representatives and governor. And don’t forget the glossy pamphlets — sometimes multiple in one day — that have arrived in mailboxes.
Mainers’ collective feelings — frustration, annoyance, ignorance or acceptance — cross ideological and demographic lines, putting political advertising in a rare category of grievances that largely foster bipartisan agreement.
That extends to politics in general. The Pew Research Center found in a 2024 survey that 65% of Americans reported feeling “exhausted” most or all of the time when thinking about politics.
“I am so sick, as most Mainers are, of the negative take and dark tone of the visuals of these ads,” said Kat Taylor, 70, an unenrolled voter who lives in Argyle Township in Penobscot County.
The retiree who previously worked at the University of Maine said she is hit with ads throughout her day, from when she tunes into NEWS CENTER Maine in the early morning to when she walks outside to check the mailbox.
Inside a Portland bar on a recent evening, a college football game was on one of the TVs. Nearly every commercial break featured at least one campaign ad.
The refrains are familiar by now, such as the “I’m Troy Jackson” opening line in one of the pro-Jackson ads, or the “Taxin’ Jackson” criticism in an ad from a pro-Republican group. (That negative ad recently and erroneously went on air in Portland, Oregon, instead of Portland, Maine.)
For those wondering if there are actually more ads in front of them this election year in Maine, the answer is yes.
The numbers prove it.
THOUSANDS UPON THOUSANDS OF ADS
The total number of ads that have aired in Maine’s official media markets of Portland-Auburn, Bangor and Presque Isle is dizzying.
According to the advertising tracking insight firm AdImpact, the Portland-Auburn market has seen more than 24,100 political ads air on TV since the week of Aug. 30. The Bangor market has seen more than 18,100 ads air since that week, while the Presque Isle region in northern Maine has seen roughly 2,750 since then.
In the first week of October alone, 5,787 ads aired on TV across the Portland-Auburn market, or about 827 ads each day, according to AdImpact.
This deluge is possible because of record spending on Maine’s highest profile races. Candidates, their affiliated political action committees, the campaign arms of national parties and dark money groups have so far spent and reserved $315 million on ads across various platforms this election cycle in Maine, per AdImpact.
That figure surpasses the state record of around $200 million in 2020 that mostly covered the U.S. Senate race between Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Sara Gideon.
Maine is the 42nd most populous state but is the 11th most expensive state for political ad spending this cycle, according to AdImpact, which said Tuesday that the total spending will likely get to around $400 million. Republican groups are outspending Democratic groups in Maine and nationally.
But there is some consolation for those tired of all the interruptions. AdImpact initially thought that number would get as high as $490 million in Maine.
DO THE ADS ACTUALLY CONVINCE PEOPLE?
Adding to the frustration of many Mainers: Political advertising is unlikely to move the needle much in any of Maine’s key races.
The gubernatorial race to succeed outgoing Gov. Janet Mills and the 2nd Congressional District contest to succeed U.S. Rep. Jared Golden have certainly drawn attention and outside interest, but ads tied to those elections are relatively few. In the 2nd District, they’re only targeted toward Mainers living in certain regions of the state.
The tight U.S. Senate race between Collins, the Republican seeking a sixth term, and former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic challenger, is a different story.
Ads upon ads have sought to sway the undecided voters who may decide the Senate contest.
An Axios analysis of dollars spent on cable, broadcast and social media along with estimates for streaming platforms found Maine has the priciest per capita Senate race in the nation, with Republican-aligned groups spending $96.99 for each Maine adult and Democratic-aligned groups spending $69.52.
But polls show the number of voters who haven’t made up their mind in that race is minuscule. And despite all of the time, money and effort that goes into producing these ads, past studies have found the effects of political spots to be small in terms of persuading voters.
The Washington Post and George Mason University’s Schar School of Policy and Government conducted a poll of Maine’s Senate race between Sept. 30 and Oct. 5, finding just 3% of respondents did not pick between Jackson and Collins.
In the 2020 election, about 819,000 voters cast a ballot in the race that saw Collins defy the polls to beat Gideon by a comfortable margin. If roughly 3% of the electorate this year is undecided, and the voting pool stays the same size, campaigns are fighting to reach about 24,500 voters.
DEALING WITH ‘THE NASTINESS’
Steve Hamblen, a 75-year-old unenrolled voter from Sanford, said he is getting inundated with ads and political canvassers at his doorstep — a reality that he said has reaffirmed his belief that the country’s campaign finance system needs reform. The U.S. Supreme Court, however, has removed limits on how much parties and corporations can spend on elections.
“The nastiness really annoys me, but people sit there and swallow it,” Hamblen said in late August. “Make up your own mind. Don’t listen to these political ads and just fall for the one-liners.”
The ads indeed make claims that are false, misleading or only partially backed up by citations in small print that are tough for the average viewer to digest in real time.
“The ads do nothing to sway my opinion. I have never been enrolled in any party and am a critical thinker,” Taylor, the Argyle Township resident, said on a recent weekday, adding that the printed ads in her mailbox “aren’t even good for starting my wood stove or composting.”
Whether the ads end up making a difference in the outcome of the Nov. 3 election is likely unmeasurable. Whether Mainers are ready for them to go away until the next cycle is an easier thing to observe.
Peggy Belkenny, an 83-year-old Democrat from Auburn, said last month she wants candidates and their ads to focus on what they would do to help people if they’re elected to office. And if they don’t?
“We’re gonna put them on a plane and send them all to Siberia,” she said. “One way.”
Staff Writer Randy Billings contributed to this report.

title: Russia celebrates Trump's sanctions waiver while Ukraine warns it will encourage attacks
text:
Russia celebrates Trump's sanctions waiver while Ukraine warns it will encourage attacks
President Donald Trump said in an executive order that the move was in America's national interest, but critics say he's "sucking up" to Russia.
Russia celebrates Trump's sanctions waiver while Ukraine warns it will encourage attacks
President Donald Trump said in an executive order that the move was in America's national interest, but critics say he's "sucking up" to Russia.
President Donald Trump waived new sanctions on Russia on Friday, two days before those penalties were set to kick in under a new bipartisan law that he signed last month.
In a new executive order, Trump argues that issuing a waiver at this time "is in the national interests of the United States," without elaborating on that justification.
The sanctions package, which targeted Russian officials and financial institutions, was designed to cut off funds for the Kremlin's invasion of Ukraine and increase pressure at the negotiating table as the Trump administration works toward a peace deal in the yearslong conflict. The law also gave Trump authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with some exceptions.
The law was named after the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., a Trump ally who died unexpectedly earlier this year while working to pass the legislation in Congress.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., who worked closely with Graham on this issue, released a statement slamming the president's decision.
"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin," Blumenthal said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also urged Trump to reverse course as Russia continues targeting Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
"Russia is trying to leave millions of our people without electricity and heating. Pressure is needed to stop this. A U.S. sanctions blackout, easing pressure on the aggressor, financial rewards for Putin – all of this only encourages him to keep attacking," Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post.
Trump has focused his frustration on Ukraine in recent days, urging Zelenskyy to stop attacking Russian oil refineries. 
Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev celebrated the sanctions suspension as a "truly historic moment."
"Economic cooperation between Russia and the United States serves the interests of both nations, contributes to global economic stability, and lays the foundation for building trust and achieving lasting peace," Dmitriev wrote.
The sanctions suspension comes after Trump struck a deal with Putin to purchase Russian diesel, which was met with bipartisan backlash from members of Congress.
Trump argues that the pact will help lower global energy prices, but experts are skeptical that it will have a significant impact at the pump, in part because the war between the U.S. and Iran is still keeping fuel costs elevated.

title: Trump puts new Russia sanctions that he recently signed into law on hold, citing national interest
text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Friday signed an executive order that puts on hold a sweeping new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest.
Trump personally signed the legislation just last month and his move came just two days before a deadline set in the law itself for its implementation. It drew shift condemnation from congressional Democrats.
Named after late South Carolina Sen. Lindsey Graham, the legislation had sought to clamp down more quickly on the flow of financial resources fueling the war against Ukraine.
Trump’s unexpected decision comes a week after he stunningly said the U.S. had agreed to purchase diesel from Russia to try to bring down global energy prices, despite that potentially hurting Ukraine in its war with Russia.
An AP-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research poll published Oct. 1 found that Americans disapprove of the president’s handling of the Iran war and blame him for higher prices. Trump’s approval ratings have sunk to near-historic lows and pressure is mounting as Republicans try to hold control of both chambers of Congress after midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Sanctions were seen as part of Graham’s legacy
Graham, a close ally and friend of the president, had just returned from Ukraine when he unexpectedly died in July. He had advocated for stricter U.S. sanctions against Russia as a way of pressuring it to end its war in Ukraine.
His colleagues in Congress responded with bipartisan support after his death and Trump attached his signature to the legislation — then changed his mind Friday.
The package had been meant to starve Russian President Vladimir Putin of the resources Moscow needs to continue its war in Ukraine after invading its neighbor more than four years ago. The bill, also drafted by Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., had sought to sanction Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers that keeps Russian energy moving.
It also directed Trump to impose up to 100% tariffs on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
Blumenthal said in a statement that Trump was turning his back on “the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies.”
“These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin,” Blumenthal said.
Democratic Virginia Rep. Don Beyer noted on social media shortly after the announcement of the sanctions being suspended that he and others had “warned” Trump might make such a move. The veteran congressman, who spoke out against the bill as it was debated, called on Congress to “fix this flawed law to stop Trump from capitulating to Putin and ensure that it truly supports Ukraine.”
The White House did not immediately explain how pausing the sanctions was in the national interest. The decision was posted on the White House website late in the evening, and the notification noted that the report explaining the decision had been submitted to Congress.
Still, it comes as Trump has increasingly lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blaming him for failing to make a deal with Putin to end the fighting.
The Trump administration, meanwhile, had remained mostly quiet since the passage of the bill with large majorities in the House and Senate following Graham’s sudden death — with lawmakers urged ahead by Zelenskyy.
Trump’s action follows announced diesel deal with Putin
Under last week’s agreement, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.”
Trump’s striking a diesel deal with Putin has been pilloried by Republicans and Democrats alike who say it will help Russia execute its war against Ukraine -- without making a different to global fuel prices, which are elevated mostly due to Trump’s war on Iran.
The sanctions that Trump has now suspended, meanwhile, also had become a campaign centerpiece for Sen. Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to serve out the remaining months in his current term. She is now running to replace him in the Senate more permanently.
Darline Graham said in a statement after Trump signed the bill, “I wish Lindsey were here to celebrate this historic day.” In a debate earlier this week with Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, Graham — who has Trump’s endorsement and is expected to campaign with him in South Carolina next week — said she had been “so proud” to help get the measure passed.
She acknowledged, however, that it was the president’s purview as to how he implemented it.
“It gives the president tools that he can use if he so chooses, to end the war through economic sanctions,” Graham said Sunday during a debate in Columbia. “So that’s up to him as to whether or not he wants to use it, or whether he wants to use something else, but I think the purpose of it is to bring down the gas prices and ultimately end the war. And when the war ends, gas prices will fall.”

title: UMaine football’s losing streak extended to six games
text:
A second-half comeback bid fell short Saturday as UMaine suffered its sixth consecutive football defeat, losing 17-14 to Bryant in Orono.
Maine’s only touchdown was an 11-yard pass from Caden Drezek to Rashawn Marshall early in the third quarter. Noah Carpenter rushed for the 2-point conversion to cut the Black Bears’ deficit to 14-11.
Bryant (5-2, 3-0 CAA) answered with a 26-yard field goal from Nicholas Stoyanovich. Maine’s Samuel Tremblay kicked his second field goal of the game, from 32 yards, early in the fourth quarter, but the Black Bears (1-6, 1-3) got the ball only one more time and were stopped on downs just beyond midfield.
Drezek, making his first start for Maine, was 18 of 34 for 234 yards. Nick Laughlin caught seven passes for 86 yards, and Marshall gained 62 yards on 19 carries.
