title: Scuffles, fires break out as protesters rally across France, joining students
text:
Clashes, fires and looting break out as protesters rally across France, joining students
Violent clashes, fires and looting marred demonstrations across France on Saturday as hundreds of thousands of people marched against rising living costs and poor conditions in schools. About 400 people were arrested nationwide, Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said.
Nuñez said 110 marches drew about 550,000 people across the country. Organizers, including the CGT labor union and students' organizations, said about 800,000 demonstrators took to the streets.
Related video above: Student protests rock France
Nuñez described troublemakers as “extremely violent, radical far-left groups” whom, he said, sought confrontations with police and targeted public buildings, including city halls and local government offices. He said those groups have been joined by offenders willing to loot shops. Most of those arrested are adults, he said.
Some incidents were still ongoing in central Paris on Saturday evening.
Associated Press reporters saw thick black smoke rising from cars, bicycles and other vehicles, and trash bins on fire. A newspaper kiosk also burned, while several shops were looted. Several people have been injured in the clashes.
Many metro stations were closed Saturday at police request, including those around the Champs-Elysées and near the presidential palace, parliament and government offices.
Meanwhile, the majority of peaceful protesters joined a march that moved toward northwestern Paris. The crowd chanted France's national anthem and waved flags, and some people played trumpets and violins.
In Lyon, France’s third-largest city where about 20,000 protesters joined the march, a fire broke out inside a tourist office.
In the southern port city of Marseille, some shops and a municipal police station were damaged, while protesters briefly forced their way into the lobby of City Hall.
Nuñez also reported violence by masked groups against local government buildings in Bordeaux, break-in attempts at Lille and Calais city halls and at a police station in Brest. Violence also broke out in Rennes, Toulouse, Montpellier and Grenoble, among other cities.
In Limoges, a middle-sized town in central France, the City Hall was set on fire. Flames were still raging Saturday evening.
Living costs and school conditions fuel anger
Protesters across France responded to calls on social media to revive the “yellow vest” movement, which emerged in 2018 against social injustice. Demonstrators expressed widespread frustration and anger at the government as gasoline, energy and food prices have spiked in recent months.
Sonia Mabrouk, 40, said she came from a suburb west of Paris with her daughter, a high school student, to protest “everything that’s going wrong,” particularly the neglect of public services. Mabrouk, who took part in the yellow vest protests, criticized “policies that favor the rich and always hit the poorest people in their wallets.”
Many protesters could be seen wearing the fluorescent yellow vests that became a symbol of the 2018 rallies. “There’s a general sense of frustration and anger,” Mabrouk said, as she marched alongside peaceful demonstrators of all ages.
Student groups protesting since mid-September through school blockades have urged supporters to join them.
The CGT, one of France’s major labor unions, also backed the protests, calling for “higher wages and pensions, lower prices and the protection of public services that meet people’s needs.”
Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who backed the high school students movement, also took part in the Paris protest Saturday.
Protester’s injury renews scrutiny of policing
Authorities opened an investigation after a young protester was badly injured Saturday and lost a hand in Saint-Etienne, Nuñez said. He declined to confirm French media reports the injury was caused by a police grenade explosion.
The incident comes as the police have drawn sharp scrutiny over their use of grenades and other riot-control weapons during recent demonstrations.
In the past weeks, France has seen thousands of arrests, hundreds of injuries and schools set on fire as the new school year descended into nationwide student protests that are influencing the country's presidential election campaign and drawing international attention.
Among protesters, particularly gruesome wounds suffered by some teenagers have been blamed on police riot-control weapons. Nuñez suspended the use of a type of police stun grenade against high school demonstrators after a 15-year-old lost a hand. But the suspension does not apply to other protests, including those staged Saturday.

title: Check your boots before hiking in Maine — here’s why
text:
This story was originally published in October 2025.
We’d been hiking for three miles before I started to feel a prickly sensation at the top of my foot near my big toe. It felt like something small, like a pine needle poking into my skin, so I ignored it.
After another quarter of a mile, it was only getting worse, so I stopped in the middle of the trail and pulled off my boot.
A brown stain marked my sock, right where I felt the discomfort. Puzzled and worried that I was bleeding, I removed my sock — but my foot looked normal, maybe a bit pink.
I upended my boot, searching for debris. Out rolled a smooshed caterpillar.
The night before, I’d left my boots outside the door of our camper, and the caterpillar must have crawled inside.
My first instinct was to feel bad for it. I’ve always had a soft spot for animals, big or small. When I was a little girl, I held an elaborate funeral for a ladybug I found on my bedroom window sill. Within me, that sentimentality is still alive and well.
Upon inspection, the caterpillar was that of a hickory tussock moth. Covered in long, white and black hairs, these caterpillars are common throughout Maine in the summer and fall. In fact, we’d seen hundreds of them along the trail that day, and I’d remarked upon it.
“Good thing those aren’t caterpillars that cause rashes,” I had commented while pointing out half a dozen of them denuding a wild blueberry bush.
Oh how wrong I was.
For the past few years, I’ve been worried about a different kind of caterpillar: the brown-tail moth.
Making headlines, this species has spread throughout Maine, stripping oak and birch trees and causing people to break out in terrible, itchy rashes. Their hairs can even cause respiratory problems.
A supervillain of the caterpillar world, the brown-tail moth has eclipsed all others, lulling me into a false sense of security. My faulty logic has been: if it’s not a brown-tailed moth caterpillar, it’s harmless. That, of course, is hogwash.
The hickory tussock moth caterpillar (Lophocampa caryae) can indeed cause problems. Their hairs are barbed and contain an irritating substance that causes some people to have an allergic reaction.
A 2001 study at the Pittsburgh Poison Center analyzed 365 human exposures to the tussock moth caterpillar over a two-year period. Routine treatment included removal of the hairs and the administration of antihistamines (for allergic reactions) and corticosteroids.
“Spines may be hollow, barbed or branched, connected to a venom gland at its base (Megalopyge) or solid and function as a mechanical irritant,” the study states.
Great. Those hairs or “spines” had been crushed into the top of my foot for miles, and I was starting to feel the effects.
Over the course of the next day or so, my foot swelled and developed a bumpy rash of tiny blisters that itched horrifically — especially at night. Multiple health organizations liken the reaction to a poison ivy rash, and I agree.
It looked ghastly, and felt worse.
Did I send a photo of my zombie foot to friends? Yes. Will I publish it in the newspaper? No. What if this is the only column you’ve ever read of mine? I’d rather not be remembered that way.
On the plus side, I no longer feel bad for the caterpillar. At least he went down swinging.
After about a week of anti-itch cream — plus a session of me attempting to remove tiny caterpillar hairs from my skin with packing tape — my foot is back to normal. No real harm done. But the experience taught me to look in my hiking boots before shoving my feet into them.
We may not have scorpions in Maine, but our caterpillars aren’t messing around.

title: Oregon father is the latest armed civilian to confront a gunman in a US mass shooting
text:
Few mass shootings in the U.S. end like the deadly attack on an Oregon elementary school: with an armed civilian opening fire on the gunman.
President Donald Trump joined others Friday in praising a father of two girls who confronted a teenage gunman during the attack at Silver Rail Elementary School, which killed three students and a teacher. Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, intervened by firing his own weapon after the shooting began at his daughters’ school in the town of Bend.
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump told reporters at the White House.
Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter who had a .40-caliber pistol legally stored in his vehicle, entered the school, heard shots and fired his gun after seeing a teacher fighting with the shooter, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.
Cases like the Oregon intervention remain rare, according to the Advanced Law Enforcement Rapid Response Training Center at Texas State University.
The ALERRT center tracked what it calls “active attack” incidents where the perpetrator used firearms, blades or vehicles from 2000 to 2025.
Out of 634 cases studied, 374 ended before police arrived. Among those, 29 ended when armed civilians shot the attacker. In another 31 incidents, civilians subdued the attacker by some other method, such as wrestling them to the ground or removing the weapon.
“They recognize they may be the only way to stop it before law enforcement arrives,” said James Keith, a spokesperson for the center.
The heroic “good guy with a gun” who can stop an attack even before law enforcement can arrive has long been a rallying cry by gun rights advocates, arguing that armed citizens can act as a first line of self-defense and public protection. In some cases, the person who intervenes has had law enforcement or military training. Other times they are just people who reacted in a moment of chaos.
In some states, lawmakers have sought to put armed citizens in position to head off an attack as soon as possible in some public spaces.
Texas created a school marshal program in 2013 to allow trained teachers and staff to carry concealed firearms on campus. It expanded safety programs and requirements for armed security and personnel at schools after mass shootings at a high school near Houston in 2018, and at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde in 2022.
Texas has some of the least restrictive gun control laws in the country, according to the Giffords Law Center to Prevent Gun Violence. The group rates Oregon among the strongest.
Some prominent examples of armed citizens who confronted gunmen to help stop mass shootings:
Twin Falls, Idaho, In-N-Out
A gunman killed three people and wounded seven more at an In-N-Out Burger on Aug. 3. Law enforcement authorities said the gunman may have killed more if not for an off-duty officer who was a customer at the restaurant, and an armed civilian who exchanged fire with the gunman.
Jordan Salinas said he didn’t hesitate to grab his gun and confront the gunman when he saw people fleeing the restaurant and heard gunfire. Under return fire, the gunman retreated and ultimately killed himself.
“He did not like it when bullets started flying both ways,” Salinas told the Idaho Statesman. “There’s a task that needs to be done, and we’re the ones who need to do it.”
White Settlement, Texas, church shooting
In December 2019, a man wearing a disguise and a trench coat pulled out a shotgun and killed two people during a Sunday service at West Freeway Church of Christ before he was killed by Jack Wilson, a 71-year-old firearms instructor who had also been a reserve sheriff’s deputy.
Wilson stayed calm as worshippers scrambled for cover.
“The only clear shot I had was his head because I still had people in the pews that were not all the way down as low as they could. That was my one shot,” Wilson said in 2019.
Sutherland Springs, Texas, church shooting
A gunman killed 26 people at a small-town church in 2017. Stephen Willeford, a former National Rifle Association instructor who lived across the street, grabbed his rifle and ran in his bare feet to open fire at the attacker, wounding him.
The gunman fled and Willeford flagged down a passing driver. The two men chased after the gunman, who eventually killed himself.
“I kept hearing the shots: pop, pop, pop” when the gunfire started at the church, Willeford said in 2017. “And I knew every one of those shots represented someone, that it was aimed at someone.”

title: Sen. Elizabeth Warren joins Troy Jackson and Hannah Pingree at No Kings rally in Portland
text:
Sen. Elizabeth Warren joins Troy Jackson and Hannah Pingree at No Kings rally in Portland
Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-MA, joined Democratic candidates for U.S. Senate Troy Jackson and for Maine governor Hannah Pingree on Saturday in Portland for a No Kings Rally.
Hundreds of supporters filled Deering Oaks Park to speak out against President Trump and Jackson's opponent, Republican Sen. Susan Collins.
"No kings means that we stand up," said Warren. "We show pride. We show backbone. We go to the polls. We vote for a fighter. We vote for Troy Jackson."
Jackson continued to emphasize his message of fighting for working Mainers, while pointing towards connections between Collins and Trump.
"You don't get to vote to fund Donald Trump's agenda and then come home and tell us how concerned you are about it," commented Jackson. "Billionaires do not own this country. And this is something across the state that I think people have to understand better than ever. A Senate seat doesn't belong to a person who has held it for 30 years. It still belongs to the people of Maine."
Pingree also spoke out against President Trump, specifically pointing to the responsibility she would take if elected to the Blaine House.
"Governors defend immigrants and teachers," stated Pingree. "Governors safeguard elections. They stand up for public health. Governors help feed kids and ensure seniors can heat their homes when Washington breaks down. Governors are the ones on the front lines. And right now, Maine needs a governor who will never back down."
Collins' campaign communications director, Blake Kernen, responded that Jackson has been campaigning with the far left of the Democratic Party. This weekend comes after Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-VT, held three events with Jackson.
Kernen added, "Senator Collins will continue campaigning on her record of independent leadership and delivering results for Maine."

title: Explore the wild backcountry of the Nahmakanta Public Land
text:
Perched comfortably on a shelf of granite just above the shoreline of Sixth Debsconeag Pond, I am both entertained and awed by the brook trout leaping out of the water like little dolphins. Must be something mighty tasty they’re feasting on. My campfire crackles next to me as I chow down on a pouch of backpacker food. The sun behind my back has sunk into the trees, and try as I might to stay awake, I’m thinking it will be an early night in the bag.
Sixth Debsconeag Pond lies at the heart of the Debsconeag Backcountry in the northeast corner of Nahmakanta Public Land, a sprawling 43,000-acre expanse that ranges across four unorganized townships—T1 R12 WELS, T1 R11 WELS, Rainbow Township and T2 R12 WELS—in the northern reaches of Maine’s famed 100-Mile Wilderness. Low but rugged mountains, dense forests and pristine waters characterize this remote region.
The Debsconeag Backcountry Trail threads through this sector of the Nahmakanta for 12 miles, making a figure-eight loop past Fifth, Sixth, Seventh and Eighth Debsconeag ponds as well as one named Stink Pond (I’d love to know the origin of that name, for sure). Several miles along Nahmakanta Lake form the outer portion of the upper loop. Mossy ledge outcrops dot the terrain and offer wonderful views of the wild country all around.
A great horned owl makes its presence known from the woods up along the pond’s northern edge. And although I haven’t noticed loons on Sixth Debsconeag Pond, in the gathering darkness I hear two call from below on Nahmakanta Lake. I stand still for a few moments amid the fragrant spruce trees on the rocky point, nip of bourbon in hand, and just listen and look. Stars begin to populate the inky black sky above. Absolutely perfect.
Tomorrow, I’ll don my ultralight daypack and finish off the rest of the Debsconeag hike before returning to camp, breaking down, and packing out to the trailhead. For now, though, I am happy to simply revel in the quiet of the night, far from any errant noise, light or traffic. No wonder, though, given that I’m situated in the midst of a 9,200-acre roadless area that makes up the lion’s share of 11,800 acres of ecological reserve. This is the place to be.
Nahmakanta Public Land, established in 1990, is a key connector in a nearly continuous corridor of conservation lands stretching from Moosehead Lake to Katahdin Woods and Waters National Monument. Owned by the state and managed for multiple uses by the Maine Bureau of Parks and Lands, the Nahmakanta features 35 miles of hiking trails (plus a segment of the Appalachian Trail) and a host of backcountry and roadside campsites.
Along the southern boundary of the Nahmakanta is the Turtle Ridge Trail, another figure-eight loop that meanders over several ridgetops and past a series of pristine ponds for 8 miles. On the southeastern edge is the Tumbledown Dick Trail, which leads past a couple more ponds and to tumbling Tumbledown Dick Falls. The Appalachian Trail winds through the Nahmakanta for 9 miles, along the namesake lake and over Nesuntabunt Mountain.
For a truly grand backpacking adventure, hikers can take to the Great Circle Trail, a 30-mile circuit that meanders through the best of the Nahmakanta terrain. This terrific new route, completed just five years ago after 15 years of trail work, connects several previously existing trails — Tumbledown Dick, the Debsconeag Backcountry Trail, a few miles of the AT, and Turtle Ridge — to several new trail segments, specifically the Pollywog Trail along Pollywog Pond to Wadleigh Pond, the Wadleigh Trail to the top of Wadleigh Mountain, and the Third Musquash Trail.
Tackle the entire Great Circle Trail loop, and you’ll gain more than 3,000 feet of elevation. There are several established campsites along the way, but you can also wild camp (except in the AT corridor), provided you practice the principles of “Leave No Trace.”
Nahmakanta Lake is, of course, the land’s magnificent centerpiece, so some time well spent there admiring its beauty is warranted. Next summer, I think I’ll bring my canoe, camping gear and cooler, and explore the 1,100-acre water body with paddle power. I’ve seen those beautiful beach campsites from high above, after all, and can just picture my camp chair there on the sand, me with cold beer in hand. Good living, that.
Carey Kish of Mount Desert Island is a Triple Crown hiker, freelance writer, and author of three hiking guides. Connect with Carey on Facebook and Instagram and at [email protected].

title: Blue Hill farm popular for berry-picking and hayrides is on the market for $4.5M
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
A popular Blue Hill berry-picking farm is up for sale for $4.5 million for the first time in a quarter century.
Married couple Jeff and Trudy Beardsworth are selling Homewood Farm after running the family-friendly Ackley Farm Road property for 25 years. The farm — which has sold everything from turkeys, chickens and lambs to pumpkins, potatoes and apple cider — has long been a local hotspot for berry-picking.
The Beardsworths, who moved to the property in 2001, announced the sale Wednesday afternoon, according to their Facebook post.
“We’ve poured our hearts, hard work and love into farming this land and making it our own,” the owners said Wednesday on social media. “Before us, Homewood Farm was owned by Ruth and Millard Bowden. We had the privilege of farming the land under Ruth’s ownership for seven years before making it our own and continuing the farm’s story for the past 25 years.”
Jeff Beardsworth, a logger by trade who started working on the farm at 27 and is now 66, said he’s not in a big rush to sell the land. He and his wife plan to relocate to Penobscot, but they’ve still planted strawberries for next season in the event they haven’t found an interested buyer by then.
“The lady who left me this place said, ‘Jeff, if the necklace gets too heavy, take it off,’” Jeff Beardsworth told the Bangor Daily News Friday afternoon. “I said, ‘What do you mean? I don’t wear jewelry.’ She goes, ‘the farm.’ So now I look at it and yeah, the necklace is getting heavy and I’ve got to see if someone else wants to enjoy it.”
Homewood Farm, listed by Voyageur Signature Properties, is a 170-acre property with views of the Blue Hill Peninsula, according to the listing.
The 4-bedroom farmhouse was first built in the mid-1800s but was expanded and renovated in 2021, preserving the barroom’s tin ceilings and walls and the kitchen’s exposed ceiling beams. The kitchen holds a vintage, cast-iron and wood-burning stove that dates back more than a 100 years.
The property includes 28 acres of fertile cropland, 30 acres of pasture and an actively managed woodland, according to the listing. It also features an antique hay barn that was relocated to the property and is more than several hundred years old, according to the listing.
The listing includes storage space, produce-packing facilities, livestock-watering ponds and ample equipment, according to the property description.
“It’s not an easy place to leave: Homewood Farm has been so much more than a home or a business — it’s been our life,” the Beardsworths said on Facebook. “There are countless memories woven into this land, and it’s hard to imagine handing it over to someone new. But while the farm is in great shape and we still have plenty of life and energy left in us, we feel it’s time to pass the torch to the next ambitious farmer, a new family, or someone with a dream of their own.”
The couple has two kids — a local dental hygienist and a son in California — neither of whom want to take over the business, he said.
“I’m not selling it because of my health — I’m just selling it because I’ve got to make a decision someday before I pass or my kids are going to make it for me,” Jeff Beardsworth said.
Locals responded to the couple’s farewell post with memories of their time at the farm. One commenter wrote of her family’s love for the annual hayrides the farm offered.
“Our family has enjoyed your farm for several years,” another commenter wrote. You have brought much happiness to many by sharing your beautiful spot. Good luck to you!!!”

title: Video shows police officer punching, using Taser on man in chair
text:
DONORA, Pa. (KDKA) — A Pennsylvania resident is calling attention to an incident between a man and a police officer after sharing video of their encounter.
The situation began with a call to Donora police about a domestic disturbance report.
The video shows Shawn Bowman sitting in a chair as an officer tries to handcuff him after officers were called to his home for the alleged domestic disturbance.
In the video, Bowman moves his hand toward the officer’s hands. The officer then punches him in the face twice and uses a Taser. Bowman falls to the ground.
Dennis Hawkins Jr., a longtime Donora resident, said he reacted after seeing the video.
“I just started shaking. I can’t believe someone in our town is going through this from a person who is supposed to protect and serve the people of this community,” Hawkins said.
Criminal complaint details
In the criminal complaint, the officer wrote that after he used the Taser, he repeatedly ordered Bowman to get on the ground and put his hands behind his back before he complied.
“If they’re not resisting or causing any threat to you, that force shouldn’t be taken. It looks like a rogue officer exercising his right to do whatever he wants to do because he has a badge on,” Hawkins said.
Community reaction
Hawkins often uses his Facebook page to bring attention to community concerns. After he shared the video, questions about the officer’s use of force came in. He said the reaction goes beyond anger.
“People are scared. It seems like no one is safe cause that guy was probably 60 years old,” Hawkins said.
Donora police were asked whether they were aware of the video. The chief was not in, and there has been no response.
“It definitely should be investigated, but its like who’s going to investigate it,” Hawkins said.

title: Maranacook girls, Winthrop boys win MVC cross country titles
text:
AUGUSTA — William Morris of Dirigo and Reagan Mattson of Maranacook dominated their competition Saturday while winning individual titles in the Mountain Valley Conference cross country championships at University of Maine at Augusta’s Elvin Fields.
Winthrop cruised to the boys team championship with 30 points, far ahead of Maranacook (72) and Boothbay/Wiscasset (93). Mattson helped Maranacook (51 points) edged Boothbay/Wiscasset (59) for the girls team title.
Morris, a senior, finished the 5-kilometer course with a time of 16:20.26, more than 35 seconds quicker than Winthrop’s Alfie Cognata (16:55.68) and Sawyer Wess (16:56.00).
“It’s not a very fast course, I wasn’t going for any (personal records),” Morris said. “Maybe it’s a lack of confidence or something, but I’m always scared I’m going to get passed. My coach has always drilled into me to never look back, but I just never seem to lose that fear, and push (as if) someone is going to pass me.”
Morris, who swept the MVC, Class C South and Class C state titles last season, has had another successful fall. He was runner-up to Scarborough’s Atticus Merriam by 0.15 seconds at the Festival of Champions in Belfast on Oct. 3.
“I’m feeling pretty good about states and regionals,” Morris said. “I feel like MVC is the strongest Class C conference. If you can place well here, you can place well at states.”
Mattson, a freshman, finished in 19:35.31, more than 1:15 faster than runner-up McKenzie Boyle (20:50.52) of Dirigo. Mattson’s teammate, Kira Pelletier, placed third (21:07.85).
“It felt good (to win), I was kind of cold to start,” Mattson said. “It was kind of rough, but I got warmed up and it was fun to run with the girls in the woods. It’s definitely a goal of mine to get out and separate myself (from the group), then you just try to take your mind off the race and try to expand the gap.”
Mattson has already made a name for herself in her freshman year. She won her first high school race, the Scot Laliberte Invitational at Cony High in Augusta, set a Winthrop course record with a time of 19.56.84 on Sept. 17, and was the top freshman girls runner (18:55) at the Festival of Champions.
“She’s been so strong all season long, she’s just a real talent,” said Maranacook coach Casey Spencer. “She consistently works hard at everything she does and it continues to pay off.”
The Winthrop boys had five runners in the top 10 in the boys race. Aside from Cognata and Wess, Sam St. Germain (17:56.67) placed seventh, Michael Van Tassel (18:04.73) was eighth and Gianni Haefele (18:53.30) finished 10th.
The Winthrop boys won MVC and Class C South titles last year but finished runner-up at the state meet to Houlton/Greater Houlton Christian Academy.
“We had a plan and we executed it,” said Winthrop coach Ed Van Tassel. “I’m happy. I think next week at regionals, we’ll have a similar type of performance. And we’ve had states circled (on our calendars) since last year.”
Maranacook’s Harper Olmstead (22:46.11) finished eighth in the girls race, giving the Black Bears three top-10 finishers.
“The team’s worked really hard,” Spencer said. “We’re feeling pretty good. We really have our eyes on the next two weekends (at regionals and states), to tell the truth. We worked really hard this past week and did our best (today), and it worked out really well for the girls.”
Temperatures were in the low 50s with a strong breeze, chilly for spectators but good conditions for runners as they danced in and out of the woods.
Morris and Mattson were named the MVC Runners of the Year. Van Tassel and Spencer are the Coaches of the Year.

title: Fisherman, 71, attacked and killed by 12-foot alligator alongside Florida lake
text:
A 71-year-old man fishing on the shore of a Florida pond was attacked and killed on Friday by a nearly 12-foot alligator, the second fatal such attack reported this year.
Steven Hamilton of Winter Garden was standing on the shoreline of Lake Apopka at Dr. Bradford Memorial Park, 15 miles (24 kilometers) northwest of Orlando, when the reptile struck around 5 p.m., the Winter Garden Police Department said.
The presence of other active alligators in the water complicated any chance of rescuing Hamilton, whose body was recovered around two hours later, Winter Garden Fire Chief Jose Gainza told FOX35.
Hamilton’s death marked the second deadly alligator attack in Florida this year.
After a 31-year-old Oviedo woman, Brittany Clark, was killed by a 13-foot alligator near her home in June, Republican U.S. Rep. Greg Steube introduced a resolution calling for the Comptroller General and U.S. Department of the Interior to study the impacts of the American alligator’s listing as “threatened due to similarity of appearance” on Florida’s ability to remove nuisance alligators from residential and commercial waterways. He said the species has been fully recovered since 1987, but it remains protected to prevent trafficking and the hunting of the similar-looking American crocodile.
Using Florida state data, the two 2026 deaths bring the total number of individuals killed by alligators since 1948 to 34. Among them was a 61-year-old woman tipped out of her canoe by an alligator in 2025 and an 85-year-old widow who was dragged out of her backyard by an alligator while walking her dog in 2023.
Police Capt. Michael Mason said authorities were not alerted in advance Friday that an alligator was near the shoreline of the lake, possibly because the lake “has tons of alligators in it.” He said police have launched a joint investigation with the Florida Fish & Wildlife Conservation Commission, whose trappers captured and killed the animal.
“Always be aware of your surroundings. Always be safe,” he said. “Wildlife: Respect it. Keep your distance. It looks like it’s docile, it looks like your Florida emblem, but it can be dangerous.”

title: Retail price impacts from the Iran war are uneven but add up for US households before midterms
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
NEW YORK (AP) — More than seven months into the U.S. war with Iran, sharply higher fuel prices are making it more expensive to drive and fly and adding to the cost of some goods, prolonging the strain on American households as the midterm elections approach.
Motorists and airline passengers have borne the clearest consequences as the fighting disrupts Middle East oil shipments. Some companies have raised delivery charges or prices on selected products. Yet the higher cost of making and moving goods has not translated into across-the-board price increases at stores.
Shoppers may not be spared indefinitely, though. Many companies have absorbed at least part of their higher production and transportation costs. A September jump in wholesale prices suggests some businesses may eventually charge more if fuel prices stay elevated.
The chief economist at Moody’s Analytics, Mark Zandi, estimated this week that the war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, including $1,100 in higher energy prices, $540 in higher interest rates and $360 in military costs. The energy portion is growing by $50 a week at current fuel prices, Zandi said.
Here’s a look at price changes since the war began and which goods and services could be most susceptible to increases in the months ahead:
Filling up fuel tanks is noticeably more expensive
BEFORE THE WAR: Regular gasoline averaged $2.98 a gallon nationwide and diesel $3.76 almost eight months ago, according to AAA. Gas peaked at $4.56 in May, below its 2022 record, while diesel reached a record $6.53 in September.
WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: On Friday, the national average stood at $4.33 a gallon for gasoline, or 45% above its prewar level, and was up 68% for diesel at $6.33, AAA reported. Gas typically costs less in the fall, and this is the first October a gallon of regular gas has cost more than $4 on average, it said.
Expensive diesel is less apparent to most U.S. residents but contributes to overall inflation by raising the cost of moving goods.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz remains dangerous and constrained, prolonging uncertainty over oil supplies and fuel prices. The Energy Information Administration said this month that it expected winter heating costs to be 21% higher for the roughly 3% of households that rely on heating oil, most of them in the Northeast, assuming the weather is mild.
Higher airfares are hard to escape too
BEFORE THE WAR: Jet fuel averaged $99 a barrel worldwide before the war, doubled to $209 in April and climbed back to nearly $195 in September after a spring decline, according to the International Air Transport Association.
WHAT’S REACHED CONSUMERS: Airlines have raised ticket prices and fees, trimmed schedules and shelved plans to add flights. Airfares cost about 22% more in September than they did a year earlier, the consumer price index showed. Average domestic airfares rose from $405 in late 2025 to $445 in the April through June period of this year, excluding optional fees, according to the U.S. Bureau of Transportation Statistics.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Fuel price volatility makes it harder for airlines to plan and could discourage them from lowering fares even when fuel prices start to fall, analysts said. United Airlines pulled some December flights and warned of further possible cuts in 2027. Fewer available seats could mean less pressure to hold ticket prices down.
Higher fares have covered substantial portions of higher fuel costs for domestic airlines but not enough to prevent a squeeze on their third-quarter profits, according to consensus estimates.
Any growth in grocery prices pains Americans after multiple years of food inflation
BEFORE THE WAR: The U.S. Department of Agriculture initially expected grocery prices to rise 1.7% this year, below the historical annual average. USDA now expects a still comparatively modest 2.4% increase.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Individual food prices can be volatile, and it’s not clear how much of this year’s expected increase is due to the war and how much is due to other factors, including tariffs, unfavorable weather and higher labor costs.
Cornell University economics professor Chris Barrett said he was surprised grocery prices haven’t risen faster given higher costs for diesel, fertilizer and refrigeration. USDA revised its 2026 fertilizer cost estimates for major crops upward by 9% to 13% and fuel, lubricant and electricity estimates by 33% to 41%.
Barrett suspects retailers are absorbing some increases to avoid alienating fed-up customers after multiple years of food inflation. Grocery prices in September were about 22% higher than five years earlier.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Experts have warned that fresh produce and other frequently replenished perishables could respond quickly to higher transportation and refrigeration costs. Barrett sees “very little prospect” of a significant reduction in fuel prices that could ease the pressure on farmers and truckers.
A strengthening El Niño weather pattern could damage crops through drought, heat or flooding, the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization warned. That could lift commodity prices, although ample inventories and good harvests elsewhere may limit the impact on groceries.
Rubber meets the road when it comes to shoe prices
BEFORE THE WAR: Nearly all shoes sold in the U.S. are imported, and roughly 70% of the materials in a synthetic shoe are petrochemical-based, according to Footwear Distributors and Retailers of America. The industry trade group opposed Trump administration tariffs last year.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: Footwear prices were 3.4% higher in September compared to 12 months earlier, according to the consumer price index. Men’s shoes went up the most, by 4.5%.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: While import costs are down from a year ago, the footwear trade group said oil prices, tariffs and geopolitical uncertainty are likely to keep retail shoe prices rising into 2027.
“Footwear companies are working hard to keep shoes affordable, but there is a limit to how much additional cost businesses can absorb before those pressures reach consumers,” FDRA President and CEO Matt Priest said.
Transportation costs add up throughout product supply chains
BEFORE THE WAR: The cost of moving goods and delivering packages was already increasing and depended on more than fuel.
WHAT HAS REACHED CONSUMERS: It’s not clear. September producer-price data showed that transportation and warehousing of goods sold to businesses as inputs cost 10.2% more than a year earlier. Prices for truck and water freight services each rose 19.3%. The indexes measure what transportation providers charged but do not show how much of the increase appeared in retail prices.
Consumers have felt the higher costs most directly when sending packages. The U.S. Postal Service raised base prices 8% in April for Priority Mail Express, Priority Mail, Ground Advantage and Parcel Select, citing increased transportation costs. UPS, FedEx and DHL also impose fuel surcharges on many shipments.
WHAT COULD COME NEXT: Shipping costs could remain elevated during the holiday season even if oil prices ease. Third-party provider AFS Logistics and financial services company TD Cowen project record parcel costs this quarter and the highest truckload rates since early 2022.
“We expect fuel to drive elevated transportation costs for the foreseeable future,” AFS Logistics CEO Andy Dyer said.
Although UPS and FedEx surcharges could decline if diesel and jet fuel prices fall, changes to carrier surcharge formulas, holiday fees and tight trucking capacity could keep total shipping bills elevated, AFS said.
__
Grantham-Philips contributed from Chicago, Yamat from Las Vegas and Durbin from Detroit.

title: Mainers offer 6 tips for family caregivers
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
Karen Groves has been taking care of her 93-year-old mother, Jean Groves, for five years.
Her mom lives at Berwick Estates, an assisted living facility near Groves’ home in South Berwick, but Groves sees her mother almost daily, taking her to twice-weekly dialysis treatments, plus other medical and hair appointments.
The retired Portsmouth Naval Shipyard engineer is never far away in case she gets a call from Berwick Estates — her mom has a variety of health, mobility and cognitive issues and has already been hospitalized four times this year.
“I feel very tied down,” said Groves, 69. “Usually once a year, one of my kids will cover for me for a few days. Then I can go away without waiting for the phone to ring. Last year I went to Vermont for four days and the mental break was amazing.”
Making time for yourself is one piece of advice Groves and other family caregivers offered to those who may be new to or still struggling with challenges that come with caring for an aging relative.
Nancy Jo Polito, 78, of Portland, wrote a book, “Taking Care of Business: Tales of a Caregiver,” about caring for her mother, Isabel Profenno Polito, who died in 2010 at age 93.
Her mother suffered from multiple health problems throughout her life, so Polito began helping out around the house when she was 5 years old and never stopped. When her mother fell and broke her wrist at age 89, she moved to a skilled nursing facility.
Polito’s concerns about the quality of care her mother received there led her to become a super advocate, regularly monitoring her mother’s meals, medications, bathing schedule, foot care and even doctor’s orders for medical tests and treatments.
“You just can’t admit someone and walk away and feel good about it,” Polito said. “You have to be an advocate to make sure they’re getting the right care.”
Here are some tips from the front lines of caregiving:
1. Get comfortable with being an advocate
It can be challenging, but it’s probably the most valuable role in caregiving — being an advocate and a witness to ensure a loved one receives proper care. That includes medical appointments, for in-home services and in long-term care facilities.
Visit and call regularly, ask questions and stop by randomly to see how living conditions measure up.
“You have to keep open communication and you have to stay on top of it,” Polito said. “I was told I was too pushy, but they like it when you don’t come in all the time.”
2. Learn what services are available
Search the internet for family caregiver programs that are available in your area. Elder care and social service agencies can help. AgeMaine, formerly Southern Maine Agency on Aging, is a good place to start.
“Be resourceful,” said Marvella Heard, 56, of Biddeford, who cares for her 79-year-old father, Samuel. “I wasn’t ready for all this. It’s complicated, like they don’t want it to be easy. It’s trial and error, but you figure things out.”
3. Meet with an elder law attorney
Whether you are a caregiver charged with overseeing a loved one’s finances and personal affairs, or you want to make long-range plans for yourself, an elder law attorney can help.
In addition to estate planning, which includes wills, trusts, powers of attorney, healthcare proxies and advanced directives, elder law attorneys handle asset protection, long-term care plans, government benefits, guardianships and elder abuse prevention.
Clare Herrmann, of Portland, cares for her husband, Jim Vollmar. The couple, both 78, found some peace of mind meeting with an elder law attorney.
“It takes all the questions out of it,” Herrmann said. “Who will take care of your finances? Who will make sure you have proper care as you age? All of that needs to be in writing and it’s hard to come up with all the ‘what ifs’ on your own.”
To find an elder law attorney, check the Maine State Bar Association’s Lawyer Referral Service or the National Academy of Elder Law Attorneys.
4. Put family controversy aside
Caring for an aging family member is often challenging on its own. Don’t let old grudges with siblings or other relatives make it more difficult.
“Put personal feeling aside and focus on caring for the person,” Heard said. “It’s very important to stick together at times like this. Be there for each other and one person won’t be overwhelmed.”
5. Take care of yourself
Reach out for assistance through elder care agencies, peer support groups and community organizations. Engage in activities that connect you with others outside the sphere of caregiving. Make time to do what makes you happy, even if it’s only for a few hours.
For Groves, that means treating any free day like an adventure, so she goes hiking or to a museum. She also enjoys volunteering and still makes time for it, teaching balance exercise classes for older adults.
“I find it gratifying and inspiring,” Groves said. “Volunteering was always going to be a big part of my retirement and I don’t want to give that up.”
6. Cut yourself some slack
It’s easy to feel guilty if you think you’re not doing enough as a caregiver, especially when a loved one gets sick or injured in a fall.
“You get waves of that,” Polito said. “You blame yourself when things happen. You feel you should have done more. You just have to let it go. It’s insurmountable at times. You can’t do it all.”

title: University official dies in freak accident while on walking tour at historic landmark
text:
SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. (KPHO/Gray News) — A senior leader of a Brazilian university died Friday afternoon in what is being called a freak accident while on a walking tour of Frank Lloyd Wright’s historic Taliesin West home in Scottsdale.
According to the Scottsdale Fire Department, Rogério Renato Mateucci, rector of the Pontifical Catholic University of Paraná, was struck by roofing material dislodged by strong winds.
Mateucci was said to be with a group on a walking tour at the late architect’s home when he was hit.
Fire officials said Mateucci, only identified as a Brazilian tourist by crews, died instantly and was pronounced dead at the scene.
No foul play was suspected. Police said they are investigating the death as a weather-related accident.
The National Weather Service reported east winds of 22 mph in Scottsdale around 2 p.m. Friday, with gusts up to 32 mph.
Taliesin West was closed to the public until further notice following Mateucci’s death.
“The Foundation extends its deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of the individual,” the foundation’s CEO Joe Spector said in a statement.
The historic home, built in 1937, served as Wright’s winter home and desert laboratory in the foothills of the McDowell Mountains. It is now a National Historic Landmark and home to the Frank Lloyd Wright Foundation.
In an Instagram post, the university said classes will be canceled Saturday and Monday, and administrative offices will be closed Monday, to mourn its highest-ranking official.

title: Trump administration aims to remove judge in golf course case, accuses her of ‘egregious’ behavior
text:
Trump administration seeks to remove judge in golf course case, accuses her of ‘egregious’ behavior
The Trump administration has requested the removal of the federal judge overseeing a legal challenge to President Donald Trump’s plans to overhaul a Washington, D.C., public golf course, accusing her of having “bias.”
Related video above: Judge bans Trump from removing trees on public Washington, DC, golf course
In a motion filed Friday, the administration’s lawyer said U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes’ “behavior in this case is nothing short of egregious,” pointing to a tense hearing earlier this week.
CNN previously reported that during Monday’s hearing, Reyes — who was appointed to the bench by former President Joe Biden — said she was “furious” with the Trump administration for cutting down 169 trees from the East Potomac Golf Course without first notifying the court, adding that “the government can’t be trusted.”
In Friday’s filing, the Justice Department lawyer said, “Judge Reyes’s conduct rises to the level of deep-seated and unequivocal antipathy toward the Trump Administration,” raising comments she made when overseeing other cases involving the administration.
“The Trump Administration is entitled to a neutral forum and an adjudicator who is capable of maintaining the appearance of impartiality,” the lawyer continued. “Judge Reyes has demonstrated she cannot do that.”
Friday’s filing is part of a legal challenge from a preservationist group and two local golfers against Trump’s plans to transform the East Potomac Golf Course into a championship-caliber course. The proposed renovation is among several construction projects that the president has launched since returning to the White House as part of his efforts to reshape the physical landscape of Washington, D.C.
Federal officials said in a recent court filing that nearly 730 trees will need to be cleared as part of the renovation plan, describing it as routine maintenance meant to eliminate potential hazards.
The administration’s lawyer also took issue with Reyes requiring “high-level” officials to be at the Monday hearing, writing that she “demonstrates a cavalier disregard for these officials’ valuable time, as well as a blatant disregard for black-letter separation of powers principles she should be aware of as a federal judge.”
The lawyer went on to point to comments that Reyes previously made when overseeing other cases involving the Trump administration to argue that there is a “pattern of animus.”
According to the filing, Reyes said the administration is “literally erasing transgender people” with its ban on transgender service members. The judge ultimately blocked the ban.

title: It was a week of good, bad and ugly sports stories in Maine
text:
Rarely do we get a week in Maine chock full of sports stories that make you do a double take. This week, we got three.
These three stories will make you nod your head in gratitude, or just make you shake your head. They’ll tear at your faith in humanity, then build it back up.
The good: Joe Russo retires
The good isn’t that Russo retired after 36 season coaching the Portland High boys basketball team, it’s that we got three and a half decades of Russo and he was able to step away on his own terms.
Russo is one of 10 coaches in state history to win at least 500 games, and he won his sixth state championship this past season. Russo’s final season may have been his best coaching job. Take away the fact that some of his players missed early season practices while they prepared for the Class A football state championship game. Set aside injuries to key players throughout the regular season. Those are issues coaches have dealt with for years.
This season, with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement running around the state under the guise of the grotesquely named “Operation Catch of the Day,” Russo had at times 17% of his team out of school, kept home by parents fearful of their son being yanked off the street and taken to God knows where.
Through the most stressful time many of those teenagers have lived through, Russo kept them together. Winning 517 games and leaving a healthy collection of Gold Balls in the trophy case are fine benchmarks, but being there when your players are facing serious life-changing threats, that’s the mark of a truly great coach.
The bad: Police investigate fight at youth football game in Livermore Falls
Yeah, shouldn’t be surprised by this one. Adults have behaved like oafs at youth sports for decades. There hasn’t been a bar to sink below for years. That bar is buried cable. You need a backhoe and a dig-safe permit to reach it.
The latest incident occurred at a youth football game in Livermore Falls last Saturday. A video of the incident shows parent Donna Jewell approach coach Dylan Rider, as she’s holding a puppy. She appears to make contact with Rider as he turned toward her. Rider pushed Jewell to the ground, then made his way toward another fight between a pair of men, one of them his father.
You can be sure everyone involved is 100% confident they are in the right. In whatever heat of the moment can happen at a youth football game, nobody every stops to consider that they’re about to play the fool. In those moments, people forget youth sports should be about teaching the game and instilling fondness and respect for the game.
It’s especially disappointing that one of those involved, Rider, is an Androscoggin County Sheriff’s deputy. If anyone should be in position to de-escalate a situation like that, it’s a police officer.
It should be simple. If you’re at a youth sports game, cheer for the kids. If something happens that draws your concern, address it with calm tact, please.
Let’s review that the next time this happens, OK?
The ugly: Westbrook athletes caught in nasty online harassment
Let’s applaud the Westbrook community for standing up to bullies. When a Facebook post suggested two members of the Blue Blazes girls soccer team are transgender, Westbrook rallied around its student athletes.
Mayor David Morse released a statement calling out the abhorrent behavior. Superintendent Peter Lancia condemned the social media posts, as did State Rep. Sue Salisbury.
There’s honest discussion and debate to have on the issue of transgender athletes. It’s apparent there are bad actors who don’t want to have anything close to civil discourse. They’d rather point fingers and bully teenagers. That is abject cowardice. They don’t have a position, they have propaganda.
Thankfully, Westbrook High leadership and others stepped up and quickly came to the defense of its students. We saw how Westbrook comes together last year when the city rallied around its state-title winning football team. It’s nice to see that happen when the reason to come together isn’t a celebration.

title: Bruins rally in 3rd period to beat Ducks
text:
ANAHEIM, Calif. — Elias Lindholm assisted on the tying goal and scored the go-ahead goal in the third period, leading the Boston Bruins past the Anaheim Ducks 4-2 on Friday night for their fourth straight victory.
David Pastrnak scored a tying power-play goal and Frederic Brunet got his first NHL goal for the Bruins, who roared back from an early two-goal deficit and improved to 6-2-0.
Less than five minutes after Pastrnak converted a give-and-go with Lindholm, the Ducks failed to mark Lindholm during a power play and allowed him to tap in a pass from Pavel Zacha with 11:39 to play. Matthew Poitras added another goal with 3:40 left on James Hagens’ second assist of the night.
Michael DiPietro made 25 saves in his second start of the season for the Bruins.
Beckett Sennecke got his fifth goal and Tim Washe also scored for the Ducks, who have lost three straight home games while giving up 13 goals. Lukas Dostal stopped 18 shots.
Ducks captain Mikael Granlund sat out with an upper-body injury, and goal-scoring winger Cutter Gauthier filled in by moving to center for the first time in his NHL career.
Anaheim had the best chances in the first period, and it took a lead with two goals 20 seconds apart in the final minute. After Washe’s long shot went in through the legs of screening teammate Jeff Malott, Sennecke finished a strong passing sequence with Gauthier and Nikita Nesterenko.
Brunet trimmed Anaheim’s lead with his first goal early in the second, connecting on a power play in the 23-year-old defenseman’s sixth NHL game.
After the Ducks failed to score on a four-minute power play, Pastrnak’s 423rd career goal broke a tie with Brad Marchand for the fourth-most in Bruins history.
The Ducks have sold out Honda Center for the first four games of a new season for the first time since 2007, when the team was coming off its lone Stanley Cup title.
Up next
Bruins: At Los Angeles on Saturday.
Ducks: At New York Rangers on Monday.

title: No Kings Rally at Capitol Park urges Mainers to vote early
text:
AUGUSTA, Maine (WABI) - “Democracy is the house that we live in. It requires maintenance and care and collective upkeep,” Anna Brown, board president of Maine Conservation Voters, remarked Saturday.
Capitol Area Indivisible, Maine Resists and 50501 Maine drew crowds to Capitol Park for a No Kings rally and urged voters to cast ballots before Nov. 3.
“We’ve been encouraging people to vote early because it absolutely reduces lines on Election Day and any potential for chaos,” explained Secretary of State Shenna Bellows. “We’ve heard a lot of anxiety about voting by mail or voting in-person on Election Day. So, we remind people that in Maine until October 29th, folks can go down to their town or city hall and cast their ballot in person with the early, no excuse absentee voting.”
Maine led the nation in voter participation in the 2022 midterms. According to Bellows, more than 178,000 Mainers have already voted this year.
“Early voting just means that you can check that off your list and then you have the time on Election Day to help other people get to the polls or to stay and be an election worker because we know that we need poll workers and poll watchers right now. So, being able to have that extra time is really valuable,” Jessica Gorton, an organizer with Capitol Area Indivisible, said.
The rally follows a lawsuit by the U.S. Justice Department seeking voter rolls from 31 states. So far, 26 states have won, including Maine, and one case has been dismissed.
“The Trump administration tried to take several actions to restrict voting rights. They tried to change the rules for voting by mail, but the Supreme Court blocked that after Secretaries of State, including here in Maine, we sued,” Bellows detailed. “Similarly, we’ve heard threats about ICE at the polls or federal agents at the polls, but that would be a violation of federal law. And the states are prepared to stand up and protect our elections for everybody.”
There are three ways to vote in Maine:
- Vote early in person at your local municipal clerk’s office through Oct. 29.
- Request an absentee ballot to vote by mail.
- Visit your polling location on Election Day, Nov. 3.

title: DoorDash driver dies, teen brother critical after being ambushed while delivering food, father says
text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WSMV/Gray News) - A man and his younger brother delivering food were allegedly ambushed by gunfire Thursday night at an apartment complex in the Nashville area.
Metro Nashville police said the shooting occurred at the Birchstone Village Apartments.
The reported victims, identified by their father as 22-year-old Jhon Diaz Santos and 14-year-old Alan, were said to be working for DoorDash that evening and drove into the apartment complex parking lot in a black Infiniti sedan.
According to authorities, a man approached Santos’ car and began shooting, police said. Two more men walked up, and one of them also started firing.
Police said Santos attempted to get away, backing his car into a fence. All three men ran off afterward.
Santos’ father, Juan Díaz, said his son had been a DoorDash delivery driver for more than a year.
Diaz said they were eating dinner as a family when Santos told him that night he was going to bring Alan out with him to make deliveries.
The father said his sons had gone out together before for food deliveries and reported nothing suspicious.
“They’d go out for two, three hours. They would come back safe. They never mentioned to us at any time at any time any suspicion,” Diaz said.
According to the father, he found out about what happened when a police officer knocked on their door, telling him his sons had an accident.
“I say, ‘Was it a car accident? Where was it?’ I say, ‘Can we go? Can you take me? I’ll follow you,” he said.
The father said it “shattered his soul” to learn that one of his sons had died.
“We don’t believe what is happening to us. One is not prepared for such a loss or news of this size,” Diaz said.
Fourteen-year-old Alan was also taken to the hospital in critical condition after being shot in the head, the father said.
Nashville authorities noted they were working on several leads while the shooting remains under investigation.

title: Hearts of Pine shut out by Forward Madison
text:
Ryan Carmichael scored in the fifth minute, then converted a penalty kick in the 40th minute, and playoff-bound Forward Madison FC earned a 2-0 win over the Portland Hearts of Pine in a USL League One match Saturday night in Madison, Wisconsin.
Madison turned a Hearts turnover into a quick attack that produced the opening goal. Hakim Karamoko drove into the penalty area and took a shot from the right side that deflected off Portland keeper Kash Oladapo. Carmichael was all alone in front and slammed the ball into the open cage.
Karamoko also set up the second goal, as he was brought down in the box by Josh Drack. Carmichael sent a low shot to the left of Oladapo for his 14th goal of the season in league matches.
Madison moved into third place with one game remaining. Portland, which is eliminated from playoff contention, ends its season with a home match next Saturday against the league-leading Charlotte Independence.

title: Pope Leo leaves the hospital 4 days after lung cancer surgery
text:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV returned to the Vatican on Saturday days after lung cancer surgery, as his surgeon said there are “no clinical reasons” to prevent his planned trip to Latin America next month.
“The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery,” Dr. Stefano Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery “in another 10 days or so.”
Leo, 71, is scheduled to make an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Peru and Argentina, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes.
“As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place,” Margaritora said.
Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. He left the hospital on Saturday, well ahead of the week-long hospital stay the Vatican had initially anticipated.
Pope says he feels ‘much better’
“I am much better, thank you,” the pope said when asked how he was as he was driven away in a black SUV.
Leo greeted patients inside the hospital accompanied by his surgeon, before waving to well-wishers outside who cried out “Holiness” as he walked to a waiting vehicle.
He paused when a 13-year-old Ukrainian girl presented him with a homemade papal doll that she said had helped her through successful cancer treatment. She had briefly met Leo at an audience in St. Peter’s Square last December—an encounter she told reporters “gave her the strength to overcome the illness.”
Since the surgery, Leo has shown signs of recovering well. He had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, held meetings with senior aides and celebrated Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.
He will take on his first official duty on Sunday, delivering the traditional Angelus blessing to the faithful in St. Peter’s Square. It comes exactly one week after the pontiff revealed to throngs in the square that the nodule had been found and would be surgically removed — an unusually candid revelation for the Vatican.
Further tests being carried out
Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, also confirmed that the nodule was discovered by chance during routine abdominal examinations. It appeared as “a small spot” at the base of the lung, which extends down to the diaphragm, he said.
He added that if the spot had been higher up, “it certainly would not have been seen.”
The cancer was in its early stages, and the pope had “no respiratory symptoms, and felt perfectly well,” Margaritora said.
He described Tuesday’s procedure to remove the lobe as “routine” and “without complications,” but acknowledged that it “stirred deep feelings ... to operate on a pope, who for the first time – at least in modern history – is undergoing surgery for a malignant tumor.”
The Vatican did not disclose that the tumor was malignant until after Tuesday’s successful surgery. It later confirmed that the pope had undergone a biopsy before being admitted to Gemelli. Experts say the state-of-the-art Ion robotic bronchoscopy would have indicated whether the tumor was malignant and possibly whether cancer had spread to the lymph nodes.
Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor’s molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor’s genetic characteristics.
Margaritora said the pope’s recovery so far had required “very little assistance from us.”
“His determination to recover quickly has been effective in every respect. It was truly commendable,” the surgeon said.
