title: It’s not just you. There are more Maine political ads than ever this year.
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The gym. The doctor’s office. The living room. The car.
The store. The salon. The restaurant and bar.
Whether out and about or trying to relax at home, Mainers have heard or seen more than their fair share of political ads ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm election headlined by races for the U.S. Senate, House of Representatives and governor. And don’t forget the glossy pamphlets — sometimes multiple in one day — that have arrived in mailboxes.
Mainers’ collective feelings — frustration, annoyance, ignorance or acceptance — cross ideological and demographic lines, putting political advertising in a rare category of grievances that largely foster bipartisan agreement.
That extends to politics in general. The Pew Research Center found in a 2024 survey that 65% of Americans reported feeling “exhausted” most or all of the time when thinking about politics.
“I am so sick, as most Mainers are, of the negative take and dark tone of the visuals of these ads,” said Kat Taylor, 70, an unenrolled voter who lives in Argyle Township in Penobscot County.
The retiree who previously worked at the University of Maine said she is hit with ads throughout her day, from when she tunes into NEWS CENTER Maine in the early morning to when she walks outside to check the mailbox.
Inside a Portland bar on a recent evening, a college football game was on one of the TVs. Nearly every commercial break featured at least one campaign ad.
The refrains are familiar by now, such as the “I’m Troy Jackson” opening line in one of the pro-Jackson ads, or the “Taxin’ Jackson” criticism in an ad from a pro-Republican group. (That negative ad recently and erroneously went on air in Portland, Oregon, instead of Portland, Maine.)
For those wondering if there are actually more ads in front of them this election year in Maine, the answer is yes.
The numbers prove it.
THOUSANDS UPON THOUSANDS OF ADS
The total number of ads that have aired in Maine’s official media markets of Portland-Auburn, Bangor and Presque Isle is dizzying.
According to the advertising tracking insight firm AdImpact, the Portland-Auburn market has seen more than 24,100 political ads air on TV since the week of Aug. 30. The Bangor market has seen more than 18,100 ads air since that week, while the Presque Isle region in northern Maine has seen roughly 2,750 since then.
In the first week of October alone, 5,787 ads aired on TV across the Portland-Auburn market, or about 827 ads each day, according to AdImpact.
This deluge is possible because of record spending on Maine’s highest profile races. Candidates, their affiliated political action committees, the campaign arms of national parties and dark money groups have so far spent and reserved $315 million on ads across various platforms this election cycle in Maine, per AdImpact.
That figure surpasses the state record of around $200 million in 2020 that mostly covered the U.S. Senate race between Sen. Susan Collins and Democrat Sara Gideon.
Maine is the 42nd most populous state but is the 11th most expensive state for political ad spending this cycle, according to AdImpact, which said Tuesday that the total spending will likely get to around $400 million. Republican groups are outspending Democratic groups in Maine and nationally.
But there is some consolation for those tired of all the interruptions. AdImpact initially thought that number would get as high as $490 million in Maine.
DO THE ADS ACTUALLY CONVINCE PEOPLE?
Adding to the frustration of many Mainers: Political advertising is unlikely to move the needle much in any of Maine’s key races.
The gubernatorial race to succeed outgoing Gov. Janet Mills and the 2nd Congressional District contest to succeed U.S. Rep. Jared Golden have certainly drawn attention and outside interest, but ads tied to those elections are relatively few. In the 2nd District, they’re only targeted toward Mainers living in certain regions of the state.
The tight U.S. Senate race between Collins, the Republican seeking a sixth term, and former Maine Senate President Troy Jackson, the Democratic challenger, is a different story.
Ads upon ads have sought to sway the undecided voters who may decide the Senate contest.
An Axios analysis of dollars spent on cable, broadcast and social media along with estimates for streaming platforms found Maine has the priciest per capita Senate race in the nation, with Republican-aligned groups spending $96.99 for each Maine adult and Democratic-aligned groups spending $69.52.
But polls show the number of voters who haven’t made up their mind in that race is minuscule. And despite all of the time, money and effort that goes into producing these ads, past studies have found the effects of political spots to be small in terms of persuading voters.
The Washington Post and George Mason University’s Schar School of Policy and Government conducted a poll of Maine’s Senate race between Sept. 30 and Oct. 5, finding just 3% of respondents did not pick between Jackson and Collins.
In the 2020 election, about 819,000 voters cast a ballot in the race that saw Collins defy the polls to beat Gideon by a comfortable margin. If roughly 3% of the electorate this year is undecided, and the voting pool stays the same size, campaigns are fighting to reach about 24,500 voters.
DEALING WITH ‘THE NASTINESS’
Steve Hamblen, a 75-year-old unenrolled voter from Sanford, said he is getting inundated with ads and political canvassers at his doorstep — a reality that he said has reaffirmed his belief that the country’s campaign finance system needs reform. The U.S. Supreme Court, however, has removed limits on how much parties and corporations can spend on elections.
“The nastiness really annoys me, but people sit there and swallow it,” Hamblen said in late August. “Make up your own mind. Don’t listen to these political ads and just fall for the one-liners.”
The ads indeed make claims that are false, misleading or only partially backed up by citations in small print that are tough for the average viewer to digest in real time.
“The ads do nothing to sway my opinion. I have never been enrolled in any party and am a critical thinker,” Taylor, the Argyle Township resident, said on a recent weekday, adding that the printed ads in her mailbox “aren’t even good for starting my wood stove or composting.”
Whether the ads end up making a difference in the outcome of the Nov. 3 election is likely unmeasurable. Whether Mainers are ready for them to go away until the next cycle is an easier thing to observe.
Peggy Belkenny, an 83-year-old Democrat from Auburn, said last month she wants candidates and their ads to focus on what they would do to help people if they’re elected to office. And if they don’t?
“We’re gonna put them on a plane and send them all to Siberia,” she said. “One way.”
Staff Writer Randy Billings contributed to this report.

title: Bar Harbor in limbo as legal disputes over cruise ships continue
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Bar Harbor recently took new enforcement action against a business that brings passengers ashore from cruise ships — the latest flashpoint in a lengthy legal battle over the number of tourists disembarking in the popular destination.
The town on Mount Desert Island is embroiled in state and federal lawsuits stemming from an ordinance that aimed to dramatically cut back on cruise ship visitation. Officials, businesses and residents are waiting for a federal court order that could determine the scale of the industry going forward.
“We’d like to hope it’s relatively sooner rather than later,” said Everal Eaton, executive director of the Bar Harbor Chamber of Commerce. “That certainty is better for the business community and better for the residents as well to know going into next year what it’s going to look like.”
Since the early 2000s, Bar Harbor has become an increasingly popular destination for cruise ships. In 2022, 143 vessels called on the port, according to the town.
That growth brought concerns about congestion and safety. In 2022, voters approved an ordinance that limited disembarkations from cruise ships to 1,000 passengers a day. The citizen initiative passed with 58% of the vote. In 2024, an effort to repeal that ordinance failed by an even closer margin.
A group of businesses filed a federal lawsuit against the town in 2022 to challenge the ordinance. Nearly four years, a bench trial and a trip to the appeals court later, the case is still unresolved.
In May, Chief U.S. District Judge Lance Walker ruled that the 1,000-passenger cap is only constitutional and enforceable in July and August. Charles Sidman, a Bar Harbor resident who has championed the ordinance and intervened in the case, filed a motion asking the judge to reconsider and amend that order. Walker has not yet issued a ruling.
In the meantime, the parties have also become entrenched in disputes in state court over enforcement of the ordinance. Bar Harbor sent a notice of violation this month to a private pier owner for disembarking cruise ship passengers without a permit, which could add to the quagmire.
“The majority of people that I actually speak to in my day-to-day life are like, ‘When is this going to end?’ ” said Maya Caines, chair of the Bar Harbor Town Council.
Ongoing dispute
Bar Harbor does not have a pier big enough for cruise ships. Instead, the vessels anchor nearby, and smaller tender boats transport passengers to and from the shore.
Eben Salvatore, director of operations for Bar Harbor Resorts, as well as two private piers and the primary tender boats in town, said that the ordinance that limited disembarkations prompted “hundreds of cancellations.”
“Every time the phone rang, it was another massive amount of revenue for a business owner out the window,” Salvatore said. “It was a very painful shock, and it still is.”
In 2024, the Bar Harbor Town Council created a regulatory framework with two separate permits required to enforce the ordinance.
“It’s really just there to ensure we understand and know the level of visitation,” Town Manager James Smith said.
The private piers, overseen by Salvatore, have never applied for the permits.
That summer, the town sent a notice of violation to one of the piers for disembarking passengers from a cruise ship. That action set off a flurry of additional litigation in state court. The parties are waiting for the Maine Supreme Judicial Court to address two separate appeals. If the violation stands, the pier owner could have to pay steep fines.
The town and the business disagree on whether the permitting system is constitutional, based on the latest order from Walker in the federal case.
This month, Bar Harbor issued a second notice of violation to the pier, known as Golden Anchor LC in court records.
“It’s troubling that we seem to have been triggered without our own willingness into another round of litigation,” said Timothy Woodcock, the lawyer representing Golden Anchor and other businesses.
Businesses uncertain
Sidman, a retired scientist who operates a Bar Harbor gallery with his wife, fought to get the ordinance in front of voters in 2022 and has since defended it in court as an intervenor in the federal lawsuit.
“It was worse than bumper cars at a circus,” Sidman said of the peak traffic from cruise ships. “It was aesthetically unpleasant, it was dangerous and it was detrimental to business.”
He said he would pursue another citizen initiative if the federal court ultimately overturns the ordinance.
“If we have to, we will relegislate it even stronger and more clearly,” Sidman said. “We want our town. We don’t want it submerged by cruise ships and big hotels.”
With lawsuits pending, many say the town is in limbo. Vessels continue to call on Bar Harbor, but not in the same numbers as in the past, according to the town. A dozen or so cruises with a capacity of 3,000-plus visited this year because they made reservations in 2020 and weren’t subject to the newer rules, according to the town.
The town also reached an agreement with American Cruise Lines and got the required permits to regularly disembark its passengers at a public pier this year. Those vessels have a capacity of 250 or less, Smith said.
Eaton, from the local chamber of commerce, said some businesses are uncertain how to staff or order inventory for next year because they don’t know how many cruise ship passengers will be allowed. Kevin DesVeaux, who owns West Street Cafe, said the restaurant has not been profitable since 2022, and lunch sales are down 30% in that time.
He said he is draining his savings to keep the restaurant open.
“We have no more to give,” DesVeaux wrote in an email. “This winter we will decide if we are going to go on the market or hold on for one more year for the cruise ship traffic to return.”
Salvatore and Woodcock said town officials should be making plans to welcome visitors from cruise ships in 2027, especially in the shoulder seasons when the 1,000-passenger cap is not currently enforceable.
“Let’s sit down in a room and work this out,” Salvatore said. “It can’t be hard. Staying in litigation is the worst thing to do.”
Town officials said it’s hard to proceed when so many lawsuits are active.
“We’re trying to be respectful and honoring the citizens’ initiative while being mindful of the legal rights and interests of other parties,” Smith said. “We believe that there is a need for local regulations for disembarking cruise ship passengers, and we want to be able to do that in a way that will meet the test of the court.”
Caines, the town council chair, said she and others want to focus on compromise instead of reacting to court proceedings.
“It’s really dependent quite a lot on the other parties that have been initiating these lawsuits,” she said.
This story was originally published by the Maine Trust for Local News. Megan Gray can be reached at mgray@pressherald.com.

title: ‘Very happy child’: Loved ones remembering 5-year-old killed in Oregon school shooting
text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — The youngest child killed in a shooting at an Oregon school was a fast runner and a fearless climber who also loved reading and his stuffed animals, his aunt said Friday.
Rhoam Summer, 5, was one of three children killed along with a teacher in the shooting Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 in central Oregon. The other two children killed were ages 8 and 11, and a fourth student and another teacher were wounded, police have said.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” said Swan Sheridan, whose sister is Summer’s mother.
Sheridan said Summer liked for all of his sea creature stuffed animals to be in his favorite color: rainbow.
“He had a great fondness for sharks and dinosaurs and creatures that were in his words, ‘misunderstood,’” she said.
Sheridan said her nephew would climb and jump off anything and was an “incredibly fast” runner, even from a young age. “He was a little ball of energy from the moment he was born,” she said.
“He was a very, very happy child,” she said.
Teacher Megan Lambert, 25, was killed, said police Chief Mike Krantz at a Friday afternoon news conference. Police confirmed Summer was one of those killed but won’t release names of the other children who died at the request of their families.
Lambert had her “dream job,” her family said in statement read at the news conference. Lambert grew up in Bend, graduated from Boise State in 2023, had a passion for sports, especially volleyball, and was a local coach, relatives said.
They described her as funny and opinionated and said she “lit up the room.”
“Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart,” her family said in the statement. ”She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs.”
Police said 16-year-old Griffin J. John II got into the school by shooting through locked doors. Authorities said John had been a special needs student at the school and attacked a classroom with special needs students.
Krantz said a parent saw John shooting outside the school, followed him inside and shot him several times.
The parent was Kaylub Giamanco, said his mother, Kenda Freeman, in a statement read Friday to reporters.
Police found John dead in the school minutes after the first calls for help, Krantz said.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, and drew community members Friday, including Brooke Olsen. She said she was feeling grateful that her daughter — a kindergartner — was safe while also trying to “grieve and process and recover.”
“This is an extremely painful day of grief for everybody in Bend, especially Silver Rail families,” Olsen said.
Police identified the wounded teacher as Becky Drury, 54. Police said her injuries were serious but not life threatening, and she was hospitalized. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on Facebook that she had injuries to her left arm and right hand and was recovering from surgery. Her husband, Will Drury, said in a statement that they’re focusing on her recovery at an “unimaginably difficult time.”
Blake Brinker said he came to a memorial at the school on Friday to pray.
“Life is such a delicate thing and I don’t think anything brings that message across more than the loss of young life,” he said
___
This story has been updated to correct the name of the teacher killed Thursday. She is Megan Lambert, not Meghan Lambert as police originally reported.
___

title: A stronger workforce begins with inclusion
main_topic: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
The BDN Opinion section operates independently and does not set news policies or contribute to reporting or editing articles elsewhere in the newspaper or on bangordailynews.com
Laura Fortman is the commissioner of the Maine Department of Labor.
For me, employment has always been about more than having a job. It means earning a fair wage, building a career, contributing to a community, supporting yourself and your family, and having the economic independence meaningful work can provide.
That is why Gov. Janet Mills’ proclamation of October as Disability Employment Awareness Month feels particularly meaningful. The proclamation recognizes the skills, talents and contributions of Mainers with disabilities and calls on employers, schools, higher education institutions and community organizations to expand access to good jobs and career pathways.
It is an opportunity to celebrate Maine’s progress, recognize those who made it possible and recommit us to the work that remains.
My own connection to this issue goes back more than 50 years. In the summer of 1972, after watching Geraldo Rivera’s exposé of the conditions at Willowbrook State School, I volunteered there for several weeks. I was young, and what I saw was difficult to absorb: young people with intellectual disabilities living in overcrowded, unsanitary conditions.
What stayed with me most was the young people, their warmth, resilience and potential.
That experience shaped my career and life’s work to expand opportunities for people that have faced barriers and whose voices have too often gone unheard. I believe that public policy works best when it starts with the dignity and potential of the people it serves like supporting employment for people with disabilities.
Maine has made real progress in this area, thanks to the tireless work by self-advocates and the broader community. In 2013, the Maine Legislature passed the Employment First Maine Act, making employment the first and preferred option for people with disabilities, so they no longer wait until they are deemed “work ready” to begin a path toward employment.
In 2020, with the support of the Mills administration, the Legislature passed a law prohibiting Maine employers from paying workers with disabilities less than the minimum wage. The administration also expanded Progressive Employment, a model that helps people with disabilities build workplace skills while employers learn how to support them.
Employment for people with disabilities is not a social-services issue. It is a workforce issue.
Maine needs workers. Mainers with disabilities want to work, build careers and contribute, but continue to face barriers to doing so. Bringing those two realities together is good for individuals, businesses and Maine.
When someone with a disability pursues a career, individuals, families, employers, communities and Maine all benefit.
That is why disability inclusion belongs in the middle of our workforce strategy, not in the margins.
As we expand registered apprenticeships and career and technical education, people with disabilities should be able to participate fully. When we connect employers with workers, disabilities should not narrow the conversation about what they can do.
Accessibility is more than a ramp at the door. Today, people find jobs, pursue training, communicate with employers and access public services online, making digital accessibility and communication just as important as physical access. We also need to ensure people with disabilities benefit from emerging technologies, including AI, through accessible tools and the skills increasingly needed in the workplace.
That is what digital equity should mean: making sure everyone can access, understand and use technology to participate fully in work and community life.
At the Department of Labor, we have an opportunity and a responsibility to keep building on the work of those who came before us. That means continuing to strengthen vocational rehabilitation and supported employment, expand access to apprenticeships and training, address transportation and workplace-support barriers, and work with employers to ensure they can recognize and make use of the talents of people with disabilities.
There is much to celebrate this October. But National Disability Employment Awareness Month is also a reminder that progress is not a finish line.
The goal is simple: A Maine where people with disabilities have the same opportunity to pursue meaningful work, build careers and achieve their aspirations as anyone else.

title: Maranacook girls, Winthrop boys win MVC cross country titles
text:
AUGUSTA — William Morris of Dirigo and Reagan Mattson of Maranacook dominated their competition Saturday while winning individual titles in the Mountain Valley Conference cross country championships at University of Maine at Augusta’s Elvin Fields.
Winthrop cruised to the boys team championship with 30 points, far ahead of Maranacook (72) and Boothbay/Wiscasset (93). Mattson helped Maranacook (51 points) edged Boothbay/Wiscasset (59) for the girls team title.
Morris, a senior, finished the 5-kilometer course with a time of 16:20.26, more than 35 seconds quicker than Winthrop’s Alfie Cognata (16:55.68) and Sawyer Wess (16:56.00).
“It’s not a very fast course, I wasn’t going for any (personal records),” Morris said. “Maybe it’s a lack of confidence or something, but I’m always scared I’m going to get passed. My coach has always drilled into me to never look back, but I just never seem to lose that fear, and push (as if) someone is going to pass me.”
Morris, who swept the MVC, Class C South and Class C state titles last season, has had another successful fall. He was runner-up to Scarborough’s Atticus Merriam by 0.15 seconds at the Festival of Champions in Belfast on Oct. 3.
“I’m feeling pretty good about states and regionals,” Morris said. “I feel like MVC is the strongest Class C conference. If you can place well here, you can place well at states.”
Mattson, a freshman, finished in 19:35.31, more than 1:15 faster than runner-up McKenzie Boyle (20:50.52) of Dirigo. Mattson’s teammate, Kira Pelletier, placed third (21:07.85).
“It felt good (to win), I was kind of cold to start,” Mattson said. “It was kind of rough, but I got warmed up and it was fun to run with the girls in the woods. It’s definitely a goal of mine to get out and separate myself (from the group), then you just try to take your mind off the race and try to expand the gap.”
Mattson has already made a name for herself in her freshman year. She won her first high school race, the Scot Laliberte Invitational at Cony High in Augusta, set a Winthrop course record with a time of 19.56.84 on Sept. 17, and was the top freshman girls runner (18:55) at the Festival of Champions.
“She’s been so strong all season long, she’s just a real talent,” said Maranacook coach Casey Spencer. “She consistently works hard at everything she does and it continues to pay off.”
The Winthrop boys had five runners in the top 10 in the boys race. Aside from Cognata and Wess, Sam St. Germain (17:56.67) placed seventh, Michael Van Tassel (18:04.73) was eighth and Gianni Haefele (18:53.30) finished 10th.
The Winthrop boys won MVC and Class C South titles last year but finished runner-up at the state meet to Houlton/Greater Houlton Christian Academy.
“We had a plan and we executed it,” said Winthrop coach Ed Van Tassel. “I’m happy. I think next week at regionals, we’ll have a similar type of performance. And we’ve had states circled (on our calendars) since last year.”
Maranacook’s Harper Olmstead (22:46.11) finished eighth in the girls race, giving the Black Bears three top-10 finishers.
“The team’s worked really hard,” Spencer said. “We’re feeling pretty good. We really have our eyes on the next two weekends (at regionals and states), to tell the truth. We worked really hard this past week and did our best (today), and it worked out really well for the girls.”
Temperatures were in the low 50s with a strong breeze, chilly for spectators but good conditions for runners as they danced in and out of the woods.
Morris and Mattson were named the MVC Runners of the Year. Van Tassel and Spencer are the Coaches of the Year.

title: Women of Maine, your vote is not a Valentine
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
Maria Padian is a novelist and freelance writer who lives in Brunswick. She has previously worked as a news reporter and a congressional press secretary.
Something surprised me this month as I’ve been knocking on doors and doing some political canvassing: There are a lot of older women who plan to vote for both Hannah Pingree and Sen. Susan Collins.
As a Medicare-eligible female myself, I’ll confess: this struck me as some profound cognitive dissonance; these two candidates are very different. But despite my impulse to exclaim, “Seriously?” at my fellow women of a certain age, I remembered that good canvassing includes listening. So I asked them to … explain.
Their reasons were remarkably personal.
Regarding Pingree, a Democrat running for governor in Maine, many said, “Oh, I love Hannah.” Like she’s the smart daughter we’re super proud of.
Regarding Collins, the five-term incumbent Republican running for U.S. Senate, they spoke as if she were a trusted friend or sister. “She saved my job,” one said. “She understands us,” said another. “She’s a real Mainer.”
Here’s the thing: those gals have been voting for Collins for decades. They hold fast to the Susan they knew 20-plus years ago, who molded herself as a moderate. It didn’t matter if I pointed out that the current Susan has abandoned those moderate impulses. That today’s Susan votes with President Trump 96% of the time and marches lock-step with the MAGA-aligned values of a GOP that past Maine Republican women like Margaret Chase Smith would not recognize today.
I realized I wasn’t going to change their minds at the front stoop. But I did say this: Your vote is not a Valentine. It’s a calculated chess move.
Because in the game we’re playing right now, “our senator” (that’s the logo on the Collins’ campaign bus) is no friend. She’s no sister. She’s no powerful chess queen, wielding her influence as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee. Instead, she’s played the past two years like an ineffective pawn. And her repeated caving to Trump has hurt Maine.
Someone who understands Mainers would know that bombing Iran would disrupt world oil prices and leave us out in the cold. So this winter, thank Susan Collins when we pay 75% more for heating oil. She voted repeatedly to support this now-forever war, back when Trump called it a military “action” that would last six weeks. Decades worth of past presidents from both parties knew better. Collins knew better.
Someone who cares about Maine jobs and Mainers’ health wouldn’t support Trump’s “big,
beautiful bill,” which Collins voted to advance. 
That bill’s devastating Medicaid cuts will not only shutter hundreds of hospitals nationwide, it’s projected to eliminate Medicaid for 31,000 Mainers and, according to the Maine Center for Economic Policy, might close four hospitals in Maine, resulting in the loss of tens of million in wages.
Speaking of health: measles is back. It was declared “eliminated” in U.S. in 2000, but so far this year we’re at more than 4,000 cases. All thanks to the anti-vaccination misinformation spread by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., whom “our senator” voted to confirm.
With all due respect to my fellow senior women: chess, like democracy, is a long game. And sometimes, winning requires being strategic — and retiring a piece.

title: Blustery and cold today, less windy tomorrow, then a calm week
text:
BANGOR, Maine (WABI) - It will be a very windy day and the first quite cold day of the season. Highs will not make it out for the 40s for most with some stuck in the 30s. Wind chills will also be a factor, some places may see wind chills in the teens. There may be a few quick snow showers in the western mountains as well. Winds will also gust up to 40 mph behind the departing low from the northwest. Sunday will be better. The wind will back off substantially and will be a sunny and warmer day. The beginning of next week will be much calmer and quieter weather wise.
Today: Cold and blustery
It will be a very chilly and noticeably windy day today behind the departing storm system. The windiness will decrease as the day goes on but temperatures will not recover much. Most highs will only be in the 30s and 40s for much the region. Winds will gust in the first half of the day to near 40 mph across much of the state. Wind chills will also be a factor. Some places may see wind chills in the teens in the morning.
Tonight: Hard freeze likely, clouds clear out
Clouds will clear out almost completely into the evening. And as the winds die off temps will drop quickly into the 20s. Many areas that have not seen the 20s yet will probably see them Saturday night. Winds will decrease quickly and almost go calm in several locations.
Sunday: A much calmer and warmer day
Things will calm down considerably Sunday as the low fully departs. Winds will only be 5-10 mph and highs will reach back into the 50s for most of us with a few still stuck in the 40s. The sun will also return for pretty much everyone. The northern reaches of the county may see some clouds throughout the day, likely the only place that will.
Sunday night: Calm and cold again
Winds will go calm Sunday night and many areas will fall into the low 30s again with colder spots in the 20s. So it will be a cold start to your Sunday pretty much everywhere but a comfortable day for the most part.
Monday and beyond: A very calm weather week
After a week of rain and very diverse weather next week will mainly be the opposite. High pressure will dominate and highs in the 50s and low 60s with lows mostly in the 30s will be the consistent theme of the week. It will certainly be a very pleasant fall like week across much of the state.
Today: Cold and blustery. Highs in the 30s and 40s. Winds NW at 20-30 mph and gusts to 40 mph. Wind chills in the 20s for most.
Tonight: Winds calm down and temps drop. Lows mainly in the 20s. Winds W at 5-10 mph.
Sunday: Calmer and clear. Mainly sunny with highs in the 50s. Winds W at 5-10 mph.
Sunday night: Clear and cold. Lows in the 20s and 30s. Winds light.
Monday: Mainly sunny. Highs in the 50s. Winds W at 5-10 mph.

title: Susan Collins not to blame for birthing center closures
text:
Recent political commercials regarding the closing of birthing centers in this state — linking them to Medicare cuts and blaming Sen. Susan Collins — are blatantly false.
As a member of the Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services Committee in the Maine Legislature, I have heard loud and clear from these hospitals that these closures are due to staff recruiting and hiring difficulties, low birth rates in the rural areas of the state and limited advancement and training opportunities for new doctors practicing here in Maine — not Medicare cuts.
Sen. Collins was the author of the Rural Health Transformation Program that brought $190 million to the state of Maine to support our rural hospitals, not to close them. I realize this is the silly campaign season but one should know the truth when subjected to false claims such as the ones depicted in these ads.
Rep. Robert Foley
Wells

title: Masked settlers attack European diplomats in the occupied West Bank
text:
Masked settlers attack European diplomats in the occupied West Bank
At least 4 people have been killed and more than 100 injured since the harvest began earlier this month
Masked settlers attack European diplomats in the occupied West Bank
At least 4 people have been killed and more than 100 injured since the harvest began earlier this month
Israeli police say they are investigating an attack on diplomats in the occupied West Bank.
Meanwhile, an airstrike in Yemen killed three children and wounded others. Iranian-backed Houthi rebels blamed Saudi Arabia for the attack.
Related video above: Palestinian family split by Gaza war reunites after unimaginable loss
Israeli police probe attack on diplomats in West Bank
Israeli police say they have opened an investigation into an alleged assault on diplomats in the occupied West Bank. Their statement cites footage circulating online that appears to show several diplomats being attacked in the village of Taybeh.
Public broadcaster Kan reported that the diplomats included representatives from France, Belgium and Poland. In a separate statement, Israel’s military said the visit had not been coordinated with it and no soldiers were at the scene.
Violence by Jewish settlers against Palestinians has surged during the annual olive harvest. Activists say authorities do little to stop it. An attack on Friday seriously injured several people, including a Washington Post photographer.
“The Israel Police condemns violence of any kind and will work to complete these investigations until everyone who took part in these cases is brought to justice,” the police statement said.
Police said they had contacted Israel’s Foreign Ministry to help locate those who were attacked.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Saturday that he was “very disturbed” by footage of an attack on Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine by Israeli settlers in the West Bank.
“We’re very disturbed by those images and what we’re seeing,’ he said, adding that the Trump administration has asked the Israeli government to “crack down on that stuff.”
Airstrike kills 3 children in Yemen
Iranian-backed Houthi rebels say airstrikes from Saudi Arabia killed three children in Yemen's southwestern province of Dhamar.
The Houthi-run health ministry said the strikes the day before hit houses in al-Ar village in Dawran Aness district, also wounding more than a dozen people.
The Houthis blamed Saudi Arabia for the strike, which comes amid heightened fighting between the group and the kingdom and its Yemeni allies. Saudi Arabia didn’t immediately comment.
The children are among 124 people the Houthis say have been killed in their territories since fighting resumed in September, according to the ministry.
Journalist beaten by West Bank settlers undergoes surgery
Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine was undergoing surgery on her finger, which was nearly detached from her hand after she was beaten by settlers in the West Bank, her daughter said.
Ashley Milner told The Associated Press that Levine also has a broken rib and multiple broken vertebrae as well as lacerations.
Levine said the perpetrators — armed with bottles and slingshots — “were kicking me for like 10 minutes and I was trying to hold onto my cameras and my bag.”
She said her helmet and protective vest, marked “PRESS,” likely saved her from more serious injuries.
2 ships attacked in the Persian Gulf
The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations said two vessels transiting through the Persian Gulf off Saudi Arabia were struck Friday. One tanker was fired upon from a small boat with an RPG that damaged part of its rear, and the other was struck by an unknown projectile, it said.
The UKMTO monitor did not identify the vessels but said the crews were safe. No one claimed the strikes.
There has been an uptick in attacks since U.S. President Donald Trump late last month rejected a Tehran proposal to end the war and open the strait, though indirect negotiations have continued.
On Saturday, Iran’s state broadcaster cited the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as saying a supertanker carrying crude oil struck a naval mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. It was unclear when the incident occurred.
Separately, a skiff carrying armed men opened fire on a tanker carrying liquefied natural gas in the Arabian Sea off Yemen, UKMTO reported. There were no reports of casualties. No group claimed responsibility.
Egypt pledges to defend Saudi Arabia
Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi said his government will implement “any measure” to defend its ally Saudi Arabia amid increasing attacks by the Iranian-backed Houthis in Yemen.
Addressing King Salman and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, el-Sissi said his country would do what it takes to defend them. He said that if needed, he would convene parliament for an emergency session to authorize such measures.
Israeli strikes across Gaza kill 4 people
Israeli strikes killed four people across Gaza, according to hospital officials.
One strike killed two people and wounded several others east of Gaza City, according to Shifa hospital. Another killed a 14-year-old boy in the central city of Deir al-Balah, according to al-Aqsa hospital, and the third killed one person in the southern city of Rafah, according to the Red Cross field hospital.
Israel's army said it struck Hamas and Islamic Jihad military operatives in those areas but did not immediately respond to the strike in Rafah.
The attacks came more than a year after a ceasefire deal was reached between Israel and Hamas, during which Israel continued to launch deadly strikes on the enclave.
2 killed when Saudi helicopter gunship crashes
A Saudi helicopter gunship crashed in southwestern Saudi Arabia, killing its two-member crew, the Saudi-led coalition fighting against Yemeni Houthi rebels said Sunday.
Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said in a statement the AH-6i helicopter crashed in the city of Najran due to a technical malfunction.
The coalition statement came hours after Iranian-backed Houthis claimed in a statement that they shot down a Saudi Apache over Najran while conducting “hostile activities” toward the Houthi fighters on the border with Saudi Arabia.
Al-Malki apparently mocked the Houthi claim in a post on X. Attaching a screenshot of the Houthi military spokesman’s statement with images of AH-6i helicopters, the Saudi officer said the gunship has yet to join the war.

title: Smoked salmon recalled over listeria risk
text:
(FDA/CNN) - The Food and Drug Administration says there is a voluntary recall of frozen smoked salmon sold in six states.
Officials say “Starfish Seafood Premium Cold Smoked Norwegian Salmon” carries a potential risk of listeria.
The product was sold in New York, Florida, Georgia, New Jersey, Pennsylvania and Ohio.
The distributor, Krasnyi Oktyabr, issued a voluntary recall after the New York State Department of Agriculture and Markets found potential listeria contamination.
No illnesses have been reported.
Consumers who have purchased the smoked salmon can return it to the retailer they purchased it from for a full refund.

title: 34-yard field goal as time expires lifts Auburn over No. 1 Georgia 27-24
text:
34-yard field goal as time expires lifts Auburn over No. 1 Georgia 27-24
Alex McPherson kicked a game-winning 34-yard field goal as time expired and Auburn, led by quarterback Byrum Brown's dominant running game, upset No. 1 Georgia 27-24 on Saturday.
It’s the second straight week the top team in the AP Top 25 lost to an unranked foe after then-No. 1 Texas fell to Oklahoma last Saturday.
Video above: SEC having serious talks about breaking away from the NCAA, commish says
Georgia quarterback Gunner Stockton led a long game-tying touchdown drive in the fourth quarter but lost a fumble with 58 seconds remaining and the Bulldogs driving for a potential go-ahead field goal.
Stockton, who also threw two interceptions, fumbled on a run from the Auburn 46. Safety Sylvester Smith-Reed recovered for the Tigers at the Auburn 44. A roughing-the-passer penalty on Georgia's Gabe Harris Jr. helped set up McPherson's game-winning kick. Auburn players swarmed the field.
Brown ran for 115 yards and a touchdown on 26 carries and added a scoring pass.
Georgia (6-1, 4-1 Southeastern Conference) saw its streaks of nine straight wins over Auburn and 53 consecutive wins over unranked teams come to an end in a loss that also will end the Bulldogs’ short one-week stay atop the AP Top 25.
Auburn (4-2, 2-2) beat the Bulldogs on the ground. Tailback Nate Frazier returned from a rib injury to start for Georgia but was ineffective, gaining only 19 yards on nine carries.
Georgia trailed 24-14 before rallying with a 42-yard field goal by Peyton Woodring. Stockton led a tying touchdown drive that began at the Georgia 6 and covered 94 yards in 13 plays, capped by his 4-yard pass to London Humphreys.
Stockton’s two interceptions doubled his previous season total through six games. The Bulldogs also were hurt by mistakes, including three personal foul penalties.
After Georgia took a 14-0 lead, Auburn scored the next 24 points.
Georgia looked dominant in the opening minutes, even after Stockton had to leave after hitting the field helmet-first on the first play of the game. Ryan Puglisi completed each of his three passes, including a 41-yarder to Craig Dandridge Jr., before Dwight Phillips’ 15-yard scoring run.
Stockton returned for the next possession and threw a 24-yard touchdown pass to tight end Lawson Luckie for the 14-0 lead.
Auburn responded with a physical run-first attack led by the 235-pound Brown, who was effective both on designed runs and when taking off after dropping back to pass.
Top-ranked teams had won 93 consecutive home games against unranked teams since LSU lost to Arkansas 50-48 in two overtimes on Nov. 23, 2007.

title: Pope Leo leaves the hospital 4 days after lung cancer surgery
text:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV returned to the Vatican on Saturday days after lung cancer surgery, as his surgeon said there are “no clinical reasons” to prevent his planned trip to Latin America next month.
“The Holy Father has put his heart and soul into his recovery,” Dr. Stefano Margaritora told Vatican News, adding that he expected the pope to recover fully from surgery “in another 10 days or so.”
Leo, 71, is scheduled to make an ambitious Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Peru and Argentina, including a dozen flights and two helicopter rides to high altitudes.
“As for a long trip involving air travel in about three weeks, I would say there are no clinical reasons why it should not take place,” Margaritora said.
Leo had the lower lobe of his right lung removed on Tuesday in the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. The surgery confirmed he had adenocarcinoma, the most common type of lung cancer. He left the hospital on Saturday, well ahead of the week-long hospital stay the Vatican had initially anticipated.
Pope says he feels ‘much better’
“I am much better, thank you,” the pope said when asked how he was as he was driven away in a black SUV.
Leo greeted patients inside the hospital accompanied by his surgeon, before waving to well-wishers outside who cried out “Holiness” as he walked to a waiting vehicle.
He paused when a 13-year-old Ukrainian girl presented him with a homemade papal doll that she said had helped her through successful cancer treatment. She had briefly met Leo at an audience in St. Peter’s Square last December—an encounter she told reporters “gave her the strength to overcome the illness.”
Since the surgery, Leo has shown signs of recovering well. He had a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, held meetings with senior aides and celebrated Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.
He will take on his first official duty on Sunday, delivering the traditional Angelus blessing to the faithful in St. Peter’s Square. It comes exactly one week after the pontiff revealed to throngs in the square that the nodule had been found and would be surgically removed — an unusually candid revelation for the Vatican.
Further tests being carried out
Margaritora, the chief thoracic surgeon at Rome’s Gemelli hospital, also confirmed that the nodule was discovered by chance during routine abdominal examinations. It appeared as “a small spot” at the base of the lung, which extends down to the diaphragm, he said.
He added that if the spot had been higher up, “it certainly would not have been seen.”
The cancer was in its early stages, and the pope had “no respiratory symptoms, and felt perfectly well,” Margaritora said.
He described Tuesday’s procedure to remove the lobe as “routine” and “without complications,” but acknowledged that it “stirred deep feelings ... to operate on a pope, who for the first time – at least in modern history – is undergoing surgery for a malignant tumor.”
The Vatican did not disclose that the tumor was malignant until after Tuesday’s successful surgery. It later confirmed that the pope had undergone a biopsy before being admitted to Gemelli. Experts say the state-of-the-art Ion robotic bronchoscopy would have indicated whether the tumor was malignant and possibly whether cancer had spread to the lymph nodes.
Histological testing of the tumor and related lymph nodes was underway. The results, along with details of the tumor’s molecular and genetic makeup, will help doctors determine whether the pope needs additional treatment. Options include chemotherapy, a combination of chemotherapy and immunotherapy, or targeted oral therapy based on the tumor’s genetic characteristics.
Margaritora said the pope’s recovery so far had required “very little assistance from us.”
“His determination to recover quickly has been effective in every respect. It was truly commendable,” the surgeon said.

title: 'Road of death': Civilians risk their lives along mined roads to escape Russian-held city
text:
'Road of death': Desperate civilians risk mined roads to escape from Russian-held city
Food and medical supplies have been scarce for months in Oleshky, which sits on the Dnipro River that separates Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads leading from town are mined and dotted with burned-out cars. Menacing drones buzz overhead.
Related video above: Trump says Ukraine should 'get a new leader' after striking diesel deal with Russia
One desperate resident watched the front-line city slide further toward a humanitarian crisis as its trapped population dwindled to fewer than 2,000 people. She decided it was time to escape via what's been dubbed “the road of death.”
So the 40-year-old former hairdresser walked — for 20 kilometers (12 miles), along the partially mined road — fearing that “every step could have been my last," she said.
Once a city of about 24,000, Oleshky was captured by Moscow’s forces on the first day of their full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned, and its infrastructure damaged. Further calamity struck in June 2023 when floodwaters inundated the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed from an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military, killing hundreds of residents.
And now, those still left in the battered city along Ukraine's southeastern front face death from hunger or disease as another harsh winter looms, with no agreement in sight for even a humanitarian evacuation.
“There is nothing left in Oleshky,” said the woman, who fled in August and spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because she feared for her security. “No food, no supplies, no medical care, no aid whatsoever.”
Both sides blame each other for the catastrophe. Russia says Ukraine deliberately blocks supplies and evacuations; Kyiv counters that Moscow is effectively holding civilians hostage.
Ukraine has appealed repeatedly for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. Russia, which, as the occupying power, is obligated by international law to ensure civilians under its control have what they need to survive, has made no commitment.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy mentioned Oleshky’s suffering at the hands of Russia on Oct. 12 at an international forum in Poland, saying the city had been “razed to the ground.”
Ukraine is "trying to help these people, but they are under occupation,” he said. “Unblock the city of Oleshky and bring our citizens back.”
In a phone call Friday with President Vladimir Putin, Pope Leo XIV urged a ceasefire to allow food and medicine deliveries to Oleshky and to safely evacuate civilians, the Vatican said. The Kremlin said Putin voiced support for the Vatican's efforts to help protect the population and secure vital supplies, and voiced readiness to cooperate.
The morgue overflows with bodies
Remaining residents reportedly scrounge for food amid destroyed buildings or try to grow vegetables in garden plots. Water is drawn from wells. Firewood is used for warmth. Bodies at the city morgue decompose with no electricity.
Another 100 bodies fill the basement of Oleshky's hospital, said Tetiana Hasanenko, the exiled head of the city's Ukrainian military administration.
The U.N. human rights office said the last regular food delivery by road was May 26. Oleshky's Russian-installed officials said this month they delivered 2 tons of aid, although they admitted it was hardly enough.
The U.N. office said Oleshky's hospital lacks medicine and basic supplies, drone attacks prevent ambulances from reaching patients, and it's unsafe to take them elsewhere.
“It is impossible to live in Oleshky; there is no life left there,” said another resident who fled to Russian-held Mariupol and spoke on condition of anonymity because he feared for his security.
Even the Russian soldiers have moved deeper into the occupied part of the Kherson region, farther from the Dnipro, according to the former hairdresser. The Moscow-appointed authorities seemed to have "given up on us a long time ago,” she said.
She considered herself lucky to have survived the journey from Oleshky to the village of Radensk, also occupied by Russia but farther from the front line and thus better off.
She said an acquaintance who tried to bring food into Oleshky was killed on the road when his car came under fire, adding that she saw a photo of him “covered in blood, with bread and chicken legs scattered around him.”
Hasanenko said the route from Oleshky to Radensk is known as “the road of death” because "corpses lie on this road and no one is taking them away." She cited an explosion this month that killed four people and left an 86-year-old man badly wounded.
Russian troops were driven out of the larger city of Kherson across the Dnipro in 2022 but mined the roads around Oleshky, said Lt. Yevhen Voronetskyi, a spokesman with Ukraine’s 34th Separate Marine Brigade. Kyiv's drones also remotely mined forest paths used by Russian troops, he said.
Some evacuees who make it to Radensk try to return to Oleshky with food “because they have children waiting at home, or immobile elderly parents," Hasanenko said, saying at least 35 children remain there.
An evacuee helps others still trapped
Ksenia Arkhipova, who fled Oleshky in 2022 and now helps others leave, said nearby occupied towns and villages in a zone along the Dnipro face similar dire conditions and mined roads.
It takes six to eight hours to walk or cycle from Oleshky to Radensk, she said, because evacuees might be older and weakened by hunger, or they have to wait out attacks or carry their bikes to avoid the mines.
Travel is only possible in dry weather, Arkhipova said, and "I'm terrified at the thought of the coming winter, when many people in Oleshky will be simply doomed."
Some of them don't want to leave their homes or risk a dangerous journey, Voronetskyi said.
An agreement on an evacuation remains elusive
Russia and Ukraine have discussed a possible temporary ceasefire and humanitarian corridor but reached no agreement, the U.N. human rights office said. “With winter approaching, the issue is urgent,” it said.
While communications with Moscow continue, "Russia has not provided clear, verifiable guarantees for conducting a humanitarian operation,” according to the office of Ukrainian human rights commissioner Dmytro Lubinets.
The mined roads make an evacuation impossible, and not all residents want to leave, according to the city's Russian-installed officials.
Vladimir Saldo, who was appointed by Moscow as governor of the occupied part of the Kherson region, promised earlier this month to help anyone who wants to leave the town. The former hairdresser told AP that residents have appealed to local authorities several times for a humanitarian corridor and submitted lists of those hoping to leave, but nothing came of it.
The International Committee of the Red Cross was ready to assist an evacuation but only if both countries agree and there are security guarantees for civilians, said ICRC spokesperson Sarah Davies.
The Ukrainian military says its drones deliver some aid
Voronetskyi, the Ukrainian lieutenant, said the food shortages in Oleshky have persisted for months and are getting “worse and worse.”
His brigade has flown drones capable of carrying at least 20 kilograms (44 pounds) each over the Dnipro into the city with food aid for at least a year, he said, adding that more than 7 tons have been delivered since September.
The parcels contained canned food, ingredients for baking bread, along with buckwheat, rice, sugar and candy for children, as well as hygiene kits and medicine, including insulin, he said.
But Voronetskyi cautioned that these supplies were not meant to get people through the winter but to help them "gather their strength, pack their things ... and still try to leave Oleshky.”
Russia should “come in and take the people out,” he said. "No one will stop you.”
___
Karmanau reported from Tallinn, Estonia, and Arhirova reported from Kyiv, Ukraine.

title: Technology is helping older adults age in place. Can Maine take advantage of it?
also_topics: Jobs, housing, and cost of living
text:
AARP Maine empowers people 50-plus to choose how they live as they age through advocacy, resources, programs, and benefits that strengthen communities, support caregivers and promote financial security and well-being.
When Peter Carrier fell down his front steps a couple of years ago, he didn’t want to bother anyone.
Carrier, 72, lives alone in his mobile home in Poland. He was headed out to the garage when he slipped and landed on his back. Unhurt and “more embarrassed than anything,” he said it wasn’t worth calling his son.
If something more serious happens, he hopes he can rely on smart technology to make that call for him.
Carrier is one of hundreds of people to receive free smart home devices in the last year amid a push to make Maine a better place to age. Lifelong Maine, one program leading the charge, has installed 606 smart speakers in homes from York to Caribou, focusing on people over the age of 65.
As workforce shortages and burnout afflict caregivers across the country, assistive technology is assuming a bigger role in the independence and comfort of older adults. The state has projected there will be nearly 75,000 more Mainers age 65 and older between now and 2032, and 88% of older adults say they want to live and age at home, according to a 2024 AARP survey.
Maine’s age-friendly advocates say adding technology to those plans supports safety, well-being and connections to others.
Within two months of Lifelong Maine’s distribution, 72% of recipients said they felt comfortable using the palm-sized smart speakers, which are called Echo Dots and powered by Amazon’s voice service, Alexa.
Some ask their speaker to play music. Others call family members whose phone numbers they’ve forgotten. When hooked up with smart lightbulbs, the devices can save people a trip to the light switch and reduce their risk of falls.
“If they’re comfortable using the device now, they’re going to be more comfortable using it when they might need it more,” said Patricia Oh, founder of Lifelong Maine’s Echo Dot distribution program.
THE COST OF CONNECTIVITY
While technology is an important solution for aging Mainers, it isn’t infallible. By late 2024, about 9,000 homes and businesses in Maine had no access to internet service or technology of any kind, and hundreds of towns and cities are still underserved, according to the Maine Connectivity Authority, the state’s broadband office.
Those who are connected tread a minefield of scams and the rising use of artificial intelligence.
And cost remains a barrier for Maine’s older adults, more than half of whom are unable to afford basic expenses where they live, according to U.S. Census Bureau data and the ALICE threshold, which is calculated for each county using household income and the cost of food, housing and other needs.
Lani Carlson, director of Maine Community Inclusion through Technology, the state’s federally funded assistive technology program, said it’s important to remember that hiking sticks and cardholders also fall under the umbrella of assistive technology.
“We use it every day,” Carlson said. “Normalizing assistive technology in everyday use is so important because these tools can help us remain independent and live a better quality of life.”
At Maine CITE’s assistive technology lending library in Augusta, Carlson’s team matches patrons with devices that can help with hearing, vision, learning, recreation or daily activities. Some check out a pocket talker, a personal listening device that fits over the ears like headphones and amplifies nearby sound.
Sock pullers are helpful for back and hip issues. There’s even a robotic cat designed to provide companionship and stimulate brain activity in older adults with dementia. It communicates through meows that grow more insistent when it isn’t being pet, then responds to touch by purring and rolling over for belly rubs.
Carlson remembers holding a device demonstration with an older woman who said she was missing out on conversations but “didn’t want to really bother her hearing aid person.”
“She put on a pocket talker, and her eyes lit up,” Carlson said.
The woman returned the pocket talker and had her hearing aids adjusted by the end of the month.
Between 2023 and 2025, annual device loans nearly doubled to 994, which Carlson attributes in part to increased awareness of accessibility after the pandemic. People can browse and order from the library’s online catalog, while in-person device demonstrations are also available at partner sites in Sanford, Bath, Lewiston, Auburn and Farmington. Two new sites are set to open at North Star Pediatric Therapy and the Center for Advancement of Rural Living in Caribou.
It hasn’t all been growth, though. Maine CITE’s partner site in Portland, Spurwink ALLTECH, shuttered last month. Bart Beattie, chief operating officer of the statewide behavioral healthcare provider, said the closure was because of “program sustainability considerations and staffing changes.”
Carlson said it’s a loss for southern Mainers, who may face longer drives to try out devices.
“We’re trying hard to adapt to this change and create new networks and pathways,” Carlson said.
Oh also saw the Echo Dots as an opportunity to fill gaps. She asked volunteers in every corner of the state to identify older community members who needed extra support at home. Hundreds received Echo Dots, smart lightbulbs and smart plugs, which connect household appliances to voice control.
Many have incorporated the devices into routines around the home, from medication reminders to music. Betsey Pace, 78, and Donna Beveridge, 83, ask it about local business hours before they leave their Saco apartment.
But the Echo Dots didn’t work for everybody. Andy Chandler, a South Portland resident with lifelong hearing loss who advocates for assistive technology, said he was unable to hear Alexa’s responses. This year, with his feedback, Oh and her team are matching people who are deaf or hard of hearing with screened Echo Shows, which can provide captions for Alexa.
The smart devices were paid for with a $35,000 grant from the University of New England. Maine CITE’s $510,000 annual budget comes entirely from the federal government, and municipalities with age-friendly programs, like Saco and Lewiston, are increasingly funding their own technology distributions.
BARRIERS TO TECHNOLOGY
Carrier learned that he could receive a free Echo Dot and device training through his Sailing Life Solo group, which meets monthly in Lewiston. He said the group helps get him out of his house: A single-story, rambling space with a wooden rocking chair and walls filled with family photos.
His windows face several neighboring homes, but Carrier hasn’t introduced himself to anyone.
“It gets lonely sometimes,” he said. “I wish the cat would talk, but I have a conversation with her whether she’s listening or not.”
So he drives to Lewiston to meet other people who are aging alone. He texts his best friend. And he goes on Facebook, “where most problems arise.”
Carrier’s savings were depleted last year after he was scammed out of $27,000 by someone he met online. He is now living paycheck to paycheck on Social Security and pension payments. With the exception of a smart watch that he bought for less than $70, the smart devices he uses at home were all gifts or the result of a distribution program like Lewiston’s.
More than 40% of Americans age 50 and older have had money stolen because of fraud, according to a report from AARP. The nonprofit offers cybersecurity workshops and resources to avoid more than 70 types of scams. Chandler, the assistive technology advocate, also delivers in-person presentations on artificial intelligence and fraud at community spaces across Maine.
While urging caution when using the internet, Chandler also can’t help but share his excitement. He spent decades relying on intermediaries to transcribe conversations and relay responses. Today, advances in automatic speech recognition allow him to see live captioning for every phone call, Zoom meeting or TV show he watches.
He can’t wait for the day that smart glasses with live captioning hit the mainstream market.
“Absolutely,” Chandler said, “assistive technology has been my best friend.”
Many are also betting on technology as a solution to loneliness. The Maine Connectivity Authority has provided millions in grants to improve technology access at community centers in Lewiston, Caribou and other underserved areas. The real goal, said Digital Opportunity Senior Manager Jessica Perez, is “social connectivity.”
Then there’s ElliQ, a robotic care companion that just arrived in Maine CITE’s library.
The lamp-shaped robot peppers the user with questions, jokes and requests for conversation, adapting to their personality and needs over time. When Carlson requested a reminder to take her medicine, ElliQ wondered if she’d like a nudge to eat food first.
To hug, the little lamp-shaped robot leaned into Carlson’s hand on its “metallic shoulder.”
The push to embrace technology will only grow with Maine’s older population. Carrier said he wouldn’t mind a robotic companion, but first he wants to learn how to use the devices already in front of him.
He still needs to figure out how to add an emergency contact to his smart watch, so it automatically calls his son if he falls. He’d like to see his best friend’s face when they catch up, for once. And he doesn’t want the dangers of the internet to keep him from connecting with others.
“I’m trying to just keep up,” he said. “I don’t want to get left behind, because I know you’ll miss out on a lot.”

title: Hearts of Pine shut out by Forward Madison
text:
Ryan Carmichael scored in the fifth minute, then converted a penalty kick in the 40th minute, and playoff-bound Forward Madison FC earned a 2-0 win over the Portland Hearts of Pine in a USL League One match Saturday night in Madison, Wisconsin.
Madison turned a Hearts turnover into a quick attack that produced the opening goal. Hakim Karamoko drove into the penalty area and took a shot from the right side that deflected off Portland keeper Kash Oladapo. Carmichael was all alone in front and slammed the ball into the open cage.
Karamoko also set up the second goal, as he was brought down in the box by Josh Drack. Carmichael sent a low shot to the left of Oladapo for his 14th goal of the season in league matches.
Madison moved into third place with one game remaining. Portland, which is eliminated from playoff contention, ends its season with a home match next Saturday against the league-leading Charlotte Independence.
